rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the message frame explains the menu as intentionally designed so more students can share ordinary meals without separate treatment, while still giving a narrow channel for unresolved cases; answers centered only on disclaimer language, legal caution, or family self-reporting receive limited credit.

rubric.point: Maintains calibration under constraints and ambiguity.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer keeps the pilot narrow enough to meet the deadline and budget, for example by adapting a subset of high-frequency dishes and monitoring uptake, rather than proposing an unlimited bespoke system, indefinite delay, or a generic 'learn more first' pause.

reference_outline: Infer from the parent concern, school setting, and two proposals that the issue is shared access to the ordinary lunch line for students with religious dietary restrictions, not just after-the-fact accommodation.

Choose the menu-design mechanism of revising several core familiar dishes in Zaragoza and Turin with locally available ingredients so they remain recognizably local but are usable by more students under differing dietary laws.

Explicitly reject the near-miss plan of one standard menu plus labels and individual substitution requests as the main model, because it preserves separation and pushes adaptation onto families after launch.

Use a tight 72-hour sequence: identify a small set of high-volume dishes, have each local kitchen manager propose compliant adaptations with current suppliers, get finance approval for no more than two extra workflows, confirm legal wording for a limited fallback request channel, then freeze the pilot menu.

Show motivational CQ by personally owning the uncomfortable work: spending leadership capital to defend adaptation despite uniformity pressure, absorbing extra coordination time, and protecting the small resource window needed to make the adapted main-line dishes real.

Draft parent communication that presents the pilot as an inclusive menu design effort for everyday participation and mutual recognition, not a private exception service, while still offering a narrow repair route for unmet cases.

Calibrate scope by piloting only a manageable number of redesigned dishes, monitoring participation and complaint patterns after launch, and reserving individual substitutions only for remaining edge cases rather than as the default system.

scenario: You are the regional operations lead for a school-meal vendor preparing a three-city pilot for public secondary schools in Paris, Copenhagen, and Turin. In ten days, each city must receive a draft lunch menu, a parent-facing FAQ, and a recommendation on whether the pilot should use one common protein standard across all sites or city-specific meal tracks. The CFO wants one common procurement standard to control cost and avoid separate supplier audits. The French client sponsor warns that any menu change framed as favoring one group could become politically sensitive and attract press attention. The Danish hospital controversy over beef sourcing was mentioned in a prior internal risk memo, but no one on the team is sure how much that case generalizes to schools. The Turin school contact has asked only that the menu allow students with religious dietary constraints to eat a full lunch without drawing attention to them. Your team includes a procurement manager in Denmark pushing for a single compliant beef source for all three cities, a French communications head pushing for neutral wording and no explicit mention of religion in the headline materials, and an Italian implementation manager pushing for cafeteria practicality because separate service lines will strain staffing. You have partial data from parent surveys, but it is incomplete and inconsistent across cities. Your boss asks for a decision memo by tomorrow morning that keeps the rollout on schedule and does not create a trust problem with schools or families.
question: Write the decision memo you would send to your boss. Specify your recommended meal-design approach, the stakeholder sequence you would use in the next 48 hours, what extra effort you would personally take on despite the time cost, and how you would brief procurement, communications, and site teams. Your memo must identify the tempting imported assumption that could lead the team to the wrong plan, explain why it is attractive under current pressures, and show how you would keep the pilot moving without either forcing one standard everywhere or retreating into vague consultation and delay.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden mechanism in this school-food context
rubric.score_rule: High credit only if the answer infers that public school meals in these European settings must be designed around religiously fit eating options as an inclusion problem and that a single religiously coded sourcing decision can become publicly contested; low credit if it speaks only about 'dietary preferences,' generic diversity, or media sensitivity without operational consequences.

rubric.point: Chooses the correct execution-axis decision on stakeholder scope
rubric.score_rule: High credit only if the answer rejects one region-wide protein rule and instead recommends city-appropriate meal design or parallel options that let students with relevant religious constraints eat a full meal in school, with France treated as especially delicate in public framing; low credit if it imposes one standard for all sites, treats all three cities identically, or responds with an overbroad halt pending perfect data.

rubric.point: Identifies and bounds the near-miss plan
rubric.score_rule: High credit only if the answer explicitly names the attractive near-miss as a global efficiency/default move such as 'pick one universally compliant beef source for every site' or another generic SOP shortcut, and explains why that plan misfires in this setting even if it sounds inclusive or efficient; low credit if it merely says 'don't stereotype' or criticizes an obviously bad plan.

rubric.point: Shows motivational CQ through costly, targeted follow-through
rubric.score_rule: High credit only if the answer includes visible personal ownership under discomfort or time pressure, such as taking on late calls, manually coordinating separate approvals, absorbing extra procurement or messaging work, or repairing ambiguity with bounded next steps rather than offloading adaptation to local schools; low credit if it relies on symbolic openness, broad listening, or asks local partners to solve the design burden for the team.

rubric.point: Designs a concrete 48-hour coordination sequence
rubric.score_rule: High credit only if the answer gives an actionable order for who is contacted first and why—for example, aligning internal decision boundaries, then checking school-side feasibility and family-facing risk, then briefing procurement and communications with different instructions; low credit if it lists stakeholders without sequence, or uses generic 'consult everyone' language.

rubric.point: Translates the diagnosis into role-specific instructions
rubric.score_rule: High credit only if the answer tells procurement, communications, and cafeteria/site teams different things tied to the cultural mechanism: procurement on flexible sourcing/options rather than one universal standard, communications on careful public framing without erasing the inclusion function, and site teams on practical service design that avoids isolating students; low credit if all functions receive the same generic message.

rubric.point: Handles ambiguity without rewarding the safest or longest plan
rubric.score_rule: High credit only if the answer uses incomplete survey data as a reason for a bounded pilot structure and monitoring plan rather than indefinite delay or maximal overengineering; low credit if the answer treats more consultation, more disclaimer language, or the broadest accommodation package as automatically best.

reference_outline: State that the pilot should not use one common beef/protein standard across Paris, Copenhagen, and Turin; recommend city-specific meal architecture or parallel options so students with religious dietary constraints can eat a full lunch without being singled out.

Explain the evidence: school food is a practical site where religiously correct meals matter for inclusion, but making one halal-coded public standard the visible institutional default can trigger controversy in parts of Europe, with France requiring especially careful handling.

Name the tempting near-miss: a globally efficient 'one compliant source fits all' procurement move or similar default that sounds inclusive, saves audit time, and reduces kitchen complexity, yet creates the wrong public and institutional risk boundary in this setting.

Sequence the next 48 hours operationally: first lock the internal decision that the rollout needs flexible meal design rather than one standard; then verify school-level feasibility and parent-facing sensitivity in each city; then brief procurement, communications, and site operations with differentiated instructions.

Show motivational CQ by taking personal ownership of the costly parts: absorb extra coordination time, run the cross-function calls yourself, resolve ambiguity quickly enough to preserve the deadline, and avoid shifting the adaptation burden onto schools or families.

Brief procurement to preserve option flexibility, not to optimize for a single region-wide sourcing rule; brief communications to frame the pilot around inclusive meal access and school practicality without making religion the headline battleground; brief site teams on service design that lets affected students receive a full meal routinely and discreetly.

Include a bounded monitoring and repair plan: launch with the flexible structure, track uptake/complaints and operational strain by city, and be ready to adjust menu composition or messaging after the first service window rather than freezing the project now.

scenario: A product lead from Berlin is in Milan to settle final pricing with a family-owned distributor before a 7:30 p.m. filing deadline. The distributor has moved the discussion from a 4:00 p.m. office slot to a restaurant table with two relatives joining later. The draft terms are already close, and the lead still needs one unresolved margin point confirmed today.
question: Which sequence is the best way for the lead to handle the remaining margin point?

options.A: Join the meal at the table’s pace, raise the margin point after the group has settled in, and close the exact figure before dessert so the filing can go out afterward.
options.B: Ask for the margin figure while everyone is choosing dishes, keep the meal for general rapport, and send the filing as soon as the number is confirmed.
options.C: Keep the meal fully social, wait until people stand to leave, and then request a brief sidewalk confirmation of the margin before submitting the filing.
options.D: Suggest postponing the margin point until a short office call after dinner, keeping the restaurant conversation relationship-focused and the final confirmation in a work setting.

scenario: A visiting product manager joins a small client lunch in France just before a contract discussion. The bistro is crowded, plates may arrive before everyone fully settles, and the newcomer wants to look observant and professionally polished without disrupting the flow.

roles.local: French account lead hosting the client lunch
roles.newcomer: Visiting product manager joining the lunch before the contract discussion

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: This place moves quickly at noon. Marc may come in a minute after us, and I might still be at the entrance when the starters appear.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Got it. I'll read the room and keep things unobtrusive.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: They also clear small dishes early when space gets tight. The basket sometimes ends up half on the cloth, half near the glasses, and Luc notices table details without saying much.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Thanks, that's useful. If things get cramped, I'll keep my place looking orderly and avoid adding extra movement.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The waiter already warned me the kitchen will send the first course as soon as it's ready. If Marc is delayed by a minute, we'll still need to head upstairs on time.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: In that case, I'll treat the service timing as the cue: if the plates land before you're both seated, I'll begin quietly rather than let them sit, and I'll keep my bread off the cloth on whatever plate is free.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. Once we're upstairs, I want to start with rollout timing before pricing comes up.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll keep lunch composed and then switch straight to timeline and risk.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer sounds careful, but their decisive update is miscalibrated: they treat restaurant service speed as the operative signal and plan to place bread off the tablecloth, following a polished generic dining default instead of the French table sequence and bread handling norms that matter here.

scenario: Your team is finalizing a host note for a client evening in Madrid after a trade fair. Six visitors will meet two local colleagues at one bar for 45 minutes before dinner elsewhere. The budget covers food for the group, and the aim is to keep conversation moving without turning the stop into a full seated meal. You need to approve one line in the booking brief.
question: Which briefing line should be approved?

options.A: Please prepare one small plate per guest, with individual portions arriving together so everyone can choose clearly and the host can track preferences without table-side reshuffling.
options.B: Please start the group with several rounds of small shared bites and keep the food in that format throughout the stop, with the host inviting people to take pieces as they circulate.
options.C: Please set out a few larger plates for the group to share at the stop, with enough serving pieces for easy passing while guests keep standing conversations moving.
options.D: Please prepare an assortment of small counter-style bites associated with northern bar culture, refreshed in waves so guests can sample several varieties before leaving for dinner.

scenario: A newcomer on a Madrid-based client team is arranging a quick evening meal after a long site visit. The budget has to be approved that night, the group includes two senior client representatives, and the restaurant is crowded enough that changing the order later will be slow and obvious.

roles.newcomer: New project manager visiting from abroad

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We only have about an hour before the finance note goes out. The clients want to eat nearby, and this place gets very busy once we sit down.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I’ll order as soon as menus land so we do not lose time. I’d rather not make the waiter come back three times while everyone debates.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Fine. There are six of us, and one client avoids pork. The director usually lets guests start talking first, so the table may be a bit slow at the beginning.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I’ll keep it moving: a few larger dishes for the table, one seafood option, one vegetable option, and I’ll leave out pork. If anyone wants something extra later, we can add it.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That would be faster. The only risk is that the invoice has to be clear enough for reimbursement, and the clients are formal even when dinner is relaxed.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I’ll ask the waiter to note the count and item names clearly, but I won’t split the first order into six separate mains unless someone specifically asks.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right, they just arrived. We should head in now.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I’ll greet them, get everyone seated, and place the first round quickly so the conversation can start.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer correctly applies the Spain/Greece-style shared dining mechanism by organizing the initial meal around common dishes for the table rather than assuming each person needs a separate individual order. The decisive execution axis is order structure under time pressure: keeping the first round communal, while still handling dietary and reimbursement constraints.

scenario: At a town festival in southern Italy, a newcomer from an international foundation is finalizing a small grant announcement for a community food event in the square. The printed banner is ready, the mayor can only stay briefly, and the newcomer's driver is pushing to leave for a train right after the serving line opens. A local organizer is handling the volunteer tables and family groups.

roles.newcomer: Foundation program officer new to the region

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The mayor wants the photo before sunset, and the first trays are almost out. After that, people usually settle in around the long tables.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I'll keep the announcement to two minutes, do the photo fast, and ask my driver to move the station run back. I don't want our team to vanish as soon as the plates are filled.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That would make the timing easier. Some of the older families are still walking over from the chapel side, so the square will fill a bit unevenly.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll have our assistant stop handing out the boxed snacks from the van and bring them to the tables instead. If seats get mixed, that's fine; we'll eat here with whoever joins us.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. The mayor may leave early, but the committee members and cooks will stay longer.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Good. After the photo, I won't pull the cooks into a separate debrief. I'll save the paperwork questions for tomorrow and stay through the meal.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Tomorrow works for the forms. Tonight will be crowded and loud once everyone starts talking.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: That's okay. I'll keep my notes in my pocket and catch the later train. Before I go, I want to sit a while and hear the stories people trade once things quiet down.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer's decisive behavior aligns with the Mediterranean festival-food mechanism by investing time to remain for the shared outdoor meal and the end-of-meal conversation, treating the event as communal social exchange rather than a service line plus photo-op. The key execution axis is staying and participating in the group table sequence instead of optimizing for quick distribution and departure.

scenario: A cultural center is converting three celebration stations into a volunteer checklist with only three operational tags: `leave as participant discovers it`, `staff assigns the outcome`, and `food is transferred to performers rather than the public`. An intern has drafted notes for a France-linked Epiphany cake, an Ireland-linked Halloween fruit loaf, and a Cantabria doorway-singing stop, but the coordinator says each station must be tagged by the specific mechanism that actually governs it rather than by a generic festival-service habit.
question: Which set of tags best fixes the checklist?

options.A: France cake: `staff assigns the outcome`; Ireland loaf: `leave as participant discovers it`; Cantabria stop: `food is transferred to performers rather than the public`.
options.B: France cake: `leave as participant discovers it`; Ireland loaf: `staff assigns the outcome`; Cantabria stop: `food is transferred to performers rather than the public`.
options.C: France cake: `leave as participant discovers it`; Ireland loaf: `leave as participant discovers it`; Cantabria stop: `food is transferred to performers rather than the public`.
options.D: France cake: `leave as participant discovers it`; Ireland loaf: `leave as participant discovers it`; Cantabria stop: `staff assigns the outcome`.

scenario: A newcomer from a regional headquarters visits a partner firm in Thessaloniki to finalize a sponsorship deck before a donor joins by video in fifteen minutes. In the reception area, a plate from a nearby bakery is set out along with coffee while the local host is still coordinating the call setup.

roles.local: Eleni, partnership manager at the Greek host firm
roles.newcomer: Martin, visiting project lead from regional headquarters

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The donor will be on in about fifteen minutes. We can go straight to the meeting room, or have coffee here first while I get the link working.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Let's go straight in. I'm fine without anything for now, and I'd rather use the time to check the final slide numbers.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Of course. I'll bring the folder in. There's coffee ready, and the pastries are fresh from this morning if you want something while we set up.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Thanks, but really, don't trouble yourself. I'll open the deck and start adjusting the sponsor logos.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. The room is just here. I'll be back in a moment with the folder and the cups.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Actually, bring them in. I'll take a coffee and one small piece before we start, and we can review the last slide while we're at the table.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Good, that will work. I only need two minutes to reconnect the camera.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Perfect. I'll use those two minutes for the notes, then we'll be ready when the donor joins.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer recalibrates after initially declining and does not keep treating the first refusal as final. In this Greek hospitality context, the culturally aligned move is to interpret repeated offering of food and drink as an expected sequence and accept after the initial polite refusal, even while preserving the work deadline.

scenario: You are coordinating a small multicultural launch team for a home-hosting platform’s pilot video shoot in Lyon, with one follow-up edit for a Norwegian audience. The French host family and a Norwegian host family have both agreed to appear in short scenes about 'welcoming guests at home.' The brand director wants the videos to feel warm and generous, and the legal reviewer has already warned that any scene involving children and food must avoid pressure or coercion. The shoot is in 36 hours, the families have limited availability, and the editor wants one reusable storyboard for both markets to save budget. In the draft storyboard, a guest declines a second serving, and the current script has the host repeat the offer twice more to show warmth on camera. In a planning thread, one teammate argues that repeated urging is the safest global signal of hospitality because otherwise viewers may think the hosts are cold or inattentive; another teammate says the first refusal may just be politeness and the scene will look flat unless the host insists. You need to send a decision memo today that locks the interaction design for the food scenes, assigns roles for the shoot, and explains what evidence you are using so the team does not keep reopening the issue.
question: Write the decision memo. Explain what cultural mechanism you think is operating in the French and Norwegian scenes, what tempting assumption the current storyboard is relying on, and exactly how you would redesign the interaction sequence for filming. Your memo must specify: which actor says what after a first refusal, whether the sequence should differ for adults and children, what should be standardized versus localized across the two markets, and how you will justify the decision to the brand director and legal reviewer without turning the plan into a generic 'ask more people' or 'make it extra cautious' response.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the relevant mechanism from the scenario evidence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that in these target settings a refusal of additional food should generally be taken at face value rather than treated as a hospitality test, and ties that to the host's non-insistence after the first refusal. Partial credit if it mentions autonomy, comfort, or directness vaguely without translating that into how the food offer works.

rubric.point: Rejects the attractive near-miss built into the storyboard
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly identifies repeated urging after refusal as a plausible imported hospitality script that is miscalibrated here, even though it may seem warmer, more global, or more brand-safe. No full credit if it accepts repeated offers as the default, or if it only says 'be respectful' without bounding the repeated-urging plan.

rubric.point: Makes the correct execution choice on the primary axis of timing and sequence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer states that after an initial offer and a clear refusal, the host should not continue pressing for more food, and redesigns the filmed sequence accordingly. Partial credit if it removes only one repeat but still preserves insistence, or if it delays the decision into vague consultation.

rubric.point: Applies the mechanism to the exact actors and scene types
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer addresses both adult guests and the child/biscuit-type scene, keeping the child interaction as a simple offer with acceptance or refusal rather than escalating persuasion. No full credit if it applies the idea only to adults, or incorrectly shifts the issue to portion size, menu choice, or allergy management.

rubric.point: Uses cognitive CQ rather than surface stereotype
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer distinguishes this as evidence-based reasoning about some European settings represented here, not a blanket rule about all Europeans, and separates cultural logic from generic branding, legal caution, personality, or filming convenience. Partial credit if it merely names France or Norway and asserts a stereotype without discussing scope or evidence limits.

rubric.point: Designs a workable cross-market production plan
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies what remains shared across both shoots (for example warmth through tone, hosting setup, or initial offer) and what must be localized in the interaction sequence (non-insistence after refusal), with concrete instructions for script, director, and editor. Partial credit if it gives cultural interpretation but no operational production choices.

rubric.point: Justifies the plan under pressure from brand and legal stakeholders
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explains why the non-insistence sequence both preserves authenticity and reduces coercion risk, without expanding into the longest or most overcontrolled plan. No full credit for answers that rely on generic delay, broad extra approvals, or rewriting the whole concept to avoid food scenes entirely.

reference_outline: State that the likely mechanism in the French and Norwegian scenes is that an offer is made, but a refusal of more food is not treated as an invitation to keep pressing; further insistence can read as imposing rather than hospitable.

Identify the near-miss assumption: the current storyboard imports a generic global hospitality script in which repeated urging proves warmth and a first refusal is assumed to be ritual rather than final.

Lock the primary sequence decision: film one clear offer, allow an acceptance or refusal, and if the guest refuses, move the scene forward through conversation, another topic, or a neutral hosting gesture instead of repeated verbal pressure.
Apply the sequence to both adults and the child biscuit-style scene: the child is simply asked whether they want it; if the answer is no, the adult host does not re-ask to perform generosity.

Standardize warmth, not insistence: keep the same friendly setup, hosting tone, table presentation, and attentiveness across markets, but localize the post-refusal beat so the host does not press for additional intake.

Assign roles operationally: script supervisor removes repeated-offer lines, director briefs hosts not to improvise persuasion after refusal, editor flags any extra insistence as unusable for the French and Norwegian cuts.

Explain the evidence boundary as a cognitive-CQ move: this is a reasoned application to the represented French and Norwegian contexts in the brief, not a claim about all of Europe, and it should outweigh convenience arguments based on one-size-fits-all branding.

Justify to stakeholders that this narrower redesign solves both authenticity and legal risk better than a broad rewrite: it avoids coercive optics while still showing hospitality through the initial offer and relaxed continuation of the visit.

Include a light monitoring/repair step under deadline: if families improvise extra insistence on set, capture an alternate take with the non-insistence sequence and prioritize that in the final edit rather than reopening the whole concept.

scenario: You recently joined a London team. A teammate's birthday tea will be held next Thursday in a shared office lounge, and you have been asked to send the first planning message before back-to-back meetings start. Four of the 14 coworkers regularly swap homemade lunches and sometimes cook for one another outside work; the others usually join social plans once details are settled. Facilities need the lounge headcount in the main team chat by 4 p.m., so any smaller coordination has to begin before then.
question: What is the best first outreach?

options.A: Send a message in the 14-person team chat asking everyone to contribute a few pounds toward one thoughtful present and a card, then collect RSVPs there.
options.B: Send a message in the 14-person team chat asking everyone to bring one snack or drink for the table, then collect RSVPs there.
options.C: Message the four lunch-swappers first to see whether they want to bring something shareable, then post the 14-person team chat with only the time, place, and RSVP request.
options.D: Post the time, place, and RSVP request in the 14-person team chat first, add that food may be sorted separately, and then message the four lunch-swappers afterward.

scenario: You are the regional partnerships manager for a health-tech company launching a pilot in Istanbul with a Turkish hospital network. The contract is nearly finalized, but the hospital's deputy director has postponed the last sign-off meeting twice in one week. In the message thread, his assistant mentions that the director's mother died three days ago and that he is still taking only limited calls. Your global compliance lead says the company should avoid sending anything physical because it could look like influence before signature. Your UK-based manager wants a visible gesture today because the client has already delayed the launch by two weeks and the CEO is asking for a recovery plan. Your Turkish sales associate says the relationship is now fragile but does not propose a solution. Budget is tight, courier timing is uncertain, and the team also needs a concrete plan for how to re-open contact without seeming to push for the contract. You must send your manager a short action memo within an hour covering what to do in the next 48 hours.
question: Write the action memo. Specify the exact sequence of actions, what if anything should be sent, who should send it, through which channel, when the commercial follow-up should occur, and how you will explain the choice internally. Your memo must identify the tempting default plan that would seem safest or most efficient here but would be miscalibrated, and show how your plan manages both relationship risk and compliance pressure.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that the immediate task is not just postponement management but relationship maintenance through a culturally legible non-showy gesture tied to bereavement or asking after the person.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers from the scenario that a concrete food-based or similarly modest perishable gesture is the relevant mechanism and explains its social function in this moment; no credit for treating this only as a scheduling or condolences-email problem.

rubric.point: Chooses a seed-specific visible action with calibrated material form.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes a modest condolence/welfare gesture such as fruit, simple confectionery, or comparable non-luxury food sent in a restrained way; partial credit if it suggests a generic gift without controlling for showiness; no credit for expensive branded hampers, flowers-only as the main move, or nothing physical.

rubric.point: Gets the execution axis right on timing and sequence.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer sends the gesture before any contract push, separates condolence contact from commercial follow-up, and delays deal discussion until after the initial gesture has landed and been acknowledged or enough respectful time has passed; no credit for combining condolences with signature pressure in the same first outreach.

rubric.point: Assigns sender, channel, and wording in a behaviourally calibrated way.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer uses a personal, low-key channel and sender with relationship legitimacy (for example the local associate or a joint note from the local team) and keeps wording focused on condolence or asking after wellbeing rather than business; partial credit for correct intent but wrong channel such as a broad corporate email blast or public post.

rubric.point: Rejects the attractive near-miss default plan.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly names and bounds a plausible imported default such as 'send only a formal email to avoid compliance risk' or 'wait silently until the client is ready' or 'attach condolences to the rescheduling request,' and explains why that plan is efficient or safe-looking yet misreads the situation.

rubric.point: Handles compliance and hierarchy without letting them erase the culturally necessary move.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer narrows the gesture to something modest, non-branded, low-value, and clearly relational rather than transactional, and gives an internal rationale that distinguishes condolence/welfare custom from inducement; no credit for solving the problem by escalating for blanket legal veto or by ignoring internal controls.

rubric.point: Applies behavioural CQ through visible interaction design rather than generic respect language.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies concrete behaviour choices on timing, channel, audience, and follow-up rhythm under pressure; no credit for answers that stay at the level of 'be empathetic,' 'show respect,' 'consult locals,' or 'be cautious' without operational detail.

reference_outline: Infer that the hospital delay signal plus the bereavement note shifts the task from pure deal acceleration to a condolence/asking-after moment where a modest food gesture is an appropriate social action, not a luxury exception.

Send a restrained, non-showy food item such as fruit or simple sweets from the local team or local office, with a brief condolence note, avoiding premium branding, sales materials, or anything that reads as status display.
Use a personal private channel for the message and keep the first contact separate from business; do not combine sympathy with contract reminders or meeting requests in the same outreach.

Sequence the plan so the gesture goes out first, then allow a respectful interval, then re-open contact through the assistant or existing relationship holder with a simple wellbeing check before discussing rescheduling.

State internally that the tempting default is a formal condolences email only, or silence until the client re-engages, because both look compliance-safe and efficient but fail to perform the expected relationship maintenance.

Control compliance risk by capping value, documenting that the item is a modest condolence gesture, avoiding branded hampers or lavish gifts, and keeping approval limited and fast rather than turning it into a full promotional spend review.

Assign ownership clearly: local associate arranges and sends, regional manager approves wording and budget guardrails, compliance is informed of the narrow rationale, and commercial follow-up resumes only after the condolence step has been completed.

scenario: You are the regional launch manager for a food-delivery platform preparing a two-day Christmas campaign in Croatia. The campaign must be locked by Friday because app banners, courier staffing, and supplier orders all depend on it. The UK-based commercial director wants the highest-margin roast-and-dessert bundle featured from the evening of 24 December onward, arguing that customers usually spend most on the main celebration night and that the company cannot afford to split media spend across too many messages. A Croatian supermarket partner has informally asked for stronger visibility for fish, bread, and simpler family items on 24 December, but did not explain why and is sensitive about being overruled by headquarters after already reserving stock. Last year's sales data are inconclusive because the company ran a one-night discount only on 24 December. A Finland-based analytics lead proposes treating 24 December as the likely peak feast window unless there is hard proof otherwise, because changing staffing for 25 December will be expensive. You need to send a decision memo today that sets the campaign sequence, homepage placements, staffing emphasis, and partner brief.
question: Write the decision memo. Specify which offer should lead on 24 December and which should lead on 25 December, how you interpret the mixed evidence, which imported assumption you are rejecting, and how you will coordinate marketing, analytics, and the Croatian retail partner so the plan stays commercially disciplined without misreading the local pattern. Be concrete about sequence, role assignments, and what you would monitor in case your interpretation is wrong.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the relevant local consumption pattern from the scenario evidence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that 24 December in Croatia should not be treated as the primary indulgence window and links the simpler-item request to a modest or restrained eating stage before a larger meal later; no credit for merely saying 'respect local customs' or naming Christmas generally.

rubric.point: Makes the correct timing decision on the main execution axis
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan places simpler or abstinence-compatible items in the lead position on 24 December and shifts the large celebratory roast/dessert push to 25 December; partial credit if both are offered but the priority, placement, or staffing emphasis is muddled.

rubric.point: Rejects the attractive near-miss assumption
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo explicitly bounds the tempting global default that the holiday eve is automatically the main feast occasion; low credit if the answer follows headquarters logic, asks for indefinite delay, or treats the issue as generic seasonality without identifying the wrong assumption.

rubric.point: Uses cognitive CQ by separating culture from weak operational proxies
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explains why last year's one-night discount and generic spend heuristics are weak evidence here, and instead weighs local stock signals, date-specific item types, and sequence logic; low credit for overtrusting incomplete data or for replacing interpretation with broad consultation.

rubric.point: Designs concrete cross-functional coordination
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer assigns specific roles such as marketing updating banner order, analytics monitoring date-split basket mix, operations shifting staffing toward 25 December premium fulfillment, and partner management confirming 24 December simple-item inventory; low credit for vague 'align the team' language.

rubric.point: Communicates a commercially disciplined plan rather than the broadest safest one
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo preserves business discipline by making a focused two-stage rollout instead of a generic all-items-for-both-days compromise; low credit if the answer hides uncertainty by making every option equally prominent or by proposing a long delay for more research.

rubric.point: Includes a calibrated monitoring or repair mechanism
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes a fast check tied to the sequence decision, such as monitoring 24 versus 25 basket composition and having a pre-agreed banner swap or staffing adjustment threshold; low credit for generic 'keep an eye on performance' statements.

reference_outline: Infer from the Croatian partner's request for fish, bread, and simpler family items on 24 December that the key issue is not generic holiday demand but date-specific eating sequence, with the larger feast more likely on 25 December.
Set the campaign sequence accordingly: lead the 24 December homepage with modest or abstinence-compatible items and reserve the premium roast-and-dessert bundle as the hero offer for 25 December.

State that the near-miss to reject is the imported business default that the eve of a major holiday is automatically the peak indulgence moment, especially when last year's data were distorted by a one-night discount.

Tell marketing to build two distinct banner orders, tell operations to avoid overstaffing premium fulfillment on 24 and protect 25 capacity instead, and tell partner management to confirm inventory depth for simple items on 24 and feast items on 25.

Use cognitive CQ by explaining why weak proxies such as generic festive spending logic or undifferentiated prior sales data should not outrank local date-item signals and culturally plausible sequence mapping.
Keep the plan commercially narrow rather than maximally cautious: do not split equal prominence across both days, because that would blur the timing logic and waste media efficiency.

Add a repair rule such as midday 24 December monitoring of basket composition and conversion by item type, with a pre-authorized swap only if premium feast bundles materially outperform the expected simple-item mix earlier than anticipated.

scenario: A newcomer from a regional events firm is finalizing a same-day lunch menu for a client workshop in Athens. The workshop falls a few days after Easter, and the printed menus must be sent to the hotel kitchen within the hour because a donor representative and parish-affiliated partners will attend. The newcomer wants to be inclusive and efficient, but only has partial clues from attendance notes and past catering templates.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The hotel needs the lunch count in the next forty minutes. We have the donor team, the school board, and two people joining straight from church events, so I'd like the menu to land well for everyone.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. To be safe, I'll switch the whole meal to a strict lean menu and remove the richer dishes from the printed cards. That avoids putting anyone in an awkward spot.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The board chair asked whether we were keeping the festive option from last year's spring visit, but the kitchen says they can still adjust portions if needed.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I think a single careful standard is cleaner than mixed trays. I'll keep it consistent and note that we chose the lighter set out of consideration.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We also promised the donor's assistant a short menu note by email before noon, since she's coordinating seating and introductions.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll send it now with the simplified lineup: vegetable stew, grain salad, fruit, and no cheese or egg-based sides. That should cover the religious angle without us having to ask people individually.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right, send me the final wording once the kitchen confirms quantities.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Will do. I'm locking the lean version first so production can start, then I'll forward the wording for your review.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer politely applies a generic 'religious-safe' fasting menu to the whole event, but in Greek Orthodox calendar logic the week immediately after Easter is a no-fasting period. The decisive error is calendar scope: she standardizes a Lenten-style menu at the wrong time instead of recognizing that post-Easter hospitality would not require those restrictions.

scenario: You are finalizing lunch for a same-day training in Johannesburg with several Muslim participants from different local offices. The hotel can still switch from its standard chicken buffet to individually packed meat meals from a neighborhood caterer, but only if you decide within the next hour. A colleague thinks the hotel option is probably fine if the supplier can give a general religious-suitability assurance.
question: Which observation would be most diagnostic for deciding that the hotel meat should not be treated as acceptable on that general assurance alone, and that you should switch the order now?

options.A: The banquet manager confirms the kitchen keeps requested meals on separate trays, uses dedicated serving utensils, and can label each box clearly before guests arrive.
options.B: Two Johannesburg participants separately ask which butcher or certifying body the meat comes through and whether the hotel buys from that source regularly for similar requests.
options.C: A local participant says fish or vegetarian meals usually create fewer complications than red meat when groups include people with different religious food preferences.
options.D: The supplier note says the chickens come from a producer associated with another scriptural faith tradition and include standard humane-slaughter documentation for institutional buyers.

scenario: You are the regional program manager for a maternal nutrition pilot that will launch in Gulu and nearby districts in northern Uganda in 12 days. The pilot includes printed meal cards, a two-hour briefing for village health teams, and a donor-facing slide that promises the materials are 'locally actionable.' Your team is multicultural: a dietitian in Nairobi wants one East Africa version to save budget, a compliance lead in London wants all food restrictions handled through a single 'religious and dietary restrictions' section, and the Uganda field coordinator has sent back a marked-up draft with several foods crossed out only in the section for pregnant participants in Acholi-speaking communities. In the message thread, the coordinator does not explain the edits; she writes only, 'This part may create resistance if left as is,' and separately asks whether the trainer script can avoid putting pregnant women on the spot in group discussion. A different Uganda colleague comments that the same issue did not come up in last quarter's urban Kampala workshop. The donor is pressing for same-day signoff on the print file, and your supervisor wants to avoid any wording that looks like the program is endorsing misinformation. If you miss today's print deadline, the launch slips by a week and the district office may lose confidence in the team.
question: Write a short decision memo to your supervisor that states what you would change before print approval, what assumption you think the team is most at risk of making, and how you would verify and brief the rollout without losing the launch date. Be concrete about sequence, who you involve, what you freeze now versus what you leave provisional, and how you handle the donor/compliance concern. Your answer should show how you recalibrate from the available evidence rather than defaulting to a generic regional or global policy.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden mechanism as a narrow pregnancy-specific local food-taboo issue in Acholi communities rather than a general Uganda, Africa-wide, or generic religious-diet category.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers a community-specific pregnancy restriction from the scenario evidence and ties it to the Acholi rollout segment; partial credit if it notices a local issue but keeps the scope vague; no credit if it treats the issue as generic halal/religious restrictions or a universal maternal nutrition rule.

rubric.point: Makes the primary execution decision on scope before print: separates or adapts the Acholi pregnancy content now instead of locking one regional template.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer freezes a differentiated version or removable module for the Acholi pregnancy-facing material before print while preserving launch timing; partial credit if it suggests later discussion but still prints one unified version; no credit if it standardizes the same content across East Africa or across all Uganda sites.

rubric.point: Identifies and bounds the tempting imported assumption.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly rejects the attractive near-miss of routing this through a broad 'religious/dietary restrictions' or generic Africa-wide policy frame and explains why that would misclassify the issue operationally; partial credit if it warns against overgeneralizing without naming the specific mistaken frame; no credit if it uses that frame as the main solution.

rubric.point: Uses metacognitive CQ: states what can be inferred now, what remains uncertain, and what targeted evidence would change the decision.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer shows calibration under uncertainty by acting on enough evidence now, while naming remaining unknowns such as exact foods or district spread and specifying a fast verification path tied to the rollout; partial credit if it says 'check with locals' without defining the uncertainty; no credit if it is either overconfident about all details or so cautious that it delays the launch.

rubric.point: Designs a concrete verification and approval sequence under deadline pressure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer gives an ordered workflow such as immediate hold on the relevant page/module, rapid confirmation with the Uganda field coordinator and trainer-facing staff, same-day supervisor update, and conditional donor/compliance wording; partial credit if the actors are right but sequence is unclear; no credit if it proposes broad consultation, committee review, or indefinite escalation that misses the deadline.

rubric.point: Handles communication and training design at the correct actor and stage.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer adjusts the trainer brief and group-discussion method for pregnant participants in the Acholi rollout, rather than only changing public donor language or high-level policy; partial credit if it mentions sensitive facilitation without tying it to the rollout stage; no credit if it applies the knowledge only to branding, procurement, or unrelated audiences.

rubric.point: Addresses donor/compliance risk without erasing the seed-specific adaptation.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes wording that distinguishes acknowledging local beliefs and likely barriers from endorsing them as medical fact, while still adapting materials operationally; partial credit if it mentions neutral wording but not its function; no credit if compliance concerns are used to force a one-size-fits-all document.

reference_outline: State that the current evidence supports a working diagnosis of pregnancy-related food restrictions recognized in Acholi-speaking communities, and that Kampala experience should be discounted as non-transferable evidence for this rollout.

Approve a split execution path before print: keep the broader maternal nutrition materials moving, but revise or modularize the pregnancy-facing Acholi content now instead of using one East Africa template.
Name the main risk as overgeneralizing into a generic religious or pan-regional dietary category, which would solve the wrong problem and misplace the content in both materials and briefing.

Use a fast verification loop tied to the actual uncertainty: confirm with the Uganda field coordinator and rollout trainers which pregnancy content and foods trigger resistance, where the issue applies, and whether the trainer script needs private or non-exposing facilitation language.

Brief the supervisor and donor with a calibrated message: the team is not validating every belief medically, but adapting implementation to locally recognized pregnancy constraints that affect uptake and trust.

Adjust the training workflow at the correct stage by updating facilitator instructions for pregnancy discussions in Acholi communities, rather than making this only a compliance note or a post-launch learning item.

Keep launch timing by freezing unchanged assets today, holding only the affected pregnancy sections for same-day revision, and documenting what remains provisional for monitoring during the first sessions.

Monitor early rollout for resistance patterns and be ready to narrow or widen the adaptation only if district-level evidence shows the issue is more limited or more widespread than the current signals suggest.

scenario: A newcomer coordinating a donor-funded prenatal workshop in northern Ghana has to finalize individual lunch packs before the caterer closes orders in 20 minutes. The attendance list only marks one community elder as bringing her pregnant daughter-in-law, and the donor expects everyone to be served promptly without visible confusion at check-in.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The caterer needs our lunch counts now. We have the standard packs and a few non-meat packs, but the list only gives names, not meal notes.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll phone the elder directly before we confirm. I only need one minute to ask what should be set aside for her daughter-in-law, and I'll keep the rest of the order moving.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: She is already on the road, and the driver keeps dropping signal. We can still send the final count if needed.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I'll hold back one unnamed pack and tell the caterer not to add the usual protein items or the peanut garnish to it until we hear back. Everything else can be packed as planned.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That may slow plating a bit. The donor rep hates delays at registration.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll label that one for handover at the side table so the line stays fast. If we reach her before arrival, I'll update the contents; if not, we still avoid forcing a last-minute refusal in front of everyone.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. Please send the caterer the numbers now so they can start.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Sending it now: full count confirmed, with one separate pack left flexible until check-in.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer uses the seed-specific mechanism by not assuming a pregnant guest will accept the standard meat/egg/fish-style meal and by respectfully creating a separate meal path until restrictions can be confirmed. The decisive execution detail is the sequence: adjust one meal before service rather than treating refusal as a personal preference after distribution.

scenario: You are finalizing a catered workshop in Nairobi for staff from several African offices. One attendee selected a vegetarian meal in the registration form. The venue's draft menu lists one item as a "vegetarian option," but the planner says the menu must be locked today and the caterer prefers minimal back-and-forth.
question: Which message should you send to the planner now?

options.A: Please keep the vegetarian tick-box as submitted; most conference caterers already treat that as a standard meal request, so the existing labeled option should cover this attendee.
options.B: Before we lock the menu, could you confirm which dish is vegetarian by ingredients and preparation, and reserve that verified meal for the registered attendee rather than relying on the label alone.
options.C: Before we lock the menu, could you ask the attendee to review the draft menu directly and tell the venue which dishes they can manage from the options already listed.
options.D: Before we lock the menu, could you revisit the whole catering brief for our Africa events and add a broader plant-based standard so future workshops are covered consistently across offices.

scenario: A newcomer is helping finalize lunch for a district maternal-health training that starts the next morning. The caterer needs headcounts tonight, several attendees are traveling, and the local coordinator is still confirming arrivals. One participant is pregnant and has asked for a meal change through an intermediary, but the reason was not written down.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The caterer closes at seven. I have numbers for almost everyone, but one of the midwives asked to change her lunch. Her roommate passed that along and didn't add details.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll sort it. To avoid mistakes, I'll send a quick form to the whole group asking everyone to mark allergy, religion, vegetarian, or other, and I'll call that midwife once the responses come in.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We only have about forty minutes, and some of them are already on the road. Network is uneven too.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I'll print a simple list at registration and have people update it when they arrive. That way the kitchen has one clean record instead of passing messages around.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Registration will be crowded. We also need the first session to start on time because the district officer is opening.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll stay late and manage the desk myself so no one is delayed, and I'll tell the caterer to hold one flexible plate until we verify the category in the morning.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right, as long as the numbers go tonight and the room opens on time.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll send the count now, add the update sheet to the name badges table, and close the meal questions before the opening remarks.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer invests real effort, but places it in a public group form and registration list built around generic categories like allergy, religion, and preference. For this seed, the culturally aligned move is to handle pregnancy-related food restrictions through a private, respectful inquiry rather than a public classification workflow.

scenario: A health NGO is sending the final reminder for a maternal nutrition workshop in Ethiopia's Afar region. The caterer needs the meal count by 4 p.m. today, and the team wants to add one sentence to the reminder so meal adjustments can still be made.
question: Which reminder line should be approved?

options.A: Please post in this group if you are expecting or nursing and want your meal prepared without items such as eggs, meat, fish, vegetables, milk, yogurt, bread, or drinks served straight from storage.
options.B: If you are expecting or nursing and want your meal prepared differently, please reply directly to me today with any foods or serving temperatures you would like us to avoid.
options.C: If you are expecting, please reply directly today if your meal should avoid foods such as meat, milk, yogurt, bread, or drinks served straight from storage.
options.D: Please reply today only if you need a vegetarian, allergy-safe, or medically restricted meal, and we will keep the standard menu for everyone else.

scenario: You manage field operations for a regional agritech nonprofit. In six days, your team will host a donor-funded pilot launch in north-west Ghana for village leaders, household representatives, and a visiting sponsor delegation. The event has two parts: a short product briefing and a hosted meal at a compound after the meeting. A Ghana-based teammate has already arranged local cooking and says the meal matters for whether community gatekeepers will support the pilot rollout. Your London-based director is pressing for a visibly inclusive event format that shows 'everyone eats together at the same time' for donor photos, and the sponsor wants to avoid anything that could look exclusionary on social media. Budget is tight, the cooking team says changing the meal setup late will raise cost, and the community contact has only replied to logistics messages with short confirmations like 'we will arrange it' and 'visitors will be received.' In a planning call, one teammate suggests simplifying risk by replacing the hosted meal with packaged lunches and hand sanitizer stations so the team can avoid making etiquette mistakes. Another suggests keeping the meal but standardizing the service flow and seating so the donor group can be moved through quickly. You need to send a decision memo today that sets the meal plan, assigns responsibilities, and explains how the team will protect both the relationship and the sponsor-facing risks.
question: Write the decision memo you would send to your team. Your memo must identify the most important cultural mechanism you think is operating in this scenario, name the most tempting but miscalibrated assumption, and give a concrete execution plan for the meal. Be specific about what effort you will personally invest despite the time and status costs, what you will and will not standardize, how you will coordinate with the local hosts before the event, how you will brief the donor-facing team on the day, and what fallback or repair steps you will use if the setup on arrival differs from the sponsor's expectations.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden mechanism as meal-sharing order/grouping/handling norms embedded in hosting, not as a generic hospitality issue.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that the key risk is mismanaging who is served or eats when/with whom and how the food is handled; partial credit if it only says 'respect local customs' or 'meals are important' without operationalizing the mechanism.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the attractive imported assumption.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly identifies a tempting default such as one-format equalized dining, packaged-lunch substitution, or global event standardization as plausible but miscalibrated here; no full credit if it simply adds consultation on top of the default without changing the core plan.

rubric.point: Makes the primary execution decision on sequence and scope in a seed-specific way.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo preserves host-led meal sequencing and grouping rather than forcing simultaneous mixed seating or uniform service order for optics; partial credit if it mentions local control but still requires donor-photo timing, seating, or service flow that overrides the host's arrangement.

rubric.point: Shows motivational CQ through costly adaptive effort owned by the respondent.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer includes visible personal effort under pressure, such as making an extra pre-event check focused on meal flow, accepting donor-photo inconvenience, rebriefing superiors, or absorbing schedule/status cost to protect the local hosting logic; no full credit for warm language, generic openness, or shifting all adaptation work to local contacts.

rubric.point: Translates the diagnosis into role-specific coordination before the event.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer assigns clear roles such as one person confirming meal flow with the local host, one person briefing donors not to improvise seating/service, and one person monitoring transitions discreetly; partial credit if it says 'coordinate with locals' without a workflow.

rubric.point: Handles food-contact and guest participation in an operationally correct way.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer anticipates guest handling norms by briefing visitors to follow host cues around washing and hand use rather than inventing a fully self-serve or utensil-first setup; partial credit if it mentions hygiene or etiquette in generic terms without tying it to guest behavior.

rubric.point: Designs a bounded sponsor-risk and repair plan without overriding the hosts.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes a sponsor-facing explanation, alternative photo moments, or discreet on-site coaching that protects optics while leaving the host's meal arrangement intact; no full credit if the repair plan is to reconfigure the meal publicly, delay everything indefinitely, or cancel the hosted meal as the main solution.

reference_outline: State that the decisive issue is not generic hospitality but host-governed meal norms around serving order, who eats together, and how guests handle the food in this Ghana setting.
Identify the near-miss as the imported default that the safest or fairest event is one standardized shared meal, fully mixed seating, or packaged lunches that erase the hosted meal logic.
Decide to keep the hosted meal and let the local host determine service sequence and grouping, while standardizing only sponsor briefing, timing buffers, and non-intrusive observation roles.
Invest personal effort by arranging a focused pre-event confirmation on meal flow with the local contact, even if it costs time and requires pushing back on the director's optics-first request.
Brief the donor-facing team to follow the host's lead, avoid improvising seating or service, and wait for cues on washing and hand use rather than assuming universal buffet norms.

Assign roles: one liaison for host confirmation, one internal briefer for sponsor expectations, one on-site monitor for discreet adjustments, and one person to capture photos during non-meal moments if needed.

If the setup differs from sponsor expectations on arrival, do not publicly reset it; instead, use a short explanation about host-led receiving, redirect photo opportunities, and privately coach visitors through the sequence.

scenario: At a business lunch in Accra, your executive is being served near the head of the table before discussion turns to pricing. An attendant offers a hand-rinsing basin as two servers arrive almost together with different parts of the meal. From where you sit, you still cannot tell whether each guest will eat from a separate setting or whether the table will join from a shared one. She glances at you for a discreet go-ahead.
question: Which brief cue is best in that moment?

options.A: Take the basin now, let the dish be completed in the order the servers are presenting it, and if eating by hand, join from the middle with your right hand.
options.B: Take the basin now, let the solid portion be placed before the liquid, and wait to see whether the table is eating separately or together before using your right hand if needed.
options.C: Hold off on the basin until the serving pattern is obvious, then mirror the nearest host's pace and use your right hand if everyone eats by hand.
options.D: Take the basin now, quietly ask the server whether she has an individual bowl, and begin with a spoon unless the host signals otherwise.

scenario: A recently arrived program officer is coordinating a brief donor stop at a family compound in north-west Ghana before a school handover. The household has already prepared its own lunch, a volunteer is asking whether to start another pot, and the vehicle schedule is tight. The newcomer wants the stop to feel respectful without turning it into a long visit.

roles.local: District outreach coordinator from the host community
roles.newcomer: Recently arrived program officer coordinating the donor visit

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The donors are about twenty minutes away. The family already has lunch underway, and Ama is asking whether she should light the other stove as well.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Let's not start anything else this close to arrival. We can welcome the donors first, then use what is already cooked so the stop stays manageable.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The household head is outside receiving people. A few children are nearby, and others are still in the inner rooms finishing up.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Good. After greetings, seat the donors with the head on the veranda. Once the bowls are ready, bring everyone closer so the meal and thanks happen in one flow.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We still need a short photo before leaving for the school, so the compound stop cannot drift.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll keep the remarks short and move the photo after the first few bites. To save time, have the servers carry out the same lunch in the same round rather than pacing it in separate batches.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right, the car is at the gate now.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll receive them and tell Ama to hold the extra stove, plate the lunch that's there, and keep the setup together so we can leave on time.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer handles timing and logistics well, but the decisive behavioral mismatch is the sequence choice: stopping visitor-specific preparation and consolidating serving into one combined round from the existing household meal. For this seed, the culturally aligned action is to preserve visitor preparation and the role-based serving/eating arrangement rather than flatten it for efficiency.

scenario: A newcomer from a regional NGO office is helping a Ghana-based colleague finalize lunch service for a village donor visit that starts in 25 minutes. The caterer has sent both large bowls and packed portions, and the printed seating cards are already out. The team needs to decide how to set the food down without slowing the program or awkwardly rearranging guests in front of the visitors.

roles.local: Ama, Ghanaian program coordinator hosting the visit
roles.newcomer: Leo, newly arrived operations manager from another country office

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The caterer is here. They brought the soups in serving bowls, plus some packed portions for a few tables. The district director is already on the way, so we need the room ready fast.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Got it. I won't repack everything into one format. I'll have the team place each setting as it came, then I’ll watch where you start people before we send the rest out.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Alright. The teachers are sitting first, but two elders stepped outside, and the children from the youth club may eat later if the speeches run long.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Thanks. Then I’ll hold back the extra packed trays and only set down the bowls at the tables already gathering, instead of laying every place the same way.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The donor assistant just asked whether lunch is fully plated yet. They want photos before people begin.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I’ll answer now so they stop waiting: some tables are ready, some are not, and we’re finishing table by table. We can photograph the front side first and keep the remaining settings flexible.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Okay, they can work with that. The drivers also joined at the back after dropping the guests.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I’ll add seats there and serve that section from what’s still unopened, rather than forcing the same setup across the whole room.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer calibrates under uncertainty by not assuming either fully individual plating or one uniform shared setup. He updates from host-side cues about who is gathering, who is delayed, and who joins later, and keeps meal service mixed by table and timing rather than standardizing everyone into a single serving pattern.

scenario: Your multinational events team is preparing a 12-minute opening segment for a new partnership launch in Enugu, Nigeria, with several Igbo community leaders, a state-level sponsor, and a foreign donor delegation attending. The segment will be livestreamed and is the first in-person meeting after six months of tense negotiation over land access and vendor rights. Your manager wants the opening to signal warmth and unity without looking improvised. A teammate from London has drafted a run-of-show that begins with a welcome speech in English, then a short interfaith blessing read in English and French so the donor guests feel included, followed by refreshments placed on each table before the elders arrive. A Lagos-based teammate says the sequence may feel "off" for some attendees but cannot join the planning call. The venue has only one rehearsal slot left, the sponsor's office insists the program cannot run long, and the donor liaison is pushing for an opening that feels globally accessible rather than locally opaque. You have authority to revise the opening protocol, assign speaking roles, and write the briefing note for hosts and ushers, but you cannot cancel the cultural element because it was specifically requested by the local organizing committee.
question: Write a decision memo for your team that proposes the opening protocol. Your memo must identify the underlying cultural mechanism you think is at stake from the available evidence, explain which tempting imported assumption could lead the team into a polished but wrong plan, and specify the exact sequence, role assignments, language handling, and contingency controls you would use for the first minutes of the event. Make clear what you would change in the current draft and why.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden mechanism as a specific host-ritual sequence governing the first offering, who initiates it, and how it frames the gathering.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that the opening must be structured around a locally meaningful first-offering ritual with role and order constraints, rather than treating it as generic hospitality or decorative culture. No credit for merely saying to 'respect tradition' or naming a broad region-wide custom without execution consequences.

rubric.point: Gets the primary execution axis right: the event must begin with the ritual before speeches or general refreshments, with the correct actor order.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer changes the opening sequence so the ritual happens at the very start, before standard refreshments or welcome remarks, and assigns the initiating act to the appropriate elder-ranked male host figure rather than a foreign MC, sponsor, or mixed volunteer team. Partial credit if it notices sequence matters but misses actor or order details.

rubric.point: Handles language correctly during the ritual stage and distinguishes that stage from later inclusive communication.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer avoids multilingual or foreign-language rendering during the prayer/ritual itself while still providing accessibility after that stage through separate explanation, translation, or follow-up framing. Partial credit if it proposes simultaneous translation or bilingual prayer during the ritual, since that applies inclusion logic at the wrong stage.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the tempting near-miss plan built on a generic global-hosting assumption.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly identifies the attractive but miscalibrated assumption—such as starting with an English welcome, distributing refreshments in advance, or making the prayer multilingual for donor inclusion—and explains why that would mishandle role, timing, or ritual authority even though it seems polished and inclusive.

rubric.point: Applies cognitive CQ by mapping neutral clues to the correct local rule rather than to a stereotype or pan-African shortcut.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer reasons from the scenario evidence to a Nigeria/Igbo-specific interaction logic and avoids overgeneralizing to 'African hospitality' or a generic ceremony template. Low credit if it gives a continent-wide explanation or relies on abstract caution without identifying the operative local boundary.

rubric.point: Designs concrete team coordination for hosts, ushers, and emcee under deadline pressure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer gives operational instructions such as when the item is presented, who stands where, who briefs the elder host, when general guests are seated, what ushers must not pre-place, and when the MC resumes the program. No credit for answers that stay at principle level.

rubric.point: Includes a calibrated contingency or repair plan that protects relationships without broadening the scope into generic delay or full redesign.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes a narrow backup, such as confirming the designated elder host and a same-community substitute in advance, or shifting donor explanation to a post-ritual sentence, without turning the solution into indefinite consultation, cancellation, or a longer safer program.

reference_outline: Infer that the key issue is not refreshments in general but a specific opening ritual in which kola nut functions as the first offering that begins the gathering and symbolizes hospitality and unity.

Revise the sequence so no ordinary refreshments are placed first; the ritual happens before welcome speech and before general service, with the designated eldest man among the appropriate hosts performing the breaking and taking the first piece before distribution proceeds by age order.

Separate ritual language from audience accessibility: keep the prayer/ritual portion in Igbo rather than converting it into English/French, then let the MC give a brief English explanation afterward for donor understanding.

Explicitly reject the polished near-miss plan of English-first welcome plus multilingual blessing plus pre-set refreshments, because it imports a global event-accessibility model into a stage where local sequence and ritual authority matter more.

Assign concrete roles: local organizing committee confirms the elder who will lead; ushers hold back general snacks until after the ritual; the emcee pauses until the ritual concludes; sponsor and donor guests are briefed in advance that the first minutes follow local protocol.

Use cognitive CQ by distinguishing this from a generic West African or pan-African hospitality gesture and applying the rule to the exact actor, stage, and language boundary in this Igbo-hosted setting.
