Add a narrow contingency: if the designated elder is delayed, activate a pre-cleared substitute from the host side rather than letting the foreign MC or sponsor improvise the act; if timing tightens, shorten later speeches instead of compressing or relocating the ritual.

scenario: A food brand in southeastern Nigeria is finalizing a festival sponsorship plan due tonight. The local events agency proposes serving small yam tastings from branded trays as guests arrive, then keeping a second round for later speeches. Another manager prefers the global festival template, where all featured foods are treated as ordinary sampling items throughout the event. The sponsorship must stay visible, but the brand does not want to misstate its role in the program.
question: Which approval decision best fits this situation?

options.A: Approve yam branding for the event, but limit tasting service to the later hospitality portion and keep the brand out of the opening moment when the new crop is first eaten together.
options.B: Approve the arrival tasting plan, but keep the first trays unbranded and move stronger branding to the later round after the opening segment is finished.
options.C: Approve the yam activation only if the brand helps shape the opening segment too, so the product is integrated consistently from the first shared bite through the later reception.
options.D: Use the global sampling template for this event as well, treating yam like the other featured foods and distributing it in both rounds without a separate exception in the sponsorship plan.

scenario: A newcomer at a regional office in Accra is coordinating a same-day visit from a senior partner from Lagos. The printed agenda is ready, but the catering order for the short welcome stop has not been finalized. The office manager is juggling a delayed driver, a tight budget, and pressure to keep the visit on schedule.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The partner lands at noon and comes here first before the bank meeting. We only have about twenty minutes in the office, and finance wants the receipt closed this morning.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. To keep it simple, I'll set out tea, bottled water, and wrapped biscuits in the conference room so nobody feels delayed.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: He is coming straight from the airport, and two directors from the local side will join him here before they all leave together.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Right, then I'll ask reception to mention that lunch is booked later near the client site, so this first stop stays light and efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The directors asked whether they should come a little earlier, but I told them we would be ready. The driver is already calling me every five minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll handle it. I'll send a polite note that refreshments are prepared on arrival and keep the room set for a quick briefing rather than adding another food order now.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. Please just make sure the room is settled before they walk in.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Done. I'll keep it neat, on time, and within budget.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer treats the host's initial food welcome as a minor logistical refreshment and assumes a later meal covers the obligation. In this Nigeria/Ghana context, the first hosted offering itself carries hospitality and recognition, so replacing it with minimal neutral snacks misreads repeated hosting cues through a generic business-efficiency frame.

scenario: You manage a three-person rollout team for a donor-funded mobile health pilot in The Gambia. At 12:40, your car is delayed by a checkpoint, so you will reach the village compound at about 1:10 instead of the planned 12:45. The village committee chair has already texted, "Come straight in when you arrive; we will finalize the device list today." Your UK procurement lead wants to keep the visit to 25 minutes because the donor review call starts at 2:00. Your Nigerian communications colleague says it may be best not to interrupt lunch and to wait quietly until people finish. You know from earlier visits that the committee often meets in a family compound rather than an office, and paperwork is usually discussed on site. When your local driver calls ahead, he learns only that "they are together now." You must send the team a pre-arrival instruction note before the car loses signal. One complication: the UK colleague does not want a full meal before the donor call, but has no medical or religious restriction. Another complication: the chair's nephew will photograph the visit for the district WhatsApp group, so any awkward moment will be visible beyond the room. The practical goal is to leave with signed confirmation of the final device list today, without damaging trust for next month's training phase.
question: Write the instruction note you would send your team. It should specify the arrival sequence, what each person should do if the hosts are eating when you enter, what wording to use if food is offered, how to handle the colleague who does not want a full meal, when to shift to the paperwork, and what immediate repair step to use if a teammate has already declined and remained standing nearby. Your note should also explain which tempting default assumption you are avoiding and why your chosen behavior is the better work plan under the time and visibility pressures.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden hospitality mechanism from the scenario evidence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that arriving during eating triggers an expectation of joining in at least minimally, rather than waiting off to the side or treating the meal as private downtime. Partial credit if it notices hospitality importance but does not convert that into a specific arrival behavior.

rubric.point: Chooses the correct execution sequence on entry
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan directs the team to enter, accept the invitation in action, and visibly participate in the meal ritual before trying to move immediately into business. Low credit if it prioritizes efficiency by waiting, watching, or pushing the paperwork first.

rubric.point: Specifies seed-calibrated visible behavior for the reluctant colleague
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer has the colleague wash hands and at least taste a small amount or otherwise participate minimally, with a polite bounded explanation if needed, rather than refusing outright because they are 'not hungry' or saying they will just observe. No full credit for generic politeness without the concrete behavioral minimum.

rubric.point: Rejects the polished near-miss default assumption
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly identifies a plausible imported assumption such as 'do not impose on hosts while they eat' or 'decline to save time and maintain professionalism' and explains why that would misfire here. Partial credit if it says not to be rude but does not name the near-miss logic.

rubric.point: Uses behavioural CQ through wording, timing, and interaction rhythm
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the note gives concrete phrasing and timing choices that fit the context, such as brief appreciative acceptance, minimal delay, and a smooth transition back to work after participation. Low credit for abstract advice like 'be respectful' or 'read the room.'

rubric.point: Designs a repair move for a teammate who already declined and stood nearby
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan includes an immediate behavioral repair, such as rejoining with a brief apology/appreciation and accepting a small taste, rather than over-explaining, joking, or leaving the person standing apart while others finish. Partial credit if it suggests apologizing later without correcting the visible moment.

rubric.point: Balances relationship protection with task completion under pressure
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer shows how a short, calibrated participation supports getting the signature today and protects next month's training relationship, instead of proposing the longest, safest, or broadest consultation plan. Low credit if it solves trust by indefinite delay or solves speed by ignoring the meal interaction.

reference_outline: Infer from 'family compound,' 'come straight in,' delayed arrival, and the likelihood that people are already together at lunch that entering during eating is part of the work interaction, not a separate private interruption.
Instruct the team to enter promptly, greet briefly, accept the invitation through action, and avoid standing aside watching others eat.

Have each visitor wash hands and take at least a small taste before shifting to business; for the colleague who does not want a full meal, use a polite bounded line and minimal participation rather than a flat refusal.

Name and reject the tempting default that professionalism means declining food, waiting quietly, or not 'imposing' on hosts during lunch; explain that this would damage trust more than a short delay would.

Give exact behavioural guidance: who speaks first, short appreciative wording, no long dietary speech, no visible hesitation, and a smooth transition such as thanking the hosts and then asking to confirm the device list once the immediate hospitality moment has been honored.

If someone already declined and remained nearby, repair immediately by re-entering the interaction with brief appreciation and accepting a small amount, instead of trying to fix it only through later explanation.
Keep the participation short and calibrated so the team still leaves with signatures and makes the donor call, showing that the culturally fitted action is also the stronger work-performance choice.

scenario: A health NGO in Fransfontein is drafting tonight’s serving brief for a goat meal after tomorrow’s workshop. Donor rules say any servings to nonparticipants must be logged separately, and the team cannot increase the total meat order. During prep, one nearby resident casually remarked that people living close by sometimes come over when an animal is being cut. A new program officer took this as a vague social comment and proposed requiring the local host to approve any sharing. A senior colleague from another part of Namibia warned against assuming the same practice applies everywhere and said overreserving would risk shorting participants. The host will be off-grid once setup begins, so staff will need a clear rule before service starts.
question: Which briefing line best reflects good judgment for tomorrow?

options.A: Keep all portions for registered participants unless the host has specifically cleared outside sharing before setup, and log any exception separately.
options.B: Set aside a small contingency share, and if nearby people ask directly during cutting, serve from that share and log those servings separately.
options.C: Prepare exactly for the participant list, then let the kitchen lead decide on the spot whether any direct requests seem legitimate enough to honor.
options.D: Pre-allocate several separately logged community portions before service, since nearby households are likely to expect meat once the goat is cut.

scenario: Your NGO team is launching a drought-resilient farming pilot in northwestern Ghana. On Thursday afternoon, you learn that a six-person delegation from the district side will stop at the field office at 8:00 a.m. Saturday before deciding whether to attend your afternoon community briefing and recommend the pilot to village leaders. The visit is short: 35 minutes at the office, then they continue to another site. Your country director in Accra wants the office to look efficient and says, by message, 'Please don't overcomplicate hospitality; tea, bread, and fruit are standard and quick.' A procurement colleague based in Nairobi has already arranged packaged breakfast items through a caterer, and canceling them will waste part of the budget. Your local operations assistant says only that 'for this group, the welcome itself will be noticed,' but does not elaborate and is unreachable for the evening because she is traveling. The delegation includes two senior men from the Dagaaba area, one younger technical officer from Wa, and three nonlocal donor observers. The field office has limited cooking capacity, no restaurant opens before 7:30 a.m., and your driver can reach nearby households or market contacts before dawn if instructed tonight. You must send a final hosting plan to the team in two hours, including who does what, what is served when, and how you will explain any last-minute change to Accra and Nairobi without making the local team look unprofessional.
question: Write the hosting and coordination plan you would send tonight. Your answer must identify the cultural mechanism you think is at work from the available evidence, name the tempting but miscalibrated plan, and give a concrete sequence for Saturday morning: what to prepare, what to serve first, who should handle the welcome, what to do with the already-ordered breakfast items, and how to brief Accra/Nairobi. Explain why your sequence is the better behavioral choice under the time, budget, and hierarchy pressure, and specify how you would monitor and repair the interaction if the first few minutes suggest your read was wrong.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that the key issue is not generic hospitality quantity but the need to welcome the Dagaaba-linked guests with the culturally meaningful staple tied to guest reception.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers a specific welcome-food mechanism from the regional/actor clues and treats it as operationally decisive; no credit for generic statements about 'offering local food,' 'being respectful,' or 'serving a nice meal.'

rubric.point: Chooses the correct execution axis: the first visible welcome offering must be recalibrated, not merely supplemented later with a local item.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer makes the culturally meaningful staple part of the initial reception sequence for the relevant guests; partial credit if it is added later as an optional extra or folded into lunch; no credit if the plan keeps the imported breakfast as the main welcome and treats the local staple as decorative.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the attractive near-miss plan of using the already-arranged standard breakfast because it is efficient, budget-safe, and broadly acceptable.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly identifies the tea/bread/fruit packaged breakfast plan as tempting but insufficient for this specific delegation and explains why efficiency or global standardization misfires here; no credit if the answer simply broadens the menu without confronting the mistaken assumption.

rubric.point: Translates the diagnosis into concrete visible behavior: sourcing, timing, serving order, host role, wording, and handling of the preordered food.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan specifies who secures the staple tonight or before dawn, who presents it on arrival, that it is served in the welcome phase, and how the preordered items are repositioned without letting them replace the main welcome; no credit for abstract recommendations without role assignment or sequence.

rubric.point: Uses behavioural CQ by choosing calibrated wording and interaction rhythm with both local and nonlocal stakeholders.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer includes brief, practical wording or briefing moves that fit the moment: e.g., a non-defensive message to Accra/Nairobi about adapting the welcome sequence for host-community legitimacy, and a Saturday interaction that avoids making the change look chaotic or overly ceremonial; no credit for generic 'communicate respectfully' advice.

rubric.point: Manages mixed audiences and constraints without overcorrecting into the largest or safest possible hospitality plan.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer keeps the intervention narrow and task-linked—focused on the decisive welcome act for the delegation while still using or repurposing the packaged items for the broader group or later timing; no credit if the answer proposes a maximal feast, indefinite delay, or broad consultation that misses the short-visit constraint.

rubric.point: Builds a credible monitoring and repair path if the inference proves incomplete or the audience composition shifts.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer gives a specific fallback, such as quietly observing whether the senior local guests are being welcomed as expected, then adjusting service order or channeling the packaged items without public fuss; no credit for vague statements like 'stay flexible' or 'ask for feedback afterward.'

reference_outline: Infer from the district visit, the Dagaaba-area seniors, and the local assistant's comment that the welcome will be judged through a specific hospitality food norm, not through generic breakfast adequacy.
Prioritize obtaining and preparing tuozaafi for the initial reception, even if this requires extra early-morning coordination and does not optimize speed or budget neatness.

Make the primary sequence actor-specific and visible: assign a local-facing host to receive the delegation and ensure the culturally meaningful staple is the first substantive welcome offering for the relevant guests rather than a later add-on.

Do not let the Nairobi/Accra standard breakfast plan remain the main welcome; repurpose packaged tea, bread, and fruit for donor observers, staff, or after the initial reception so the sunk cost is bounded rather than driving the core interaction.

Send a concise management note tonight explaining that the adjustment is a targeted reception calibration for local legitimacy and stakeholder trust, not a loss of professionalism or uncontrolled catering expansion.

Use behavioural CQ through exact phrasing, timing, and rhythm: avoid public debate over the change on Saturday morning, avoid presenting the adaptation as exotic entertainment, and keep the welcome orderly and matter-of-fact.

Monitor the first minutes of arrival for whether the senior local guests are being received in the intended way; if cues suggest the read is off, shift smoothly by broadening service without announcing a correction or embarrassing anyone.
Keep the plan narrow under pressure: one critical hospitality adjustment tied to project credibility, not a general 'serve many local dishes' response or an all-purpose consultation delay.

scenario:
You manage operations for a regional NGO that is launching a three-day health-training workshop in Addis Ababa for 28 participants. The workshop includes staff from two Ethiopian partner organizations, a donor representative flying in from Europe, and facilitators from Kenya and India. The donor expects a networking lunch on Day 1 and has already approved a catering budget built around buffet service with chicken, beef, eggs, and dairy-heavy desserts because it is the cheapest package the hotel can still guarantee on 48 hours' notice. The country director wants the event to feel welcoming and does not want a visible food problem in front of the donor.

You receive partial signals, but no one has given a direct briefing. One Ethiopian partner asked whether the lunch break could start later than originally scheduled. Another participant replied to the invitation, 'I may join the meal after the session depending on the day.' A third person thanked your team for arranging hospitality but said they would 'likely not take anything at midday.' Several invitees have not answered the meal form at all. The hotel sales manager keeps pushing for a single final menu today and says split service after dark would increase labor costs. Your supervisor says, 'We cannot keep changing plans for every preference; just choose one standard lunch and note vegetarian options.'

You have one hour before the hotel cutoff and a donor briefing call in two hours. You cannot cancel the meal budget, but you can redesign timing, menu logic, invitation wording, and who gets asked what before confirming.
question: Write a decision memo to your supervisor that recommends how to finalize the meal plan today. Your memo must: (1) diagnose what uncertainty matters most in this Ethiopia setting and what tempting assumption would mislead the team, (2) specify the immediate evidence you will seek and from whom before the cutoff, (3) make a concrete decision on meal timing/menu structure if full clarity does not arrive in time, and (4) explain how you will brief the donor and hotel so the plan stays workable without publicly putting attendees on the spot.

rubric.point: Identifies the operative uncertainty as fasting schedule and observance pattern, not generic dietary preference.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that the key issue is whether attendees are observing different fasting schedules in Ethiopia and links this to midday participation, timing, and animal-source foods; partial credit if it mentions religion or diet vaguely; no credit if it treats the issue as ordinary vegetarian preference or simple RSVP unreliability.

rubric.point: Rejects the attractive near-miss of one default lunch with token vegetarian coverage.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly bounds or rejects the supervisor's 'standard lunch plus vegetarian option' logic as miscalibrated for this case; partial credit if it says to be flexible but still centers the default package; no credit if it keeps the global buffet plan and assumes that one vegetarian tray solves inclusion.

rubric.point: Uses targeted evidence-gathering that reduces the right uncertainty before the cutoff.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes rapid, specific follow-up to the Ethiopian partner focal points or participant clusters to determine who expects midday food, who needs a later meal window, and whether animal-source items are inappropriate, while keeping unknowns visible; partial credit if it says 'ask participants' generically; no credit if it waits for full survey completion, asks only to confirm the original menu, or overweights one ambiguous cue.

rubric.point: Makes a concrete execution decision on the primary axis of timing/menu structure under incomplete information.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer recommends a contingency design such as shifting the main hosted meal later, or building a menu that can serve attendees who may not eat at midday while avoiding dependence on animal-source dishes for the core offering; partial credit if it suggests both lunch and dinner without prioritization or operational detail; no credit if it insists on the original midday meat-centered buffet because the budget and schedule favor it.

rubric.point: Applies metacognitive CQ by separating what can be inferred now from what remains uncertain and by defining what evidence would trigger adjustment.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer clearly distinguishes current signals, remaining unknowns, and a revision rule for final confirmation or on-site adaptation; partial credit if it shows caution without an update logic; no credit if it is either overconfident ('they are all observing X') or inert ('delay everything until certain').

rubric.point: Designs stakeholder communication that protects relationships and avoids public pressure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies private or focal-point-based checks, donor framing around participant access and attendance, and hotel instructions that avoid forcing individuals to refuse hospitality publicly; partial credit if communication is respectful but generic; no credit if it asks participants to declare sensitive observance publicly at the event or frames the change as mere personal preference management.

rubric.point: Handles operational constraints without letting cost or hierarchy erase the cultural mechanism.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer shows how to stay within the deadline and budget while redesigning the service logic, rather than treating cost pressure as a reason to ignore the signals; partial credit if it acknowledges constraints but gives no workable path; no credit if it defers entirely to the cheapest package or proposes an elaborate plan disconnected from the cutoff.

reference_outline: State that the crucial uncertainty is not 'who wants vegetarian food' but which attendees may be observing different fasting schedules in Ethiopia, affecting whether they eat at midday at all and whether core dishes should rely on animal-source foods.
Name the near-miss explicitly: finalizing the hotel's standard midday buffet with a token vegetarian option because it fits budget, donor expectations, and generic global event practice.

Immediately contact partner focal points or a small set of participant representatives for rapid confirmation on meal timing and fasting-related menu constraints, rather than blasting a broad public question or waiting for complete RSVPs.

If not all replies arrive, commit to a plan that does not depend on broad midday consumption and does not make animal-source dishes the default core meal; shift the main hospitality window later or structure the hosted meal so late eaters and midday non-eaters are still accommodated.

Brief the donor in operational terms: attendance, hospitality quality, and avoiding a visible mismatch require a calibrated meal format, not just a cheaper buffet; frame the adjustment as improving participation rather than catering to isolated preferences.
Instruct the hotel on flexible timing and menu composition with a protected non-animal-source core offering and, if used, clearly secondary optional items rather than a meat-centered default.

Keep metacognitive calibration visible: specify what is inferred from the current clues, what remains unknown across attendees, and what on-site monitoring or final same-day check will trigger a timing or service adjustment.

scenario:
You are the program manager for a UK museum’s Africa season launch in London. In 9 days, the museum will host a public evening co-produced with a Benin City cultural foundation, a UK-based Edo community association, and two internal teams: fundraising and events. The sponsor wants a visually strong 'first harvest' moment because ticket sales are behind target, and the events team has already drafted a run-of-show with a welcome cocktail, a tasting station built around this week’s newly imported yam shipment, a short blessing, a donor announcement, live drumming, and a surprise on-stage engagement between two junior staff members from the community association. 

You have partial signals that something is off, but no one has stated a rule directly. In the email thread, the Benin City liaison approves the venue map and guest list but does not comment on the tasting or music sections. A UK-based Edo volunteer replies only, 'Please avoid making the opening too festive before the formal observances are complete.' Another message from a palace-affiliated guest’s assistant asks whether 'the first presentation of produce' will happen privately or in front of donors, and whether the principal guests are expected to remain for the full evening. Meanwhile, fundraising says changing the sponsor-facing segment this late could jeopardize next year’s grant, and legal says there is no compliance issue with the drafted program. 

Your line manager wants a concrete plan by 4 p.m. today: what to keep, what to resequence, what to verify, and what to tell each stakeholder so the event can still proceed on time without embarrassing the museum or its Benin partners.
question: Write the decision memo you would send your line manager. Give a concrete execution plan centered on sequence and evidence use: what you infer from the current signals, which parts of the draft program you would pause or redesign immediately, what assumption a competent UK events team might be tempted to make here but should not, and how you would brief fundraising, events, and the Benin-facing contacts today. Your answer should show what you are prepared to act on now, what remains uncertain, and what specific evidence would change your plan before launch.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden mechanism from the neutral cues
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that the opening cannot treat the newly arrived yam and surrounding program as a normal celebratory harvest feature, and links this to a bounded ritual/observance sequence rather than generic sensitivity or generic religious caution.

rubric.point: Makes the correct sequence decision on the core execution axis
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer immediately removes or holds the new-yam tasting from the public opening and prevents any sponsor-facing 'first harvest' reveal until the appropriate observance stage is clarified; partial credit if it merely adds a disclaimer or moves tasting later without tying the move to the observance sequence.

rubric.point: Applies the sober-period implications beyond the food item
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer also flags that the drumming and surprise engagement/wedding-like public celebration are high-risk elements to pause or redesign now, rather than treating the issue as food-only. Partial credit if it notices only one of these additional elements.

rubric.point: Distinguishes broad from role-specific participation
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer avoids assuming that every attendee must follow the same restrictions in the same way, while still recognizing that the museum’s public program should not force principal Benin-linked guests or the wider Edo-facing audience into a breach. Answers that overgeneralize the same requirement to all participants without nuance lose credit.

rubric.point: Rejects the attractive near-miss plan
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly rejects a plausible imported assumption such as 'there is no legal issue, so proceed and simply label the ritual portion respectfully' or 'keep everything but offer alternatives for those who opt out.' Answers that rely on compliance logic, generic inclusion options, or donor preference as the main frame do not score highly.

rubric.point: Shows metacognitive calibration under uncertainty
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer separates what can already be inferred strongly enough for immediate action from what is still unknown, identifies which cues matter more than silence or generic approval emails, and states what targeted confirmation is needed without delaying all decisions.

rubric.point: Designs role-specific coordination for the same day
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer assigns concrete messages or actions to fundraising, events, and Benin-facing contacts today—for example, freezing certain segments, proposing substitute sponsor moments, and asking narrowly framed questions about observance timing and who must not be publicly placed in a conflicting role. Generic 'consult stakeholders' answers receive low credit.

reference_outline: Infer from 'avoid making the opening too festive before the formal observances are complete' plus the question about first presentation of produce that the event draft is colliding with a restricted pre-celebratory period, not just a matter of taste or branding.
Act immediately on the strongest evidence: remove or suspend public serving, display, or donor-centered debut of the newly imported yam until the proper observance sequence is confirmed.

Treat the issue as broader than menu choice: pause live drumming/percussive celebration and cancel or redesign the surprise engagement because the opening should not be framed as a festive climax if the relevant observance has not been completed.

Do not overcorrect into 'everyone must follow identical restrictions'; instead redesign the museum program so no Benin-linked principals, Edo partners, or the event’s public symbolism are put into the wrong stage or role.
Name and reject the tempting near-miss: proceeding with the drafted celebration because legal cleared it, sponsor pressure is high, and abstaining guests could simply decline food or leave early.

Use metacognitive CQ by stating a provisional read: enough evidence exists to change sequence now, but the team still needs targeted confirmation on observance completion, whether any produce presentation must occur privately, and which guests have role-specific constraints.

Brief fundraising with a replacement sponsor-visible moment that does not center first consumption or festive breakthrough; brief events to freeze the risky segments immediately; brief Benin-facing contacts with narrow operational questions rather than a vague request for cultural education.

Set a repair/monitoring plan: if confirmation later shows the observance will be complete before the event, some held elements may be reinstated in the correct order; if not, keep the program sober and shift celebration language, music, and produce handling out of the opening.

scenario: A public-sector training team in Calgary is closing lunch orders for a small workshop. Four registrants checked "religious meal" on an old form with no follow-up field. The caterer can still provide either sealed certified-halal turkey boxes from a separate vendor or vegetarian pasta boxes from the regular kitchen, which also prepares pork dishes and desserts containing gelatin. A colleague forwards last year's note saying Muslim attendees at another session "mostly just took the vegetarian option." But one of the four current registrants has already asked whether the vegetarian meals are prepared separately, and another wrote earlier, "Either option is fine if it meets the requirement." Procurement wants a final count in 15 minutes.
question: Which plan best handles the situation before the deadline?

options.A: Order four certified-halal turkey boxes, since they are individually sealed and more likely to work for everyone than the regular vegetarian meals.
options.B: Send the four registrants a short message naming both lunch options and how each is prepared, ask each person which option works for them, and submit only the choices people explicitly confirm.
options.C: Use last year's vegetarian pattern as the default, then follow up only with the registrant who specifically asked about separate preparation.
options.D: Submit a split order of two certified-halal boxes and two vegetarian boxes, because the current signals suggest the group probably has mixed preferences.

scenario: At a U.S. university in Boston, a newcomer helping with a same-day alumni-student networking reception has to finalize the dinner count before a caterer cutoff. The RSVP sheet includes one note asking for a religious meal, but the registration team is overloaded and the event director wants the seating chart sent in the next hour.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We need the final meal count to the vendor by 3 p.m. One RSVP has a note saying they need a religious meal, and the student workers are still fixing name badges.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Since it's only one note and we don't have details yet, I'll keep the standard dinner order and avoid guessing. If the guest asks at check-in, we can see what sides or salad work.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The venue is off campus, so once the trays leave, changes are basically over. The guest list also has several people coming from Roxbury and Cambridge, but not everyone filled out the form completely.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Right, I don't want to make a visible mistake by labeling the wrong meal. I'll ask registration to quietly watch for that guest and handle it discreetly on site if needed.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Okay. I can send the seating chart now, but the caterer will still take a short update for another twenty minutes if you want anything added.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Let's leave the order as is. Better to stay neutral than order something too specific without confirmation.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Got it. I’ll release the count in ten minutes, then.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Thanks. After that I'll draft a cleaner RSVP question for future events so we have less ambiguity next time.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer miscalibrates by treating the safest option as non-commitment and delaying action until check-in. In this U.S. campus inclusion context, the culturally aligned move is to provide an appropriate religious meal proactively and, if needed, directly clarify the attendee's request before the cutoff rather than defaulting to the standard dinner.

scenario: A food-services manager at a seniors' residence in Alberta is finalizing a special lunch for Indigenous residents next week. Purchasing needs one main-order decision by tomorrow afternoon, and the team can still make one short round of calls tonight if there is a clear reason. A draft plan uses a plant-based entrée with bannock and berry dessert, based on the idea that it will be broadly acceptable across households.
question: Which observation would most justify spending the extra time tonight to revisit the main entrée plan before ordering?

options.A: The residence's monthly menu data show the plant-based lunch usually gets the highest overall uptake across the building, including on weeks when several Indigenous residents attend the dining room.
options.B: During RSVP calls, residents from the same lunch list mention different preferred main dishes tied to where they grew up or lived before moving into the residence.
options.C: Several residents sound pleased that bannock and berry dessert are included, and one family member asks whether a fish option could also appear on the serving table.
options.D: A community volunteer says wild game and fish are meaningful foods in many places, and suggests pausing the order until a broader cultural menu review can be organized.

scenario:
You are operations lead on a multicultural project team preparing a two-day public launch event in Los Angeles for a wellness app. Your core team includes a country manager in Germany, a procurement lead in Singapore, a brand director in Brazil, and a U.S. partnerships manager who will host local creators, volunteers, and press. The CEO wants vendor commitments locked within 48 hours because a sponsor is threatening to pull a co-marketing budget if the event plan slips again.

One invited U.S. creator, Ava, is central to the local turnout: she is bringing a volunteer network and has already posted once about being excited to support the launch. In message threads over the last week, she has not only asked whether meals are "strictly vegan," but has also separately asked whether the event gift bags include leather or wool items, whether the after-hours networking venue can confirm how food is sourced and handled, and whether the volunteer activity can be changed from a visit to a fashion resale partner to a neighborhood mutual-aid kitchen. No one on the team has said this is required; the German manager says these look like optional lifestyle requests and suggests offering one vegan meal plus a polite note that the rest of the program is fixed. The Singapore procurement lead prefers to avoid reopening vendor contracts and proposes marking Ava as a special-diet attendee only. The Brazilian brand director warns that changing visible event elements for one person may trigger fairness complaints from other guests.

You cannot cancel Ava without hurting local attendance and trust, and you do not have budget to redesign the full event from scratch. You also cannot ask legal for a long review because the sponsor deck must go out tomorrow morning.
question: Write a decision memo to your team that sets the execution plan for the next 48 hours. Your memo must: (1) diagnose what is likely happening in Ava's requests from the available evidence, (2) identify the most tempting but miscalibrated assumption in the team's current proposals, (3) specify exactly which parts of the event you would revisit now versus keep fixed, (4) assign who must do what with vendors and with Ava, and (5) show what effort you are personally willing to absorb to keep both task progress and local trust. Be concrete about sequence, scope, wording, and fallback if Ava's expectations turn out to be broader than you inferred.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the mechanism as a broader organizing practice rather than a narrow meal preference.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer uses the pattern across food, materials, venue, and volunteer activity to infer that the requests likely reflect a value system shaping identity, community alignment, and boundaries; partial credit if it notices the pattern but still treats it mainly as a dietary accommodation.

rubric.point: Rejects the attractive near-miss of handling Ava through the standard 'special diet' workflow only.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly bounds the team's tempting generic plan as too narrow because it would solve the menu line while missing other event touchpoints; no credit for answers that simply add politeness, a disclaimer, or a vegan entree to the existing plan.

rubric.point: Makes the primary scope decision correctly on which event elements to revisit immediately.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer revisits the cross-cutting elements most directly implicated by Ava's pattern now (food sourcing/handling, gift-bag materials, and the volunteer or social activity) while preserving lower-risk fixed elements where possible; reduced credit if it either overreacts by reopening the entire event or underreacts by limiting action to catering.

rubric.point: Designs role-specific coordination instead of generic consultation or delay.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo assigns a concrete owner sequence such as: one person verifies vendor handling and material specs, one person negotiates limited substitutions, one person communicates directly with Ava using targeted questions, and one person protects sponsor timing; low credit for broad statements like 'check with everyone' or 'consult local stakeholders more.'

rubric.point: Shows motivational CQ through costly, sustained adaptive effort with boundaries.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the respondent takes ownership of inconvenient follow-through such as late vendor calls, manual substitution work, or direct repair conversations rather than shifting the burden to Ava or waiting for locals to explain everything; no credit for effort-free inclusivity language or for intrusive overcommitment without prioritization.

rubric.point: Uses calibrated wording and repair logic under ambiguity.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes wording that tests the inferred scope without forcing Ava to educate the team broadly, and includes a fallback if her expectations are narrower or broader than inferred; reduced credit for answers that demand a full cultural explanation from her, promise total redesign immediately, or hide behind noncommittal caution.

reference_outline: State that Ava's pattern likely signals more than a menu choice: the same principle appears to shape what she eats, what materials she uses, which spaces she joins, and which community activity fits her participation.

Name the near-miss explicitly: treating this as a standard dietary checkbox or one-person preference request is attractive under deadline and budget pressure but misses the cross-touchpoint nature of the issue.

Choose a narrow but real revision scope for the next 48 hours: verify strict vegan food handling and sourcing claims, swap or remove animal-derived gift-bag items, and replace or offer an equivalent volunteer/social activity that does not conflict with the inferred value boundary; keep unrelated event components fixed.

Assign roles and sequence: respondent personally owns the direct message/call with Ava and final integration; procurement checks ingredient handling and material specs with vendors; partnerships negotiates the activity substitution; brand updates sponsor-facing language only after the revised scope is confirmed.

Use wording that is specific but not presumptive, such as confirming whether the team should align food, materials, and volunteer components consistently, instead of asking Ava to teach the team her beliefs in general.

Show motivational CQ by accepting visible cost: absorb after-hours vendor work, spend political capital to reopen limited contracts, and stay engaged through ambiguity rather than withdrawing, overpromising, or pushing all adaptation onto Ava.

Include a fallback and monitoring plan: if Ava confirms a narrower scope, lock only the necessary substitutions quickly; if broader conflicts remain, offer a bounded alternative path and communicate internally which limits are operational rather than dismissing the concern as personal preference.

scenario: A newcomer at a museum in southern Arizona is helping finalize a donor breakfast tied to a community cultural program. The printed menu, table cards, and media preview must be approved by noon. A local coordinator from the host community is managing logistics, while the newcomer has been asked to keep the event inclusive and on schedule after a caterer substitution changed several dishes.

roles.newcomer: Museum events manager new to the region

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The caterer swapped two items this morning, and the donor team wants the menu cards sent to print in an hour. We also still need a short intro slide for the breakfast.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I can absorb the reprint cost and redo the slide myself. To avoid guessing, I'll bring sample cards and the revised dishes to the advisory table at 10:30 so they can react before anything goes out.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That would mean pulling a few people from setup. The donor office usually prefers quick signoff from one point person.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I know it's extra work, but I'd rather lose thirty minutes than reduce this to a branding check. I'll keep the donor office updated, and if the room setup slips, I'll stay late and cover that reset with facilities.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Alright. The caterer also asked whether you want the small tasting cups set near the registration desk so guests can try them as they arrive.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Let's do that. Since it's a welcoming event, having the samples right at check-in should show openness, and I can mention on the slide that the foods are part of living traditions so people understand the context.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The donor photographer will be there early too, and the print vendor needs final wording by 11:15.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll get the wording approved at 10:30, keep the intro concise, and make sure the tasting station and signage are ready before guests enter.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer shows real effort and takes on cost, but misplaces that effort by treating culturally significant foods as welcoming samples for general arrival traffic and display. For this seed, food is tied to sacred ceremonial relationships rather than handled through a generic museum hospitality format.

scenario:
You are operations lead for a Toronto-based nonprofit that is launching a youth mentorship partnership with a New York donor network. The first in-person planning session will be held at a community center in Toronto on Thursday evening, followed immediately by a photographed welcome meal. The donor representative wants the meal to signal unity and has already written in a draft run-of-show: "After the remarks, everyone will gather around one buffet and we’ll invite all mentors, parents, and board members to share the same meal together before the press photos." Your team has 36 hours to finalize the event brief, catering instructions, and MC script. Press coverage is important because next-quarter funding depends on visible community participation. Budget is tight, so the easiest option is one caterer, one buffet line, one set of serving ware, and one public invitation to eat together. 

The participants include local board members, several families connected to a Jewish partner organization, a U.S. donor team, two Muslim youth mentors, and a Canadian corporate sponsor that wants the event to feel seamless and "inclusive without complicated exceptions." In the email thread, one board member asked only, "Can we avoid making anyone feel singled out at the meal stage?" Another replied, "We should not overcomplicate this; people can always choose not to eat." No one has stated a formal dietary rule, and no one has asked for a separate room or separate program. Your supervisor tells you that if you change the meal plan, you must preserve the sponsor’s unity message, keep the event on time, and avoid a public moment where attendees have to explain personal food choices.
question: Write a brief decision memo for your supervisor that recommends exactly how to redesign the meal stage. Your memo must: (1) diagnose the hidden cultural risk in the current plan from the evidence given; (2) identify the most tempting but miscalibrated assumption in the current email thread; (3) specify the visible execution choices you would make on wording, sequence, audience, catering setup, and follow-up within the next 36 hours; and (4) explain how your plan preserves sponsor goals while reducing relationship and trust risk. Be concrete about who says what, when, and in what channel.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the specific risk in making the meal a single public act of shared eating rather than treating it as a neutral logistics choice.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that the current design risks turning participation in the same food into a boundary-signaling act for some Jewish participants, not merely a generic dietary inconvenience. Partial credit for mentioning dietary sensitivity without explaining why the shared-meal expectation itself is the problem.

rubric.point: Rejects the tempting near-miss that "people can always opt out" or that one inclusive buffet is automatically the most respectful default.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly bounds this assumption as attractive under budget, schedule, and sponsor pressure but miscalibrated because it shifts the burden onto attendees in a public moment. No credit for answers that keep the same public invitation and rely on individual self-selection alone.

rubric.point: Makes the primary execution-axis choice on sequence and public framing of the meal stage.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan changes the event rhythm so remarks, networking, and food access do not publicly require everyone to join one shared eating moment in the same way at the same time. Acceptable answers may decenter the meal from the unity script, separate gathering from eating, or redesign photos and transitions; low credit if the answer merely adds more food options while preserving the same public expectation.

rubric.point: Uses behavioural CQ through calibrated wording, audience, and channel rather than generic politeness.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies concrete phrasing and channels such as a private check-in with the partner organization or key host, revised MC language that does not publicly summon everyone to share one meal, and catering instructions that avoid spotlighting who is or is not eating what. No credit for broad statements like "be respectful" or "ask everyone their needs" without channel and timing.

rubric.point: Assigns roles and workflow steps that fit the 36-hour constraint.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer names who should contact whom, who rewrites the run-of-show, who adjusts the caterer brief, and when these happen before the event. Partial credit for a sound idea without an executable owner-sequence.

rubric.point: Preserves sponsor and donor objectives without using the wrong visible behavior.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes an alternate way to signal unity—through remarks, welcome format, seating flow, photo timing, or shared program moment—while not tying unity to everyone eating the same food together. Low credit if unity is preserved only by making the plan broader, slower, or more consultative without changing the key public behavior.

rubric.point: Includes calibration or repair if the inference is incomplete or if a change raises concern.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer includes a narrow verification or fallback step that checks the redesign with the relevant partner privately and quickly, without escalating into a general survey or delaying the event. No credit for answers whose main strategy is to postpone, over-consult, or gather exhaustive dietary data from all attendees.

reference_outline: Infer from the mixed-faith guest list, the board member’s concern about singling people out, and the draft script that the main risk is not only menu compliance but making one shared public eating act the visible marker of belonging.

Identify the near-miss: under deadline and sponsor pressure, a competent planner may keep one buffet and assume anyone uncomfortable can quietly decline; explain why that still creates a public boundary moment and pushes the cost onto attendees.

Redesign the sequence so the unity moment happens in remarks, introductions, or photos before or apart from any eating decision; do not have the MC invite everyone to share the same meal as the symbol of togetherness.

Revise visible behavior: use neutral MC wording such as welcoming guests to continue conversations and refresh themselves as they wish, avoid calling attention to who joins which food option, and brief hosts not to urge everyone to eat the same thing together.

Handle coordination privately and quickly: contact the Jewish partner-side organizer or host counterpart in a direct one-to-one channel to validate the redesign and catch any obvious miss, rather than sending a broad attendee questionnaire or public email.

Adjust catering and room setup operationally: structure service so guests can participate in the event without a single central public decision point about one shared meal; preserve timing and sponsor optics through layout, signage, and photo order rather than through one buffet script.

Give owners and timing: operations rewrites the run-of-show today, supervisor approves sponsor-facing language, caterer receives revised service instructions tonight, and the MC/hosts get a short behavioral briefing before the event.

Include a repair boundary: if donor or sponsor objects that the meal no longer visibly proves unity, propose an alternative symbolic moment and explain that this protects participation and trust while still meeting the event’s public goals.

scenario: At a client lunch in Toronto, a local account manager and a newcomer consultant are finalizing how to handle a catered tasting meal for visiting executives. They have only a few minutes before the guests arrive, and the newcomer wants the meal to stay efficient so the team can keep discussing the contract.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The clients will come straight from the site visit, so lunch has to stay smooth. Catering left small plates at each seat and a few shared dishes in the middle.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Got it. To keep the conversation moving, I'll help from my seat instead of having people pause. If something is out of reach, I'll just lean over and place a bit onto their plates as we talk.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We do need to keep things moving, and the VP hates long breaks in the discussion.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Exactly. I'll also keep one spoon with the condiments so everyone can use the same one quickly rather than ask staff to circle back.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Catering is short-staffed today, so there may not be much table service once everyone sits.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: No problem. I'll watch who needs what and top up plates from where I am, even if I have to reach across once or twice. That should look attentive and save time.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Alright, the clients are almost here. We just need lunch to feel polished.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll keep it efficient and quiet so the meeting stays on track.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer enacts the wrong meal-sharing logic: reaching across others' place settings, serving directly into others' plates from his seat, and normalizing one shared utensil for multiple diners. In North American dining contexts, the key mechanism is individual place-setting boundaries and orderly sharing, so the execution is culturally miscalibrated even though it sounds efficient and considerate.

scenario: A visiting program manager is arranging a post-workshop dinner in Boston for four U.S. employees and five local freelancers. Company policy allows only employee meals to be expensed. At 2 p.m., the reserved restaurant calls to say that parties of nine must use a fixed family-style menu on one bill. A nearby restaurant can still take the group, but only if the manager transfers the booking now and sends each guest's entree choice before 4 p.m. The team has had a long day, and changing plans will take extra coordination.
question: Which plan is best?

options.A: Keep the current reservation, explain in advance which meals the company can cover, and send the itemized bill afterward so freelancers can reimburse their portions digitally.
options.B: Transfer the booking, collect entree choices that afternoon, and tell everyone the company will cover employees while other guests handle their own orders at dinner.
options.C: Keep the current reservation, explain in advance which meals the company can cover, and ask the restaurant to group the freelancers' items together so they can divide that part among themselves.
options.D: Offer the group the choice to switch restaurants if they want; otherwise keep the current reservation and sort out payment with the server once everyone is seated.

scenario: A newcomer on a university exchange team in the United States is helping at a faculty family's welcome dinner for student mentors. One platter of grilled vegetables and one large pasta bowl will be set in the middle of the table, but the team is short on time because the dean may arrive early. The newcomer wants to help in a way that keeps the evening moving and shows commitment without making the hosts do extra work.

roles.local: Maya, a U.S. graduate assistant helping coordinate the dinner
roles.newcomer: Rafi, a newly arrived exchange staff member

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The dean might get here before the last students, so we need the table ready in ten minutes. The big bowls can go in the center once the host brings them out.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Got it. I'll handle the place settings and stay back from introductions if that helps. Do you want the extra small plates stacked near the sink or at each seat?

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Either works. We usually keep things fairly relaxed here, but tonight is a little tight.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I'll put one at every seat and keep serving spoons with the center dishes. It takes a minute longer now, but it should make the table flow cleaner once everyone sits.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Thanks. I still need to check name cards and the host's dessert trays, so I may disappear for a bit.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: No problem. If the food comes out before you get back, I'll start by helping people get some onto their own plates so the host isn't juggling that too.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That would help. The dean just texted that he's parking now.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'm on it—plates are set, spoons are out, and I'll keep the line moving once the bowls land.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer's decisive behavior matches the U.S. serving norm by preparing individual plates for food taken from shared dishes and planning for people to portion food onto their own plates before eating. The key execution axis is separating food from the mutual serving dishes into personal plates, even under time pressure.

scenario: You are helping a U.S. manager host six new hires at her home after a Saturday training session. She wants the dinner plan sent to a grocery-delivery service within an hour. The meal will include two mains, several sides, and a small dining table, and the manager asks you to specify the serving sequence.
question: Which serving sequence best fits this setting?

options.A: Put the mains and sides in the middle, invite everyone to start from the shared dishes, and let guests continue taking bites from those dishes through the meal.
options.B: Portion the mains and sides onto each plate in the kitchen before anyone sits down, then bring completed plates to the table and keep extra food off the table.
options.C: Bring the mains and sides to the table in serving dishes, have each person take a portion onto their own plate as dishes are passed, then eat from that plate.
options.D: Pass the mains and sides around once for guests to sample onto plates, then leave the dishes open for everyone to keep eating directly from as conversation continues.

scenario: You work in London for a museum-food festival partnership preparing a public program on Indigenous food traditions of North America. The launch is in 10 days, the museum director wants sponsor-ready copy tomorrow, and the legal team has warned against unsupported cultural claims after a previous exhibition complaint. A UK-based content lead has drafted a panel and tasting-introduction script that says the event will highlight how 'North American Indigenous communities used ceremonial feasts to share valued foods fairly across the continent.' The draft draws on one academic review, a photo set from the Pacific Northwest coast, and an older internal deck that grouped several communities under one regional heading. A Canadian operations manager likes the draft because it is simple for press, while a US brand manager argues that broad wording will help attendance and avoid 'overcomplicating distinctions.' You have budget for only one additional round of revisions and one late-evening call outside normal hours if you choose to use it. No one on the team is a specialist in the source communities, and if you slow the launch too much the director may cut the food segment entirely.
question: Write a decision memo for the team that states what you would change before approval, who you would involve, and what extra effort you would personally take on over the next 24 hours. Your memo must identify the most tempting but flawed assumption in the current draft, explain the cultural mechanism you think is being misframed from the available evidence, and give a concrete revision-and-approval sequence that balances deadline pressure, sponsor expectations, and relationship risk.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden scope problem from the evidence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that the source supports a specific ceremonial food-sharing practice in a narrower northwestern Indigenous context rather than a continent-wide North American generalization; no credit for merely saying 'be more accurate' or 'avoid stereotypes' without identifying the scope error.

rubric.point: Rejects the attractive broad-brand near-miss
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly identifies the tempting assumption that one example can be scaled into a generic North American claim and explains why that broad wording is miscalibrated under the evidence; partial credit if the answer objects to the wording but keeps similarly broad framing for convenience, safety, or audience simplicity.

rubric.point: Makes the key execution choice on wording and approval scope
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan narrows the panel/script to the supported subregional ceremonial context and freezes broader claims until verified, instead of approving the draft with disclaimers, vague qualifiers, or a generic 'some Indigenous groups' formula that still treats the evidence as continent-wide.

rubric.point: Shows motivational CQ through costly, bounded follow-through
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the respondent takes visible ownership of inconvenient next steps such as using the one late call, reworking copy personally, or absorbing status/time cost to keep the narrow revision on track; no credit for friendly but low-cost suggestions that shift the burden to others or default to postponement.

rubric.point: Designs a concrete 24-hour coordination sequence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies a workable order of actions across roles, such as redrafting first, checking the source against the draft claim, getting targeted sign-off on the narrowed wording, and briefing sponsor-facing colleagues on why simplification must stop at that boundary; partial credit for broad consultation without sequence.

rubric.point: Uses evidence weighting rather than generic caution
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer distinguishes between what the academic review, photo set, and old internal deck can and cannot justify, giving the review the highest weight and treating the deck or visuals as insufficient grounds for expansion; no credit for answers that treat all artifacts as equally supportive.

rubric.point: Builds a repair and risk-control plan under launch pressure
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer includes a practical fallback such as replacing the overbroad line with narrower confirmed wording now and parking any broader comparative claim for post-launch review; no credit for answers whose main solution is indefinite delay, maximal review by many parties, or cutting the issue from the program without trying to salvage a precise version.

reference_outline: State that the current draft overextends one documented ceremonial food-sharing practice into a claim about Indigenous North America as a whole, and note that the Pacific Northwest source cues are the relevant evidence.
Revise the panel and script immediately so they describe the supported ceremonial food-sharing practice in its narrower northwestern context instead of using continent-wide language.

Personally own the extra effort: redraft the copy tonight, use the single after-hours call if needed to resolve the wording boundary, and absorb the discomfort of pushing back on director/brand pressure rather than letting the broad version pass.
Tell the Canadian operations manager and US brand manager that simplification is still possible, but only within the narrower verified frame; reject audience-friendly broadening as the main trap.

Route approval in a tight sequence: source check against the exact sentence, targeted sign-off on the narrowed text, then sponsor briefing with a short rationale for why broader phrasing is unsupported.

Weight evidence carefully: the academic review supports a specific ceremonial complex and food-distribution role, while the old deck and images do not authorize expansion to all Indigenous communities in North America.

Use a bounded fallback if certainty remains incomplete by deadline: publish the narrow confirmed wording now, remove unsupported general lines, and schedule any broader interpretive framing for later review rather than forcing locals or future partners to repair the museum's overclaim.

scenario: A newly relocated analyst in Chicago is invited by her U.S. manager to Thanksgiving dinner at the manager's home. She does not eat meat, has an early airport departure the next morning, and the manager asks for a reply by this afternoon so grocery plans can be finalized.
question: What is the best next step now?

options.A: Thank the manager warmly, decline to avoid intruding on family holiday time, and suggest meeting for brunch that weekend instead.
options.B: Accept the invitation for dessert and conversation, mention your diet, and offer to bring a vegetarian dish after eating beforehand.
options.C: Ask what dishes are planned before committing, then offer to add a vegetarian shared dish if needed and confirm once the menu is clear.

scenario: You are leading a small multinational account team for a software vendor. Your operations manager, based in another region, suggests a streamlined approach: let everyone order and settle their own preferences at the table, split the bill transparently so no one feels obligated, and avoid awkwardness by handling payment in front of everyone. The VP asks you for a short execution memo covering exactly what your team should do before the dinner, at the table, and at the close so the evening supports the deal and does not create social friction.
question: Write the execution memo. Specify the concrete sequence of actions, who does each step, what should be said or not said, and how you will handle ordering, dietary uncertainty, server coordination, payment, and the end of the meal. Your memo must also identify the tempting but miscalibrated assumption in the operations manager’s plan and explain why it is risky here. Keep the plan practical under the time and budget pressure; do not answer with generic advice to 'be respectful' or 'check with locals.'

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden hospitality mechanism from the scenario evidence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that the hosted meal should be run by actively anticipating and taking care of guests’ needs rather than treating the dinner as a neutral peer meal where each person manages themselves.

rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies visible host behaviors such as making clear to the server who the host is, ensuring the guest has the opportunity to order, and managing the meal flow so guests are attended to first; no full credit for generic friendliness without these execution details.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the polished near-miss plan
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly identifies the attractive misunderstanding in the operations manager's suggestion—treating fairness, transparency, and guest autonomy as reasons to split payment and sort everything out publicly at the table—and explains why that would mis-handle the hosted setting here.

rubric.point: Balances relationship management with business constraints
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer keeps the plan operational under deadline and budget pressure by using a narrow, efficient host script rather than defaulting to the broadest, slowest, or most consultative plan.

reference_outline: Infer from the hosted-client-dinner setup, the assistant's note, the silent attendee, and the VP's role that success depends on anticipatory hosting, not a self-service or split-cost meal logic.

Before the dinner, assign one team member to contact attendees quickly for allergies, dietary restrictions, or travel-related constraints, then brief the VP so guest needs are known in advance rather than discovered publicly at the table.
At arrival or early in service, discreetly identify the VP or designated company representative to the server as the host so ordering and billing can be managed without public negotiation.

Sequence the table interaction so guests are attended to first, including giving them the first opportunity to order, while the host watches for needs instead of leaving choices and logistics entirely to the guests.

Reject the operations manager's 'split transparently at the table' approach as a polished near-miss: it looks fair and efficient but shifts hospitality work back onto guests and makes the hosted nature of the meal clumsy or conditional.

Arrange for the bill to be paid privately if possible, including gratuity appropriate to a hosted meal in the U.S./Canada context, so the close remains smooth and does not force public discussion of cost-sharing.

Use concrete brief wording and role cues, such as a short pre-dinner message asking about restrictions and a quiet check-in with staff, because the key CQ test is visible behavior in timing, channel, and sequence rather than merely naming etiquette.

scenario: A newcomer is helping organize a U.S. university fundraising reception for visiting alumni. roles.newcomer: New staff member from an overseas campus

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We need the final reception setup by noon. The dean will only stop in for twenty minutes, but several alumni are driving in after work, so I want the room ready when they arrive.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. Since the print bill came in high, I trimmed the catering order to light nibbles and arranged for the hotel bar next door to stay open. I'll add a note in the reminder email that guests can order whatever they like there if they want something more substantial.

dialogue.text: The hotel can handle overflow traffic, yes. We also have name tags, a photographer, and the student speakers confirmed. I just need to know what to tell advancement before I sign off.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer

dialogue.text: All right. The guest list includes a few older donors and two former board members, so it will be a fairly formal crowd. The dean's office mainly cares that check-in stays smooth.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I'll keep the entrance simple and have the tickets tucked into each name badge so nobody queues twice. I'll also ask the student volunteers to point people toward the bar area first, before the remarks begin.

dialogue.speaker: Local

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Will do. I'll confirm the reduced platters, the badge inserts, and the bar arrangement now so we stay within budget and don't need another approval round.
