dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Got it. I'll make it efficient, but still friendly, so they feel we've made an effort right away.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer invests real effort in welcome and relationship-building, but misplaces that effort by assuming immediate physical familiarity with a mixed European group of mostly first-time contacts. The seed-specific mechanism is to begin with low-contact interaction unless relationship and local setting clearly support more contact; the execution error is the newcomer's chosen greeting style at first contact.

scenario: You are the UK-based program manager for a consumer-health company launching a pop-up blood-pressure screening booth at a trade fair in Lyon, France, in nine days. The booth team will include two French partner representatives who will host local guests, one Italian sales lead, and one Finnish clinical trainer. A senior sponsor wants the first morning to feel 'warm and premium' because a municipal hospital buyer may stop by unannounced, and the French partner has hinted that your team sometimes comes across as distant. At the same time, legal has warned against any guest complaint about inappropriate contact at the booth. You must finalize a 10-minute pre-opening briefing and a one-page interaction script for staff who will greet visitors, VIPs, and partner staff they have only met by email. Current draft notes from different teammates conflict: the Italian lead proposes teaching everyone a more affectionate greeting style to avoid seeming cold, the Finnish trainer wants a strict no-contact rule for all first meetings, and the sponsor wants one consistent behavior so the team looks polished on camera. No one on the French partner side has given an explicit greeting preference in writing. The opening hour will be crowded, introductions will be fast, and there will be little time to recover from awkward moments in front of clients.
question: Write the core of your briefing plan for the opening hour. Specify the greeting rule you will give for first in-person contact, how staff should physically sequence the first 5-10 seconds with French partner representatives and new visitors, what you will tell them to do if the other person moves into a more familiar greeting, and how you will explain why your plan is not the same as either a universal no-contact rule or a 'match local warmth proactively' rule. Your answer should make concrete choices about wording, body action, timing, role assignment, and risk control under the deadline.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden mechanism as relationship-stage dependent touch rather than a single national-style rule.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that first-contact behavior must stay restrained because the people are still strangers or email-only contacts, and that touch can expand only if the relationship or the other person's lead makes that appropriate; generic statements like 'be respectful of French norms' do not earn this point.

rubric.point: Sets the correct first-move sequence for opening greetings.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan explicitly starts with a hand-based or clearly non-intrusive greeting posture for first meetings and avoids initiating cheek-kiss or broader touch; answers that proactively script cheek kisses, hugs, shoulder touches, or any more intimate first-contact gesture lose this point even if framed as warmth.

rubric.point: Handles initiation timing correctly when the other person chooses a more familiar greeting.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if staff are instructed to wait, read the counterpart's movement, and adapt only after the other person initiates a more familiar greeting; answers that tell staff to ask everyone in advance, mirror instantly without a restrained first beat, or keep rigidly refusing all non-hand greetings lose credit because they miss the timing hinge.

rubric.point: Rejects or bounds the tempting near-miss plans.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly explains why 'be warmer by initiating local-style closeness' is miscalibrated for strangers and why a blanket zero-contact policy is also too blunt for the setting; answers that reject only one side, or rely on generic legal caution without distinguishing the two traps, earn partial credit at most.

rubric.point: Translates the diagnosis into visible behavioural instructions.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer gives concrete, observable directions such as stance, hand availability, interpersonal distance, greeting wording, who speaks first, and what the host does during crowded introductions; broad advice like 'use good judgment' or 'be culturally sensitive' does not earn this point.

rubric.point: Designs a role-specific briefing that preserves task performance under pressure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan assigns who models the greeting, who welcomes VIPs, and how the team stays consistent during fast, public introductions without slowing the opening; answers that default to lengthy consultation, case-by-case improvisation, or delaying the script until local partners clarify lose this point.

rubric.point: Includes a calibrated repair move if a greeting becomes awkward.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer provides a quick, low-drama recovery that keeps the interaction moving, such as smoothly shifting into verbal welcome and booth guidance without making the miscue bigger; answers that escalate into lengthy apologies, public explanations, or formal incident-style handling for minor awkwardness lose credit.

reference_outline: State that the key variable is not 'France equals affectionate greeting' or 'professional setting equals no touch,' but whether the people are still first-time or low-bond contacts; opening behavior should therefore begin narrowly.

Instruct staff to open with a visible, restrained greeting sequence: eye contact, verbal welcome, hand available for handshake or equivalent restrained first-contact option, no self-initiated cheek kiss or broader touch with people known only by email or as new visitors.

Specify the timing rule that if the French partner representative or visitor clearly initiates a more familiar greeting, staff may follow smoothly rather than block it, but they should not pre-empt that move.

Explain why the 'show warmth by initiating local closeness' plan is attractive under sponsor pressure yet wrong for strangers, and why the strict no-contact rule is overcorrective because it ignores that some counterparts may appropriately lead a more familiar greeting.

Give behavioural briefing details: one person demonstrates the opening sequence, VIP greeters rehearse the first line and body position, staff avoid shoulder or arm touch in first contact, and the booth lead monitors consistency during the first crowded hour.

Include a quick repair script for near-misses: if timing misaligns, pivot immediately to a verbal welcome and task-oriented transition such as introducing the booth or next person, without freezing, over-apologizing, or debating etiquette in public.

Show work-performance logic: the plan protects brand and legal risk, still allows warmth when invited, and keeps greetings fast and coordinated enough for a crowded launch rather than turning the issue into a long consultation exercise.

scenario:
You manage field rollout for a health-services NGO. In 36 hours, your mixed team must start a pilot registration drive in a Gambian district center and two nearby villages. A donor representative will observe the first morning, and your regional director has warned that any visible delay will be treated as poor execution. The local district office has arranged a first-stop courtesy visit before field activity begins. Your team includes a 27-year-old female operations lead from Kenya, a 32-year-old male logistics officer from the UK, and two Gambian enumerators in their early 20s. Message history shows the UK officer wants to 'keep introductions efficient' by opening with the agenda and then moving into role assignments; the Kenyan lead wants to avoid awkwardness by having everyone offer the same professional greeting to every stakeholder; one enumerator privately notes only that 'the first five minutes will matter more than the slide deck.' You also know the first visit will include an older male district figure, a younger male clerk, and later a women-led village volunteer group. Budget does not allow a separate rehearsal trip, and the donor expects the team lead to model a single protocol that can be repeated across all three stops.

Your supervisor asks you for a short execution memo: how will you structure the first-contact sequence, who does what, and how will you keep the team engaged with the plan even though it costs time and may feel uneven or uncomfortable to some members?
question: Write the execution memo. Diagnose the hidden interaction mechanism you think is operating, identify the most tempting imported assumption your team is likely to follow, and give a concrete first-contact plan for the district office and the village stop. Your memo must specify sequence, role assignment, what you would brief the team to do or not do, how you would handle uncertainty without pausing the rollout, and what adaptive effort you would personally take on to keep the plan working under deadline and observer pressure.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the operative mechanism from the scenario evidence rather than giving generic etiquette advice.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires inferring that the opening must prioritize greeting before business, that the greeting pattern changes by counterpart and setting, and that the district elder, younger staff, and village women should not all be handled with one uniform professional script. No credit for answers that only say to 'be respectful' or 'learn local customs.'

rubric.point: Makes the correct execution choice on the main axis of sequence and actor-specific greeting.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires a concrete opening order for the district visit and village stop: greeting first, business second; younger team members not waiting passively for the elder to initiate; and different handling for the women-led village group than for the older male district figure. Partial credit if the answer notices sequence but still proposes one identical greeting action for all actors.

rubric.point: Applies the mechanism to exact behavior details that affect work performance.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires operational consequences such as using the appropriate hand in handshakes where used, assigning who should greet the elder first, warning against direct eye contact from the younger greeter to the elder, and avoiding forcing handshakes in the village women's context. Partial credit for naming one or two of these cues without integrating them into the rollout plan.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the tempting near-miss plan.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires identifying the attractive but wrong assumption that a global, equal, efficiency-oriented greeting protocol should be applied to everyone, and explaining why that would misfire under donor pressure even if it looks professional or inclusive. No credit if the answer endorses uniform treatment, generic agenda-first efficiency, or broad 'let locals adapt to us' logic.

rubric.point: Shows motivational CQ through costly, sustained adaptive effort rather than tone alone.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires visible ownership of the inconvenience: for example, spending scarce prep time briefing and practicing the uneven sequence, accepting that the opener will be slower, taking personal responsibility to cue colleagues in the moment, and staying engaged through ambiguity instead of withdrawing or over-delegating cultural burden to Gambian staff. No credit for low-cost statements like 'be open-minded' or 'ask the team to be patient.'

rubric.point: Designs a bounded uncertainty and repair strategy that preserves rollout momentum.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires a practical fallback such as having one Gambian enumerator quietly cue transitions if the team misreads the interaction, using a short non-business greeting buffer before the agenda, and correcting a misstep through adjusted sequencing at the next stop rather than stopping the whole rollout for broad consultation. Partial credit for vague monitoring without a repair channel.

reference_outline: Infer that the critical issue is not generic friendliness but a context-sensitive greeting sequence in The Gambia: greeting must come before business, greetings differ by age/status and by whether the counterpart is an elder male official or women in a village setting.

For the district office, open with greetings before agenda; assign the younger Gambian enumerator or other younger team member to greet the older male figure first, avoid prolonged direct eye contact in that elder greeting, use the right hand for any handshake that occurs, and only move to the project purpose after the greeting cycle is complete.

Do not use one identical protocol for every person: the male district elder and younger clerk can be handled differently from the women-led village volunteer group, where forcing handshakes from women would be a misapplication even if done in the name of consistency or equality.

Explicitly reject the near-miss plan of 'professionalize and standardize introductions for everyone' or 'get straight to the agenda to satisfy the donor'; explain that this saves minutes upfront but creates trust loss in the very first interaction.

Show motivational CQ by absorbing the cost personally: run a fast pre-visit briefing despite time pressure, explain why the sequence matters, rehearse who speaks first and who hangs back, and remain committed even if colleagues find the non-uniform protocol awkward or inefficient.

Use a bounded repair and monitoring method: one local enumerator quietly signals if the greeting is moving too fast or if a handshake should not be initiated, the team lead delays agenda talk until the social opening lands, and any mistake is repaired through adjusted behavior at the next stop rather than by freezing the rollout.

scenario: Your company is launching a farm-data pilot in western Kenya with a county agriculture office, a cooperative board, and a donor observer. You are briefing a mixed team: a 29-year-old product lead from Germany, a Kenyan analyst in her early 30s, a U.S. donor representative, and two engineers joining remotely. The in-person arrival window is only 12 minutes before the room must be handed to another event. The global VP has warned the team not to let greetings delay the demo because the donor is already questioning schedule slippage. However, the county office has not confirmed the final seating chart, and the people entering first may include a board chair in his late 60s, two younger technical officers, and a woman who runs a village collection network. Notes from a previous visit say the visitors were described afterward as 'efficient but not well-oriented to the room,' and one local photo from that visit shows the Kenyan host still holding an older guest's hand while speaking, with his head slightly lowered. A draft protocol from headquarters recommends 'greet everyone briskly in the order they arrive, make eye contact, keep it equal, and avoid any gesture that could seem selective or old-fashioned.' You need to send a short coordination memo tonight so the product lead can rehearse tomorrow morning.
question: Write the coordination memo for the arrival and opening minute of the meeting. Your memo should identify the most important interaction mechanism the team needs to infer from the evidence, explain why the headquarters draft is a tempting but miscalibrated plan here, and give a concrete greeting sequence for the first minute: who initiates with whom, in what order, how long to stay in each greeting, what to do if a senior person and younger officers arrive together, and how to handle the woman from the village network without creating a public awkward moment. Include how you would brief the non-Kenyan product lead so she applies the logic correctly even if the exact lineup changes at the door.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden mechanism from the scenario evidence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that the key issue is greeting order and manner keyed to seniority and local handshake pacing, not generic friendliness, confidence, or equal-treatment optics alone; low credit if it only says 'be respectful' or names etiquette without operational consequences.

rubric.point: Sets the correct first-minute sequence on the main execution axis
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan prioritizes greeting elders or senior figures first when multiple people arrive together and avoids defaulting to arrival order or alphabetical equality; partial credit if seniority is mentioned but not turned into an actionable sequence.

rubric.point: Applies the handshake norm at the right stage and degree
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies using the right hand, allowing the handshake to last longer than a fast Western business clasp, and not forcing immediate release or rushing into the demo; partial credit if it mentions handshake etiquette but misapplies it to everyone identically or treats speed as the main virtue.

rubric.point: Handles the ambiguous woman-stakeholder case without imported assumptions
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer avoids prescribing a universal initiate-or-avoid rule based on a different country in the seed set and instead proposes a non-awkward, observant approach that lets the local interaction cue whether a handshake is initiated; low credit if it imports the Gambian village norm into Kenya or insists on a rigid global default.

rubric.point: Rejects or bounds the headquarters near-miss plan
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explains why 'equal brisk greetings in order of arrival with direct eye contact' is attractive under donor and time pressure yet culturally miscalibrated here, especially because it can mis-sequence senior people and shorten greetings in a way that reads poorly; low credit if it merely says the draft is wrong without explaining the specific failure mode.

rubric.point: Demonstrates cognitive CQ rather than stereotype recall
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo shows rule-mapping logic from mixed evidence and gives a portable decision rule for changing lineups, such as how to identify who should be greeted first and what cues matter at the doorway; low credit if it just lists facts about Kenya or relies on blanket statements about Africans, elders, or handshakes.

rubric.point: Builds a workable coordination plan under pressure
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer assigns roles or cues clearly, such as having the Kenyan analyst quietly identify the senior-most entrant while the product lead pauses the start and completes the key greetings before beginning the demo; low credit if it solves the issue only by delaying the meeting, consulting indefinitely, or making everyone else handle it.

reference_outline: Infer from the photo note and prior feedback that the problem is not mere warmth but a locally legible greeting sequence: senior figures should be greeted first, and the handshake may last longer than the headquarters script assumes.

In the first minute, instruct the product lead to pause the demo setup, use the right hand, and greet the senior-most person first if a mixed group arrives together, then proceed to other attendees rather than following arrival order mechanically.

Brief the team that a slightly lowered gaze or non-dominating posture can read better with elders than assertive direct-eye-contact performance; do not make this a theatrical gesture, but avoid a rushed, stare-and-release style.

Use the Kenyan analyst as a discreet real-time spotter for status ordering at the door, not as a substitute greeter; the non-Kenyan lead still performs the key greeting herself so respect is visible from the accountable project lead.

Do not import a universal rule from another market or from a generic equality SOP: the headquarters draft is attractive because it seems fair and efficient, but here it risks publicly bypassing elders and compressing the very interaction that establishes proper entry into the meeting.

For the woman from the village network, avoid forcing either a handshake or a conspicuous non-handshake script; let the local cue determine whether she initiates or reciprocates, while keeping the greeting warm and non-publicly awkward.

Give the product lead a portable doorway rule: identify the highest-status or oldest local figure first, complete that greeting at local pace with the right hand, then continue through the room, rather than optimizing for speed or visual equality alone.

Risk-control move: if the team realizes mid-entry that they greeted younger technical officers first, repair immediately by turning to the senior figure before starting content, acknowledging them first in the verbal opening rather than pretending sequence does not matter.

scenario: A documentary team in Arusha will begin a one-day shoot at a Maasai-owned tourism site tomorrow morning. The producer has drafted a one-page arrival protocol for camera crew, drivers, and interviewers, and wants one approval route before it is added to the call sheet. The site owner will receive the team first, then introduce several younger staff members who will guide setup. Legal wants a documented briefing today, but the crew cannot run multiple rehearsals on site.
question: Which approval decision should the field manager make for the arrival protocol?

options.A: Approve one uniform greeting protocol for all hosts and staff, documented through HR, so the crew avoids ranking people differently during the first arrival sequence.
options.B: Approve the protocol after the local coordinator checks the opening exchange specifically against how the team will first address the site owner, then issue the same card to everyone.
options.C: Approve the protocol only after the site owner signs off on the crew’s greeting approach for every person they will meet that day, from arrival through setup.
options.D: Approve the protocol after the youngest bilingual guide reviews the full arrival sequence for the whole crew, then file that review as the local cultural clearance.

scenario: At a health NGO in Banjul, a newcomer needs a senior administrator's signature before noon so printed outreach passes can go with the driver. The office is busy, the administrator is older than the newcomer, and several staff and visitors are moving in and out. The newcomer is trying to judge how to handle the urgency without making the situation worse.

roles.local: Mariama, a Gambian program assistant coordinating the print run
roles.newcomer: Daniel, a newly arrived operations officer

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The driver leaves at noon. If this pass is not signed in about fifteen minutes, today's village stop gets dropped. The administrator is in, but the office has been full all morning.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I do not want to create a scene over one signature. Before I go in, is this the kind of thing where people usually wait to be called closer, or is it better to keep it quick and just present the form?

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: It depends on the moment. Sometimes people pause at the doorway first. Sometimes someone just needs one paper and is gone quickly. He is also still seeing people this morning.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: All right, so the main uncertainty is how much room there is for a long exchange. If others are moving fast, I will keep mine even shorter.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The printer is warm, and I can have the driver ready. We only need the page signed and back here.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I will not slow it down by adding extra words. I will stop at the entrance, catch his eye so he knows I am there, hold up the pass, and go straight to the deadline and signature.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. I will stay by the copier in case he signs immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Good. I will keep it efficient and let the urgency speak for itself.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: Daniel calibrates to speed and office traffic, but updates on the wrong uncertainty. His decisive plan is to begin with the request itself, using eye contact and urgency as the opener, instead of starting with the expected greeting sequence when approaching an older senior in The Gambia.

scenario: A project lead from abroad is about to open a neighborhood water-committee session in Brazzaville. The country team has a seating list with attendees' names, and the lead has about eight minutes before the agenda must start. The room includes committee officers, local residents, and two municipal staff who arrived with the group.
question: Which briefing gives the best scope for how the lead should handle the entrance greeting?

options.A: Use one warm room-wide greeting at the door, then move straight into the agenda and catch people individually during the break if time allows.
options.B: Work the entrance line by greeting the committee officers and municipal staff one by one, then open the session with a collective greeting for the residents.
options.C: Treat the entrance itself as the moment to greet each person individually by name with a brief physical greeting, then begin once that round is complete.
options.D: Keep the formal opening collective, then make time after the session to greet everyone by name with a brief physical greeting before people leave.

scenario: You are the regional events lead for a multinational health-tech firm. In 48 hours, your team will host a small partnership breakfast in Johannesburg for a South African hospital group that may sign a pilot deal this quarter. Your supervisor in London wants the reception to feel 'warm and relationship-first' because a competitor's launch last month was described as too transactional. A branding manager in Paris has already drafted a host briefing that tells greeters to avoid 'cold, distant handshakes' and to use a more familiar greeting style to create instant rapport. The guest list includes six South African attendees from different functions and age groups, plus your internal team from the UK, Kenya, and Germany. Two of the South African guests have met your country manager before; the others are first-time contacts. You also have a seating-chart note that some guests know each other well, while others are joining because they were added late by the client sponsor. The room is small, arrivals will be staggered, and there is no time for a full rehearsal. You need to finalize the reception protocol, the host script, and the fallback plan for awkward greetings before close of business today. No one on your team is based in South Africa, and the supervisor wants a one-page decision note rather than a long cultural memo.
question: Write the one-page decision note you would send to your supervisor. It must: (1) diagnose the most important cultural uncertainty in the greeting plan from the evidence you have, (2) identify the tempting but miscalibrated assumption in the Paris draft, (3) set a concrete arrival-greeting sequence for hosts on the spot, including what they should do first, when they may adapt, and how they should handle mixed groups, and (4) explain how you will monitor and recalibrate in real time without making the reception feel stiff or hesitant.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the key uncertainty as relationship- and context-dependent greeting variation within the South African setting, not as a single countrywide norm.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer states that the main issue is deciding greeting form case by case based on familiarity, group composition, and first-time versus known contacts; no credit for treating South Africa, Africa, or 'business culture' as having one expected greeting style.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the imported assumption that a more familiar physical greeting should be standardized to signal warmth.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly identifies the Paris draft's logic as attractive but overgeneralized and explains why applying one warmer default to all arrivals would be miscalibrated; partial credit if it objects only on generic risk, consent, or professionalism grounds without the seed-specific execution reason.

rubric.point: Sets the primary execution axis correctly: begin with a neutral first-contact greeting and adapt only after relationship cues justify it.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan makes the first move a neutral option such as a standard verbal greeting with handshake-ready body language, then allows adaptation for clearly known relationships rather than pre-committing to familiarity; no full credit if the answer recommends avoiding all physical greetings entirely or standardizing cheek-kiss-like familiarity from the start.

rubric.point: Applies the sequence to exact actors and stages, including mixed groups and staggered arrivals.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies who greets whom, how to greet each person in a small arriving group, and how to avoid copying one greeting across all members just because one person is known; partial credit if the answer stays at a generic 'read the room' level.

rubric.point: Uses metacognitive CQ by distinguishing what can be inferred now from what must be checked through live cues during the event.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer names both a working hypothesis and a real-time update method, such as watching whether a known pair initiates greater familiarity, tracking whether first-time guests mirror or hold distance, and revising host behavior accordingly; no credit for 'ask locals' or 'be respectful' without stating what uncertainty is being monitored.

rubric.point: Designs a brief host script and fallback repair move that preserves flow under pressure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer gives operational wording or equivalent script logic for first greeting, name use, introductions, and a smooth recovery if a host misreads familiarity; partial credit for generic advice about apologizing or being polite.

rubric.point: Prevents overcorrection into delay, inertia, or broad consultation that would miss the deadline.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan keeps the event moving with a usable protocol today rather than outsourcing the decision to more research or making every greeting contingent on advance checking; no credit if the answer's main move is to postpone, circulate surveys, or add excessive approvals.

reference_outline: State that the evidence does not support one default intimate greeting for South African guests; the decisive issue is familiarity and subgroup variation, especially between known contacts and first-time encounters.
Flag the Paris draft as a polished near-miss: it confuses 'show warmth' with 'standardize a more familiar greeting' and would wrongly scale a context-specific behavior across all guests.

Set the reception protocol: hosts greet each arrival by name if possible, open with a neutral verbal greeting and handshake-ready posture, and let the guest or an already-established relationship determine whether the interaction becomes more familiar.

Specify mixed-group handling: greet each person individually rather than copying the first greeting across the whole cluster, because one known relationship does not generalize to added attendees or strangers in the same arrival group.

Assign roles: the country manager greets the two returning contacts and may mirror their established level of familiarity if they clearly initiate it; other hosts use the neutral opening for all first-time guests.

Add metacognitive monitoring: brief hosts on what they know, what remains uncertain, and which live cues matter; discount weak cues such as a supervisor's branding preference, and update only from direct interaction patterns at the door.
Include a repair move: if a host starts the wrong level of familiarity, pivot immediately to a verbal welcome, name introduction, and directional hosting task without dramatizing the mistake.

Close with work-performance logic: this narrower protocol still feels warm, protects trust with first-time contacts, and avoids the reputational cost of imposing the wrong greeting under deadline pressure.

scenario: At a youth enterprise launch in Banjul, a newcomer is helping a local coordinator seat guests and distribute pledge cards before a deputy minister arrives. Several older guests are already seated, some are eating, and the printed cards came back late from the copy shop.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The cards finally came. We have maybe eight minutes before the deputy minister walks in, and some of the senior guests are already settled.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I’ll help. I can move fast through the front rows while you handle the dais and the photographer.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That helps. A few people at the back are still chatting with each other, and two of the elders started their tea already.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I won’t stop the whole room. For the people already seated, I’ll acknowledge them from where I am and keep the line moving.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We also need the pledge cards in their hands before the remarks start, otherwise the minister’s aide will collect blank ones.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I’ll carry the mic notes in my right so they don’t get bent, and I’ll pass the cards with my left as I go row by row. It’s quicker, and I won’t disturb those who are eating.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right, I’m going to the entrance now. The first car just pulled up.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Got it. I’ll finish the back section and meet you at the front before the remarks begin.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer invests effort and protects the schedule, but the decisive behavior is culturally miscalibrated: in The Gambia, greetings and passing items should not be done with the left hand. He also chooses a distant acknowledgment for seated guests, which is acceptable in some cases, but then combines it with left-hand distribution instead of using the right hand or a repair such as supporting the left with the right when necessary.

scenario: A donor team is arriving at a Makhuwa community in Tanzania to secure final agreement on a borehole location before a contractor deadline that afternoon. Their local coordinator says the hosts will expect a formal opening exchange before any site discussion. The visiting team knows one host is an older man, another is a recently married woman who chairs the village committee, and a third is a younger initiation leader. The team has five minutes outside the meeting place to decide how to handle the opening.
question: Which briefing sequence should the team lead use right before entering?

options.A: Ask the oldest visitor to open the formal greeting to the oldest host first, then have the rest of the team follow in age order before turning to the borehole decision.
options.B: Enter, wait for the hosts to signal the order themselves, keep the team silent until someone invites a reply, and let the coordinator explain any uncertainty after introductions finish.
options.C: Brief every visitor to deliver the formal greeting to each principal host on arrival, using the visible posture cues carefully, then sort out who carries authority once the meeting begins.
options.D: Brief the team that the opening should track the host group's standing rather than age alone; if that is still unclear at first contact, let the coordinator open and the team follow that lead before moving to the agenda.

scenario: A newcomer is coordinating a public handover event in southern Tanzania where district guests, village elders, and a donor representative will all be present. The printed running order from headquarters lists each local committee member by personal name because the donor wants the stage script locked before noon.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The district car is already on the road, and the MC wants the final stage script in twenty minutes. Headquarters sent the committee list exactly as it appears in the database.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I saw that. I’ll keep the printed order unchanged for the donor file, but I’m rewriting the spoken introductions before I send them to the MC.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The MC is a schoolteacher, so she will read whatever is on the page. We also have reserved front seats for the older committee members.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I’ll mark the script line by line and hand it to her directly. On stage she can welcome the older men with forms like bambo and the others with relationship terms, instead of reading the database names aloud.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That will differ from the slide deck. The donor team usually likes every name to match across materials.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I’m fine with that mismatch for ten minutes. The slides can stay as filed, but the live wording should fit the room, and I’ll brief the donor rep before people sit down.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. The MC is waiting near the generator tent, and the village chair has already arrived.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Good. I’m taking her the marked copy now and will start the welcome without using the personal-name list.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer aligns with the Ngoni address mechanism by avoiding personal names in live address and using relational or formal noun-based forms instead. The decisive execution axis is spoken public address at the event, even while preserving the headquarters name list in back-end materials.

scenario: You manage regional rollout for a health NGO that is launching a maternal-care SMS reminder service in south-western Tanzania. The final approval meeting is in 48 hours with a district sponsor, two senior community coordinators from a Ngoni-speaking area, and your internal director in Nairobi, who is pushing for a scalable script that can later be reused in Kenya and Zambia. The current draft call script and onboarding leaflet greet recipients and local coordinators by personal first name because your CRM autofills names and your compliance lead argues that using exact legal names reduces record confusion. However, during two field visits, your Tanzanian staff noted that older coordinators introduced themselves through family or role relationships, and one coordinator consistently referred to another senior woman without using her personal name even after hearing it. No one has directly objected to the draft. The Nairobi director wants you to avoid a custom local exception because budget is tight and translation time is limited. At the same time, the district sponsor has warned that if the launch feels socially awkward, trust in the service could drop quickly and the pilot may lose village-level support. You have authority to change the greeting approach, but only if you can propose a concrete rollout and repair plan that does not derail the launch.
question: Write a decision memo for the approval meeting that recommends how the team should handle forms of address in the SMS onboarding, staff call script, and in-person briefing. Your memo must: diagnose the likely cultural mechanism from the available evidence; identify the tempting imported assumption in the current draft; specify the execution choice on one main axis of your plan; assign who must do what before launch; and explain what extra effort you will personally invest to keep the launch on schedule while reducing relationship risk.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden mechanism from scenario evidence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that the risk is not generic politeness but the social meaning of how people are addressed, including likely preference for kinship, relational, or honorific terms over personal names in this setting. Partial credit if it mentions hierarchy or respect vaguely without linking it to address-form choice.

rubric.point: Makes the correct primary execution-axis decision on wording across channels
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan changes the default naming practice at the greeting stage across the relevant materials and interactions, rather than keeping first-name address as the default and merely adding a respectful tone or optional check later. Partial credit if the answer limits the change to only one channel or delays it until after launch.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the imported near-miss assumption
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo explicitly identifies the attractive near-miss: a global-SOP or compliance-style belief that using personal legal names is the safest universal default. High-scoring answers must show why that logic is tempting under CRM, scale, and record-keeping pressure yet miscalibrated here. Low credit if the answer simply says 'consult locals more' or keeps first names for efficiency.

rubric.point: Translates diagnosis into role-specific execution
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer assigns concrete tasks such as revising script placeholders, separating backend record names from outward address terms, briefing field staff on address choices, and setting an approval owner for the revised wording. Low credit for generic statements about being respectful or culturally sensitive.

rubric.point: Shows motivational CQ through costly adaptive follow-through
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the respondent takes ownership of visible extra effort under pressure, such as personally absorbing rework, arranging a fast verification loop, rehearsing the revised script, or protecting local-facing adjustments despite director pressure. Low credit if the plan shifts the burden to local staff to fix it informally, postpones the problem indefinitely, or offers only warm intent without effort.

rubric.point: Designs bounded calibration and repair under launch constraints
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes a narrow, practical monitoring or repair mechanism tied to the address issue, such as checking early reactions to greetings, allowing staff to switch to role/kinship/honorific forms immediately, and correcting misaddress quickly without reopening the whole rollout. Low credit if the answer proposes broad delay, large new research phases, or generic risk reviews.

reference_outline: State that the main risk signal is the pattern of avoiding personal-name use in senior local interactions, so the team should treat forms of address as a trust-sensitive mechanism rather than a cosmetic wording issue.

Show motivational CQ by accepting the cost of adaptation: spend limited time before launch to rework the script, push back on reuse pressure, and stay engaged through ambiguity instead of either forcing the generic template through or withdrawing into 'local staff can handle it.'

scenario: You are the project lead for a three-country nonprofit team preparing a one-day community design workshop in Songea, Tanzania, to launch a maternal health pilot. question: Write a brief execution memo for your team covering the opening sequence and participant-facing materials for tomorrow morning. rubric.point: Diagnoses the region-specific address logic from the evidence

rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly bounds the UK director's first-name-equals-rapport approach as a plausible global or nearby-market practice that is misapplied here; partial credit if it merely says to 'be careful' or 'adapt locally' without naming why the first-name plan is risky in this case.

rubric.point: Applies the mechanism to the exact execution axis of wording and materials
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer makes concrete, seed-consistent choices for spoken address and printed/displayed names, such as using relational/honorific forms in introductions and on participant-facing materials for the relevant senior local attendees, rather than defaulting to personal names; deny full credit if the answer uses correct cultural knowledge but applies it only to private emails, only to juniors, or only after the event starts.

rubric.point: Uses cognitive CQ to separate valid evidence from bad generalization
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explains why the repeated local naming pattern in this specific area outweighs continent-wide assumptions, generic NGO equality norms, or habits from Kenya or urban Tanzanian colleagues; partial credit if it cites 'Africa is diverse' without showing which evidence matters and which comparison is invalid.

rubric.point: Designs a workable team coordination plan under time pressure

rubric.point: Includes a calibrated fallback and repair path
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes a narrow risk-control move consistent with the inferred mechanism, such as defaulting to the safer local relational/honorific forms where evidence is strong, using more neutral titles where evidence is uncertain, and correcting discreetly if needed; deny full credit for maximalist plans that make everyone hyper-formal or for generic apologies without a seed-specific repair channel.

reference_outline: Infer from the Songea setting plus the repeated internal use of forms like 'Mawu,' 'Dadi,' and 'Bambo' for senior invitees that the decisive issue is a local address system in which personal names are not the safest default for those stakeholders.

Do not generalize from a generic international norm that first names create warmth, and do not generalize from other African settings or from Kenya workshop practice; the evidence here is subregional and actor-specific.

Change the opening script so facilitators greet and introduce the senior community representatives using the local relational/honorific-style forms rather than personal names, while keeping ordinary operational content unchanged.

Revise or hand-correct the highest-visibility badges, name tents, and thank-you slide entries for the senior local representatives first; if some cases remain uncertain, use a neutral formal title rather than reverting to first names.

Use a narrow fallback: where evidence is strong, apply the local form; where evidence is mixed, choose the least presumptuous formal option and watch the first exchanges for confirmation rather than launching a broad consultation process that misses the deadline.

Protect relationship risk through execution, not generic politeness: the plan should preserve workshop momentum, avoid public misaddress in the opening minutes, and signal that the team can read local interaction logic rather than importing a continent-wide default.

scenario: A newcomer helping at a university partnership event in Accra is told to speed up guest check-in before a donor walkthrough. dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The vice chancellor's guests are arriving early, and the donor team will pass this desk in ten minutes. Badges are alphabetical, envelopes are by table number, and we cannot let the queue stall.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I can take the next arrivals and call names quickly while you handle the donor group if that helps.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That works. The radio is noisy, so just keep things moving and make sure each guest leaves with the right envelope.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I’ve got the folder in one arm, so I’ll steady each envelope with that hand and pass it over with the other. If I need to indicate a table on the seating board, I’ll step around and show it from close by instead of signaling across the room.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Fine. Some of the faculty are already clustering near the board, and the photographer keeps asking people to shift. It may get cramped.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I’ll keep the pace brisk and call people forward one at a time. If my hands are full for a moment, I’ll say excuse me and adjust before handing anything over.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Good. Also, one guest may ask for his place before his badge is printed, so you may need to direct him fast.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I’ll walk him to the board and indicate the row from beside him, then come straight back to the desk so the line keeps moving.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer's execution fits the West African left-hand interaction norm: they avoid using the left hand alone in social exchange, plan to support or excuse any unavoidable left-hand involvement, and avoid distant hand-signaling by moving closer rather than pointing across the room.

scenario: You are the regional rollout lead for a retail wayfinding pilot in southwest Nigeria. question: Write the execution plan you would give the team today. Your answer must: (1) diagnose the most likely interaction risk from the available evidence, (2) identify the tempting but miscalibrated imported assumption a competent global team might follow, and (3) specify exactly how the product specialist, store staff, and you should handle pointing, positioning, wording, sequencing, and real-time repair during the live walkthrough. rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden interaction mechanism from neutral clues.

rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies how to brief privately before the event, how to cue the specialist in the moment without public correction, and how to phrase directions during the demo so adaptation is visible but not awkward; partial credit for the right content with wrong channel or timing, such as correcting the specialist publicly during the walkthrough or sending only a generic written note.

rubric.point: Handles hierarchy and role assignment under deadline pressure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer assigns roles to protect both task clarity and relationship management, for example having you or a local-facing staff member lead guest-facing movement cues while the specialist handles product explanation, or otherwise sequencing speakers so elders/owner are not directly finger-targeted; partial credit for suggesting someone else leads without linking the change to the specific interaction risk.

rubric.point: Designs a credible repair plan if a misstep happens live.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes a narrow, low-drama repair move such as smoothly restaging attention with the correct gesture/form, shifting who demonstrates, or verbally redirecting focus to the fixture without calling out the breach; partial credit for generic apology plans; no credit for making the safest plan a full stop, public cultural explanation, or event delay.

rubric.point: Avoids overbroad or misapplied cultural reasoning.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer keeps the adaptation tied to the relevant actors, moments, and visible behavior in this walkthrough rather than turning it into a broad rule to avoid all pointing, avoid all directness, or over-consult indefinitely; partial credit for accurate cultural knowledge applied too broadly or at the wrong stage.

reference_outline: Infer from the Lagos message, elder audience, Yoruba-speaking owner, and rehearsal behavior that the risk sits in gesture form during the live walkthrough, not in product content.

Keep the plan narrow and performance-oriented: preserve sponsor clarity, avoid delaying the event, and adapt the exact visible behaviors that carry relationship risk in this setting.

scenario: A renewable-energy NGO is setting up a same-day launch in northern Namibia with a local host committee. question: Write a brief execution memo for your event team. scenario: You are meeting a procurement director in Banjul for the first in-person kickoff before a site drive. On video calls he was informal and fast-paced. scenario: A newcomer is helping run a same-day investor visit in Chicago. roles.newcomer: Recently transferred project lead assisting with guest flow

dialogue.text: We met the visitors downstairs already, and now they're heading to the product room. We only have twelve minutes there before finance takes over.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll keep the room change crisp, but I'll still greet each guest properly at the door so the handoff feels polished.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Thanks. It's mostly the same six people all morning, just different leads joining in each room.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Right, so I'll reintroduce myself briefly in each session and give each of them the same firm welcome again, then point them straight to their seats.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Okay. Product is ready, and legal wants us to stay on time because the VP can only drop in for a few minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll be fast about it—eye contact, quick grip, name, and move them along. That should keep it respectful without slowing the agenda too much.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Got it. I'll welcome the VP as she arrives, and when the visitors enter I'll give them the same brief formal greeting again before we start.

question: Write the briefing. rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the briefing gives actionable instructions such as who initiates introductions, what returning greetings should sound like, how to introduce a new attendee without re-running the ritual for familiar contacts, and how teammates should stay aligned under time pressure.

rubric.point: Handles edge cases without broadening into an overcautious plan
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer addresses late arrivals and teammate concerns with narrow, stage-specific adjustments—for example, verbally acknowledging known contacts while physically greeting only truly new introductions—rather than recommending delays, room-wide reset greetings, or blanket consultation.

Monitor execution by watching for two failure modes: teammates reverting to the all-purpose formal routine for repeat contacts, or overcorrecting into overly casual first introductions that lose confidence.

scenario: A U.S. product lead is about to moderate a client roundtable in Montreal. The printed agenda and spoken introductions must be finalized in 15 minutes for a room that will include the client team, the lead's U.S. colleagues, and several senior banking executives. During planning, the client director signed emails with her given name, and two client managers addressed each other by given name in a private chat thread. The lead now has to decide whether the public introductions and name placards should stay formal or switch to given names.
question: Which additional observation would be most diagnostic in deciding that the public introductions should remain formal rather than treating the earlier first-name cues as enough to switch?

options.A: At arrival, several attendees who have not met before exchange firm handshakes, then move quickly into business talk without using any visible title cues.
options.B: Minutes before the session, the client director sends a short text from her phone signing only her given name and asking whether the slides are in the final order.
options.C: A senior U.S. sponsor greeting the room says, "Please, call me Tom," and several participants smile and repeat his given name in response.
options.D: Before guests enter, two client coworkers of similar rank use given names backstage, but once the audience gathers they refer to each other with surnames and titles on the floor.

scenario: A newcomer on a university partnership team in Montreal is helping with a fast-moving donor breakfast. dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The dean's car is ten minutes out, and our emcee card still needs the opening line for Professor Leduc. She and Marianne were chatting easily backstage yesterday, so I only need something clean for the microphone.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Got it. Since they already know each other, I'll keep the room relaxed and write, "Please welcome Marianne Leduc," so it doesn't sound overly ceremonial.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We also have two donors from Toronto and a provincial reporter in the front row, so the first minute will carry most of the tone for the morning.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll make it polished overall, but I still think using her given name on stage shows closeness and keeps the breakfast from feeling too rigid.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The slides are already locked, but the cue card and spoken intro are still yours to finalize. We need to send the card to the emcee now.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I'll send the final card right away with "Marianne" in the spoken welcome and keep the rest formal so we stay on schedule.

dialogue.speaker: Local

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Done—I sent the cue card and noted that the shorter form should help the opening sound friendly.

brief_reason: In Quebec/Canada, public address for a senior academic should stay more formal; the newcomer wrongly extends private familiarity into a public on-stage introduction and drops the title/instructor-status form.

scenario: You are a U.S.-based program manager coordinating a three-city kickoff roadshow for a software rollout. One stop is in Montreal, where your Quebec client sponsor has invited a small group of local partner managers to an evening reception before the first workshop. None of the Montreal attendees have met your visiting VP in person, but several of them have worked closely for months with the Quebec account lead, who is also attending. The VP wants a one-page arrival brief tonight because she lands two hours before the event and will not have time for a rehearsal. She is worried about seeming cold in a relationship-driven market and suggests: “If this is the French pattern, I’d rather greet everyone warmly than default to stiff corporate formality.” Meanwhile, legal has warned against any plan that creates avoidable discomfort with clients, and the Quebec account lead is hard to reach because he is on a train with spotty service. You have only these clues: email threads show some Montreal partners using first names with the Quebec lead, the formal invitation lists titles and surnames, and a photo from a previous private celebration shows some local colleagues greeting each other at close range. You also need to coordinate with a German solutions director, who prefers explicit protocol, and a Brazilian sales manager, who keeps saying the VP should “just follow the room.”
question: Draft the core of the VP’s arrival brief for the Montreal reception. Your answer must: (1) diagnose the most likely greeting mechanism at work from the limited evidence, including what remains uncertain; (2) identify the most tempting but miscalibrated assumption the VP could import; (3) specify exactly how the VP should greet the first three categories of people she encounters at the event, in sequence; and (4) explain what live cues, backup wording, and coordination steps you would use to recalibrate in the room without making the plan either overconfident or inert.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that the key distinction is not 'French-style warmth' in general but whether the interaction is a first-time introduction versus an already-familiar relationship.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers a narrow relationship-based greeting boundary from the evidence and applies it operationally; no credit for simply saying to be respectful, local, or warm.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the attractive near-miss assumption that because the setting is Montreal and some locals greet closely, the VP should proactively use cheek-kiss greetings with new client contacts.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly names this as a tempting overgeneralization and explains why it is miscalibrated under first-meeting conditions; partial credit if it advises against it without identifying the faulty inference.

rubric.point: Gives a concrete sequence for three actor categories: unknown Montreal partners, the Quebec account lead or clearly familiar local colleagues, and ambiguous cases where others seem already socially close.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan differentiates the greeting by actor and stage, such as handshake plus self-introduction for first-time contacts, while not extending familiar-style greetings to the wrong people; no full credit for one rule applied to everyone.

rubric.point: Uses metacognitive CQ by separating what can be inferred now from what must be checked live, and by naming which cues should be weighted and which should be discounted.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer states a provisional default, identifies uncertainty, and specifies live evidence that would justify updating; no credit for generic 'read the room' or blanket 'ask someone first' with no target uncertainty.

rubric.point: Designs backup wording and role coordination that protect relationship quality and legal/brand risk without freezing action.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer includes executable wording for introductions and a coordination move such as briefing the VP on a default script and assigning the account lead, if reachable, to handle any familiar contacts after arrival; partial credit for vague mention of preparation.

rubric.point: Avoids polished but wrong alternatives such as delaying all greetings until someone else moves first, or copying whichever local behavior appears first in the room.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explains why broad caution or pure mimicry is also miscalibrated here: it fails to distinguish private familiarity among locals from first-time introductions involving the VP.

reference_outline: State a provisional diagnosis: some Montreal attendees may greet each other with close familiar gestures, but the VP is still entering as a first-time introducer with most or all client-side partners.
Set the primary execution rule: the VP should default to a handshake and self-introduction with people she has not personally met, even if others in the room appear more familiar with one another.

Differentiate actor categories operationally: greet unknown partner managers first with handshake plus name/role; greet the Quebec account lead according to their own existing relationship; treat ambiguous third parties as first-time introductions unless they unmistakably initiate otherwise.
Name the near-miss trap: overreading Montreal/French cues or a private social photo into a universal arrival protocol for the VP, and thereby initiating cheek-kiss greetings with new contacts.

Apply metacognitive CQ: note that email first-name use and close-range photos are relevant but not decisive for the VP’s own role; use stronger live evidence such as whether a person steps in to initiate familiarity specifically toward the VP, not just toward local colleagues.

Provide briefing language: for example, 'Start with a handshake, your name, and your role; if someone clearly initiates a more familiar greeting, follow their lead calmly rather than launching it yourself.'

Coordinate around pressure: send the VP a short default script now, try to confirm with the Quebec account lead only if reachable, and brief the German and Brazilian teammates that the event plan is neither rigid universal protocol nor pure mimicry.

Include repair/calibration: if the VP senses a mismatch, she should pivot smoothly with a warm verbal welcome and continue the introduction, rather than overexplaining or turning the moment into a cultural discussion.

scenario: A London-based partnerships director is flying to Canada for two first-time client meetings on the same trip: a bank in Toronto, then a media cooperative in Montreal. The Montreal host writes partly in French, and the local account manager says the second stop will include a small office reception right after the meeting. Because the director lands late, he asks for one short briefing line on how to handle greetings without slowing the schedule.
question: Which briefing direction should the team give him?

options.A: Use a light cheek-to-cheek greeting at both stops, since a warmer opening is widely read as polished in international business and avoids starting either visit too formally.
options.B: Use a handshake in Toronto, and switch to a cheek-to-cheek greeting in Montreal from the first introduction, since that city more often accepts a warmer professional opening.
options.C: Use a handshake in Toronto, and keep the Montreal office greeting non-physical until the reception, where a cheek-to-cheek greeting is the better starting point for first introductions.
options.D: Use a firm handshake for the first introduction at both offices, and stay ready for a warmer greeting later in Montreal if counterparts themselves move the interaction that way.

scenario: A London startup team lands in Canada tomorrow for two events: a first-time investor meeting in Toronto and, the next evening, a small dinner in Montreal at the home of a long-time adviser, where some guests know the CEO personally and others do not. The operations lead has one hour to send a short arrival brief and wants one scope decision that keeps the team aligned without writing separate playbooks.
question: Which group should the operations lead explicitly cover in the brief now?

options.A: Brief everyone attending the Toronto meetings, and brief the Montreal dinner attendees only for guests they have not already built a close personal relationship with.
options.B: Brief the full traveling team to use the same no-contact greeting approach with every person they meet in both cities, including family hosts and long-standing personal contacts.
options.C: Brief only the Toronto meeting team, and leave the Montreal dinner group unbriefed because the social setting there can include more familiar forms of greeting.
options.D: Brief everyone who will meet someone for the first time in either city, including the Montreal home dinner, to open with a firm handshake across all new introductions.

scenario: At a Toronto museum fundraiser, a newcomer from abroad is covering the welcome area because the host is delayed in traffic. Several guests are first-time donors from Toronto and Boston, and one board member keeps mentioning last year's Montreal gala photos while rushing the team to open the doors on time. The newcomer has to greet arrivals smoothly without slowing the line or creating awkward first impressions.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The first donors are already in the lobby. Most of them haven't met us before, and the chair wants the line moving because the remarks start in twelve minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Got it. I saw last year's Montreal photos in the deck, but this crowd sounds mixed. I'll keep the welcome quick at the table and not assume everyone wants the same style.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Yes, we have Toronto guests, two couples from Boston, and one family friend of the chair who knows everyone already. Name tags are alphabetical, and the photographer will be shooting the entrance.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I'll greet each person with a simple hello from behind the sign-in table, and if someone clearly offers a hand first time around, I'll return it once and move them straight to badges.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That should keep us on schedule. The chair may arrive halfway through, so I might step away when she calls.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: No problem. I won't lean in across the table or hold people there for chat; after the greeting I'll point them toward the gallery so the entrance doesn't bunch up.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Thanks. One donor is bringing a guest whose name might not be on the list, so there may be a brief pause at check-in.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: If that happens, I'll still welcome them verbally first, sort the list calmly, and keep a little space so nobody feels crowded while we fix it.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer calibrates to U.S./English-Canadian greeting norms by avoiding assumed social touching, allowing a first-meeting handshake only when the other person initiates, and maintaining personal space during conversation instead of importing a warmer Montreal-style or generic global greeting routine.

scenario: A newcomer on a university partnership team in Montreal has to finalize the printed program for a donor-facing research event by the end of the afternoon. The local coordinator is juggling late sponsor changes, and several speakers are faculty members from Quebec institutions. The newcomer wants to be inclusive and avoid sounding stiff, but the program and stage script also need to feel polished in a public setting.

roles.local: Local coordinator at a Montreal university

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The printer needs the speaker page in an hour. I still have two bios coming in, so if you can lock the emcee script and name cards first, that would help.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Got it. To keep the tone friendly, I’ll make the script consistent with first names once people have been introduced, and I’ll send each speaker a quick note so it feels personal.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Thanks. Some of them know each other well, but the room will include donors, board members, and media, so the wording will travel beyond the team.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I’ll be careful in the emails and mention that I’m happy to adjust if anyone prefers something else. For the printed cards and emcee copy, I’ll keep everyone approachable and uniform.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We also have Professor Leduc joining straight from another campus, and the dean’s office asked for a clean final PDF before 4.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I can absorb that. I’ll redo the layout myself so we don’t miss the deadline, and I’ll update the cards to Marie Leduc, Alan Shore, and Sophie Bouchard to match the conversational style in the welcome slide.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right, send me the proof when the bios arrive. I may still be in the sponsor call, so just flag anything that affects seating.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Will do. I’ll keep the titles out of the public-facing materials for consistency and save the fuller credentials in the internal notes.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: In Quebec/Canadian public professional settings, especially in academia, the newcomer should keep last names and appropriate titles in public materials until invited otherwise. The miscalibration is the public execution axis: they politely offer flexibility in private emails but still strip titles and surnames from donor-facing scripts and name cards by applying a generic friendly-first-name default.

scenario: You lead operations for a joint university-industry research showcase that will be streamed from Montreal in 36 hours. The event page, speaker cards, moderator script, and automated confirmation emails must be finalized tonight because the sponsor is buying paid promotion at 8 a.m. tomorrow. The team is split across Boston, Toronto, and Montreal. Your U.S. design lead argues that the fastest option is to standardize all presenters under first names because several speakers signed earlier messages with their first names only. A Canadian communications manager is pushing for a more formal version but has not specified a rule, and legal wants to avoid using incorrect gendered courtesy titles in outbound email. One featured speaker teaches at a Quebec university and signs email as "Samir Bouchard, PhD"; another is listed on the draft agenda as "Alex Chen" with no title shown anywhere, but their faculty profile URL contains "/prof-chen/"; a third U.S.-based industry panelist replied, "Please call me Dana." The sponsor also wants the moderator to sound warm and contemporary rather than stiff. You need to send one decision memo tonight that sets the naming convention for the public materials and the moderator briefing, and it must be specific enough that junior staff can implement it without asking each speaker individually before the deadline.
question: Write the decision memo you would send to the team. Your memo must: (1) diagnose what uncertainty actually matters here and what should not be over-weighted, (2) identify the tempting but miscalibrated naming plan, (3) set a concrete naming and form-of-address rule for the event page, email salutation, and live moderator script, and (4) explain how you will monitor for mistakes and repair them quickly if a speaker objects after materials are published.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden mechanism as a context-specific formality and title-calibration problem, not just a generic branding or friendliness choice.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that name use must vary by role, channel, and certainty level, with special care for academic speakers and the Canadian/Quebec context. No credit for treating this as merely 'be respectful' or 'match the warm tone.'

rubric.point: Rejects the attractive near-miss of universal first-name standardization based on partial cues.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly bounds the fast global-default plan as tempting but wrong because first-name signatures, warm branding, or U.S. startup norms do not justify flattening all speakers to first names. Partial credit if it rejects the plan without explaining why those cues are insufficient.

rubric.point: Sets a seed-specific execution rule across channels.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies a differentiated convention such as: use professional titles plus surname when status/title is known or when uncertainty remains, especially for university instructors; omit gendered courtesy titles when preference is unknown; use first name only where the person has clearly invited it or where the context supports it. The rule must separately cover public listing, email salutation, and spoken introduction.

rubric.point: Applies the rule correctly to the concrete actors in the scenario.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer operationalizes likely treatment for the Quebec academic, the faculty member with indirect evidence of professorial status, and the panelist who explicitly invited first-name use. No credit for accurate principles applied to the wrong person or channel.

rubric.point: Shows metacognitive CQ through evidence weighting and visible uncertainty management.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer distinguishes what can be inferred now from what remains uncertain, identifies at least one cue that should be discounted or treated as weak evidence, and avoids both overconfidence and inert delay. Answers that simply say 'ask everyone' or 'wait until confirmed' do not earn full credit.

rubric.point: Designs an implementable workflow for staff under deadline pressure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer assigns a default rule junior staff can apply tonight, gives an approval or exception path for ambiguous cases, and keeps the plan narrow enough to meet the deadline. Generic calls for careful review or broad consultation are insufficient.

rubric.point: Includes a targeted repair plan for post-publication objections.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer gives a concrete repair channel and sequence, such as immediate correction of digital materials, updated moderator script, and concise acknowledgement to the affected speaker without turning the issue into a broad public discussion. No credit for vague promises to apologize if needed.

reference_outline: State that the key issue is how to calibrate titles and names under incomplete evidence across U.S./Canadian academic contexts, with extra caution for Montreal/Quebec and for academic roles.

Set the primary execution rule: when a speaker is an instructor or high-status academic and no explicit invitation to use first name exists, default to professional title plus surname in public materials and live introductions; when gender preference is unknown, do not invent gendered courtesy titles.

Treat weak cues carefully: a first-name email sign-off or a desire for a warm sponsor tone is not enough to justify first-name use for all; a faculty-profile cue may support a cautious formal default more than an informal one.

Apply the rule actor by actor: keep the Quebec academic formal, treat the likely faculty member formally unless clearer contrary evidence appears, and use first name for the industry panelist who explicitly invited it.

Differentiate channels operationally: speaker cards/event page can use the formal professional form where relevant, confirmation emails should avoid unknown gendered courtesy titles while remaining formal where status is known, and moderator script should preserve formal introductions unless invited otherwise.
Show metacognitive calibration by stating what is known tonight, what remains uncertain, and what evidence would trigger a revision before airtime without blocking production.
Give staff workflow: junior coordinators implement the default convention now, flag only true exceptions for quick lead review, and avoid a mass outreach that would miss the deadline.

Provide a repair plan: if a speaker objects, correct the website and script immediately, send a brief direct acknowledgement using the preferred form, and document the update so the same error is not repeated live.

scenario: A U.S. program lead is flying to Montréal for a one-day workshop with a Canadian client. The day starts with a small prep huddle among the project team, then moves into a formal client session where those analysts will present to senior directors.
