rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer gives an operational sequence such as confirming the hosting family plus relevant clan coordinators, aligning documentation and resource use to the collective support structure, and setting budget boundaries around defined roles or contributions; no credit for abstract advice without workflow.

rubric.point: Shows motivational CQ through visible, bounded effort rather than friendliness alone.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer includes a real cost the respondent would absorb—extra calls, schedule reshuffling, direct follow-up, repeated clarification, or taking ownership of difficult coordination—while still keeping limits; no full credit for passive waiting, shifting the burden to locals to 'tell us what to do,' or enthusiastic but intrusive overreach.

rubric.point: Builds a workable risk-control and repair plan under budget and deadline pressure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer balances relationship protection with constraints by defining monitoring signals, fallback boundaries, and a repair channel if turnout or obligations exceed assumptions; no full credit for the longest or safest plan unless it is tied to this exact scope problem.

reference_outline: Infer that the delayed observance is a major later-stage obligation, not a minor after-event, because it occurs long after burial due to cost and still mobilizes multiple clan members to help.

State that the near-miss is the global-default assumption that bereavement support should stay confined to the immediate household and that the earlier funeral-related assistance already addressed the main need.

Set stakeholder scope at the family-plus-obligated clan support structure: confirm the host household, identify the relevant clan-side organizers/helpers, and scope the grant to support the collective performance functions rather than only private family expenses.

Sequence outreach this week: first verify expected participant roles and obligations with the host side and clan coordinators, then revise budget lines and filming permissions, then brief headquarters on why a household-only design risks public failure.

Use motivational CQ by owning costly follow-through personally: make extra coordination rounds, absorb schedule inconvenience, keep engaging despite ambiguity, and avoid offloading all interpretation work onto local contacts.
Keep boundaries: do not turn the grant into an open-ended village subsidy; define what collective logistics or participation support the project can cover and what remains outside scope.

Prepare repair and monitoring steps such as checking whether key obligated participants were omitted, watching for signs that the plan is being read as household-only, and adjusting documentation or resource placement quickly before the event day.

scenario: Your team is hosting overseas clients at an evening temple program in Thailand during a major festival. A final one-page participant brief must go out within the hour, and there is no time for another local review. You are deciding whether to replace a general line like "follow the volunteers' guidance" with one explicit instruction about how attendees should handle the ritual items if a robed cleric assists near the entrance.
question: Which observation from setup is the most diagnostic reason to add that explicit instruction now?

options.A: At the hotel welcome, several guests from different countries instinctively reached to shake hands with every host, even after staff had shifted the greeting into a wai-style exchange.
options.B: During the temple walkthrough, when a robed cleric stepped forward to help with spare candle sets, several women in the group started extending the items straight toward him.
options.C: On the practice circuit, multiple guests carrying the candle sets began following the outer path in the opposite direction until a volunteer redirected the group near the second turn.
options.D: At the hall entrance, several guests paused to photograph the interior and stepped onto the raised floor with their shoes still on before turning back to remove them.

scenario: You manage regional communications for a museum-and-tourism partnership preparing a 3-minute opening film and press kit for an upcoming cultural program in Lombok, Indonesia. One segment covers the Lingsar festival. The launch is in 6 days, the Jakarta sponsor wants a single clear storyline for media use, and the legal team wants wording that can be defended if challenged by either community. Your local production coordinator has sent notes from two preparatory meetings: in one, Sasak participants emphasized one origin story and described the gathering in terms that fit their community's public framing; in the other, Balinese participants used a different founding account and highlighted different meanings and purposes. No one directly objected to the project, but when the draft script tried to merge both accounts into one reconciled explanation, edits came back slowly, several lines were rewritten without explanation, and one approval comment said, "better not to force the same meaning in every part." Another internal teammate argues the safest route is to pause publication until the team can verify the single historically correct version, because publishing inconsistent accounts could look sloppy. A sponsor representative pushes the opposite direction: choose one unified narrative now so the campaign feels coherent across channels. You must brief your team today and lock the production workflow tomorrow.
question: Write a decision memo for your team that sets the content strategy and workflow for this Lingsar segment. Your memo must: (1) diagnose what is happening from the evidence in the scenario, (2) identify the most tempting but miscalibrated assumption your team might import, (3) decide how the film script and press kit should handle the differing accounts on the key execution axis of wording/message frame, and (4) specify who should review what, in what sequence, and what signals would make you revise your approach before launch. Be concrete: generic advice to 'be respectful,' 'ask more people,' or 'delay until certain' is not enough.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that the issue is not simply missing facts but a workable coexistence of different community narratives and meanings around the same festival.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers from the slow edits, rewritten lines, and comment about not forcing one meaning that the task is to preserve cooperative ambiguity in representation; no credit for treating the problem only as a fact-checking gap or interpersonal miscommunication.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the tempting imported assumption that one official, reconciled, single story must be produced before communication can proceed.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly names the pressure toward one unified or historically verified storyline as attractive but miscalibrated here, and explains why enforcing it would create risk; partial credit if it merely says 'avoid assumptions' without identifying this specific near-miss.

rubric.point: Makes a seed-specific wording decision for the film and press kit that preserves multiple accounts without collapsing them into one voice.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer gives an operational message frame such as parallel attribution, side-by-side or community-attributed language, or carefully bounded umbrella wording that does not resolve contradictions; no full credit for vague neutrality, generic inclusivity language, or a blended script that smooths differences into one explanation.

rubric.point: Designs a review sequence matched to the ambiguity rather than a generic broad-consultation loop.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies role-based review steps tied to wording scope—for example, separate checks on community-attributed passages before final legal/brand consolidation, and a final pass to ensure the package does not imply one imposed meaning; partial credit for 'consult stakeholders' without stage, scope, or sequence.

rubric.point: Applies metacognitive CQ by stating what can be inferred now, what remains uncertain, and what evidence would justify revising the plan.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer distinguishes actionable inference from unresolved uncertainty and names concrete revision triggers, such as explicit objection to attributed wording, refusal of one community to appear under the shared framing, or legal requirements that force a different packaging choice; no credit for open-ended caution with no commitment.

rubric.point: Controls deadline, sponsor, and legal pressure without defaulting to the safest-longest delay or the fastest brand-coherent simplification.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer offers a narrow executable plan that can ship on time while containing risk through wording boundaries, attribution, and scoped approvals; partial credit for either indefinite pause or immediate single-story lock-in.

reference_outline: State that the evidence suggests the festival can be cooperatively represented even when communities maintain different founding narratives and interpretations; the problem is the script's attempt to force coherence, not merely incomplete research.

Name the near-miss explicitly: imported brand/legal logic says to verify one authoritative story or merge accounts into one clean narrative, but that move is the main risk because it overwrites how cooperation is sustained in this case.

Set the wording/message-frame decision: use attributed or parallel phrasing in the film and press kit, e.g. describing the festival as shared by Sasak and Balinese communities while assigning origins/meanings to the relevant speakers or communities rather than the institution asserting one reconciled account.

Sequence reviews by scope: first revise script lines that make a single interpretive claim; then send community-specific passages to the relevant participants or coordinators for wording fit; then legal/brand reviews the bounded institutional framing; final producer check ensures no edit has silently collapsed the accounts back into one meaning.

Show metacognitive calibration: commit to publishing with a provisional but operational frame, list what remains uncertain, and define revision triggers such as explicit pushback against attribution wording, sponsor demand for a single claim in all assets, or evidence that one passage wrongly assigns meaning across communities.

Handle pressure practically: tell the sponsor that coherence will come from structure and attribution rather than one explanatory thesis, and tell legal that defensibility comes from not overclaiming beyond what each community is prepared to own.

Include a repair path if late conflict appears: narrow or remove only the contested explanatory line, keep the shared event description, and avoid solving the dispute by selecting one community's account as the master narrative unless the stakeholders themselves converge on that change.

scenario: In Chiang Mai, a newcomer on an events team is helping produce a same-day New Year social clip for a hotel sponsor. The team must capture both a morning family-facing visit at a temple compound and later street scenes before the editor's 2 p.m. deadline. The local colleague handles community contacts, while the newcomer is assigning crew flow and on-site behavior.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The editor wants the first cut by two, so we need morning footage from the compound and then faster scenes outside town gate later. Families will already be there early, and the caretaker dislikes delays.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I'll keep the temple unit tiny: one camera, no presenter intro there, phones on silent, and I'll ask the crew to wait for the attendant's cue before they move. We can get the louder opening lines on the truck once we leave.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That helps. We also promised the sponsor at least one shot with senior guests, otherwise they'll say the clip looks like any travel reel.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll take that myself so it stays quick. I brought the small silver bowls from props, and I'll cue the lens only after the family starts. If it takes a second pass outside for branding, we'll do it there instead of holding anyone up inside.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The sponsor may still ask why the morning section feels restrained compared with the afternoon one.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: That's fine—I want that contrast. I'll brief the client now that the early sequence will be short, close, and quiet, then we'll switch to the high-energy street material after lunch.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Okay. Security also asked us not to block the side walkway when school alumni arrive.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll stand the crew off the path, cut any extra direction once we're inside, and keep all retakes for the public area after we exit.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer matches the seed-specific mechanism by preserving the morning sacred sequence as quiet, guided, and non-casual, and by placing respectful water-pouring footage with elders before shifting to energetic public scenes later. The decisive axis is timing and setting: restrained temple conduct first, playful festival coverage afterward.

scenario: Your team in Vietnam is approving one briefing line for freelance photographers covering a national memorial day. They will shoot both the morning temple-based observances and the afternoon public festivities, and the line needs to fit on a single call sheet.
question: Which briefing line should be approved?

options.A: Wear subdued clothing and ask permission before photographing anyone at the event, including wide crowd scenes, formal observances, and the afternoon celebration areas.
options.B: Wear subdued clothing, follow cues during the morning observances, and ask before taking close photos of people directly involved; use normal event shooting for the afternoon public activities.
options.C: Wear subdued clothing and ask permission before photographing monks and officials during the morning observances; candid coverage of other attendees and the afternoon activities can proceed normally.
options.D: Wear subdued clothing and keep a respectful distance; as this is a public national event, candid photography is acceptable throughout both the morning observances and afternoon activities.

scenario: You lead APAC employee-relations programs for a multinational in Tokyo. A senior Japanese client contact has invited your three-person project team to visit his family home during Obon after you deliver a pilot report that afternoon. He describes the visit as important for trust because his late father founded the business, and he says his mother and aunt will also be present. Your team includes a German operations manager who wants to bring a premium fruit box and place it at the family memorial space as a sign of sincerity, and a Singaporean account lead who proposes arriving early so the team can 'help with preparations' and avoid looking casual. The client’s assistant has only written: 'Please come after the report meeting; family will receive you at home.' You also know the family is affiliated with a Buddhist denomination, but no one on your team is sure whether that changes what will happen at the house. You have one evening to brief the team, one chance to send a confirmation note, and your VP wants the visit handled smoothly because contract renewal is being discussed the next morning. If you ask too many broad questions, your VP may see it as slowing execution; if you rely on a generic memorial-visit script and improvise on site, you risk a visible misstep in front of the family.
question: Write the visit plan you would send to your team and the short confirmation you would send before the visit. Your answer must identify the hidden cultural mechanism you think is operating, the tempting but miscalibrated assumption your teammates are making, and the exact sequence you would use from pre-visit confirmation through the first minutes inside the home. Be concrete about what you would ask in advance, when you would arrive, who handles the offering, what the team should and should not do on entry, and how you would brief the team to adapt if the household’s practice differs from what they expect.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the key mechanism as household- and timing-specific memorial practice rather than a single standard Obon script.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that visible actions must be calibrated to this particular family’s observance and schedule; no credit for treating Obon as one fixed national routine or for naming a religion/festival without execution consequences.

rubric.point: Uses advance confirmation to resolve the exact participation sequence.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan explicitly confirms arrival timing and whether guests should attend any arrival-linked or departure-linked observance, and whether they should enter a memorial/altar room immediately or wait to be guided; partial credit for vague 'check local customs' language without these concrete decisions.

rubric.point: Sets the first-contact behavior and offering handoff correctly.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer instructs the team to give the offering to the host in a controlled handoff rather than placing it themselves at a memorial space, and specifies visible execution such as who hands it over and how; no credit if the team places the gift directly on the altar or memorial area, even if framed as respectful.

rubric.point: Rejects the polished near-miss plan created by generic memorial-visit logic.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly bounds at least one attractive but wrong assumption, such as arriving early to help without confirmation, assuming all households want guests present for every rite, or assuming the most respectful act is to approach the memorial space immediately and place the offering there.

rubric.point: Demonstrates behavioural CQ through wording, timing, and interaction rhythm.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the response includes concrete wording or channel choices for the confirmation note and team briefing, showing calibrated timing and visible action under pressure; partial credit for abstract advice like 'be respectful' or 'follow their lead' without preplanned behavioral cues.

rubric.point: Builds a constrained team coordination plan that still protects trust and contract risk.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if roles are assigned clearly, with one person leading greetings and offering handoff, others avoiding initiative at the wrong moment, and a fallback if the family’s practice differs from expectations; no credit for broad delay, over-consultation, or improvisation that offloads responsibility onto the host.

reference_outline: Infer that the operational issue is not 'how to behave at Obon in Japan' in general, but that this family’s Obon timing and home sequence may differ by household, region, and denomination, so the team must not assume one standard script.

Send a short confirmation before the visit that asks only the decision-critical questions: exact arrival time after the meeting, whether the family would like the team present for any welcome or farewell observance, whether there will be a memorial/altar space to greet, and whether guests should go there immediately on arrival or wait in another room first.
Plan to arrive at the confirmed time rather than early, because unsolicited early arrival or attempts to help prepare can disrupt household rhythm during a memorial observance.

Brief the team that the fruit box is handed to the host with both hands by the designated lead, with a simple prepared phrase, and that no one should independently place it on a family memorial/altar space.

Assign roles: respondent or account lead handles greeting and offering, operations manager does not take initiative toward the memorial area, the third teammate watches for host cues and mirrors movement only after the host directs the group.

State the near-miss explicitly: a globally respectful-seeming plan would be to arrive early, enter the memorial room promptly, and place the offering there; explain that this is miscalibrated because the actor, timing, and placement decision belong to the household.

Use behavioural CQ by scripting exact visible conduct for the first minutes: greeting, waiting point, handoff order, movement only when invited, and adaptation if there is no visible altar or if expected rites are omitted.

Include a repair/calibration step under pressure: if the home setup differs from expectations, quietly pause, let the host lead, and shift without forcing the team’s prepared script, while keeping the visit smooth enough for next-day contract discussions.

scenario: In Kathmandu, a newcomer working for a cultural foundation is helping produce a same-day public livestream and printed program note for Sakela. A sponsor wants a clean 'heritage celebration' presentation, but the feed also has to match what actually happens on the ground and avoid upsetting participants or city officials.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The sponsor wants the opening caption locked in the next twenty minutes. They prefer something simple about dance, music, and seasonal tradition. Also, our camera team keeps asking whether they should stay only near the main circle.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll keep the caption concise, but I won't frame the whole program as only performance. I'll also station one camera by the stage and one with the moving crowd so we don't miss the full program if it shifts.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That may make the sponsor nervous. They said families abroad are expecting colorful coverage, not a complicated feed, and the permit window is tight.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll avoid advocacy language in our own wording, but the note will say the gathering includes collective addresses and songs as part of the day, and the crew should record them without treating them like an interruption.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We also have the printed handout for guests from the embassy row. The draft headline currently says 'community folk festival.' Do you want that left as is so it stays neutral?

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: No, I'd revise it before printing. 'Community celebration' is safer than reducing it to folklore, and I'll remove the line telling ushers to redirect visitors away from the speech area unless there is a security issue.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. The sponsor rep will probably ask why the setup became broader than a dance coverage plan.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll tell them the coverage needs to reflect the event as participants are actually holding it today, so the crew stays flexible and the program note doesn't narrow it inaccurately.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer correctly recognizes that Sakela in Kathmandu Valley should not be treated as only folkloric or private-religious. The decisive culture-fit is the execution choice to present and cover speeches, songs, and collective public expression as part of the event rather than filtering them out as off-program or mislabeling the gathering as mere folklore.

scenario: Your Bangkok team must print a one-page executive briefing by 5 p.m. for a December 5 evening candle event in a public square. An HQ draft schedules a team photo beside a large commemorative portrait at the entrance and says guests can "settle in during the opening music." A local coordinator has not edited the draft; she only sent a site map with a portrait zone and a marked audio cue before candle distribution.
question: Which sequence should you use for the briefing?

options.A: Send the draft to legal and inclusion reviewers first, keep the portrait photo stop, add optional language for the opening music, then print once the wording is cleared.
options.B: Hold the draft unchanged, ask the local coordinator to rewrite the arrival and music sections fully, then print her version if it returns before the deadline.
options.C: Remove the portrait photo stop now, add an instruction to rise when the opening music begins, send the revised draft for a quick cue check, then print.
options.D: Add the instruction to rise now, print immediately to protect the deadline, and decide onsite whether to move the group photo away from the portrait area.

scenario: A newly assigned outreach coordinator from Shanghai is helping a community partner in Kuching finish a donor newsletter during a festival weekend. The city has already advertised an afternoon open event, and the partner wants the page to feel warm rather than purely official. Layout closes tonight, while several committee families will separate into their own evening rounds after the public program.

roles.newcomer: Newly assigned outreach coordinator from Shanghai

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We need four usable photos by 7 p.m. The hall program is open to the public, and the donor team asked whether the page can feel less like a stage recap.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I can cover the welcome line and food tables first. If the page still feels formal, I can add one quieter image later so it reads more lived-in.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Once the hall segment ends, committee families peel off in different directions. Not everyone wearing today's badges stays together after that.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I won't try to follow several groups. If one committee car still has a seat, I'll join for just one stop, take a single family-table shot, and head straight back.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The layout team mainly needs the partner group represented, and Mrs. Ting may only send caption details later because she'll be moving between relatives.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. The city notice keeps describing the whole day as an open celebration, so I'll lock the public set first and use the evening stop only if the spread still looks too official.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Please text me the file names before closing. After the crowd breaks up, I may only be able to answer short messages.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Will do. I'll send the public selects by six, then ride with the committee car for one supper frame if timing works.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer updates on the wrong evidence. After cues that the public program and the later family rounds are not one continuous shared setting, they still treat the city's open-event framing and access to a committee car as enough basis to extend coverage into a family-centered evening stop. The miscalibration is on scope, sequence, and evidence use, not tone.

scenario: You are the regional operations lead for a multicultural event team preparing a one-night sponsor activation in Penang during the seventh lunar month. The activation will use a temporary outdoor stage beside a row of neighborhood shoplots, with 120 folding chairs, a sponsor photo wall, and a livestream camera lane. The local venue contact has sent a site photo showing several small food setups and burned-stick ash near the curb from previous nights, and has marked a 'best camera angle' that centers the first row. Your Singapore-based brand manager wants every visible seat filled for optics because the sponsor is worried about low turnout; your German production vendor wants to clear the curb and front aisle early for safety and faster guest flow; and your Malaysian Chinese community partner has only said by text, 'Please avoid rearranging some things outside before we arrive; we can sort details at dusk.' The sponsor deck must be locked in two hours, and trucks arrive at 5 p.m. You cannot cancel the event, move the street permit, or add major budget. Your plan will be judged by your director as a test of whether you can run culturally sensitive public activations without causing neighborhood backlash.
question: Write a brief decision memo for your team that sets the setup sequence, seat-use rule, and who is allowed to move what on site before the community partner arrives. Your memo must identify the most likely local mechanism behind the ambiguous cues, explain which tempting default event plan would misread them, and show how you will protect sponsor goals without turning the answer into a generic 'consult more' delay. Be specific about the evidence you are using, the execution choices you are making, and how you will brief the brand manager, vendor crew, and on-site staff.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden local mechanism from the scenario evidence rather than treating the issue as generic clutter, superstition, or crowd-management preference.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that both the front-row seating area and the curbside food/ash setups may have ritual significance during Hungry Ghost observances in this Malaysian Chinese context, with operational consequences. Partial credit for recognizing only one cue or naming the festival without explaining what it changes.

rubric.point: Makes the correct primary execution-axis decision on placement and movement authority before dusk.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly keeps the first row unavailable for ordinary guest seating and prohibits general crew from stepping over, clearing, kicking aside, or casually relocating curbside offerings, ash, or related items before the community partner handles them. Partial credit if the answer protects the area but assigns the wrong actor or timing.

rubric.point: Rejects the polished near-miss default plan that would optimize optics and safety by filling every visible chair and clearing the curb as standard event prep.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer identifies why a normal global event heuristic—maximize visible occupancy, remove obstructions, standardize seating—would be attractive yet miscalibrated here. Low credit if it merely says 'be respectful' or 'follow local customs' without bounding the mistaken plan.

rubric.point: Applies cognitive CQ by separating cultural evidence from process, personality, and generic legal/safety explanations.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer shows why the text message, timing, site photo, and festival period together outweigh a purely operational reading, while still acknowledging safety and sponsor pressure. Partial credit if it jumps to a label with no evidence chain or treats the issue as only religion, only hazard, or only community politics.

rubric.point: Designs a concrete coordination plan for the brand manager, vendor crew, and local staff.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies role-based instructions such as reserving/reframing the front row, rerouting the camera angle or fill strategy, marking no-move curb zones, limiting who can authorize changes, and briefing crew not to touch certain materials. Partial credit for broad consultation with no workflow.

rubric.point: Protects sponsor and safety goals through a narrow workaround instead of the biggest or broadest precaution.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer offers specific alternatives—such as changing framing, redistributing guests, using later rows, or creating a protected perimeter—without cancelling, overdelaying, or shutting down the whole frontage. Low credit for maximal avoidance plans that ignore task completion.

rubric.point: Includes calibration and repair steps if the initial inference is partly wrong.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer includes a fast verification and contingency path that does not itself violate the likely norm—for example, holding the areas untouched until the partner arrives, then confirming exact boundaries and adjusting signage or camera placement. Low credit if the repair plan requires prior disturbance of the likely sensitive spaces.

reference_outline: Infer from the seventh lunar month timing, outdoor stage, first-row camera focus, curbside food setups, ash, and the partner's 'avoid rearranging some things outside before we arrive' message that this is not ordinary street clutter; the likely mechanism is ritual treatment of front-row seating and curbside offerings during Hungry Ghost observance.

Decide the primary execution axis early: do not allocate the first row as normal sponsor-visible seating, and do not let general crew clear, step through, or move curbside offerings, ash, or related materials before the community partner takes ownership at dusk.

State the tempting near-miss explicitly: a competent global events plan would fill every front seat for optics and clear the curb for safety and flow, but that imported default would misread the local meaning of the spaces and objects.

Brief the German vendor in operational terms: freeze the curbside zone, create a no-touch perimeter, reroute foot traffic and equipment paths, and escalate any requested movement through one named local-facing lead rather than ad hoc crew action.

Brief the Singapore-based brand manager with a sponsor-preserving alternative: keep the visual density from row two backward, adjust camera framing, use side angles or tighter shots, and avoid promising a fully occupied front row.

Give on-site staff a role-specific rule: no guest seating in the protected front row, no one steps over or kicks aside ash, sticks, or food setups, and only the designated lead can approve changes after local confirmation.

Show cognitive CQ by explaining why this inference comes from combining time period, object placement, audience layout, and the partner's wording, rather than assuming a generic hazard, an individual preference, or a broad stereotype about festivals.

Use a narrow calibration step: hold the areas untouched until the partner arrives, confirm exact boundaries and what may be relocated, then update markings or seating use without disturbing the protected elements first.

scenario: A regional operations manager in Shanghai must decide today whether to keep budget on a polished office celebration with visible seasonal décor and a host, or reassign the same budget to staggered early departures and coverage during the holiday week. No one has asked for a change, and reworking coverage would leave the manager handling two late client calls personally. Which observation would most strongly justify redirecting the plan?
question: Which observation is most diagnostic?

options.A: The internal social feed shows the China team posting enthusiastically about lobby decorations, citrus gift baskets, and last year's office performance, with higher engagement than posts about standard holiday benefits.
options.B: Several employees ask whether close relatives could join the office event briefly, and one team suggests adding a family photo corner near the entrance before the evening program begins.
options.C: Department coordinators report that employees are volunteering for a larger pre-holiday group lunch and want the office celebration to end with a collective toast and team photos.
options.D: Shift leads notice employees quietly trading coverage to leave earlier for long return trips, while still declining extra office programming and not raising formal requests for a bigger event.

scenario: You manage APAC partnerships for a museum network. A Tokyo-based sponsor has invited your multinational project team to attend part of an Obon family gathering at the sponsor chair's home in Japan before the final signing dinner for a memorial-exhibition deal. The chair's assistant has only said, in English, that the team may 'stop by the house first' and that 'a small offering would be appreciated.' Your regional director wants a simple standard plan by tonight because flights, gift purchasing, and driver scheduling must be locked within 12 hours. The finance lead is pushing for one uniform itinerary and a branded gift handoff so the team does not miss the dinner. Your Japan account manager is offline on a domestic train for most of the day. Team members from Singapore and Germany ask whether they should just arrive 30 minutes before dinner, bring the gift inside, and place it where the family display area is likely set up so they do not burden the host. The sponsor relationship is high-value, but the chair is senior and private, and an awkward visit could damage trust more than a delayed internal schedule. You must send a coordination note to your director and team now.
question: Write a decision memo that sets the team's execution plan. Your memo must identify what you think is going on from the limited evidence, explain which attractive default plan you are rejecting, and give a concrete sequence for the next 12 hours: who contacts whom, what exactly you need to clarify before arrival, how much inconvenience your team should absorb, how the offering should be handled on entry, and what fallback you will use if you still cannot get complete answers before departure. Make the plan specific enough that your director could judge it as work performance, not just etiquette awareness.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that the visit cannot be treated as a standard fixed-time pre-dinner stop and infers household-level variation from the limited Obon context.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer uses the evidence to conclude that timing and participation details may differ by household or local practice and therefore must be confirmed directly; no credit for generic statements such as 'be respectful' or 'customs may vary everywhere.'

rubric.point: Rejects the tempting imported default of a uniform itinerary plus self-directed gift placement.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly identifies the near-miss plan as attractive under deadline and logistics pressure yet miscalibrated because it assumes a generic default sequence; partial credit if the answer rejects it without explaining why that assumption is specifically risky here.

rubric.point: Specifies the exact pre-arrival clarifications that the team must pursue despite inconvenience.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan names the need to ask in advance about arrival time, meal expectations, any role or presence around home preparations, and whether the team should be present for particular beginning or ending observances; partial credit if it asks only for a general schedule confirmation.

rubric.point: Assigns role ownership and shows motivational CQ through costly but bounded adaptive effort.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer makes someone own the follow-up immediately, accepts friction such as extra calls, schedule uncertainty, or changing transport plans, and keeps the burden on the visiting team rather than waiting passively for the host to educate them; no credit for respectful withdrawal or for pushing all adaptation onto the Japanese side.

rubric.point: Gives the correct entry-stage handling of the offering and keeps actor and placement calibrated.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer states that the offering should be presented to the host at the entrance with both hands rather than placed by visitors on the family altar or display area; partial credit if it mentions careful gift handling but leaves placement or recipient ambiguous.

rubric.point: Designs a fallback that is narrow and risk-controlled rather than broad, safest, or endlessly consultative.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the fallback limits the team's participation to what has been explicitly confirmed, preserves flexibility on arrival time, and avoids improvising around meals, altar-related actions, or fire-related presence; no credit for generic delay-everything plans or for proceeding with the original standard itinerary unchanged.

rubric.point: Translates cultural diagnosis into work-facing communication for director and teammates.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo frames the plan as protecting sponsor trust and execution quality through a specific sequence, not as abstract cultural sensitivity; partial credit if it names relationship risk without giving concrete instructions teammates can follow.

reference_outline: State that the Obon home visit likely has household-specific timing and participation expectations, so the team should not assume a universal pre-dinner pattern from the sparse invitation.
Reject the one-size-fits-all itinerary and self-placement of the gift because those moves apply a generic outsider default to a context where sequence and host mediation matter.

Immediately assign one owner to contact the assistant or family liaison with a short clarification list: exact arrival window, whether the visit overlaps with a meal, whether guests should be present for any welcome or farewell observance, and whether there is any expectation around preparations before entering.

Show motivational CQ by absorbing the cost on the visiting side: keep transport and dinner timing flexible, accept rebooking or waiting time, and continue follow-up even if the answers come slowly rather than dropping the issue for convenience.
Instruct the team that on entry the offering is to be handed to the host with both hands and not placed directly by visitors on the family altar or display area.

If complete answers do not arrive, narrow participation to confirmed actions only: arrive only at a host-confirmed time, avoid assuming inclusion in meals or ritual moments, and do not improvise involvement in home or altar-related actions.

Explain the plan to the director as sponsor-risk management tied to execution quality: a small investment in clarification and flexibility reduces the chance of a visible misstep with a senior private host.

scenario: At a Kaamatan event, a newcomer from a sponsor team is helping coordinate a short stage-side product handoff and guest hospitality during a tightly timed opening program. The sponsor wants visible participation and quick photo coverage, but the opening sequence includes formal remarks and a later ritual segment. Seating near the front has name cards, and volunteers are circulating trays of drinks and snacks to VIPs and visitors.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We need your team ready by the side stairs in ten minutes. After the opening starts, movement gets harder, and the front rows are already assigned for committee guests.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I’ll keep our two reps standing at the side until our cue instead of filling those empty front seats, and I’ll brief our photographer to stay off the center aisle.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Thanks. The sponsor director also asked whether we can make the hospitality feel more lively, since some visitors are shy about taking refreshments.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I can help the volunteers by inviting people once, but I won’t have our staff press anyone to take a drink or keep topping up cups just for energy. We can make the table look full without pushing it.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That helps. One more thing: while the emcee and elders are up front, I may be stuck backstage and unable to signal much.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I’ll keep my team on text-only updates and no side coaching once that section begins. If our director wants a quick introduction for visibility, I’ll tell him we hold it until the transition point.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Good. After that transition, the sponsor handoff has to happen fast because the press wants the photo before lunch.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Fine by me. We’ll move quickly when the break opens, do the handoff in one pass, and leave the untouched trays for later service instead of clearing them into giveaway bags.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer’s decisive behavior matches the Kaamatan conduct mechanism on execution: they avoid using unallocated seats, prevent unnecessary talking/noise during solemn parts, avoid pressuring people to drink, and avoid waste by not repurposing untouched refreshments prematurely. The superficially rigid, fast, and text-driven style is not the deciding issue; the key is the sequence and restraint during formal segments.

scenario: In Kuala Lumpur, a newcomer helping a Chinese Malaysian community group is coordinating a sponsor photo and livestream clip at an evening street performance during the Hungry Ghost month. The sponsor wants visible audience energy before the troupe starts, and the clip must be sent within the hour.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The sponsor just asked for a quick photo and ten-second clip before the first song. We only have a few minutes once the lights come on.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Got it. I’ll help fill the shot so it doesn’t look flat. I can ask the volunteers and some families near the road to take the seats closest to the stage for two minutes, then we’ll clear out.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The walkway is already crowded, and some households have set things out along the curb, so moving people around may be slow.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I’ll keep it efficient. I can step across the curb area, bring people forward from both sides, and avoid delaying the performers. After the clip, I’ll thank everyone and move them back.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We also need the troupe manager in a good mood, so please keep the setup smooth.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I’ll do it myself so your team doesn’t have to get stressed, and I’ll make it sound like a sponsor request, not an order.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right, I need to check the audio feed. Send me the frame before you post it.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Will do. I’m heading to the front now to stage the audience tightly and grab the clip before the opener starts.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer invests real effort and sounds considerate, but the decisive behavior is culturally miscalibrated: he plans to occupy the seats nearest the stage for the shot and to step across curbside items set out during Hungry Ghost observances. The seed-specific mechanism is that those front seats may be intentionally left empty and roadside offerings should not be stepped over.

scenario: A multinational's Shanghai sales team is finalizing a one-line briefing for Lunar New Year visits to local distributors. Compliance has already approved either prepaid shopping cards or cash gifts up to the same value cap. Sales leads must place the order tomorrow, and the route includes both long-standing distributor partners and a few accounts that were reassigned this month.
question: Which briefing line should be approved for the visit pack?

options.A: Use prepaid shopping cards rather than cash-style gifts for distributor visits in China; they show appreciation while avoiding the awkwardness of handing over money in a business setting.
options.B: For Lunar New Year visits in China, prepare festive cash envelopes for every distributor contact on the route, including newly reassigned accounts and first introductions this quarter.
options.C: For Lunar New Year visits in China, prepare festive cash envelopes for distributors with an established working relationship, keeping the amount within the existing gift cap.
options.D: For Lunar New Year visits in China, reserve festive cash envelopes for annual contract renewals, and use prepaid shopping cards for the seasonal courtesy visit itself.

scenario: You are the regional partnerships manager for a multinational education company. Your Beijing team has just signed a university alliance, and the local host has added your company to the guest list for the dean’s daughter’s wedding next Saturday. The host university matters because a renewal decision on a pilot program will be discussed two days after the wedding. Your global finance director in London says the company should avoid anything that looks like a personal cash transfer and suggests sending a premium boxed gift basket worth the equivalent of RMB 2,000 with a congratulatory card signed by senior staff. Your Shanghai-based account lead says the host’s assistant already asked how many attendees from your side will come and requested names for a seating chart, but gave no guidance on gifts. A junior teammate mentions that at another event she saw guests write something in a ledger at the entrance before going in. You have a hard cap of RMB 1,500 in discretionary spend, cannot ask the host directly what amount to give without risking awkwardness, and your vice president wants a one-page decision memo today because brand, audit, and relationship risk are all in play. Your team includes a German finance partner, a Singaporean operations lead, and two China-based staff who will attend in person.
question: Write the decision memo. Specify what gift mechanism you would use, how you would determine the amount and who it should be associated with, what the two China-based attendees should do at the venue, and how you would explain your plan to finance and the vice president. Your memo must identify the most tempting imported assumption in this case, show why it is miscalibrated here, and make one clear choice about timing/sequence at the event that reduces relationship risk without creating a larger expectation problem.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that the core issue is not whether to give something generous, but how the gift amount functions as a socially legible signal tied to relationship level and comparison with others at the event.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explains that the amount itself must be calibrated to expected convention because it communicates closeness and affects surrounding expectations; no credit for answers that discuss only kindness, anti-bribery optics, or general wedding etiquette.

rubric.point: Chooses a cash-based wedding gift mechanism rather than substituting a premium non-cash corporate present.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan explicitly rejects the attractive boxed-gift default as the imported near-miss and uses an appropriate monetary mechanism for this social event; partial credit if cash is suggested but treated as optional or secondary.

rubric.point: Calibrates the amount to the correct relationship scope and avoids over- or under-signaling.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer states that the amount should be set to a locally conventional level for this host relationship and not inflated to impress or equal the full discretionary cap; partial credit if the answer says to 'match local norms' but does not connect that to closeness signaling or expectation effects.

rubric.point: Assigns the gift and attendance roles correctly on the primary execution axis of event sequence.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer places the in-person China-based attendees as the ones who handle the entrance-stage gift process and associated recording moment before joining the event, rather than mailing something later, sending only a card, or delegating the act to remote executives.

rubric.point: Uses cognitive CQ to separate seed-specific evidence from generic corporate heuristics.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo weighs the ledger clue, the wedding context, and relationship stakes against the global anti-cash heuristic, and shows why the generic policy instinct is incomplete rather than universally wrong; no credit for vague statements like 'respect local culture' without evidence comparison.

rubric.point: Designs a finance-facing explanation that bounds compliance risk without erasing the local logic.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes a narrow, documented rationale such as treating this as a culturally conventional social gift tied to attendees/relationship and keeping the amount within a calibrated band, rather than solving risk by escalation, blanket prohibition, or maximal documentation alone.

rubric.point: Rejects plausible but misapplied alternatives.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly rules out at least one polished near-miss such as using the largest budget-safe amount to show respect, standardizing the same expensive gift used in other markets, or avoiding the gift entirely and relying on a congratulatory note; partial credit if alternatives are rejected only on generic grounds.

reference_outline: Infer from the wedding context, guest handling details, and entrance ledger clue that the event likely uses a socially visible monetary gift practice where the amount is legible and consequential.
Choose a monetary wedding gift mechanism handled in person by the China-based attendees, not a premium non-cash substitute driven by a generic global gift default.
Set the amount by the actual relationship category between the company/team and the host family, aiming for a locally conventional band rather than the maximum available budget or a token amount.
Sequence the action so the attendees present and record the gift at the entrance-stage process before joining the banquet, because timing and placement are part of proper execution here.

Explain to finance and leadership that the risk is miscalibration, not simply cash itself: too much or too little sends the wrong relational signal and can create expectation distortions relative to others.

Use a bounded compliance control: document business context, attendees, occasion, and rationale for calibrated conventionality, while avoiding a showy or exceptional amount that could look like influence-buying or false intimacy.

Reject the tempting imported assumption that the safest universal answer is a high-end physical gift or no cash; show that this would miss the local mechanism and could create more awkwardness than a properly calibrated monetary gift.

If uncertainty remains, narrow it by using discreet local pattern knowledge from the China-based team or comparable recent events, not by asking the host directly for the amount or defaulting to the broadest corporate-safe gesture.

scenario: A newcomer operations manager in Jakarta is preparing a donor site visit scheduled for the week before Lebaran. The donor expects a polished event and a full office turnout, but vendor confirmations are slowing down and several staff have already mentioned long-distance travel plans. The newcomer must finalize staffing and payments without delaying the visit.

roles.local: Rina, Indonesian HR and office manager

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The donor wants the office tour on Tuesday afternoon, and catering still needs a deposit today. A few team leads also asked when the holiday payment advice will go out.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll release the holiday payment notice this afternoon and have payroll process it this week instead of bundling it with month-end. For the visit, I'm shrinking the program to a core crew and asking department heads by 3 p.m. who will still be in town.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That gives us less ceremony than the donor expected. We also usually rely on drivers and two outside printers for these visits.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I'll switch the printed packs to a simple in-house version and send the donor a tighter agenda today rather than promise the full setup. I'd rather confirm only people and suppliers we can actually count on next week.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Finance may ask why you're moving the payment earlier than the regular cycle, and the donor country team likes seeing a busy office.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll note it as a holiday obligation and keep the finance explanation short. For the donor, I'll frame it as a focused working visit and avoid scheduling roundtables that depend on everyone being physically here.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. If you send me the revised headcount by tonight, I can start calling the departments and the caterer.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: You'll have it tonight. I'm locking the visit around confirmed availability now, not around our usual pre-holiday attendance assumptions.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer correctly applies Indonesia-specific Lebaran operations logic on two execution axes: he advances the holiday payment rather than treating it as a normal payroll-cycle item, and he plans the event around expected pre-Lebaran absences and service disruption instead of assuming standard staffing and vendor capacity.

scenario: A regional payroll system cutover is scheduled for the month-end that falls two days after the main holiday week in Indonesia. The plan needs final HR signoff, a bank file check, and employee support coverage. The Jakarta team says staff can finish data cleanup before then, but several people have already arranged intercity travel and the employer may announce extra shared leave days. HQ can approve one country-specific scheduling override without moving the rest of APAC.
question: Which override scope is the best one to approve for Indonesia?

options.A: Treat the whole fasting month in Indonesia as a reduced-capacity period and move all payroll milestones for that country to the following month, keeping the rest of APAC on the original plan.
options.B: Keep Indonesia on the regional prep timeline, but move only the signoff, bank check, and support window out of the combined holiday closure period once the employer confirms its added leave days.
options.C: Keep the cutover date, but shift Indonesia's signoff and bank check into the last workweek before the holiday block, while freezing employee support until staff return from travel.
options.D: Use the published public-holiday dates only, and require Indonesia to follow the same signoff, bank check, and support schedule as other APAC markets unless individuals request personal leave.

scenario: A Berlin events lead is approving one sentence in an English invitation for visiting staff who will join a Latvian partner team's late-June gathering at a family property outside the city. The shuttle leaves at 20:00, indoor beds are limited, and finance wants the packing note finalized today.
question: Which invitation line should be approved?

options.A: Please plan for an overnight gathering, bring something small to share, and pack camping gear if you can sleep outdoors, as people usually remain outside until sunrise.
options.B: Please join us for an evening bonfire, with food and return transport arranged by the hosts, so you can travel light and expect to be back in town before midnight.
options.C: Please plan to stay late, bring a dish to share, and pack a tent if you want to continue after the singing, while others can leave once the main bonfire ends.
options.D: Please arrive after dinner, bring something for breakfast, and pack overnight gear, as the group will settle around the fire toward morning before heading to sleep.

scenario: You are a Berlin-based project lead at a Nordic consumer-tech company. A Swedish product designer on your team, Lina, mentioned in a small Thursday call that her family will be at their summer place outside Uppsala for Midsommar and said, smiling, that 'a few people may stop by if they are nearby.' Your VP, who is joining from the US office, immediately told you privately to 'lock this in' because she wants at least two non-Swedish team members there to strengthen trust before a tense post-holiday launch review. Budget is tight, train tickets rise sharply after noon, and you need to send a team logistics note within two hours so people can decide whether to travel Friday morning. You also know that one French teammate has already asked in the group chat whether Lina's family will 'handle the food situation,' and a Polish teammate asked whether they should bring 'a bottle for the host.' Lina has not followed up with details, and you do not want to put her on the spot publicly or miss a genuine opening. Your plan will be judged by your VP as execution under pressure and by Swedish teammates as relationship judgment.
question: Write a brief decision memo to your VP that sets the participation plan and the exact next-step sequence for you and the two interested teammates. Your memo must: (1) diagnose what is most likely going on from the available evidence, (2) identify the most tempting but miscalibrated assumption an outsider might make here, (3) specify the wording, channel, audience, and timing of the next messages, and (4) explain how your plan balances speed, relationship risk, and practical preparation for the event.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the invitation as requiring careful confirmation rather than treating it as an open casual drop-in.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers from the scenario that attendance should not be presumed and that the team must seek confirmation in a calibrated way before making travel commitments; no credit for treating Lina's remark as a public open invitation or for proposing to simply announce who is coming.

rubric.point: Uses the correct behavioural sequence for expressing interest and preparing participation.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan has the interested teammates reach out promptly in a limited channel with interest framed through contribution, then asks what food item would fit, rather than first asking for hosting details, expecting the host to provide everything, or waiting passively for Lina to organize all logistics.

rubric.point: Handles drinks and food preparation with the right scope and ownership.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer assigns attendees responsibility for bringing their own drinks for the full event and for coordinating a suitable food contribution with Lina; partial credit if it mentions bringing something but leaves host responsibility ambiguous; no credit if it assumes a host gift or a single shared bottle is the key preparation.

rubric.point: Rejects the attractive near-miss imported assumption.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo explicitly bounds a plausible outsider default such as 'the host will cater once invited' or 'a bottle for the host is enough' and explains why that plan is efficient but miscalibrated here; no credit for generic statements about 'different cultures have different norms.'

rubric.point: Chooses the right channel, audience, and timing under pressure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer avoids turning the matter into a group-chat coordination before Lina privately confirms scope and contribution expectations, while still acting quickly enough for travel decisions; partial credit for the right content in the wrong channel or too-late timing.

rubric.point: Applies behavioural CQ through visible wording and interaction rhythm.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the response includes or closely specifies concrete phrasing that is neither overly passive nor presumptive, such as expressing interest, offering to bring specific contributions, and asking what would fit best; no credit for abstract advice like 'be respectful' or 'check with her first' without wording or sequencing.

rubric.point: Builds a workable contingency if the answer is no or limited.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan includes a face-saving fallback that protects Lina from pressure and gives the VP an alternative trust-building step without escalating publicly; no credit for plans that force a yes/no in front of the group or treat refusal as a coordination failure.

reference_outline: Interpret Lina's comment as a possible opening but not as a casual public invitation that the team can operationalize on its own.
Advise the VP not to announce attendance yet; first send a prompt private message to Lina from the project lead or the specific interested teammates, not the full team chat.
Use wording that expresses interest by coupling it with contribution: for example, say the teammates would be glad to come if appropriate and ask what food item would fit best for them to bring.
Tell attendees to plan to bring their own alcohol or non-alcoholic drinks for the whole event rather than assuming host provision or relying on a symbolic host bottle.
Explicitly reject the efficient outsider default that once someone hints at an event, the host will manage food and drink logistics for guests.
Keep the audience narrow until Lina confirms scope; only after confirmation send the practical travel note to the two teammates with their preparation responsibilities.
Include a fallback if Lina's family gathering is not suitable for extra guests: thank her, avoid pressure, and propose another low-key post-holiday relationship-building step for the VP.

scenario: You are an event partnerships manager at a European consumer brand. Your team is finalizing a small co-sponsored employee-and-client gathering in Latvia tied to the 23-24 June holiday period. The Latvian sales lead has secured use of her family’s rural property, and the CFO has approved only a modest budget on the assumption that using a private site will keep costs down. A German operations manager wants a tight evening program ending by 22:30 so everyone can return to city hotels and submit receipts cleanly. A Swedish HR partner is pushing for a low-burden attendance model so guests can 'drop in if they want' without pressure. The local sales lead has sent scattered notes over two weeks: she asked whether the grounds team could come earlier in the week, whether guests had dietary contributions in mind, and whether the invitation should mention overnight gear. No one has answered clearly. Yesterday, your VP asked for a final execution memo by noon because several invited clients have still not RSVP’d and legal wants the invitation language locked today. If you make the event feel too demanding, some senior invitees may decline; if you over-standardize it into a short hosted reception, the Latvian team fears it will feel off and damage trust. You cannot add major budget, move the date, or send a vague 'we’ll confirm later' note.
question: Write a decision memo for your internal team that sets the event design and invitation approach. Your memo must: (1) diagnose what cultural mechanism is most likely driving the local sales lead’s scattered requests; (2) identify the most tempting but miscalibrated imported assumption in the current team debate; (3) make a concrete call on the main execution axis of guest commitment and event sequence; and (4) show what extra effort you personally will own under time pressure so the plan does not simply shift the adaptation burden back to the Latvian side. Be specific about invitation wording, who brings or prepares what, whether and how to handle overnight logistics, and how you will reduce relationship risk if some invitees cannot fully participate.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden mechanism as a shared-participation hosting model rather than a standard one-way hosted reception.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers from the property-preparation, contribution, overnight-gear, and timing clues that guests are expected to help complete the social setting and stay meaningfully engaged; low credit if it merely says 'respect local traditions' or names the holiday without execution consequences.

rubric.point: Rejects or sharply bounds the attractive near-miss of a short optional drop-in event with centralized hosting.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explains why a brand-safe, low-burden, hotel-return plan would misread the local participation logic even though it seems efficient and inclusive under budget and legal pressure; low credit if it treats that plan as the default and adds only polite local touches.

rubric.point: Makes the correct execution-axis decision on guest commitment and sequence.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer commits to an event design that signals preparation ahead of time, shared contributions, and a realistic overnight/late-participation structure instead of a brief evening reception; partial credit if it mentions contributions or staying late but keeps the core structure as a short optional program.

rubric.point: Translates the diagnosis into role-specific logistics and invitation wording.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies who prepares the site, what guests are asked to bring, how overnight gear is framed, and how expectations are communicated without making the request sound accidental or purely optional; low credit for generic 'coordinate with local team' language.

rubric.point: Shows motivational CQ through costly personal ownership under ambiguity and discomfort.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the respondent takes on visible extra effort such as personally repairing the unanswered threads, consolidating contribution tracking, absorbing inconvenience in the schedule, or staying engaged through the demanding format rather than delegating uncertainty back to locals or diluting the format to avoid discomfort.

rubric.point: Balances participation demands with relationship-preserving flexibility.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer creates a bounded way for constrained invitees to decline parts of the format without redefining the whole event into a generic reception; low credit if it either pressures everyone into full participation or makes the event so optional that the core mechanism disappears.

rubric.point: Uses evidence from the scenario, not generic festival stereotypes or broad consultation moves.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan is tied to the specific message history and constraints in the case; low credit if the answer relies on generic advice such as 'ask the locals,' 'be inclusive,' 'delay until more information,' or references cultural labels without deciding actor, stage, and scope.

reference_outline: Infer from the unanswered notes that the local lead is not asking for incidental extras; the site, guest contributions, overnight gear, and extended timing are part of how the event is socially completed.

State that the main mistake would be converting the gathering into a brief centrally hosted reception with optional attendance and hotel return, because that follows a generic corporate event default rather than the local participation logic.
Set the event sequence around advance preparation, arrival with contributions, late-night participation, and on-site sleeping options; do not keep the core design as a short evening program.

Assign roles concretely: local lead coordinates property readiness, central team funds and tracks essential supplies, guests are explicitly asked to bring shareable food or equivalent agreed contributions, and overnight gear is named directly in the invitation rather than buried in FAQs.

Own the motivational-costly work personally: send the repaired invitation today, call key invitees who may hesitate, maintain the contribution list yourself, and absorb the inconvenience of supporting a longer format instead of simplifying the event for your own comfort.

Preserve relationships with bounded flexibility: allow some guests to attend only part of the event if necessary, but frame partial attendance as an exception to manage practically rather than the default design principle.

Reduce risk by clarifying expectations early and specifically, not by broad delay: explain the format, contribution norms, and sleeping logistics in one coherent message so invitees can opt in knowingly and the Latvian team is not left to fix mismatched assumptions at the last minute.

scenario: A Stockholm-based team has just finished a demanding product launch, and a Swedish colleague invites the newcomer to Midsommar at her family's summer place outside the city. The newcomer wants to sound appreciative and organized because trains and shops will close early, and he also wants to avoid arriving empty-handed. The exchange happens in the office chat while people are still wrapping up work.

roles.local: Swedish colleague hosting part of the Midsommar gathering
roles.newcomer: Recently relocated employee joining the celebration for the first time

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: A few of us are going to my family's place for Midsommar on Friday. If you want, you can come with us from the office after lunch, but I need to confirm car seats tonight.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'd love to, thanks. I'm still learning how these weekends work here, so I'll keep it simple and fit around your plan.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Good. We'll stop once on the way, but after that it's a long drive and the small shop near the water closes early.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Perfect, then I won't create extra errands. I'll bring a bottle for the evening and maybe some mixers, and I can settle up with you later if there are shared costs.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: No stress about settling up now. We just need to leave on time because people start arriving before dinner.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. To keep it easy for everyone, I won't ask you to organize anything for me. I'll just come ready for the whole day and count on whatever food and drinks the house already has.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Alright, send me by six if you're taking the spare seat, because I have to text the driver.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Will do. Thanks again—I'll travel light and won't need any special planning from your side.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer sounds considerate and logistics-aware, but the decisive behavior misfires on the seed-specific mechanism: for a private Midsommar invitation, the culturally calibrated move is to offer a concrete contribution under the shared-guest format, not to assume the household will cover all food and drink for the day. Bringing only something for his own evening drinking while relying on the house for the rest enacts the outsider default the seed warns against.

scenario: A documentary team in Latvia plans a 90-second opening shot at a cemetery on a June Saturday. The producer wants a visually strong arrival sequence near the main path, but moving the shoot to another window will disrupt the rest of the day. Before locking the setup, the producer asks the fixer to watch the site for ten minutes and report one concrete observation.
question: Which observation would be the most decisive reason to change the planned opening setup window?

options.A: Several family groups arrive from different cars carrying tools and flowers, then begin cleaning and arranging individual graves well before any formal gathering starts.
options.B: Small groups gather near the entrance after arriving from other towns, greet each other quietly, and remain there talking before walking farther into the grounds.
options.C: Municipal workers have already tidied the main paths, and later arrivals mostly walk slowly between plots carrying candles, bouquets, and folded programs.
options.D: Visitors from abroad take photos of older monuments from the side paths, and no staff member stops them as long as they keep their voices low.

scenario: You are coordinating a multicultural employer-branding team for a Nordic-Baltic logistics company. The Riga office will host a rural client-and-staff gathering outside Cesis on 23–24 June, and headquarters wants the event to serve two goals at once: strengthen the relationship with a Latvian municipal partner and capture social content for a regional recruitment campaign. The draft plan from headquarters treats it like a standard evening summer party: a shuttle from Riga arriving at 19:30, branded snack boxes for each attendee, a midnight departure so the film crew stays within overtime limits, and optional giveaway accessories in company colors. The local office has not objected directly, but in recent message threads several people have separately asked whether guests may bring their own food, whether there is space on the property for extra cars and sleeping gear, and whether the wardrobe note should distinguish between what women and men are expected to wear. Another note from the municipal partner asks whether the wood delivery has been confirmed early enough and whether the sunrise shot is still in scope. Your German finance lead is pressing for one locked run-of-show by tomorrow because insurance, transport, and branded materials must be approved now. Your Swedish brand director wants the event to look authentic but says the company should not over-script people or appear to costume them. You have one memo to send tonight recommending the event design and coordination plan.
question: Write the decision memo: recommend the event design, participant briefing, and stakeholder sequence you would use. Your answer must identify the cultural mechanism you think is driving the mixed signals, explain which tempting imported assumption would misread them, and make concrete choices on the key execution axis of timing/overnight structure. Specify what you would change in logistics, what you would tell headquarters, what you would ask of hosts versus guests, and how you would preserve authenticity without turning the event into a generic all-purpose consultation exercise.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden mechanism from scenario evidence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that this is not a standard short evening party but an all-night, host-prepared yet guest-contributing celebration whose meaning depends on preparation, overnight continuity, and dawn endpoint; partial credit if it notes 'important local holiday' without linking the evidence to overnight structure, shared contribution, and role-specific dress.

rubric.point: Makes the correct timing and overnight design decision
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if it explicitly rejects the midnight-departure format and redesigns transport, staffing, filming, and safety around staying through the night into sunrise, with sleep/return options rather than assuming same-night exit; no full credit for answers that simply extend the party a little later or say 'check with locals first' without deciding.

rubric.point: Applies the seed-specific participation logic to hosts and guests
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if it distinguishes host responsibilities such as site preparation and core hospitality from guest participation such as bringing food to share and, where relevant, sleeping gear, instead of treating the event as fully catered individual consumption; partial credit if it mentions sharing generally but does not assign it to the right actors or stage.

rubric.point: Handles visible symbols and authenticity at the right scope
