scenario: You are coordinating a three-person Asia-Pacific public affairs team for a museum partnership in Auckland. On Tuesday morning, the museum texts that its Māori community liaison has died unexpectedly, the partnership launch scheduled for Thursday will be postponed, and several staff and community members will be at the marae over the next few days. Your director in Singapore wants a same-day response plan by 2 p.m. because sponsors are asking whether your company will send representatives, flowers, a condolence note, and a replacement meeting request. The Australian brand manager pushes for an efficient plan: send two senior managers for a short visit on Wednesday morning, have the local account executive give condolences directly to the deceased’s spouse and adult children, leave once the note is handed over, and use the visit to confirm when the launch can be rescheduled. You have only one Auckland-based staff member available in person, a regional vice president may join briefly if needed, and there is pressure not to look absent or disorganized. Message history from the museum is sparse: one note says people are arriving from different parts of the country, another says the family is 'with everyone at the marae,' and a third says, 'Please don’t worry if the people you expect to speak are not the ones addressing visitors.'
question: Write the decision memo you would send your director. Specify the in-person visit plan and departure sequence, who should speak to whom and who should not be assumed to lead the exchange, what should and should not be attempted during this visit, and how you would brief your Auckland staff member and vice president so the team shows support without disrupting the local process. Your memo must identify the tempting but miscalibrated plan in the current discussion and explain why your chosen behavior sequence is the better operational fit under the deadline.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that the visit must be planned around an extended mourning process rather than a short transactional condolence call.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers from the scenario that attendance may need to accommodate a multi-day, high-traffic setting with people arriving from afar, and therefore rejects a quick drop-in framed as a brief handoff. No credit for merely saying 'be respectful' or 'funerals differ by culture.'

rubric.point: Sets the primary execution sequence for the visit and exit in seed-specific behavioral terms.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan gives a concrete visit rhythm: attend primarily to pay respects, avoid treating departure as casual, and include an explicit leaving sequence that accounts for cleansing actions before fully exiting the viewing/burial space. Partial credit if the answer slows the visit down but omits the departure behavior.

rubric.point: Assigns speaking roles without assuming closest kin are the main public interlocutors.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer instructs the team not to target the spouse or adult children as default lead speakers and instead to follow the visible speaking structure on site, allowing that others may address visitors. Partial credit if the answer says 'wait to see who is leading' but still centers closest family as the intended primary contacts.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the attractive near-miss plan under business pressure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly identifies the polished but wrong plan as using a global condolence/default stakeholder script: short senior visit, direct approach to nearest kin, quick exit, and rescheduling discussion during the mourning visit. The answer must explain why that plan is efficient but behaviorally mis-sequenced here. No credit if it rejects the plan only because 'more consultation is safer.'

rubric.point: Uses behavioural CQ through exact briefing on wording, timing, audience, and interaction rhythm.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo gives actionable instructions such as whom to let take the lead on-site, how to phrase the purpose of the visit, when not to introduce business scheduling, and how the vice president should avoid dominating the interaction. Partial credit for general advice without visible behavioral detail.

rubric.point: Protects task performance while preserving relationship trust.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer separates condolence attendance from launch-rescheduling logistics by proposing a later channel, timing, or contact point for business follow-up, while still meeting sponsor/internal pressure with a clear immediate plan. No credit for indefinite delay or for folding all issues into one visit.

rubric.point: Designs a constrained but credible staffing plan.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer uses the limited Auckland staff member and optional vice president in a calibrated way: enough presence to avoid seeming absent, but not a status-heavy delegation that turns the visit into a performance or rushed executive appearance. Partial credit if staffing is plausible but unexplained.

reference_outline: Infer that this is not a standard short condolence stop: people are traveling long distances, the gathering spans multiple days, and the team should plan presence around paying respects rather than a quick ceremonial handoff.

Choose a behavioral sequence in which the Auckland staff member attends to represent the company, the vice president joins only if briefed to follow local rhythm and not take over, and the purpose of the visit is condolence only, not schedule recovery.

Do not assume the spouse or adult children will be the people publicly receiving or leading exchanges; instruct staff to follow the speaking pattern that emerges on site and address the appropriate speakers or hosts rather than forcing nearest-kin contact.

Separate the mourning visit from business matters: do not ask for a new launch date during the visit; instead send a later follow-up through the museum contact or another suitable channel after the immediate mourning stage.

Brief the team on departure behavior: they should not simply hand over flowers, leave abruptly, and head out as from a normal office call; the exit should include the expected cleansing actions before fully leaving the relevant space.

Name the near-miss clearly: the efficient global-default plan is attractive because of deadline and sponsor pressure, but it misfires on timing, audience, and exit sequence even if the intention is respectful.

Show behavioural CQ with exact instructions on wording, role restraint, timing, and channel: say the visit is to pay respects, avoid pushing for clarity in the moment, let on-site structure determine who speaks, and reserve business coordination for a later message.

scenario: A New Zealand nonprofit is sending two staff to a memorial gathering for the father of its Tongan partner director. question: Which observation would most strongly justify planning for the longer on-site presence?

options.A: After the formal remarks, the room settles into small quiet clusters, close relatives remain seated together, and venue staff begin clearing cups while later arrivals are directed to return another day.
options.B: Before the main gathering starts, women from the partner office begin circulating tea and food trays while early guests sit quietly and organizers keep checking whether the principal family has arrived.

scenario:
You lead event operations for a regional broadcaster that will livestream the opening night of a major annual self-government celebration in the Cook Islands. Your team includes a Sydney-based broadcast producer, a Wellington social-media editor, and a local logistics coordinator in Rarotonga. A government communications office wants strong opening visuals for international audiences, and your sponsor wants a short teaser clip posted within 10 minutes of the ceremony starting. Budget is tight, so you can only place one roaming camera team in the most symbolically important part of the opening sequence. 

In the planning notes, you see that the opening involves a flame being lit in one location, carried into Avarua, and then used later in the formal opening with senior political figures. You also see two inconsistent pieces of prior message history: last year's external agency treated the opening mostly like a parade and focused on crowd energy, while a local volunteer's email about this year's event asks crews to avoid distracting behavior near one central object and says audience noise expectations change during certain segments. No one on your team can get a full rehearsal because roads will close early, and the government office keeps pushing for 'the most dramatic close-up possible' as soon as the procession reaches town.

You must send a same-day execution brief in the next hour covering camera placement, staff behavior, posting sequence, and who gets authority to change the plan on site if the opening runs late.
question: Write the execution brief you would send. It should state: (1) what hidden mechanism you think is shaping the opening and which tempting outsider assumption could cause a mistake; (2) where you would place the roaming camera team and when you would or would not push for dramatic close-ups; (3) how you would sequence livestream, teaser posting, and on-site decision authority under sponsor pressure; and (4) what extra effort you personally would take before the event to reduce uncertainty without shifting the burden entirely onto local staff. Be concrete about roles, timing, limits, and fallback actions.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that the opening is not just entertainment footage but includes a protected protocol segment tied to the transported flame and formal civic sequence.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers an operational consequence from the clues: some moments/objects in the opening require deference, low disruption, and different filming behavior than a generic parade. No credit for merely saying 'respect the culture' or naming a festival.

rubric.point: Rejects the attractive near-miss of treating the earliest high-energy arrival shots as the main capture target for aggressive close-ups.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly bounds the sponsor/government pressure for instant dramatic footage and explains why a global event-coverage default would misfire here. Partial credit if it mentions caution but still centers success on getting as close as possible throughout the arrival.

rubric.point: Makes the primary execution-axis decision on timing and placement for the roaming camera team.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer places the single roaming team so it can capture the formal ignition/transfer sequence without intruding on the central object or quiet segments, while using other coverage methods for parade energy earlier. Partial credit if it uses correct cultural knowledge but applies it to the wrong stage, such as over-protecting all parade footage or focusing only on performances.

rubric.point: Designs a concrete posting sequence that preserves the ceremony's order instead of letting teaser speed override the protocol-heavy moment.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer delays or edits the teaser plan so the first fast post comes from a safer segment or after confirmation that the formal moment has been captured appropriately, with explicit conditions for what cannot be clipped live. No credit for generic 'check before posting' language without a sequencing rule.

rubric.point: Assigns on-site authority and escalation in a way that protects the protocol boundary under delay pressure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer gives a specific person or role near the ceremony the power to block intrusive repositioning or posting during sensitive moments, with a narrow escalation route. Partial credit if authority remains with the remote producer by default or if everyone must agree, causing delay or pressure on locals.

rubric.point: Shows motivational CQ through visible, costly follow-through rather than low-cost politeness.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer includes personal effort such as making extra pre-event calls, reviewing prior ceremony footage, staying available for live adaptation, or taking on inconvenient coordination work to reduce ambiguity without demanding that local staff solve everything. No credit for answers that simply say 'ask the local coordinator' or 'wait for guidance on the day.'

rubric.point: Builds a repair/fallback plan for uncertainty that is bounded and operational.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies fallback content, alternative camera behavior, or a hold-post rule if the timing shifts or the team cannot verify whether a segment has entered a more formal/protected phase. Partial credit for broad delay, broad consultation, or the longest/safest possible plan without execution triggers.

reference_outline: Infer from the transported flame, later ignition by senior political leadership, and notes about quiet behavior near a central object that the opening contains a civic-protocol core, not only festival spectacle.
Name the tempting near-miss: using a generic global broadcast logic that treats the procession arrival as a free-for-all visual peak and rewards immediate close, dramatic footage everywhere.

Place the single roaming team where it can cover the formal ignition/hand-off sequence from a respectful distance and stable angle; use fixed/wider shots or secondary coverage for crowd energy earlier rather than chasing the central object aggressively.

Set a posting order: livestream continues, but the fast teaser should come from a non-sensitive parade or crowd segment unless and until the formal moment is completed and cleared by the on-site authority; do not rush out a clip centered on the protected object/sequence.

Give on-site decision authority to the local logistics coordinator or designated ceremony-side lead to freeze repositioning, silence crew movement, and hold social posting if the event shifts into a quieter or more formal phase; remote producer escalates only for non-protocol technical tradeoffs.

Show motivational CQ by absorbing effort personally before the event: make extra calls, confirm sequence markers, review prior openings for cues, and remain on live standby, instead of pushing ambiguity resolution onto local staff at the last minute.

Include a bounded fallback: if timing slips or the team cannot verify the phase, default to wide respectful coverage, capture ambient crowd material for the sponsor clip, and postpone any close-up package until the formal segment is complete.

scenario: A regional nonprofit is sending a two-person media team to record short footage at an annual civic commemoration on Tanna for a donor update due next week. question: Which approval decision is most defensible for the field manager to sign off today?

options.A: Approve filming if the crew keeps a respectful distance, secures standard event permission from organizers, and gathers individual consent from anyone shown closely in the footage.
options.B: Approve filming once the provincial tourism office confirms visitor access rules, and require the crew to follow whatever viewing limits and seating directions officials provide on arrival.
options.C: Approve filming after the local host circulates the plan to several community leaders in advance, and let the crew rely on whichever boundary guidance appears most restrictive on the day.
options.D: Approve filming with existing permits, but require the host to identify the person controlling access around the formal performance area and route the crew through that person for placement changes on site.

scenario:
You are leading a multicultural museum-production team in Santiago that has 9 days to finalize a traveling exhibition launch tied to Tapati Rapa Nui. The sponsor from mainland Chile wants strong visitor numbers and has asked for a teaser campaign promising 'rare access to ancestral practices.' A Rapanui liaison has already sent you three things: a draft list of performance clips that were filmed during last year's festival, a note saying the festival is one of the few moments when older practices are shown in ways that contemporary audiences can see, and a separate request that clan names and youth-participant captions be reviewed carefully before anything is released. Meanwhile, your legal manager says that because the footage was recorded in a public festival, the safest default is to treat all clips alike unless there is a documented restriction. Your marketing lead from Spain wants to cut a fast trailer focused only on the most visually dramatic scenes. Your Chilean government contact wants the ministry logo placed on all digital materials before Monday's approval meeting. You have budget for only two same-day review calls, and if you miss the Monday meeting the launch will likely be delayed by a month.

In the last internal thread, some teammates argued that the cleanest approach is to release the full trailer now, then handle any sensitive concerns later through takedowns or caption edits. Others argued for freezing all public-facing material until a complete cultural review is done, even if that means missing the sponsor deadline. No one on the thread has explained exactly which parts of the package may create different kinds of risk, and the Rapanui liaison is offline for the next 14 hours because of travel.
question: Write a decision memo for your team that sets the next 48-hour plan. Your memo must identify what you can reasonably infer from the information already available, what you should not assume, and how you will decide which materials move forward now versus later. Be explicit about stakeholder sequence, what evidence deserves the most weight, what tempting default assumption you are rejecting, and how you will brief the sponsor and ministry contact without either overpromising access or stalling the whole launch.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the core mechanism behind public visibility at Tapati Rapa Nui
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that festival visibility does not make all representations interchangeable; it treats the festival as a specific public interface balancing community heritage needs with outsider audiences, not as blanket permission or blanket prohibition.

rubric.point: Uses the right execution axis: selective release sequencing rather than all-or-nothing treatment
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer separates materials into at least two release paths for the next 48 hours based on role, content, and review need; no credit for 'release everything now' or 'hold everything until total certainty.'

rubric.point: Weights evidence narrowly and updates assumptions metacognitively
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer states what the current evidence does support, what remains uncertain, and what specific missing evidence would change the decision; low credit for generic 'consult more' or for using public-footage status as decisive proof.

rubric.point: Rejects the polished near-miss default
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly bounds the attractive imported assumption that public festival footage can be managed later through standard legal/marketing cleanup because it was publicly recorded; partial credit if the answer notices risk but still treats all clips under one generic public-event rule.

rubric.point: Designs stakeholder sequence around the actual pressure points
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan sequences internal legal/marketing alignment, targeted review of clan/youth/caption-linked materials, and a sponsor/ministry briefing that preserves momentum without finalizing the wrong assets; low credit for broad meetings with everyone or vague stakeholder inclusion.

rubric.point: Translates diagnosis into concrete package decisions
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer names which kinds of assets can advance now (for example, neutral launch framing, dates, approved logos, non-claiming copy) and which require hold/review (for example, dramatic ritualized clips, lineage-linked labeling, youth or clan-specific representations); low credit for abstract respect language without asset-level consequences.

rubric.point: Applies metacognitive CQ under ambiguity
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer shows calibrated revision: it does not collapse into certainty, but it still acts provisionally on enough evidence now, identifies one or two cues that should not be over-weighted, and states how the next review call will test the right uncertainty rather than merely confirm the team's default frame.

reference_outline: State a working diagnosis: Tapati Rapa Nui is a rare public setting where older practices are presented across multiple simultaneous relationships, so 'public' here means managed interface rather than unrestricted content equivalence.
Choose the primary execution move: do a selective two-track release plan within 48 hours instead of either full release or full freeze.

Advance low-risk materials now: event announcement, schedule, sponsor/ministry branding placement, and copy that frames the exhibition as engagement with living heritage without promising unrestricted access to all ancestral content.

Hold and triage higher-risk materials for the limited review windows: visually dramatic reenactment clips, clan-linked naming, youth-participant captions, and any asset that turns community-facing performance into generic tourist spectacle.

Use evidence weighting explicitly: give more weight to the liaison's separate caution about names/youth review and to the note that the festival serves both community and outsider functions; give less weight to the legal default that all public footage is equivalent just because it was recorded in an open event.

Sequence stakeholders tightly: first align legal and marketing on the selective-release rule, then use one review call to sort asset categories and one to confirm wording/caption boundaries, then brief sponsor and ministry with a provisional package and a clear rationale for why some assets await confirmation.
Name and reject the near-miss: do not rely on global event-marketing logic that promises rare access now and fixes sensitivity later through takedowns or edits.

Show metacognitive calibration: specify what remains unknown, what exact answer from the next calls would change release status, and how to communicate uncertainty without sounding indecisive or letting deadline pressure force the wrong inference.

scenario: A newcomer coordinating media coverage for a community celebration on Ambrym needs to deliver a short photo package to a donor by the same evening. The local organizer is juggling seating and clothing arrangements for guests, and transport back to town leaves soon.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The truck for town leaves not long after the afternoon program. If you need pictures for your donor tonight, it will have to be quick. We still have to place visitors and sort what everyone should wear.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I’ll keep the camera work light and stay out of the way. To avoid guessing, I’ll ask someone on your side where guests should stand and whether there are moments I should not shoot.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That helps. Some visitors from Port Vila are coming too, and they always want a fuller set of images than we expect.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I can handle that. Rather than only taking the open dance area, I’ll also ask if one of the senior men can walk me through the inside spaces for a few contextual shots, then I’ll share only a tight selection with the donor.

dialogue.text: We are already short on time, and there are children running around everywhere. The committee still wants the visitors settled before things begin.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I’ll move fast: first the public performance, then a very brief escorted look behind the scenes so I can avoid using random phone photos from guests later. I’ll keep the group small and dress plainly.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right, just make sure your file is ready before the truck goes.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I will. I’ll get the overview images early, then confirm names and send the package before we leave.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer sounds careful and consultative, but the decisive behavior is miscalibrated: they plan to seek access to interior male-restricted ceremonial space for donor context shots instead of limiting coverage to the public parts and following local guidance only within permitted areas. scenario: A newcomer from an NGO is helping finalize a printed program and a short donor note for a clan-hosted life-stage feast on Lihir. brief_reason: The newcomer shows strong follow-through and accepts real cost, but directs that effort into adding spoken visitor appreciation in the immediate slot after Rarhum. The seed-specific error is the sequence and form of participation around Rarhum: guests are expected to remain quiet and highly respectful there, so creating a donor-facing verbal close at that point is culturally miscalibrated even though it looks organized and considerate.

scenario: You are helping a family committee on Aitutaki draft one English WhatsApp update about a cousin’s twenty-first celebration during the late-December return season. question: Which draft message is the best one to send now?

options.A: We’ll keep the birthday on the original date so travel plans stay stable, and anyone who arrives later can join a separate family dinner and send a gift contribution remotely.
options.B: We’ll move the birthday to the first free evening after the dance rounds, while keeping the hall work and donation collections as separate volunteer activities for those available earlier.
options.C: We’ll shift the birthday to the first evening when most return groups are on island, and we’ll confirm it now with a shared prep roster and pooled family-and-village contribution list.
options.D: We’ll keep the birthday week unchanged, ask each returning household to nominate someone for the hall roster, and leave the celebration itself as a private meal for the immediate family.

scenario:
You lead a three-person field production team preparing a short festival documentary segment in Wogosia, Oceania, for a regional broadcaster. The local organizing committee has approved filming of the opening day procession and a pre-ceremony food-preparation sequence, but final camera positions must be locked by 5 p.m. today because boat transport and battery deliveries are being scheduled tonight. Your team includes a female producer from Australia who handles on-site interviews, a male camera operator from Fiji, and a remote executive producer in Singapore who keeps pushing for a single continuous shoreline shot that shows both the food handoff and the ceremonial structures in one elegant sequence for the sponsor reel. 

The committee’s written note is brief and non-explanatory: 'Certain structures and adjoining areas are under stricter limits during preparations. Please avoid disruptions and coordinate movements carefully.' In today’s walk-through, you notice that some participants carrying food containers take a longer route behind the structures instead of the direct beach path, and one elder quietly redirects your producer when she starts to follow the shorter front route. Nobody gives a full explanation, and the executive producer messages that changing the shot plan now will increase cost and may make the sponsor think your team is disorganized. 

You must send a same-day operations memo that assigns roles, movement routes, and communication rules for tomorrow morning’s shoot. If you are too vague, the crew may improvise on site. If you over-restrict access without justification, the executive producer may overrule you and demand the original continuous shot.
question: Write the operations memo you would send to your team and executive producer. Your memo must: (1) diagnose what mechanism is likely driving the movement pattern and access limits from the available evidence, (2) identify the most tempting but miscalibrated assumption behind keeping the original shot design, and (3) set a concrete filming plan with exact role assignments, approach routes, no-go areas, briefing wording, and a fallback if the sponsor challenges the change. Focus on the execution choices that matter most tomorrow morning rather than giving a general cultural-respect statement.

rubric.point: Infers that the key issue is not only ceremony access but route-specific and space-specific restriction around the structures during preparation.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer translates the evidence into an operational diagnosis about movement paths and adjoining ritual space, not just 'some sacred areas' or 'be respectful.' Partial credit if it notices restriction but treats it as a generic filming-permit issue.

rubric.point: Adjusts the plan on the primary execution axis: who moves where, from which side, and in what sequence.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly prevents the female producer from using the front beach approach near the restricted structures and redesigns coverage so needed footage is captured without crossing that route or entering restricted space. Partial credit if it merely says to 'ask before approaching' or 'keep distance' without route and role consequences.

rubric.point: Rejects the attractive near-miss of preserving the continuous shoreline shot through generic consent, safety, or equal-access logic.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer names a plausible imported assumption—such as once filming is approved, the team can use any efficient path if they are polite or escorted—and explains why that would still misfire here. No credit for attacking an obviously rude or reckless plan instead of the polished near-miss.

rubric.point: Uses behavioural CQ through visible wording, timing, and briefing discipline rather than abstract sensitivity.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo includes concrete pre-brief language, channel, and timing such as locking routes before arrival, instructing no on-the-spot improvisation, and giving concise wording for how crew should respond if redirected. Partial credit if the answer is culturally aware but leaves execution to informal judgment in the moment.

rubric.point: Designs a workable alternative shot plan that still meets production goals under deadline and sponsor pressure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer replaces the original single sweeping shot with a feasible segmented sequence or angle plan that preserves sponsor value while respecting the movement boundary. Partial credit if it cancels too much coverage without replacement or proposes an ideal but logistically vague redesign.

rubric.point: Assigns roles and authority clearly enough to prevent accidental breach under ambiguous local feedback.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if one person is made responsible for route enforcement/on-site stop decisions and the team members’ tasks are differentiated by location and access, with no assumption that all crew can shadow each other. Partial credit for general coordination without explicit role boundaries.

rubric.point: Builds in a repair and escalation plan if the sponsor or remote executive resists the change.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes a narrow, performance-oriented justification and fallback—such as explaining that route restrictions create a non-negotiable placement limit during preparation, offering substitute footage, and escalating only the revised plan rather than reopening access debate. Partial credit if it relies on broad statements like 'the locals prefer this' or suggests delaying the whole shoot.

reference_outline: Diagnose from the elder’s redirection, the longer rear movement pattern, and the committee note that restrictions likely apply to approach paths and the area in front of the ceremonial structures during preparation, not just entry into a ritual moment.

Change the execution plan by banning the front beach approach near the structures for the female producer and any unnecessary crew movement there; assign coverage from permitted distance/angles and use the male camera operator or fixed-position capture only where movement can stay outside the sensitive route.

State the near-miss explicitly: assuming broad filming approval means any efficient path is acceptable if the crew is respectful, escorted, or trying to minimize disruption; reject this because the hidden boundary is spatial and directional, not just about intention.

Send a pre-shoot memo tonight and repeat a short in-person briefing before departure: no improvising for a better angle, no following participants along the direct front route, stop and reset immediately if redirected, and route questions go through one designated lead.

Offer a sponsor-safe alternative package: separate shots of food preparation, rear-side handoff arrival, ambient shoreline footage from a compliant distance, and later structure visuals from approved placement, instead of one continuous front-facing shoreline sequence.

Assign one on-site decision owner—ideally the team lead or camera lead—to enforce movement boundaries, while the producer handles interviews only from pre-cleared positions and the remote executive is informed that access constraints affect shot geography, not overall delivery.

Use concise escalation wording focused on production reliability and stakeholder trust: the revision reduces the risk of invalidating local cooperation or losing the shoot entirely; if challenged, defend the placement limit and offer edited continuity in post rather than renegotiating route access on the morning itself.

scenario: You manage visitor operations for a regional museum team preparing a short documentary and photo package about a community ceremony in the Solomon Islands. The local committee has approved limited access on the festival day, but only for a 40-minute window between the fish offering and the next scheduled segment. Your crew includes a female producer, a male camera operator, and two local logistics hires. A sponsor in Australia wants a visually strong sequence showing food being brought to the ceremonial structures, and the museum director has warned that if the crew misses that sequence, the entire trip may be judged a failure. Budget is tight, so there is no second filming day. In message history, the committee repeatedly confirms timing, says the food portion will still be visible, and notes that the producer should finalize shot order before arrival. No one states any explicit access rule. A draft plan from headquarters proposes the most efficient setup: have the producer walk the route first, stand in front of each structure to cue camera angles, then ask whichever nearby helpers are free to carry bowls into view so the team can capture one continuous shot. Another teammate argues this is safest because it treats everyone equally and avoids making assumptions about gendered roles. You need to send a field-execution memo tonight.
question: Write the field-execution memo you would send to your crew. Your memo must do four things: (1) infer the likely cultural mechanism shaping access and movement from the available evidence; (2) identify the tempting but miscalibrated assumption in headquarters' plan; (3) give a concrete filming and coordination sequence for who approaches which areas, from what direction, in what order, and who must not do what; and (4) specify the exact wording, role assignment, and on-the-spot repair steps you will use if the planned shot becomes difficult under time pressure. Do not answer with generic respect, broad consultation, or 'wait and see' advice—give an operational plan that still protects the work objective.

rubric.point: Diagnoses a specific access-and-movement restriction tied to the ceremonial structures and the food-delivery stage.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that the key issue is not general sensitivity but a narrow rule about who may approach the ceremonial houses, especially during food delivery, and that movement path matters. No credit for vague claims such as 'be respectful around sacred spaces' without operational consequences.

rubric.point: Rejects the attractive near-miss plan based on equality, efficiency, or standard film blocking.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly identifies headquarters' plan as tempting but wrong because it places the wrong person in front of or into the restricted zone and treats role interchangeability as neutral when it is not. Partial credit if the answer merely says 'confirm locally first' without naming the execution error.

rubric.point: Sets the correct behavioural sequence for approach, placement, and role assignment.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer assigns any approach to the canoe-house area and front-facing shot setup to permitted male roles, keeps the female producer out of entry/front-path execution there, and preserves the food-delivery objective by using a back-entry or offset capture plan rather than canceling the shot. No full credit if correct knowledge is applied to the wrong actor, wrong path, or wrong stage.

rubric.point: Uses behavioural CQ through exact wording, channel, and timing rather than generic deference.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo includes concrete briefings such as pre-assigning roles before arrival, using concise private crew instructions, and giving active real-time wording that prevents the wrong movement before it happens. Answers that rely on soft generalities like 'follow their lead' or public improvisation under pressure do not score highly.

rubric.point: Balances task delivery with cultural risk control under deadline pressure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer preserves the sponsor's filming goal through an alternative shot design, sequence, or camera placement while explicitly refusing the faster but miscalibrated route. No credit for answers that solve the risk by abandoning the work objective when a narrower adaptation is available.

rubric.point: Provides a concrete repair plan if the crew is already moving into a restricted pattern.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies how to stop or redirect the action immediately and discreetly—for example, rerouting the wrong crew member, switching who carries/positions items, or changing angle/channel without debate in front of ceremonial space. Low credit for broad statements about apologizing later or escalating after the breach.

reference_outline: Infer from the timing note, food visibility emphasis, and repeated preplanning requests that the sensitive point is the post-offering food-delivery interaction at the ceremonial canoe houses, with restrictions tied to who may enter or pass in front.

Do not use the headquarters default of letting the female producer walk the route first or cue angles from directly in front of the structures; identify that as a plausible global-production shortcut that misreads local access rules.

Pre-brief the crew before arrival: female producer stays in an off-path coordination position, male camera operator or permitted male helper handles any approach near the houses, and food movement is captured without the producer entering or crossing the front approach.
Design the shot around permitted movement: capture delivery from a side or back-entry angle, or stage coverage in two segments rather than one continuous front-facing efficiency shot if needed.

Use behavioural CQ visibly: send exact role instructions in advance, give short private commands at the moment of movement, and intervene before the wrong person steps into the restricted path rather than correcting after the fact.

If pressure rises, protect both goal and boundary by switching operators, redirecting route, or dropping the continuous-shot preference—not by widening access, improvising equality-based role swaps, or relying on generic politeness.

If a breach is about to occur, stop action quietly, pull the crew member back, reassign the movement to the permitted male role, and resume with a modified angle; repair should be immediate and discreet, not a public discussion.

scenario: A university team from overseas will attend a morning welcome at a marae near Auckland before signing a research partnership that afternoon. The team lead must brief six visitors today. Finance can reimburse a single team expense quickly, but individual cash claims are slow, and the host contact is reachable before close of business.
question: Which sequence should the team lead use before the visit?

options.A: Set one team cash amount this afternoon, prepare it in an envelope, and check with the host contact on arrival where in the morning program it should be presented.
options.B: Ask the host contact today how guest contributions are usually handled and when they are given, then organize a pooled amount the team is comfortable offering and brief one presenter.
options.C: Wait until the group reaches the marae, ask a local staff member how visitors usually contribute, then collect equal cash from everyone and present it later that day.
options.D: Use the fast finance route first to buy a formal hosted gift on the university card, then contact the host only if a special presentation step still needs arranging.

scenario: A newcomer helping coordinate a year-end village program on Aitutaki is juggling an outside sponsor's documentation requirements and the village fundraising flow. A visiting group has just finished its segment, and the newcomer must decide how to handle the sponsor envelope, the fund table, and the transition to the next item.

roles.local: Moana, a village committee member managing the day's schedule
roles.newcomer: Eli, a newly arrived program coordinator working with an external sponsor

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The sponsor rep wants the envelope counted and photographed before sunset, and the next youth team is already waiting by the side path. The school repair table is still open.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I can separate the sponsor paperwork from the village collections so nothing gets mixed. I'll have the MC acknowledge the visiting group, then I'll take the envelope straight to the table for the receipt.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: They came over early this morning and are still gathered near the front. A few aunties are carrying things in now, so the space will tighten up fast.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I'll keep the front clear. I'll skip any handover there, get the sponsor photo done, and note a contribution for the repair fund under their group's name once the rush settles.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The drummer is asking whether to hold the break, and the sound desk wants a cue in the next minute.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: No need to hold it. A short thanks from the mic is enough for now, and I can process the village side after the program so the accounts stay neat.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right, I can clear the path and send the next team in.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Great. Let's move them straight on and I'll close out both the sponsor receipt and the repair-fund entry at the end.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: Eli sounds organized and supportive, but misreads the event as something that can be handled with public thanks now and a clean ledger entry later. The seed-specific issue is timing and scope: the host side's reciprocal giving/participation belongs in the exchange itself, not as an after-program accounting action.

scenario: A marine cleanup team on Niue needs local shoreline helpers for a Monday dawn launch. The only access point for the first pickup is beside a church green. The visiting lead must lock the sequence today because fuel, boat time, and radio permits are already booked. A local coordinator's factual note says many residents attend both morning and afternoon services on Sunday.
question: Which sequence best fits the situation?

options.A: Send the full Sunday briefing now, ask helpers to reply once services finish, then do the shoreline walk near the church-side pickup point before sunset.
options.B: Send a short note now holding Monday dawn plans, avoid Sunday activity around that pickup area during service times, then confirm details with helpers later Sunday evening.
options.C: Let each helper choose any Sunday time for a private call, gather preferences through the day, then issue the final Monday sequence to everyone that night.
options.D: Meet the helpers briefly near the pickup point before the morning service starts, leave the afternoon open, then send the final Monday instructions after the second service.

scenario: You are coordinating a three-country production team for a tourism board and an airline partner that want a 90-second launch video announcing a new route to Niue. The editor in Auckland needs final footage by Monday 18:00. The local host in Niue has already booked a boat operator, two village interviewees, and shoreline access near a church-facing bay. A sponsor executive in Sydney pushes for the most 'efficient' plan: film the coastline, drone pass, and two family scenes on Sunday because roads will be quieter and the international crew can fly out that evening. The local host's recent messages are neutral but specific: 'Saturday is busy with setup; Sunday morning and later afternoon many people are occupied; some places are better avoided at certain times; Monday is cleaner for community-facing shots, but we lose the early edit window.' The boat operator has not refused, but replied only, 'Can do if confirmed soon; some hours are easier than others.' The brand team also wants one shot of visitors entering the water near the bay because similar footage performed well in other Pacific campaigns. Budget allows only one extra half-day if you change the sequence, and your supervisor will judge your plan on both delivery and stakeholder management.
question: Write a decision memo for your supervisor that recommends the shoot sequence for Saturday-Monday. Your memo must: (1) diagnose the most important local mechanism shaping the schedule from the evidence given, (2) identify the tempting imported assumption behind the sponsor's Sunday plan and why it is miscalibrated here, and (3) give a concrete coordination plan covering which scenes move, which scenes stay possible, who needs which message first, and how you will protect both deadline and local relationships without simply expanding consultation or postponing everything.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden scheduling mechanism from the evidence, not just 'religion matters.'
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that Sunday in Niue has protected worship/rest/family expectations with reduced normal activity, and that this affects both business availability and appropriateness of visible recreational or community-facing filming during service-linked periods. Partial credit for vague mention of a holiday or church without execution consequences.

rubric.point: Applies the mechanism to the exact scenes, times, and locations in this case.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly avoids Sunday boat/water/community-facing filming near the church-facing bay or village-linked areas during likely service times, and reallocates those shots to Saturday or Monday. Partial credit if Sunday is treated as generally 'sensitive' but the answer still keeps the water/bay sequence or interview setup in the wrong window.

rubric.point: Rejects the polished near-miss plan based on the wrong imported assumption.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer identifies the sponsor logic as a generic efficiency heuristic such as 'quiet roads = good filming day' or 'weekend availability = lower disruption' and explains why that global default misreads local meaning here. No full credit for answers that merely say the sponsor is being disrespectful without naming the mistaken operational assumption.

rubric.point: Uses cognitive CQ by separating plausible explanations and weighting evidence correctly.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer shows why the local host's indirect timing cues, the boat operator's conditional wording, and the church-facing bay detail together outweigh a generic production reading such as weather, logistics, or personal preference. Partial credit if the answer notices the cues but treats them as too ambiguous to act on.

rubric.point: Provides a concrete role-and-sequence coordination plan.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies who is told first and why, such as aligning supervisor/sponsor expectations before reconfirming with the local host and operator, then issuing a revised call sheet with scene-level changes. Partial credit for broad statements like 'communicate with stakeholders' without order, role, or decision content.

rubric.point: Designs a deadline-preserving alternative rather than the broadest or safest delay.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer protects Monday delivery through a narrower reschedule—for example moving scenic and water footage off Sunday while preserving usable indoor, transit, prep, or non-sensitive B-roll elsewhere, or buying the single extra half-day strategically. Low credit for cancel-everything Sunday plans, indefinite consultation loops, or answers that sacrifice the edit deadline without justification.

rubric.point: Frames the supervisor-facing justification in operational rather than purely symbolic terms.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo links the schedule choice to concrete work-performance risks: community trust, access continuity, cooperation of hosts/operators, and brand damage from visibly mis-timed imagery. Partial credit for answers that cite culture accurately but do not translate it into production risk boundaries.

reference_outline: Infer from the host's indirect timing message, the church-facing bay location, and the operator's noncommittal response that Sunday carries protected worship/rest expectations in Niue, so apparent physical availability does not equal filming permission or social acceptability.

Make the primary execution-axis decision on timing: do not place boat, swimming, or village/church-adjacent community shots in Sunday service-linked windows; shift those to Saturday if possible or Monday with the extra half-day.

Bound the near-miss explicitly: the sponsor's 'quiet Sunday = efficient filming' logic is a generic production default that misreads a day when reduced activity signals observance, not open operational slack.

Sequence communication by first securing internal approval for a revised call sheet, then resetting sponsor expectations, then confirming scene-level availability with the Niue host and boat operator so local relationships are not put in the position of refusing a bad plan.

Keep progress by using Sunday only for low-visibility, non-disruptive work if needed—such as internal review, ingest, edit prep, or non-community-facing material away from sensitive areas—rather than treating the whole day as a standard exterior shoot window.
Use cognitive CQ by weighing local indirect evidence over generic weekend heuristics, and by avoiding a nearby-market assumption that Pacific coastal footage norms transfer unchanged to Niue.

Include a repair/control mechanism: if any Sunday element must remain, narrow it to activities with no water entry, no village/church-adjacent staging, and no dependence on local families or operators during likely service periods, with a fallback Monday pickup plan.

scenario: A foreign university team is sending two women and one man to a same-day partnership signing at a state training institute in Malaysia. The newcomer's job is to finalize what the delegation will wear for the ceremony, campus walk-through, and official photo before the garment courier closes. The institute has asked for a tidy group presentation, but no detailed dress rule has been stated.

roles.local: Farah, Malaysian operations coordinator at the host institute
roles.newcomer: Elena, newly arrived regional partnerships manager

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The deputy director added a building tour after the signing, and the photographer will take pictures in the lobby and the meeting room. If your team needs anything pressed or altered, I have to tell facilities within the hour.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Got it. I was going to put our delegates in the fitted navy company polos for consistency, but I'll switch the two women to the long-sleeved, looser set we brought for formal visits and keep the polos for the man and the travel day.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That changes the look a bit. The rector's office also asked whether your side wants the group photo before lunch, because everyone will go straight from the signing table.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Let's keep the photo before lunch. I'll send one revised wardrobe line now so your team can set the seating and backdrop once, even if our branding shows less in the pictures.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. One of your delegates asked whether ankle-length trousers are fine or if she should borrow from the welcome rack downstairs.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: She can stay with her own dark trousers if the cut is loose and the top falls well below the hip; otherwise I'll have her take one of the spare longer options before we leave the hotel.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Understood. I just need final names for the front row and who will step onto the stage for the exchange.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Use the same speakers as planned. I'll message the final clothing notes and arrival order in five minutes so you don't have to rework the stage list twice.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer’s decisive behavior matches the seed-specific mechanism by proactively shifting the women’s public presentation toward looser, more body-covering formal dress for a Malaysian state-institution setting. The key execution detail is wardrobe selection before the event flow is locked, even at the cost of branding consistency and speed.

scenario: A regional NGO is finalizing an outdoor launch event in Thimphu that will be photographed for local press. The country manager must approve the wardrobe note today. The cast list includes foreign staff, Bhutanese office employees, and several short-term community liaisons from southern districts. A draft from headquarters says the event memo should use one rule for all local participants to avoid inconsistency in public materials.
question: Which approval line is the most defensible for the manager to authorize in the event documentation?

options.A: Approve the memo with national attire as the rule for all Bhutanese participants, and require any different local dress to be cleared case by case through HR before release.
options.B: Hold the wardrobe memo until counsel and a wider review group confirm whether subgroup-specific exceptions can be documented without creating unequal treatment in public-facing event records.
options.C: Approve the memo with national attire as the default for official public-facing roles, while documenting that local coordinators may clear participants' own community dress where that is already customary.
options.D: Approve a uniform participant-choice memo that removes country-specific attire guidance from the record, so the event file does not appear to endorse a public dress expectation.

scenario:
Your regional events team is finalizing a dawn-to-noon filming schedule in Bali for a global hospitality brand. The shoot includes a short welcome sequence in the outer area of a major temple complex, followed by interviews at a nearby hotel. The client has already sold the campaign internally as showing 'real local atmosphere,' and the temple access window cannot be moved because a separate ceremony will begin later that day. A women-led cast list and wardrobe pull were approved yesterday by the Singapore brand director, who wants the same linen resort look used in a Phuket campaign: sleeveless tops, open shoulders, and light wrap skirts for a 'natural tropical' aesthetic. 

This morning, the Balinese venue coordinator sent a brief message: 'Please ensure attire is proper and correctly arranged for entry. We can help on site if needed, but timing is tight.' No one explicitly rejected the current wardrobe. The producer from Australia argues that the safest move is to keep the approved outfits for brand consistency and just bring shawls in case someone is told to add coverage at the gate. The Indonesian account manager is worried about losing face with the temple side if changes happen publicly at arrival, but also warns that re-costuming everyone now may trigger a delay, a budget overrun, and conflict with the Singapore director, who has final visual sign-off. 

You lead the cross-border project team. You must send a decision memo within 30 minutes telling wardrobe, production, and client-facing staff what to do before the vans leave.
question: Write the decision memo you would send. It must state: (1) what cultural mechanism you infer from the available evidence, (2) which tempting assumption in the current team discussion you would reject or tightly limit, and why, and (3) the exact pre-departure sequence for wardrobe, approvals, and on-site coordination. Make your plan concrete enough that the team could execute it immediately under the deadline, and explain how your choices show sound judgment rather than generic caution.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden mechanism from the scenario evidence
rubric.score_rule: High credit identifies that temple entry for Balinese women requires modest, correctly worn attire as a condition of respectful participation, not merely a flexible visitor-style preference or a last-minute cover-up issue. Low credit treats the issue as generic conservatism, brand sensitivity, or 'dress neatly' without connecting it to the temple setting and correct wearing.

rubric.point: Chooses the correct execution axis: pre-departure wardrobe correction rather than gate-side improvisation
rubric.score_rule: High credit explicitly moves the key decision upstream by changing and checking outfits before travel. Low credit proposes keeping current looks and adjusting only if challenged on arrival, or leaves the decision to the venue gate, which misreads timing and scope.

rubric.point: Rejects or bounds the attractive near-miss plan
rubric.score_rule: High credit directly identifies the tempting imported assumption that globally approved resort styling plus backup shawls is sufficient, and explains why that plan is miscalibrated here even though it seems efficient, brand-safe, and flexible. Low credit accepts shawls as the main solution, or criticizes the current plan only in vague 'be respectful' terms.

rubric.point: Applies cognitive CQ through evidence weighting and scope control
rubric.score_rule: High credit shows why the venue coordinator's wording about 'proper' and 'correctly arranged' should be weighted as diagnostic evidence about entry requirements, despite the absence of an explicit rejection email. It separates culture from generic process noise and avoids overreacting into unnecessary cancellation of the whole shoot. Low credit either ignores the signal, or turns it into broad uncertainty requiring indefinite delay.

rubric.point: Designs a concrete role-and-sequence plan under pressure
rubric.score_rule: High credit assigns immediate actions such as wardrobe revising women's temple looks before departure, client-facing staff informing the Singapore director that temple-segment attire must be adjusted for entry compliance, and on-site staff using the venue helper only for final fit confirmation rather than first-line problem solving. Low credit gives generic advice to 'coordinate with everyone' without sequencing roles or approvals.

rubric.point: Handles approval and relationship risk without letting brand logic override the cultural requirement
rubric.score_rule: High credit preserves stakeholder relationships by framing the change as a location-specific production necessity for the temple segment while protecting hotel/interview looks separately if needed. Low credit either prioritizes visual consistency over entry requirements, or proposes a maximal rebrand of the whole shoot when a narrower adjustment would solve the actual problem.

reference_outline: Infer from 'proper' and 'correctly arranged for entry' in a Bali temple context that the issue is not just neatness but women needing modest, correctly worn temple-appropriate clothing before arrival.
Make the primary decision on timing: do not send the cast in sleeveless, open-shoulder temple looks with backup shawls as the main plan; recostume and check before vans leave.
Tell wardrobe to prepare covered, modest temple outfits for the temple sequence specifically, including a fit check that garments are worn correctly rather than loosely improvised at the gate.

Tell the Singapore brand director immediately that the temple segment requires a location-specific wardrobe exception; preserve approved resort styling for the later hotel interviews if the schedule allows, rather than forcing one look across both settings.
Use the Balinese venue coordinator only for final confirmation or minor adjustment on site, not as the person who discovers first that the team arrived misdressed in public.

Explicitly reject the near-miss logic that generic tropical-resort standards and emergency shawls are an efficient compromise; explain that this treats a likely entry-and-respect requirement as optional styling correction.

Show cognitive CQ by distinguishing among three explanations: brand preference, generic modesty assumptions, and temple-specific attire logic; choose the third because it best explains the wording and the stakes.

Add a calibration step under deadline: if a temple-compliant women’s wardrobe cannot be assembled in time, reduce or redesign the temple segment before departure rather than testing borderline outfits at arrival.

scenario: A museum in Phnom Penh is opening a small exhibit on village textiles and needs one last promotional photo by the afternoon. A newcomer from the regional marketing team is helping style a Cambodian intern for the image using pieces already pulled from storage. The museum director is traveling, the budget is tight, and the photo will go straight to local print once approved.

roles.newcomer: Mina, newly arrived regional marketing manager

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The photographer can only stay until three. We have the checked wrap, a cream blouse, and a long woven cloth from storage. If we miss this slot, the newspaper ad slips a week.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Got it. To keep the image feeling contemporary, I'll use the wrap as the main skirt piece and drape the woven cloth loosely behind her shoulders so it doesn't block the necklace.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The director asked for something that still reads clearly to older visitors, not a fashion shoot. The intern also has to walk through the front hall afterward.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll keep the silhouette long and tidy below, and I'll pin the cloth so it stays in place while she walks, but I'll leave the blouse line open in the photo so it feels lighter and less costume-like.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We only have ten minutes once makeup finishes, and the printer wants the final file immediately. Please make sure the outfit is ready before the school group comes through.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer

scenario: You are a project lead at a global consulting firm. The Japanese client sponsor has already thanked your firm for 'joining properly' and will likely be in photos with the guests. You have one hour before everyone leaves for the airport, no time to shop after arrival, and the US director outranks you and dislikes being micromanaged. You may send one written briefing now and make one follow-up coordination move later today. question: Write a short decision memo to your team describing exactly how you would handle this in the next hour. Your memo must: (1) diagnose what cultural mechanism is most likely operating from the available evidence, without relying on generic global event assumptions; (2) identify the most tempting but miscalibrated interpretation of the invitation; (3) specify the sequence, wording, and target of your written briefing and your one follow-up coordination move; and (4) explain what you would treat as sufficiently certain now versus what remains uncertain, including how your plan manages both relationship risk and time pressure.

rubric.point: Infers the operative dress standard from the invitation and event context
rubric.score_rule: Awards credit only if the answer concludes that the event should be treated as requiring guest-appropriate formality beyond everyday casual wear despite the English wording, and ties that inference to the Japanese wedding context and photo/host implications. No credit for vague statements like 'dress respectfully' or for treating the note as a generic casualization cue.

rubric.point: Correctly identifies and bounds the attractive near-miss assumption
rubric.score_rule: Awards credit only if the answer explicitly rejects the tempting imported assumption that 'no dress code' plus 'come comfortably' means ordinary smart-casual or a generic global default. Partial credit if the answer notices ambiguity but does not name this specific misread or still leaves it operational.

rubric.point: Applies seed-specific exclusions and allowances to the exact people/items at stake
rubric.score_rule: Awards credit only if the answer operationalizes the likely problems with the cream dress, the all-black outfit unless lightening/softening accessories are added, and the chinos-based outfit as likely underdressed, while also recognizing that guests do not need traditional local attire and can use formal Western options. No full credit for naming colors or formality in the abstract without mapping them to these actors.

rubric.point: Designs the briefing on the primary execution axis of timing and sequence
rubric.score_rule: Awards credit only if the answer gives a concrete order of action for the next hour: an immediate group message that sets a working standard and flags specific risk boundaries, followed by one targeted coordination move aimed at the highest-risk or highest-power mismatch. No credit for broad 'check with everyone individually first,' indefinite delay, or a long consultative process that ignores the travel deadline.

rubric.point: Uses metacognitive calibration rather than overconfidence or inertia
rubric.score_rule: Awards credit only if the answer distinguishes what is sufficiently inferable now from what remains uncertain, and still acts. High credit requires a provisional but actionable recommendation, not just 'ask a local' or 'better safe than sorry.' Also penalizes answers that treat the inference as certain without acknowledging residual uncertainty about exact venue styling or host expectations.

rubric.point: Chooses wording and stakeholder handling that protect hierarchy and trust
rubric.score_rule: Awards credit only if the memo proposes language that avoids publicly singling out the senior director while still steering choices precisely, and uses the one follow-up move strategically, such as a private note or direct check with the person whose planned outfit carries the highest visible risk. No credit for blunt correction in a group thread or for purely generic politeness with no execution detail.

rubric.point: Rejects polished but wrong risk controls
rubric.score_rule: Penalizes answers that rely mainly on the longest, safest, or broadest plan: e.g., postponing advice until arrival, telling everyone to wear black because it is always formal, telling them kimono is expected, or escalating to the client for dress confirmation when the available evidence already supports a narrower decision.

reference_outline: Diagnose from the invitation, event type, and photo-sensitive sponsor context that the practical guest baseline should be treated as semi-formal rather than everyday casual, even though the English note appears to soften the instruction.
Name the key near-miss: importing a global assumption that 'no dress code' or 'come comfortably' means standard smart-casual latitude; explain why that would misread this specific context.

Send an immediate short group briefing that sets a concrete floor: formal Western wedding-guest attire is appropriate, avoid white or near-white looks in photos, avoid an all-black look unless balanced with lighter or dressy accessories, and do not assume traditional local clothing is required.

Map guidance to the three people: steer the US director away from cream, flag the Singapore manager’s all-black plan as needing softening/light accessories, and tell the German analyst to upgrade from chinos to a conventional suit-level or equivalent semi-formal outfit.

Use the one follow-up move privately with the highest-risk or highest-power person, likely the US director, with face-saving wording framed around event photos and host expectations rather than personal taste or correction.

Show metacognitive CQ by stating what is known enough to act on now, what remains unknown (exact venue formality, family style preferences), and what evidence would matter only if it can be obtained without delaying action.

Manage time and trust by avoiding a broad consultation loop or client escalation; the plan should be narrow, fast, and relationship-protective because the downside of under-correction is high and the available cultural evidence is already decision-relevant.

scenario: You are the regional operations lead for a software company preparing a three-day client workshop in Tokyo for a major Japanese manufacturer. question: Write the coordination plan you would execute tonight. rubric.point: Rejects or bounds the attractive near-miss plan
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer identifies the tempting imported assumption as treating 'business casual' and hot weather as a universal permission for broadly casual dress, or treating one global message as more efficient than calibrated guidance, and then limits that assumption operationally. rubric.point: Uses behavioural CQ through calibrated channel, audience, and timing
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer chooses visible execution details that fit the context: quickly correcting guidance tonight, handling the VP's earlier message in a tactful way such as a brief private alignment plus an immediate operational note to staff, avoiding a public contradiction that creates confusion, and tailoring wording to different audiences without losing clarity. rubric.point: Designs role-specific instructions and backup workflow
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer distinguishes what junior analysts, senior visitors, and Japan-based staff should do, and includes concrete fallback steps such as borrowing jackets, purchasing compliant items on arrival, bringing a jacket for the kickoff even if not worn all day, or checking photos/items privately before Monday. rubric.point: Balances task performance with relationship and hierarchy risk
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer protects client trust and internal hierarchy simultaneously: it preserves delivery readiness, avoids embarrassing junior staff in front of the client, and manages the VP's authority without either blunt public correction or passive compliance. Low credit if it prioritizes speed, brand energy, or deference to headquarters at the expense of local execution risk.

reference_outline: Infer from the Tokyo client setting, senior-executive kickoff, factory tour, junior-presenter roles, and vague summer flexibility note that attire should be conservative and coordinated, not interpreted through a broad global 'business casual' lens.

Make the primary execution-axis decision on wording and audience: send an immediate operational correction tonight that defines the workshop as conservative client-facing business attire, with only limited summer relaxation such as optional jacket or tie depending on the moment, not broad casual wear.

Privately align with or inform the VP rather than publicly framing the earlier note as wrong, while sending the team a clear staff instruction so uncertainty is removed before travel and shopping windows close.

Give role-specific guidance: junior analysts should err most formal because appearance carries stronger status and professionalism signals for them; senior visitors also avoid casual items even if they can use lighter summer business wear; Japan-based staff can follow the same client-facing standard rather than improvising.

Use behavioural CQ by choosing exact phrasing, timing, and rhythm: fast correction, tactful handling of hierarchy, segmented guidance by audience/role, and practical backup steps instead of vague advice or delay.

scenario: A newcomer from an international NGO is accompanying a local coordinator on a coastal field day in Southeast Asia. After a beachside donor visit, the pair are unexpectedly invited to a community elder's nearby home for tea and a quick thank-you photo before a tightly scheduled media stop back at the hotel. The newcomer has a spare change of event clothes in the van and must decide how to handle the transition without delaying the day.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The elder who helped arrange today's visit just asked if we can stop by his place for tea before the hotel interview. His family is already waiting, so we probably only have fifteen minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Of course. I'll make it quick and change out of the swim shirt into the event polo in the van so I look more presentable for the photo.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Good. After that we'll go straight to the press setup by the waterfront, so there won't be another break.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I'll keep the same outfit for both stops—polo, neat walking shorts, and my cap since the sun is strong. That saves us from changing twice.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We'll be carrying the camera case and donation folder, and the lane to the house is narrow, so we should move fast once we arrive.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll head in first with the folder so we don't keep them waiting, and I'll leave my sneakers on until everything is set down and the photo is done.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right, let's go before the driver loses the parking spot.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Perfect—I can still look tidy for the media piece, and we won't lose time between locations.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer's decisive behavior applies a global efficiency and presentability logic across both locations instead of using situational modesty for a private home visit in this Southeast Asian context. The miscalibration is on execution sequence and dress setup: keeping shorts/cap for the home stop and planning to enter before removing footwear, even though the norm changes by setting.

scenario: A documentary team in Bali is told tonight to prepare backup outfits for three non-Balinese presenters who may be taken into a temple compound at dawn. The local coordinator only sends a few phone photos: one elder in an all-light outfit near offerings, while other attendees appear in muted ceremonial dress with covered legs and matching waist cloths. The producer wants one wardrobe direction sent to the vendor now so fittings can start before sunrise.
question: Which wardrobe direction should the team send now?

options.A: Prepare complete ceremonial sets with covered legs and waist cloths, using a plain light-colored version as the default backup while keeping the garment pieces properly matched and modest.
options.B: Prepare complete ceremonial sets for everyone in all-white outfits, keeping the silhouette modest and the garment pieces matched across the group for visual consistency.
options.C: Prepare modest ceremonial sets in dark or jewel tones with matching waist cloths, avoiding light-colored outfits so the team does not borrow visual cues tied to the ceremony.
options.D: Prepare several neutral modest outfits first, focusing on covered shoulders and legs, and leave color open so each presenter can choose what feels least presumptuous on arrival.

scenario: In Hanoi, a newcomer is coordinating a sponsor booth for a university recruitment fair starting the next morning. The sponsor’s regional team wants a visibly Vietnamese look for photos, the rental shop closes in an hour, and the local office has only two staff available to re-sort outfits tonight.

roles.newcomer: Ethan, newly arrived regional marketing manager

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The sponsor approved the mood board, and the rental shop can still send six traditional sets tonight if we confirm in the next 45 minutes. We have three male interns, two female hosts, and one MC for the opening.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I know this is late, but I’m going to rework the plan instead of dressing everyone the same. Please keep the sets for the two hosts and the opening moment only; I’ll have the men in dark business wear and I’ll call the sponsor myself if they push back.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That means reprinting the lineup board and updating the run sheet tonight. The sponsor asked for 'full traditional presence' in the photo brief.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I’ll stay and fix the brief, the captions, and the lineup order with you. We can still give them a strong local image at the entrance and opening, but I don’t want to force the same outfit across the whole male team just because it looks neat in a template.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The MC is asking whether he should match the hosts during the career talk too, since the photographer will still be there after the ribbon moment.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Let’s keep his formal look for the opening segment and switch him after that. I’d rather absorb the extra coordination than run the entire day on one imported visual rule.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right, then we need final sizes and the revised shot list in fifteen minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Send me the size chart now. I’ll trim the order, rewrite the shot list, and notify the sponsor that the opening visuals stay strong while the rest of the team uses standard event dress.

label: appropriate
