rubric.point: Chooses the right immediate sequence and channel
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer stops fittings and the wardrobe demo immediately, then uses a targeted private channel first to obtain exact guidance on wardrobe/script/photo use from the community participant or responsible community-side contact before sending a broader team reset; lower credit if it starts with a reply-all debate, a public correction, or a general consultation round that burns the deadline.

rubric.point: Uses calibrated wording in the team-facing reset
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer replaces language that frames the items as 'costumes' and gives concrete substitute wording and instructions for slides, scripts, labels, and production notes; lower credit if it only says 'change the language' without operational replacements or if it keeps educational content but retains the original framing terms.

rubric.point: Provides a workable replacement for the segment objective
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer preserves the sponsor's educational/engagement goal through a new format that does not depend on non-Indigenous staff wearing the items, such as approved visuals, host narration, credited participant-led explanation, or removing the try-on mechanic while keeping the segment on schedule; no credit for canceling the whole segment or offering only vague future consultation.

rubric.point: Demonstrates behavioural CQ through timing, audience, and interaction rhythm
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer shows visible adaptation in who is told what, when, and how—for example, halting the risky action now, avoiding public embarrassment, using precise wording, assigning short-term holding instructions, and sequencing a private clarification before broad rollout; lower credit for correct cultural knowledge delivered through the wrong channel or too late.

rubric.point: Adds constraint-aware monitoring or repair
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer includes a 2-hour control plan such as freezing wardrobe assets, revising deck/script ownership, documenting approved terms, and setting a decision checkpoint before the board review; lower credit for broad caution, open-ended delay, or a maximal process that ignores the deadline.

reference_outline: Infer from the wardrobe script request and the proposed try-on/demo setup that the issue is not generic inclusion but whether ceremonial or honor-bearing clothing is being misframed and used by the wrong people in the wrong context.
Immediately stop the fitting/demo and freeze any slide, caption, rehearsal blocking, or photo list that treats the items as 'costumes' or has non-Indigenous staff wear them.

Contact the community-side participant privately first by phone or direct message for rapid clarification on acceptable wording, visuals, and whether any clothing-related content should appear at all; do not begin with a reply-all justification thread.
Send a short team memo that renames the material, removes the volunteer wear-and-show concept, instructs brand and production to hold fittings, and assigns script/deck edits within the hour.

Preserve the segment objective by shifting to approved explanation rather than borrowed enactment: host narration, credited community-led description, approved images, or another non-wearable educational format that can still meet sponsor needs.
Explicitly reject the near-miss assumption that appreciative intent, broad representation, or a family-friendly interactive design makes the wardrobe plan acceptable.

Show behavioural CQ in the exact execution pattern: private clarification first, broader operational reset second, public-facing language cleaned before board review, and no performative over-apology that wastes the timing window.

Set a deadline-bound repair loop: confirm revised script/photo list, assign one owner for terminology checks, and enter the 5 p.m. review with a narrowed, safer segment rather than an unresolved broad consultation.

scenario: A newcomer on a university events team in Canada is finalizing same-day staging for a public opening gathering. A student club wants volunteers at the entrance to look 'festive' for photos, and the print vendor needs the welcome sign wording within an hour. The local coordinator is juggling donors, venue rules, and a late AV setup.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The student club just sent over a box of entrance accessories and asked whether our volunteers can wear them for the opening photos. Also, the sign proof still says 'traditional costume showcase' under the welcome line, and the printer wants approval in 45 minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll handle both now. I'll tell the volunteers to stick to the black event shirts and name badges only, and I'll ask the printer to remove that subheading for the first run so we don't lock in the wrong wording.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That may upset the club—they were pushing for a more visible welcome. One donor also likes big photo moments, and we haven't reached every community contact this morning.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I won't hold the print job waiting for a universal sign-off on the styling idea. I'll send a short note saying we're keeping volunteer dress neutral for the entrance, and I'll ask for a quick review of the revised welcome line before noon.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The club president is in the lobby now and wants to know what changed before she goes onstage. The MC script is already being reformatted.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll tell her directly that we kept the front-of-house team in standard event wear and tightened the wording on the sign so the entrance setup doesn't imply something we weren't asked to present. If she wants, we can still highlight the student hosts by name in the program slide.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Okay. Just keep it brief—we're about to seat people, and facilities is asking whether the extra photo props stay at the doors or go backstage.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Send them backstage for now. I'll clear the sign proof, speak to the club president in the lobby, and keep the entrance line moving.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer calibrates quickly under uncertainty by not treating imitation ceremonial wear as a neutral event costume choice in a Canadian public-event context, and by correcting the wording without waiting for perfect consensus. The decisive culture-fit is the execution choice: keeping non-Indigenous volunteers in standard attire and removing misleading ceremonial language rather than repurposing identity-linked regalia for a festive entrance display.

scenario: A nonprofit in Bolivia is finalizing posters for a teacher-training scholarship. One featured candidate normally appears at public events in her community’s formal layered skirt, shawl, and hat, but the regional office has suggested matching blazers for all poster subjects to keep the campaign "institutional." The studio booking is tomorrow, reprints are expensive, and the candidate has already set aside time for one fitting only.
question: Which wardrobe direction should the project lead choose now for this candidate’s poster image?

options.A: Photograph her in the formal outfit she ordinarily uses for public occasions, and align the poster’s background, framing, and typography with the other subjects rather than matching their clothes.
options.B: Use the same blazer-and-blouse combination planned for the other subjects, keeping clothing uniform across the series and leaving distinction to each candidate’s quote and school placement.
options.C: Keep the layered skirt for recognizability, but switch to a plain jacket and remove the hat and shawl so the image reads more institutional beside the other posters.
options.D: Shoot the main poster in the blazer version, then capture a second image in her usual public outfit for local channels that want a more community-specific variation.

scenario: You lead a multicultural museum-education team preparing a 90-second video and visitor brief for a sponsor-backed field visit in Salvador, Bahia. The video crew will accompany two researchers and one donor representative to document a visit to a Candomble terreiro for an internal learning series due in 48 hours. The sponsor expects strong visuals and has already approved a draft wardrobe note from headquarters: 'All visitors wear white to show respect; smart summer clothing is fine.' A Brazilian logistics coordinator has only sent two short messages: 'Please do not frame this like a cultural attraction' and later, after seeing the draft, 'I still need to confirm whether this house can receive this group.' No one has answered yet on footwear, filming boundaries, or whether the donor representative may join the full visit. One teammate in Spain argues the white-clothing note is safer because it signals formality and keeps the team visually consistent on camera. A U.S. compliance manager says not to change the sponsor-facing brief unless you have explicit written evidence, because the donor is senior and travel starts tomorrow morning. You must send one final operations memo tonight covering wardrobe, who contacts whom, what remains provisional, and what the team should do on arrival if instructions differ from the memo.
question: Write the operations memo you would send tonight. Your answer must: (1) identify the most important assumption in the current plan that you would treat as unstable, and why; (2) specify the sequence of confirmations, including who should contact whom and what you can decide before a reply arrives; (3) set the wardrobe and arrival protocol you would use under uncertainty; and (4) explain how you would brief the sponsor-facing stakeholders without either overcommitting or stalling the project. Be concrete about wording, timing, and what evidence would make you revise the plan.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the unstable assumption in the current draft as the imported dress rule and visitor-access assumption, not merely 'lack of information.'
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer identifies that the current plan wrongly treats the site like a generic visit with a universal symbolic dress default and guaranteed access; partial credit for saying 'confirm details' without specifying those assumptions; no credit if it accepts the white-clothing note as the safe baseline.

rubric.point: Uses the right evidence hierarchy before finalizing wardrobe and attendance scope.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer prioritizes direct confirmation from the specific terreiro or its authorized contact on openness to visitors, dress code, filming, and entry conditions, while treating headquarters preference and adjacent-market logic as weaker evidence; partial credit for broad consultation without naming the specific source of authority.

rubric.point: Makes a seed-specific interim wardrobe decision under uncertainty.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer replaces the white default with a provisional instruction such as conservative, neutral clothing with shoulders and knees covered, plus readiness to adapt immediately on-site; partial credit if it says 'dress respectfully' or 'modestly' without operational details; no credit if it keeps white as the default or recommends visually branded coordinated clothing.

rubric.point: Defines an arrival protocol that calibrates rather than freezes.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer instructs the team to comply immediately with site requests on arrival, including footwear changes if asked, and to treat on-site direction as a trigger to update the plan; partial credit for generic 'follow local guidance'; no credit if the answer relies on the preapproved memo as fixed unless written approval is reissued.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the polished near-miss plan.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly explains why 'everyone wear white because it is safer/respectful/consistent on camera' is a tempting but miscalibrated shortcut; partial credit for changing the plan without explaining the trap; no credit if it preserves the shortcut for sponsor management reasons.

rubric.point: Applies metacognitive CQ through explicit provisionality and revision triggers.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer states what can be inferred now, what remains unknown, and what specific incoming evidence would change wardrobe, attendee scope, or filming behavior; partial credit for generic caution or 'wait for confirmation'; no credit if it either overcommits or becomes so cautious that no actionable plan is sent.

rubric.point: Designs stakeholder communication that preserves progress under hierarchy pressure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo gives sponsor-facing wording that keeps the trip moving while clearly marking site-dependent elements as provisional and narrowing who needs immediate confirmation; partial credit for broad delay or mass escalation; no credit if the answer either hides uncertainty from the sponsor chain or halts the whole visit without first using the available confirmation route.

reference_outline: State that the current risky assumption is not just incomplete logistics but the belief that a generic respect signal and visitor entitlement can be standardized before confirming with the specific terreiro.

Immediately route confirmation through the Brazilian logistics coordinator to the specific terreiro or authorized host contact on four points: whether this house can receive the group, whether the donor representative may attend, what dress is expected, and whether footwear or filming restrictions apply.

Issue a provisional wardrobe instruction tonight: conservative, neutral clothing; covered shoulders and knees; no automatic white requirement; avoid framing attire for visual branding; pack footwear that can be removed easily if requested.

Brief the team that the site is an active place of worship rather than a general-access cultural stop, so access and behavior are conditional; treat any on-site instruction as controlling and comply immediately, especially if asked to remove shoes or adjust participation.

Send sponsor-facing wording that preserves momentum: travel proceeds, final visitor protocol remains subject to host confirmation, and the team is using a site-specific brief rather than a universal template to avoid preventable offense or access problems.

Name revision triggers: confirmation that the house is not open to this group, a house-specific dress instruction, a restriction on filming, or an arrival request that changes footwear/participant scope; update the memo and attendee plan accordingly rather than defending the original draft.
Reject the near-miss explicitly: a white-clothing rule may sound respectful and camera-ready, but using it as the default before host confirmation is overgeneralization, not prudent planning.

scenario: At a teacher-training center in La Paz, a donor photo call is scheduled for the next morning with school directors, trainees, and local press. The branded jackets are stuck in transit. The newcomer is under pressure to make the group look coordinated for a formal public-facing event without delaying the visit.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The jackets still have not arrived. Tomorrow's photos include the donor team, two school directors, and a reporter. The room is booked from eight, so we need a decision tonight.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I'll solve the coordination another way. I won't ask the women on staff to switch into the city-market outfit some families wear for big days just to make the pictures look more local.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That would have been the fastest visual fix. Some of the trainees have those clothes at home, though not everyone does, and we'd need to send people across town.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'd rather spend the budget on neutral blazers from the rental shop by the plaza and keep the clothing expectations the same for everyone on stage. We can bring in the woven table runners from storage so the room still reads as ours.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The rental shop closes in forty minutes, and the donor photographer asked for a shot of the teaching team together with the directors.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll go now, cover the rush fee, and rework the shot list so the teachers and directors still look coordinated. If any staff member comes dressed that way on her own tomorrow, fine, but I don't want us assigning it as event wardrobe.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. I can have maintenance steam the blazers and set the runners before sunrise.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Great. I'll text the photographer tonight with the revised setup and drop the jackets here before nine.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer invests extra time and money to avoid using socially and politically meaningful women's dress as a generic styling tool in a formal public-facing professional setting. The decisive axis is who assigns that appearance and for what institutional purpose, not whether the tone is warm or cautious.

scenario: A regional university in Bolivia is filming a scholarship campaign that will run in city buses, provincial radio pages, and its admissions website next week. The brand team wants the visuals to feel locally grounded, but the legal office has asked for one wardrobe briefing that can be applied consistently across all female presenters in the shoot. One presenter from community outreach usually appears in a full pleated skirt in public events; the other presenters do not.
question: Which wardrobe briefing should the campaign lead issue for this shoot?

options.A: Tell all female presenters they may choose for themselves whether to wear the full pleated skirt on camera, as long as everyone stays within the campaign's general professionalism standard.
options.B: Ask all female presenters in Bolivia-facing campaign materials to use the full pleated skirt, so the local version carries a recognizable public marker across every channel.
options.C: Limit the full pleated skirt to the provincial and community-outreach scenes, while keeping the city-campus and website shots in the standard corporate wardrobe used elsewhere.
options.D: Do not assign the full pleated skirt as a campaign styling element; keep each presenter in her usual professional public dress, including it only where it is already part of that presenter's own public identity.

scenario: A bridal studio in São Paulo is preparing a styling brief for a Muslim bride. The studio mainly stocks mainstream wedding gowns, but its seamstress can alter one look before the first fitting tomorrow. The bride's inspiration folder mixes embellished white dresses, fitted bodices, draped headpieces, and custom sleeve ideas.
question: Which direction should guide the brief for the first fitting?

options.A: Use an international Muslim-bridal template as the base look, then localize fabrics and ornament after the bride reacts to the silhouettes available in the studio.
options.B: Treat the first fitting like ordinary modest daywear planning, keeping bridal trend elements restrained until later rounds clarify how much ceremony styling the bride wants.
options.C: Build the look from current Brazilian bridal silhouettes first, then solve coverage through add-on layers and matching pieces once the main dress shape is approved.
options.D: Start by mapping the bride's celebration-specific coverage expectations, then construct the bridal look creatively from available gowns, alterations, and accessories rather than a fixed imported formula.

scenario: You lead a three-country event-production team preparing a wedding microsite and guest-facing style guide for a couple in São Paulo. The launch is in 36 hours because printed inserts, venue screens, and the RSVP page all have to go live together. The Brazilian account manager has sent only fragmentary notes: the ceremony will be religious, there may also be a larger evening celebration, and the bride wants the materials to feel 'elegant, celebratory, and unmistakably hers.' No one has provided a finished wardrobe brief. A designer in Spain proposes using a photo layout with progressively more glamorous outfit examples for the party section than for the ceremony section, arguing that guests usually read wedding receptions as a more relaxed dress phase. A U.S. brand director supports this because it reduces rework and matches global wedding-industry patterns that separate formal ceremony attire from freer party attire. Meanwhile, the couple has already rejected one draft for feeling 'generic' and the venue partner is pressing for final visuals today. You cannot ask the couple 20 open-ended questions because the account manager says they are overwhelmed and slow to respond, but you can send one tightly scoped clarification request and you can redesign the guide structure before launch.
question: Write a decision memo to your team that sets the dress-guidance approach for the microsite and inserts. Your memo must: (1) diagnose the most important cultural mechanism you think is operating from the limited evidence, (2) identify the tempting assumption in the Spain/U.S. proposal and explain why it is risky here, (3) decide how the guide should handle ceremony and party sections on the main execution axis of visual/content sequencing, and (4) specify one clarification request, one internal approval step, and one fallback if the couple does not answer before launch. Be concrete about wording, examples, and what should and should not vary across the two event segments.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden mechanism as continuity of modesty expectations across wedding formats, with variation in styling rather than a switch to less covering for the party.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires inferring from the Brazil Muslim wedding context that ceremony format may vary but baseline covering expectations likely do not relax between segments; partial credit for noticing religious/formal sensitivity without tying it to continuity across both ceremony and party; no credit for generic 'be respectful' statements.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the attractive near-miss that reception attire should be framed as more revealing, freer, or categorically less modest than ceremony attire.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires naming the imported wedding-industry assumption as the risk and explaining its misfit in this case; partial credit for saying 'don't assume' without specifying the mistaken direction; no credit if the answer preserves a staged relaxation model or treats it as the safest default.

rubric.point: Makes a seed-specific execution decision on sequencing and scope for the guide.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires proposing parallel guidance across ceremony and party that keeps the same modesty baseline while varying style cues, embellishment, fabric, color, silhouette detail, or formality expression; partial credit for merging everything into one vague section or for separating sections without controlling the baseline; no credit for using ceremony vs. party as a modesty gradient.

rubric.point: Applies cognitive CQ by distinguishing culture-specific logic from generic global SOP, brand convention, or adjacent-market intuition.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires showing why the globally common wedding heuristic is not enough evidence here and using scenario facts to choose the narrower interpretation; partial credit for mentioning 'different cultures differ'; no credit for answers driven mainly by process convenience, industry norm, or abstract inclusion language.

rubric.point: Designs one tightly scoped clarification request that tests the right uncertainty without outsourcing the whole decision.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires a targeted question such as whether any guest-facing examples should differ by event segment in style details while keeping coverage expectations consistent, or asking for approval on draft wording that preserves one baseline; partial credit for broad requests for all attire preferences; no credit for recommending delay until full consultation.

rubric.point: Specifies an internal approval route and fallback that control reputational risk under deadline.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires a concrete step such as holding brand/legal or account approval on the no-relaxation baseline before publication and using a conservative-but-elegant launch version if no reply arrives; partial credit for generic 'get sign-off'; no credit for fallback plans that default to global party norms because they are common or visually attractive.

rubric.point: Translates the diagnosis into operational wording or example design choices.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires concrete execution consequences such as avoiding copy like 'more relaxed/revealing for the evening' and instead using phrasing that differentiates celebration style, ornamentation, or sophistication without implying reduced coverage; partial credit for abstract references to tone; no credit for culture labels without design implications.

reference_outline: State that the key inference is not 'religious ceremony equals strict, party equals relaxed' but that in this Brazil Muslim wedding context the expected degree of body covering likely remains stable across both the religious ceremony and any larger celebration.

Explain that the Spain/U.S. proposal imports a plausible global wedding heuristic—reception attire becomes freer—and that this is the main trap because it mistakes event-phase difference for a change in modesty boundary.

Set the primary sequencing decision: keep separate ceremony and party sections only if both preserve the same modesty baseline, and let the difference appear through styling variables such as embellishment, luxury, color richness, tailoring, or festive detailing rather than exposure.

Send one narrow clarification request asking the couple or account manager to confirm whether they want distinct style expression across ceremony and celebration while maintaining the same coverage expectations, instead of asking for a full attire brief.

Require internal approval on the exact guest-facing wording and imagery so that no screen, insert, or RSVP page implies that evening attire should uncover more; route sign-off through the account lead or brand approver before launch.

Use a fallback launch version if no reply arrives: publish elegant, non-generic guidance that treats both segments as modest in baseline and avoids any copy that frames the party as a relaxation of coverage rules.
Show cognitive CQ by weighing incomplete evidence correctly: ceremony size and presence of a party are relevant, but they do not by themselves justify changing the underlying attire boundary.

scenario: Your company is launching a client-facing field-sales program in Colombia and Brazil in three weeks. A global brand director in London wants one appearance guide and one photo kit for all South American reps so the campaign can go to print on time. The regional sales VP, based in São Paulo, argues that visible role credibility matters in first meetings and wants the guide to make seniority legible. The Colombia country manager has sent mixed signals: she rejected the first draft as 'too coastal/startup' for the first Bogotá roadshow, but she also approved similar lighter looks for an event in another Colombian city last quarter. HR warns against making the guide so rigid that it looks discriminatory, and procurement says there is budget for only one core kit plus minor local variations. The team includes a Brazilian operations lead pushing conservative, status-marking businesswear for client visits, and a U.S. program manager pushing a 'modern global smart-casual baseline' to simplify rollout. No one has time for a full market study, and the printer needs final wardrobe specs, role assignments, and image selections in 48 hours.
question: Write a decision memo for the rollout team. Specify: (1) the cultural mechanism you think is driving the conflicting feedback, based only on the scenario evidence; (2) the tempting but miscalibrated assumption the team should reject or tightly limit; (3) your concrete design for the appearance guide and photo kit across Colombia and Brazil, including what stays common and what must vary; and (4) the approval and communication sequence you would use in the next 48 hours so the team can ship on time without undermining client credibility. Be specific about which actors, locations, and meeting types drive your choices, and explain why your plan is better than using one 'safe' South America-wide standard.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden mechanism as subnational and role-signaling, not just 'South America is formal.'
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires inferring that the relevant issue is intra-Colombia variation plus business attire as a professionalism/status signal in some settings, rather than treating Colombia and Brazil as one uniform dress market or reducing the issue to generic conservatism.

rubric.point: Uses the correct execution axis: where and for whom the guide must vary.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires mapping variation to actor and place: e.g., stricter/client-facing highland or formal business contexts versus other Colombian settings, and role-sensitive expectations in Brazil. Partial credit if the answer says 'adapt locally' without specifying location, role, or meeting type.

rubric.point: Rejects or bounds the polished near-miss of a single global smart-casual baseline.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires explicitly identifying the one-guide-for-all-default as attractive under deadline/brand pressure but miscalibrated here, and limiting it to non-client-facing or low-stakes contexts rather than making it the main standard.

rubric.point: Designs an operational guide and photo kit with concrete common vs variable elements.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires proposing one core framework plus tightly defined local modules or image swaps tied to geography, role seniority, and client-facing context; low credit for generic advice like 'be professional' or 'let managers decide case by case.'

rubric.point: Applies cognitive CQ by weighing ambiguous evidence and choosing the right explanatory frame.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires distinguishing culture from generic brand preference, personality, or HR caution, using the mixed clues in the scenario to infer the narrow mechanism without overclaiming a continent-wide rule.

rubric.point: Sets a workable 48-hour approval route that protects speed and cultural accuracy.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires a specific sequence such as freezing the common baseline, routing Bogotá/client-credibility decisions through the Colombia country manager, routing Brazil role-signaling decisions through the regional sales VP or Brazil lead, and avoiding a broad all-market consensus process that misses the deadline.

rubric.point: Controls risk without turning 'more consultation' into the answer.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires narrow calibration and repair steps—such as labeling the guide by city/context and first-meeting type, monitoring early client reactions, and scheduling a post-launch revision—rather than solving the case by delaying, surveying everyone, or using the broadest/safest possible standard.

reference_outline: Infer from 'too coastal/startup' for Bogotá plus prior approval in another Colombian city that the key issue is not Colombia-wide but location-specific, with inland highland business settings requiring a different professional signal.

Treat Brazil evidence as reinforcing that attire can mark professionalism and role/status in business interactions, so the guide must account for who is meeting the client, not only climate or brand style.

Reject the imported assumption that one polished global smart-casual standard is the safest choice for all South American markets; note that it is efficient for brand and procurement but wrong at the level of local business interpretation.

Build one core regional guide for internal consistency, then add mandatory local/client-facing modules: stricter first-meeting looks for Bogotá and similarly formal settings, and role-differentiated businesswear guidance for Brazil where seniority/professional standing should read clearly.
Limit any lighter or startup-coded looks to non-client-facing, lower-stakes, or explicitly approved local contexts rather than using them as the default visual identity across Colombia.

Use a fast approval sequence: finalize shared baseline immediately, get Colombia city-specific signoff from the country manager for Bogotá-facing materials, get Brazil role/seniority signoff from the regional sales VP or Brazil operations lead, then send only final localized image swaps to brand and procurement.
Communicate the rationale in operational terms—client credibility, first-meeting interpretation, and role clarity—rather than vague cultural labels or continent-wide claims.
Add a narrow repair loop: tag assets by market/context, collect feedback from the first roadshows, and schedule a rapid revision after launch instead of delaying the print deadline.

scenario: A newly arrived regional product lead is in Quito for a same-day meeting with a conservative institutional client. The local coordinator is juggling a delayed luggage issue, a building access deadline, and a press photographer who wants a quick corridor photo before the presentation.

roles.newcomer: New regional product lead visiting from abroad

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The client moved the presentation up thirty minutes. Security also wants badges issued before 9:15, and the photographer is already outside the conference room.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. Please start badges without me for two minutes and tell the photographer to take the team shot first. I’m going upstairs to swap out of the travel polo and have the hotel press the dark jacket.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We can still make the time if we leave in eight. The coast team usually keeps these visits pretty relaxed, so the client deck matters more than anything.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: The deck is ready. I’d rather arrive with the materials and the room aligned, even if I miss the first photo. I’ll be back down before the car pulls out.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. I’ll hold your badge at reception and send the assistant ahead with the sample units.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Good. Also, move my sneakers into the luggage van and bring the leather pair from the side pocket. We don’t need to brief everyone on it—just keep the schedule moving.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Fine. The client’s deputy director may join late, so we may start with only half the table there.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: That’s fine. I’ll open once everyone important is seated, but I’m still changing before we go.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer correctly calibrates to Quito’s higher workplace formality by changing out of visibly casual travel clothes before the client meeting, rather than applying a single relaxed standard across Ecuador. The decisive axis is regional formality matching under time pressure, not generic politeness.

scenario: A newcomer from a global museum partner is helping finalize the wardrobe and textile styling for a traveling exhibit opening that will feature makers from northwest Argentina and the Chilean altiplano. The print shop needs the styling board within the hour, and a sponsor has already praised the draft for looking "elegant" and "premium." The local coordinator has only seen the files briefly between other logistics calls.

roles.local: Local coordinator for the Andean textile exhibit
roles.newcomer: New museum design manager from abroad

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The printer closes the board in 45 minutes. I just need the wardrobe page and loom backdrop locked so the opening packets can go out.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I moved quickly and simplified that page already. I kept the garments against soft taupe, light blue, and stone so the sponsor deck feels refined and the photos don't compete with the jewelry.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: You changed several pairings from the first photo pulls. The earlier version felt louder, but the makers did spend time choosing those pieces.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I noticed, so I kept their silhouettes and stripe layouts. I just toned the palette down and evened the bands so it reads more polished to international guests.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We still need something the visiting artisans will recognize as theirs when they arrive tonight. I can't reopen the whole deck with the sponsor on email.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I won't reopen the whole deck either. I'll keep this page only, add a short credit line to the makers, and send the printer the quieter version now so we don't miss the deadline.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right, send me the final export when it's queued. I have to get back to seating and transport.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Sending it in five minutes with the softened wardrobe page and backdrop locked.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer's decisive move follows a generic global 'refined neutral palette' design default by muting and evening out the color pairings on the exhibit styling page. That conflicts with the seed-specific Andean textile logic here, where strong brilliant colors and visible contrast between bands carry meaning; the miscalibration is in the concrete design treatment, not the newcomer's tone or project management.

scenario: A producer in La Paz is preparing a televised panel featuring women from several nearby highland communities. The sponsor asks for a more visually unified stage, and a local coordinator says backup garments or accessories could still be arranged overnight. The producer has only phone photos of the planned outfits: they look broadly similar, but the colors and small details differ from person to person. There is no time for broad community research before the morning rehearsal.
question: Which wardrobe decision is the best one to make now?

options.A: Approve backup outfits in one sponsor color family, while letting each speaker keep her own hat and jewelry so some local distinctions still remain visible on camera.
options.B: Keep each speaker's clothing as she planned it, and if the set needs visual unity, limit standardization to the backdrop and name placards after one coordinator check on added accessories.
options.C: Keep the skirts each speaker brings, but standardize shawls and hats across the group so local identity stays present while the broadcast still reads as one panel.
options.D: Let each speaker wear her own outfit, but ask women from the same area to align on a shared shawl color so their affiliation is presented more clearly to viewers.

scenario: You are the regional creative operations lead for a museum-commerce collaboration in Cusco, Peru. A Lima-based sponsor wants a 48-hour decision on packaging and launch visuals for a limited textile collection tied to an Andean community partnership. The draft prepared by your multinational team uses one striking woven motif from a photographed garment across all product tags, tote bags, and the campaign landing page, with the caption "traditional Andean design from Peru." The sponsor likes the speed and says a broad national framing is safer for international customers. A procurement manager from Spain wants all artisans to wear the same provided hat and shawl set at the launch for a cleaner brand image. In a review call, the Cusco field coordinator does not directly object, but repeatedly separates "that workshop," "the women coming from the other side," and "what appears in ceremony clothing" when discussing who will attend the launch. A junior marketer from the U.S. interprets this as minor styling variation and suggests moving ahead, then doing a courtesy credit line later if anyone complains. You need to send a decision memo today that keeps the launch on schedule, avoids insulting partners, and gives the sponsor a workable execution plan.
question: Write the decision memo you would send to the sponsor and team. Specify: (1) what you infer from the available cues and what you still treat as uncertain; (2) the immediate execution decision on the current packaging/visual draft and launch wardrobe plan; (3) the sequence of who should verify what, through which channel, and by when; and (4) how you will explain why the tempting "broad Peru/traditional Andean" approach is not a sufficient basis for this rollout. Make your plan concrete enough to judge as project performance, not just cultural sensitivity.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that the issue is not generic styling but the possibility that specific garments, motifs, and dress details signal community, status, residence, or ceremonial meaning within a narrower Andean context.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer translates the cues into an operational risk about misidentifying or flattening socially meaningful dress signals in the Cusco-area context; no credit for saying only that clothing is 'important' or 'symbolic' in a general way.

rubric.point: Rejects the current broad national framing as a near-miss rather than a safe default.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly bounds the tempting plan of labeling the design as simply 'Peruvian' or 'traditional Andean' and explains that this overgeneralization could wrongly merge distinct communities or ceremonial meanings; partial credit if it merely asks for more specificity without showing why the broad frame itself is miscalibrated.

rubric.point: Makes the primary execution-axis decision on evidence weighting and immediate rollout scope.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer freezes or narrows reuse of the motif and standardized wardrobe now, while allowing other launch work to continue, because the current evidence is strong enough to act provisionally; no credit for either full-speed rollout or total project paralysis.

rubric.point: Uses metacognitive CQ by separating what can already be inferred from what remains uncertain and naming what evidence would change the decision.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer distinguishes likely risks already visible in the coordinator's wording from unresolved specifics such as exactly which motifs or dress elements are appropriate for which participants, and sets targeted checks to resolve that uncertainty; no credit for generic 'consult locals' or for treating the hypothesis as proven fact.

rubric.point: Designs a role-specific verification sequence under deadline pressure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer assigns concrete next steps such as the field coordinator confirming community- and garment-specific meaning with the relevant partner contact, the creative team pausing only affected assets, and the sponsor receiving a same-day revised decision path; partial credit for vague consultation without roles, channel, or timing.

rubric.point: Handles the launch wardrobe issue as more than branding consistency.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer stops the plan to put all artisans in one provided hat/shawl set and proposes participant-specific or self-selected dress pending confirmation, because externally standardizing visible dress markers may erase or misassign identity signals; no credit for treating the wardrobe issue as mere comfort or aesthetics.

rubric.point: Provides concrete wording or message framing for sponsor communication.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo frames the change as a quality, partnership, and accuracy control—e.g., avoiding false attribution or inappropriate reuse of community-linked or ceremonial visual elements—rather than as abstract respect or vague reputational caution.

rubric.point: Penalizes polished but inert caution.
rubric.score_rule: No full credit if the answer defaults to indefinite delay, broad stakeholder expansion, or a generic cultural review process that ignores the 48-hour deadline; high-scoring answers must preserve schedule on unaffected work while narrowing the culturally exposed decisions.

reference_outline: State that the field coordinator's distinctions suggest the photographed garments and motifs may mark different communities, roles, places of residence, or ceremonial contexts, so the current draft cannot be treated as a generic Peru-wide visual asset.

Decide immediately to pause only the motif-heavy packaging tags, landing-page hero visual, and standardized launch wardrobe plan, while continuing unaffected production tasks such as logistics, pricing, and non-sensitive copy.

Tell the sponsor that the broad label 'traditional Andean design from Peru' is a risky overgeneralization because it collapses narrower social meaning into a national marketing shorthand and could misattribute specific community-linked dress elements.

Have the Cusco field coordinator contact the relevant community liaison or workshop lead today to verify which visual elements are appropriate for commercial reproduction, which are specific to a subgroup or locality, and whether any garments or motifs are associated with ceremonial use rather than general display.

Instruct the creative team to prepare a fallback version using neutral product photography and provenance wording that stays specific but provisional, rather than reusing the questioned motif before verification is complete.

Cancel the one-costume-for-all launch styling plan and shift to participant-approved attire or no imposed dress standard until it is clear which hats, skirts, shawls, or other visible details can be represented without misassigning identity markers.

Show metacognitive calibration by writing what is known now, what remains uncertain, and what evidence will trigger either reinstating a specific motif with proper attribution or keeping the neutral version.

Include a repair path: if confirmation arrives late or reveals misuse, publish with the neutral version, document attribution rules for future assets, and brief sponsor and team on why visual consistency cannot override narrower dress meaning in this partnership.

scenario: A newcomer creative producer is helping a municipal team in La Paz stage a tourism photo call with neighborhood market vendors and dancers. The mayor's office wants polished images before noon, and the wardrobe assistant has started regrouping garments on one rack by color so the lineup looks more consistent on camera.

roles.local: Local event coordinator from La Paz

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We lost twenty minutes on lighting, and the mayor's office wants the first group on the steps in half an hour. The assistant combined the clothing by color to speed dressing.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: For the camera, a tighter palette could help. I was about to have the front row swap a few pieces so the image reads more uniformly.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The women who arrived first have been quietly putting things back on separate chairs. No one has complained to me, but they are checking the rack pretty closely.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then let's stop the mixing now. I'll relabel every chair by wearer, return each set to the person it came with, and build the shot around their own combinations instead of a matched palette.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That will slow us down. We still need a clean frame, and the press team keeps asking for something that looks coordinated.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: We'll keep it clean through spacing and background, not by reshuffling what people brought. I'll brief the photographer in front of everyone so we don't keep re-sorting the clothing rack.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. The school director is also joining one frame, so the lineup may matter to the office more than the styling notes do.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll lock the order with her team, but wardrobe stays with each person's own set unless they themselves ask for a change.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer recalibrates away from a generic branding/default-styling approach and preserves each person's own clothing set rather than mixing items across wearers. That matches the seed-specific mechanism that distinctive Bolivian dress features can signal identity, status, and social belonging, so the key execution axis is keeping garment combinations attached to the individual wearer instead of standardizing them for visual consistency.

scenario: A nonprofit is finalizing facilitators for a literacy program in highland districts across Bolivia, Peru, and Ecuador. One district office asks for a "more professional" team for school visits and attaches staff photos. Several facilitators wear locally distinctive skirts, hats, or jackets in daily life. Contracts must be confirmed today, and the country manager must decide what approval route to use if appearance concerns affect school-facing assignments.
question: Which manager decision is most defensible?

options.A: Approve a single appearance-standard review through HR, documenting only role-based dress criteria and keeping school assignment decisions separate from locally distinctive clothing or accessories.
options.B: Approve placements now, but require any appearance-based reassignment request from schools to be logged separately and cleared by the country education lead before changing school-facing roles.
options.C: Approve placements only after the field team records each facilitator's visible community-linked dress details and obtains district-level sign-off for school visits in every target area.
options.D: Approve contracts after school principals review facilitator photos in advance, with any concerns documented in the partner file before final school-facing assignments are released.

scenario: A learning platform is localizing its scholarship homepage for Bolivia before a university fair in La Paz. The page is already built, and design can replace only one photo today without moving the deadline. Current visuals show a female science tutor leading a lab demo in a blazer, two mixed student scenes, and a parent waiting outside a school gate. A regional partner’s only brief is that the page should feel credible beyond the main cities, while still looking aspirational for families comparing providers.
question: Which visual change is the best next step now?

options.A: Replace one student scene with a classroom photo where several girls wear Andean skirts, while keeping the female tutor image unchanged to preserve a consistent professional lead visual.
options.B: Replace the tutor photo with one showing a female instructor leading the lesson in locally rooted dress, while leaving the rest of the student and parent images as they are.
options.C: Replace the parent-at-gate photo with a welcoming image of a woman in locally rooted dress arriving with a child, while keeping teaching staff in standard businesswear for clarity.
options.D: Keep the current staff and student photos, and swap in stronger local textiles and mountain imagery around the page so clothing does not carry too much representational weight.

scenario: You lead regional rollout for a financial-literacy campaign in Bolivia. The first public workshop is in La Paz in 9 days, and the donor's country director wants the launch photos to look 'distinctively local' because they will be used in a board update the same week. Your team includes a brand manager in India, a Bolivian field coordinator, and a procurement officer who needs clothing and image-use approvals locked within 48 hours. A draft brief proposes a 'traditional Bolivian look' for the three women who will greet participants at the registration desk, including renting matching skirts and hats from a costume supplier so the visual identity is consistent with the event backdrop. The field coordinator has not objected, but in email she keeps separating 'community hosts' from 'promo staff,' and she asks whether the registration role could be reassigned after wardrobe is finalized. The donor also expects one of the women featured in photos to later join a roundtable with bank managers and municipal staff. Budget is tight, and changing vendors after tomorrow will trigger a penalty. If you slow the launch, your manager will likely escalate because the donor already thinks Bolivia is behind schedule.
question: Write a decision memo for your team. Explain what hidden issue you think the emails are signaling, what tempting assumption the current draft is making, and what concrete plan you would execute in the next 48 hours. Your memo must specify: who should and should not be assigned to the visible greeting/photo roles, whether the clothing plan should be kept, altered, or dropped, what follow-up effort you will personally own despite the deadline, and how you will brief the donor and internal team so the launch still moves forward without creating a trust or status problem later in the event.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that the clothing choice is not a neutral visual theme but can signal socially loaded identity and status in Bolivian professional space.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer translates the appearance issue into consequences for role perception, authority, or treatment at the event; no credit for merely saying to 'respect tradition' or 'be culturally sensitive.'

rubric.point: Identifies the attractive near-miss assumption in the draft and rejects or tightly bounds it.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly challenges the idea that Indigenous-coded dress can be used as a generic local aesthetic, branding device, or matching costume for staff; partial credit if it notices a problem but treats it as only a consent, PR, or photography issue.

rubric.point: Makes the correct execution choice on role assignment and wardrobe under deadline.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan avoids assigning rented 'traditional look' attire as a uniform for promo or greeting staff and avoids placing someone in that dress purely for launch visuals; high-scoring answers either keep people in their own authentic attire/standard professional dress or redesign the visible roles so clothing is not instrumentalized. Answers lose credit if they keep the clothing concept but add softer wording, optionality, or broader consultation without changing the core role-risk.

rubric.point: Uses motivational CQ by taking costly personal ownership rather than shifting the burden to Bolivian colleagues.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the respondent absorbs a visible cost in time, status, or convenience—for example, personally rewriting the brief, calling procurement and donor stakeholders, or reworking the photo plan that same day—instead of saying 'ask locals what they prefer' and waiting. No credit for respectful withdrawal or delay that leaves the local team to solve the issue alone.

rubric.point: Designs a bounded communication sequence that protects progress and relationships.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer sequences internal correction first, then a concise donor reframing that preserves launch momentum while removing the problematic visual premise. Answers lose credit if they make the first move a public values statement, a broad meeting, or a full postponement when a narrower fix would work.

rubric.point: Interprets the field coordinator's email cues as evidence relevant to execution.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer uses the split between 'community hosts' and 'promo staff' and the request to revisit registration assignments as clues that clothing, role, and perceived standing are entangled; partial credit if it notices ambiguity but does not connect it to staffing and event hierarchy.

rubric.point: Includes a repair and monitoring step for the live event.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer adds an operational safeguard such as confirming final role wording, checking photo shot lists, or ensuring that whoever joins the roundtable is not visually framed in a way that undercuts professional standing. No credit for generic statements about 'monitor reactions' without specifying what to watch or change.

reference_outline: State that the core issue is not fashion preference but the social meaning attached to Indigenous-coded women's dress in Bolivia, which can shape how a person is categorized and treated in both greeting and professional discussion roles.
Name the near-miss: the draft assumes a globally familiar branding logic that 'local-looking' clothing can be assigned as an aesthetic layer for staff without changing how those staff are perceived.
Stop the costume-rental plan for greeting/photo uniforming; do not use matching rented skirts and hats to create a 'traditional Bolivian look' for promo visibility.

Separate authentic community participation from staged branding: if community hosts attend in their own chosen attire, do not script or wardrobe them for image goals, and do not assign attire-driven symbolism to registration staff.

Reassign visible launch roles so authority-bearing functions and later roundtable participation are not undermined by a photo-first wardrobe concept; use standard professional/event-appropriate dress unless an individual is appearing in her own chosen clothing.

Personally take ownership within 48 hours by rewriting the brief, contacting procurement to cancel or redirect the order, and giving the donor a substitute visual plan that still meets the board-update need without instrumentalizing attire.

Brief the donor narrowly: frame the change as protecting credibility and stakeholder trust at the event, not as a vague cultural concern; offer alternative imagery such as venue, materials, participants in natural dress, or community context.

Use the field coordinator's wording as evidence that role category and clothing are already being read differently on the ground, so the issue must be fixed before wardrobe is finalized rather than left for onsite improvisation.

Add live-event controls: approve captions and shot lists, confirm who appears in launch photos versus professional roundtable settings, and check that no one is visually positioned in a way that reduces standing while still keeping the launch on schedule.

scenario: A regional brand team is preparing a same-day media shoot and evening investor reception in Lima for an upscale residential project. Three male executives from the developer will appear in fitted jackets on camera and then host guests. The newcomer has to keep the schedule moving, avoid embarrassing anyone, and make the team look polished for a status-conscious audience.

roles.newcomer: Regional brand lead newly assigned to Peru

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The jackets arrive at noon, the photographer starts at three, and the developer's directors go straight from the shoot to the reception. They're particular about how the event lands with this crowd.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Got it. I'll keep the run sheet tight and send the directors their call times now so we don't lose the afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: One director asked whether there is any time between fitting and makeup. We only have about an hour if traffic behaves.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll use that hour. I'm reserving short slots at the traditional shop beside the hotel, staggered right after jacket fitting, so each director can be cleaned up before camera. I'll have wardrobe photos sent ahead so the look stays consistent on stage.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That adds another stop. The finance director hates detours, and we still need the press notes signed.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll send a runner with the notes and keep the appointments to twenty minutes each. I know it's a bit strict, but the camera, the jackets, and the evening crowd all work together here, so I'd rather lock it in than leave it to hotel grooming.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. If you can keep them on time, production will be relieved.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll message each director separately with his slot, car pickup, and revised call time, then meet them at the fitting room so the sequence stays fast.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer's decisive behavior matches the seed-specific Lima norm by actively arranging classic barbershop grooming for upper-status male presenters and coordinating it with clothing fit and body presentation, rather than relying on a generic minimal-grooming default. The key execution axis is sequence: grooming is built into the prep flow after wardrobe fitting so appearance is matched, not treated as incidental.

scenario: A production team in Cusco is preparing a dawn video shoot for a regional tourism campaign. Four local performers from nearby highland communities will appear together in ceremonial dress, but the wardrobe rack was packed by color and garment type rather than by person. The creative director wants the group to look visually balanced on camera and asks for one fitting rule before tonight’s final styling session.
question: Which direction should guide the fitting?

options.A: Build the strongest group look from the full rack, provided each performer stays in complete ceremonial dress from the region instead of mixing ceremonial and everyday clothing.
options.B: Keep each performer’s hat and mantle matched, but exchange skirts, belts, or ponchos across nearby communities to balance the palette while preserving a recognizably local silhouette.
options.C: Keep each performer’s outfit elements aligned as the wearer’s own local combination, and adjust visual balance through accessories, spacing, or background choices rather than cross-swapping garments.
options.D: Keep community-linked combinations intact for the women, but standardize the men’s hats and ponchos across the group so the ensemble reads more cleanly on camera.

scenario:
You are a regional launch manager for a museum-tech company preparing a paid livestream and on-site exhibition opening in La Paz with partner communities from Bolivia and southern Peru. The event brochure, stage visuals, host script, and dressing-room workflow must be locked by tomorrow 16:00 because the sponsor’s legal team needs final files and the streaming vendor charges a rush fee after that. A senior brand director in Madrid wants the event to feel 'welcoming and photogenic' and has proposed a fast fix: set up a 'try-on corner' before the ceremony so foreign staff, influencers, and guests can wear the featured garments for photos, then move some pieces onto mannequins near the bar afterward to keep the visual story going through the reception. 

Your local operations team has sent practical notes but no explicit cultural explanation: one note says some garments are being brought by families rather than by the museum; another says the dressing room list should distinguish which items are assigned to whom and at what moment; another says the reception layout should avoid mixing all textiles into a single display rack after the formal segment. A Peruvian production assistant asks whether the host should invite 'everyone on stage to model the pieces together' for efficiency. A Bolivian venue coordinator says only that the sequence matters and that a mistake during the opening would be harder to repair publicly than a late lighting cue. 

You must send a decision memo tonight that tells the Madrid director, the stage manager, wardrobe lead, and host exactly how to proceed without derailing the launch, insulting partners, or missing the sponsor deadline.
question: Write the decision memo you would send. Specify the execution plan for the garments across three moments: pre-event preparation, the formal ceremony, and the post-ceremony reception. Your memo must identify the hidden cultural mechanism you think is operating from the available evidence, name the tempting but miscalibrated assumption behind the Madrid proposal, and give concrete instructions on wording, who may handle or wear which items, where the items should be placed, and how to repair or contain risk if a global stakeholder pushes back. Do not answer with general respect or 'consult locals more'; give a workable sequence under the deadline.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that the garments should be handled as socially and ceremonially meaningful items tied to specific people and statuses, not as generic decorative costumes or interchangeable props.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires inferring operational significance from the evidence about family-brought items, assignment lists, and sequence sensitivity; low credit if the answer only says 'be respectful' or names culture without translating it into handling rules.

rubric.point: Sets the main execution axis correctly by separating garment handling and placement across pre-event, ceremony, and reception rather than using one efficient all-purpose display/try-on plan.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires a sequence in which access, wearing, and placement are narrower before and during the ceremony and do not default to public try-ons or mixed post-event display; low credit if accurate concerns are raised but applied at the wrong stage or only after the ceremony.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the attractive near-miss plan that treats the garments as engagement assets for guests, influencers, or broad cast participation.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires explicitly identifying the imported assumption that visual inclusion and audience participation are automatically positive here, and replacing it with a narrower plan; low credit if the answer merely softens the try-on corner or allows mannequins/bar-area display as a compromise.

rubric.point: Gives role-specific behavioural instructions on wording, audience, and handling.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires concrete visible behavior such as instructing the host not to invite general modeling, limiting handlers to designated wearers/wardrobe staff, using wording that presents garments through the people or families assigned to them, and choosing private correction channels for staff; low credit if the answer stays at policy level without who-says-what-to-whom.

rubric.point: Applies behavioural CQ through calibrated timing, channel, and interaction rhythm under pressure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires choosing actions that may cost speed or visual simplicity—such as a private pre-brief tonight, a locked assignment sheet, and a narrow on-stage sequence—because the visible execution detail matters; low credit if the answer picks the right values but wrong channel or timing, such as correcting the issue only in a public rehearsal or after guests arrive.

rubric.point: Designs a practical alternative that still meets sponsor and brand needs without enacting the misunderstanding.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires substituting safe visual storytelling methods such as approved explanatory captions, focused camera framing, or designated speakers/wearers rather than broad interactive use; low credit if the answer solves the cultural risk by cancelling visibility entirely or delaying all decisions.

rubric.point: Includes a containment or repair path if headquarters or event staff continue pushing the efficient global-SOP approach.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires a concrete escalation or fallback boundary—for example, stating non-negotiable handling limits, rerouting disputed visual ideas to signage or digital content, and privately stopping unauthorized try-ons immediately; low credit if the answer relies on vague consultation or assumes goodwill will prevent mistakes.

reference_outline: State that the evidence suggests the garments carry socially specific ceremonial meaning linked to identity and role, so they cannot be treated as general event costumes or neutral display fabric.

In pre-event preparation, issue a private assignment sheet naming which items belong with which designated wearer or family-linked presenter, limit handling to wardrobe staff and assigned participants, and brief the host and stage manager tonight rather than improvising tomorrow.

For the formal ceremony, prohibit audience/staff/influencer try-ons and reject a group 'everyone model them together' segment; the host should introduce participants in a way that keeps garments attached to their designated wearers rather than to generic spectacle.

For the reception, do not move all garments to mannequins near the bar or into a mixed rack; either return them to assigned custody, keep them off-limits in a controlled area, or use approved photos/text panels for continued storytelling.

Name the near-miss explicitly: the Madrid plan assumes inclusion, photo engagement, and efficient reuse are universally positive, but here that would flatten garments with role, status, and ceremonial significance into props.

Use behavioural CQ by choosing the right channel and rhythm: send a concise decision memo now, run a private pre-brief with stage/wardrobe/host, give short exact wording for the host, and reserve any pushback conversation with headquarters for a non-public channel before showtime.

Offer a brand-safe substitute that preserves visuals and sponsor value—close-up filming of designated wearers, captioned program notes, or a moderated explanation segment—without broad physical access.

Set a repair boundary: if unauthorized use starts, wardrobe or stage management stops it immediately off-mic, removes the item from casual circulation, and shifts to the substitute visual plan rather than debating the principle publicly.

scenario: You are the operations lead for a regional nonprofit team preparing a two-day community heritage event on Rotuma. A donor delegation, several chiefs, church-linked community leaders, and local families will attend. The first evening includes a welcome inside a family house, and the second day includes a formal public ceremony. Your team must finalize a dress brief by tonight for 12 visiting staff and volunteers coming from Fiji, Australia, and New Zealand, plus approve the photo look for the printed program and social posts by tomorrow morning. Budget is tight, so the team wants one reusable outfit guideline for all visitors. The brand manager pushes for a colorful Pacific-themed look with statement accessories and branded caps because the photos need to look lively and recognizable. A logistics coordinator argues that a generic 'smart casual, culturally respectful' note is enough, since asking people to source special layers or change accessories this late may cause delays and complaints. Message history shows that local hosts have so far only said things like 'please come tidy' and 'the church and chiefs will be there,' without giving a full dress code. You need to send the final brief and rollout plan now, including who gets what instruction, when, and how you will handle arrivals at the house and the formal ceremony if some visitors show up dressed differently from the brief.
question: Write a short decision memo that sets the dress-and-appearance rollout plan for the visiting team. Your memo must: (1) diagnose the hidden cultural mechanism from the scenario evidence, (2) identify the most tempting but miscalibrated generic assumption, (3) specify the exact outfit, accessory, and arrival-sequence instructions you would send to different visitors before travel, and (4) explain how you would handle on-site correction at the house and at the formal ceremony without derailing the event or publicly embarrassing guests. Be concrete about timing, wording, audience, and who is responsible for each step.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that the issue is not generic neatness alone but a ceremony-and-household dress protocol tied to modest presentation, respect, and formal standing in front of chiefs and church-linked hosts.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers a specific formal-conduct mechanism from the clues and translates it into dress consequences; no credit for saying only 'be respectful' or 'dress conservatively' without linking house entry, ceremony context, and visible appearance control.

rubric.point: Sets seed-specific visible instructions on clothing and accessories for the right people and stages.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan requires neat, clean, non-gaudy presentation, removes hats from the relevant settings, and addresses women's full lower-body coverage for public/ceremonial participation with ceremony-appropriate layering rather than a single generic unisex dress note. Partial credit if one element is correct but applied too broadly, too vaguely, or only at one stage.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the attractive near-miss plan of using one global 'smart casual/respectful' standard or brand-first colorful styling.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explains why the generic default is tempting under deadline, budget, and brand pressure yet operationally wrong here. No credit for simply proposing more consultation or delay without making the dress decision.

rubric.point: Uses behavioural CQ through calibrated wording, channel, timing, and audience.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the respondent chooses concrete delivery behavior such as a pre-arrival direct brief to visitors, separate role-specific instructions where needed, private correction rather than public call-out, and an arrival checkpoint before entering the house or joining ceremony flow. No credit for correct content delivered in the wrong channel or only after guests are already in the public setting.

rubric.point: Designs a workable sequence for house entry and ceremony participation under pressure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer distinguishes what must happen before travel, on arrival at the house, and before the formal ceremony, including who checks for hats/accessories/coverage and how spare items or adjustments are handled. Partial credit for a correct rule with no executable sequence.

rubric.point: Handles repair without making the answer the broadest or safest possible plan.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the repair plan is narrow and practical: discreetly pause, adjust clothing/accessories, re-sequence entry, or assign a staff member to intercept rather than stop the whole event, publicly lecture, or escalate immediately to local leaders. No credit for generic 'be sensitive' language with no action.

reference_outline: Infer from 'church and chiefs,' the indoor family-house welcome, and the formal public ceremony that appearance rules are stricter than a generic island-event dress code and govern respect signalling in both house and ceremonial settings.

Send the brief before travel, not after arrival: require neat, clean, well-groomed dress; prohibit flashy or gaudy jewelry/clothing; tell all visitors not to wear caps or hats at the house welcome or near the ceremony.

Differentiate instructions by role/body rather than forcing one reusable unisex note: women should be told to ensure ankle-length coverage in public/ceremonial participation and to arrange the expected under/over ceremonial layers if they will appear in the formal ceremony rather than assuming an ordinary dress is enough.

Do not accept the brand-manager shortcut of colorful statement styling or the logistics shortcut of 'smart casual, culturally respectful'; explain that these save time but miss visible rules on modesty, accessories, and hat removal.

Use behavioural CQ in delivery: send a concise written brief plus a packing checklist, assign one staff lead to privately confirm compliance on arrival, and brief photographers/designers to avoid showing prohibited hats or flashy styling in the program and social imagery.

At the house, intercept privately before entry if someone still has a cap or unsuitable accessory; at the formal ceremony, quietly adjust, lend backup garments/accessories if prepared, or hold someone out of the visible front sequence until corrected rather than correcting them publicly in front of hosts and chiefs.

Build a minimal contingency under deadline: prepare spare plain wraps/layers and a no-gaudy-accessories fallback kit, and document who has authority to make quick appearance corrections so the event keeps moving without normalizing the wrong standard.

scenario: A newcomer coordinating a donor-funded youth literacy project in Port Vila is invited to give a two-minute thank-you at a Saturday handover held in a village church hall. The printed banners and books have already arrived, and the driver is leaving in twenty minutes. The newcomer came from a school visit in the heat and has only packed office clothes plus one extra outfit bought the night before.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We need to leave soon if we're going to arrive before the opening prayer. The chiefs, pastors, and the school committee will all be there, and you'll say a few words after the books are set out.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I came straight from the school and I'm still in my field trousers. I did buy one spare outfit last night, so I'll change before we load the boxes, even if it makes us cut the photo setup short.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The hall gets crowded quickly. Once we arrive, there probably won't be a room free, and people usually come over to greet guests right away.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I'll switch here now and carry the cartons after. I can skip the branded polo and use the long dress instead; the logos matter less than arriving ready.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The donor team likes clear event pictures, and they were expecting you in project colours.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll still stand with the books for one quick photo, but I'd rather give them a plain shot than spend the welcome in the wrong clothes. If needed, I'll explain the branding change myself.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right, I'll tell the driver to wait by the gate for five minutes. We can stack the boxes while you change.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Thanks. I'll be fast, and if the hem needs pinning I'll handle it in the truck so we don't push that work onto anyone there.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer invests time and status cost to change into a more formal, modest outfit before a church-based public event with elders and community leaders present. That matches the Vanuatu-specific mechanism that dress at church services, ceremonies, and meetings is socially meaningful and should be more formal/modest, rather than treating field trousers as acceptable under a generic global default.
