options.D: Keep the rollout note fixed once senior leaders support it, and let each team lead decide locally how much wider discussion is needed before implementation.

scenario: A newcomer at a software vendor in Lisbon is trying to secure sign-off on a pilot budget before a regional deadline. The local office contact has arranged a review with a department head and two managers the newcomer has not met before. Headquarters wants a decision this week, but the local team warns only that the meeting slot is short and the director will join for the first half before leaving for another appointment.

roles.newcomer: Ethan, newly transferred regional partnerships lead

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The review is at 10:00 with Director Ferreira, Sofia Ramos, and Paulo Nunes. We have twenty-five minutes before the director leaves, so we should use the time well.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I reworked the deck last night and printed a short briefing for Director Ferreira and the others. I also moved the pricing appendix to the end so we can walk through the case properly instead of rushing to the ask.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That helps. They have seen the summary note, but not your revised numbers. The director usually opens the meeting, then the managers go into details.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I’ll open briefly, address Director Ferreira and the managers formally, and let the discussion breathe before I press for a decision. If the detailed review runs long, I can stay after the director steps out and work through the assumptions with Sofia Ramos and Mr. Nunes.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: HQ has been asking whether we can get an answer today. They may expect a firm update right after the meeting.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I can still give HQ an update today, but I’d rather not force a yes-or-no in the first minutes. I’ll aim to leave with a clear next step and, if needed, send a written follow-up this afternoon under Director Ferreira’s attention.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. One more thing: the room changed, so we may walk in just as they arrive.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: No problem. I’ll be ready at the door with the printed copies, greet Director Ferreira first, and keep the opening concise so we can spend most of the time on the discussion.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer invests extra time and status-sensitive effort in a formal, hierarchy-aware first meeting: he uses titles and surnames, acknowledges the senior person first, and avoids rushing an immediate decision, favoring a thorough discussion and follow-up. That execution fits Portuguese business formality and pacing better than a generic global push for fast first-name efficiency.

scenario: You are a product lead based in Singapore, newly assigned to coordinate a 10-day decision sprint for a joint rollout involving a Swedish design team and a Dutch operations team. The deliverable is a final recommendation on whether to launch a new self-service claims feature next month or delay by one quarter. A global sponsor in New York wants a crisp go/no-go answer by Friday because marketing slots are already reserved. The Swedish country manager and Dutch operations head will both attend the main decision meeting, along with two senior engineers, three junior specialists who built the pilot workflow, and a compliance analyst. In the past two meetings, the most senior people spoke last, several junior participants stayed quiet until the end, and follow-up messages showed that key implementation concerns emerged only after the meeting. Your sponsor now asks you to run the final 45-minute meeting 'efficiently' and avoid visible disagreement in front of leadership. You also know that if the recommendation slips, the sponsor may bypass the local teams and decide centrally. You have one chance to set the meeting format, pre-read instructions, speaking order, and follow-up process.
question: Write a concrete meeting-and-follow-up plan for this final decision sprint. Your answer must: identify the hidden interaction problem you think is causing late-emerging concerns; explain the tempting but miscalibrated meeting design that an outsider might choose under these pressures; specify exactly how you would structure the pre-read, who speaks when in the meeting, how senior leaders should be used, what wording you would use to invite contributions, and how you would close the meeting and follow up afterward. Make clear how your plan protects decision speed without defaulting to either top-down closure or endless consultation.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that the core risk is not lack of expertise but a meeting pattern that suppresses or delays contributions from less senior participants whose input is operationally decisive.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer links late-emerging issues to waiting on senior voices or treating leaders as the main decision speakers; partial credit for vague comments about 'psychological safety' or 'more input' without identifying the interaction pattern.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the attractive near-miss plan of getting senior alignment first and then inviting others to confirm or react.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explains why a senior-first or sponsor-driven format looks efficient yet would likely produce artificial agreement, late objections, or disconnect; no credit for simply saying 'be inclusive' without naming the miscalibrated sequence.

rubric.point: Uses a seed-specific speaking sequence that draws out junior and hands-on contributors before leadership closes the discussion.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly sequences contributions so that implementation-facing or junior participants speak early enough to shape the decision before senior wrap-up; partial credit if juniors are included but only after managers frame the answer or at the very end.

rubric.point: Applies behavioural CQ through concrete wording, timing, and role design rather than abstract principles.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer gives visible execution details such as pre-read prompts, named turns, facilitator phrases, time boxes, or how to ask for dissent and alternatives; no credit for answers limited to attitudes like respect, openness, or sensitivity.

rubric.point: Positions senior leaders as facilitators or synthesizers rather than sole authorities during the live decision process.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer shows leaders being used to frame the decision criteria, listen, synthesize, or remove blockers after others contribute; partial credit if leaders still dominate the substantive discussion even politely.

rubric.point: Balances speed and closure with a narrow, concrete follow-up mechanism that captures unresolved risks without reopening the whole decision.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer closes with a defined recommendation, owner list, and short post-meeting validation path for residual concerns; no credit for broad delay, open-ended consultation, or 'gather more views' without a boundary.

rubric.point: Avoids wrong-scope use of cultural knowledge.
rubric.score_rule: No full credit if the answer overcorrects into endless consensus-seeking, removes leadership ownership entirely, or treats all disagreement as needing prolonged alignment; high-scoring answers must preserve decision momentum while changing the interaction rhythm.

reference_outline: Identify the likely mechanism from the evidence: problems surface after meetings because key knowledge holders are not shaping the discussion early, and a senior-last or senior-centered rhythm is still causing others to wait rather than contribute openly in time.

Name the near-miss explicitly: under sponsor pressure, an outsider might pre-align with the Swedish manager and Dutch operations head, let them set the answer first, and use the meeting mainly for confirmation; this appears efficient but will likely recreate late offline objections.

Send a short pre-read with a forced input structure, such as decision criteria, top two launch risks, top two mitigation options, and one go/no-go recommendation from each participant before the meeting, so junior specialists arrive expected to contribute substance.

Run the meeting with the facilitator opening on decision criteria and process, then call first on the pilot-build specialists and compliance analyst, then senior engineers, and only after that ask the country manager and operations head to synthesize tradeoffs and confirm the decision boundary.

Use explicit wording that makes contribution active and time-bound, such as asking each hands-on contributor for the strongest reason to launch and the strongest reason to delay, rather than vague invitations like 'any comments' after leaders have spoken.

Use senior leaders behaviourally as enablers: ask them not to anchor the answer in the first minutes, but to listen, test assumptions, and close on ownership, escalation needs, and sponsor messaging after others have spoken.

Close with a clear provisional recommendation, named owners for any final checks, and a tightly bounded post-meeting window for surfacing only new implementation blockers, so the process does not drift into indefinite consensus-seeking.

Monitor and repair if needed: if a senior person speaks too early or silence appears, reset the rhythm in the room by redirecting to those closest to the workflow rather than accepting polite non-response as agreement.

scenario: A visiting VP has one 25-minute call with the Stockholm team to lock a pricing choice before Monday's launch gate. Everyone already received the pre-read and several people commented in the shared file. The VP's preferred option is known internally, but execution will depend on sales, operations, and analytics moving together right after the call. There is no time for another full-team meeting.
question: Which meeting plan is the best fit?

options.A: Ask everyone to add any last concerns in the document before the call, use the live meeting for the country manager and department heads to settle the choice, then circulate the decision to the full group immediately afterward.
options.B: Open with the VP's preferred option, take a quick round of reactions from everyone on the call, then have the country manager confirm the final decision once no major objections are voiced.
options.C: Have the country manager frame the trade-off, invite the people who commented in the shared file to speak to their points early in the call, let the others react, then check where the group stands before closing.
options.D: Use the call to surface views from the full team, but end without deciding; have the country manager collect any remaining reactions one-to-one right after and confirm the choice by message later that day.

scenario: A newcomer product director in Stockholm needs sign-off on a client-facing rollout plan by the end of the day. The client is pressing for a launch date, but the plan will affect engineering, support, and sales enablement. The local colleague has gathered the relevant team members for a short internal meeting before the director sends anything externally.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We have 35 minutes before the client asks for the revised timeline. Engineering can do the earlier date only if support and sales change their prep.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then let's use the time well. I'll put the draft on the screen now, and I want each function to say what would block them from standing behind this version today.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The country manager is traveling, so if needed you can still send a recommendation upward after this. People here have already read the pre-read.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Good. I won't wait for a top-line approval first. If there are objections, let's surface them in the room and change the plan until the people executing it can support it.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Support is worried about weekend coverage, and sales wants the client date kept because procurement has booked internal reviews.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. Sales, give me the immovable milestones. Support, name the minimum staffing buffer. Engineering, tell us the latest point your handoff still works. We'll build one version all three can live with, not three separate promises.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: If we leave this room with one date, I can update the client deck immediately. It may be a little later than what procurement hoped.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Do that. I'll send the client the single date we settle here, plus the dependencies we all accepted, instead of a faster date that half the team would have to unwind next week.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer aligns with the Nordic mechanism by using the meeting to reach genuine cross-functional buy-in among the people who must implement the plan, rather than defaulting to a top-down recommendation for speed. The decisive execution axis is who is included in the decision before commitment: the newcomer pushes visible, direct discussion in the room so the final agreement is one everyone present can stand behind.

scenario: You are a regional product lead based in Singapore, assigned to launch a shared internal workflow tool across the Stockholm, Copenhagen, and Oslo offices. The CFO wants a go/no-go decision by Friday because the current vendor contract expires in 12 days, and your global VP has already told headquarters that the Nordics are 'the easiest region to standardize.' A draft recommendation from you was circulated on Monday with a request for comments by end of day Tuesday. By Wednesday afternoon, the country managers have sent only brief notes, but several product specialists, operations analysts, and one junior UX researcher have added detailed comments in the shared document, raising implementation concerns, data-field differences, and training suggestions. Your VP messages you privately: 'Country heads are supportive enough. Lock the decision with them today and announce tomorrow so we don’t lose momentum.' At the same time, the Swedish implementation lead says the launch will go faster if 'people feel the issues are worked through before the switch,' but does not explicitly ask you to delay. Budget allows only one extra coordination block before Friday, and if you miss the contract deadline, procurement will force a 3-month extension with the current vendor at a higher cost. If you overrun the Nordic team’s patience, adoption risk will be visible in the first month because usage data will be compared publicly across regions.
question: Write a decision-and-rollout memo for your VP (about 250-400 words) that states what you will do between now and Friday. Your memo must: (1) diagnose what is happening in the Nordic input pattern, (2) identify the tempting but miscalibrated assumption in your VP’s plan, (3) choose a concrete stakeholder sequence for the next 48 hours, and (4) show how you will keep momentum without either forcing a top-down decision too early or drifting into open-ended consultation. Be specific about who you involve, what effort you personally take on, what you ask from senior managers versus junior contributors, and what boundary you set for final decision timing.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden mechanism from the evidence pattern
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that meaningful pre-decision buy-in is being built across levels, including junior staff, and that the sparse manager comments do not mean the decision is ready for top-down closure. No credit for vague statements like 'they value teamwork' or 'people want to be heard' without linking this to the current decision stage.

rubric.point: Rejects or bounds the attractive near-miss plan
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly identifies the tempting imported assumption as 'manager sign-off is enough to decide now' or an equivalent global-default shortcut, and explains why that would create downstream implementation drag or visible adoption risk here. Partial credit if it notes risk but still treats extra input as optional courtesy rather than decision-critical.

rubric.point: Chooses the correct execution axis: stakeholder sequence before final commitment
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan uses the limited extra coordination block to surface and resolve cross-level implementation concerns before announcing final rollout, then closes by a firm deadline. Answers lose credit if they either announce first and invite fixes later, or broaden consultation indefinitely without a bounded decision point.

rubric.point: Shows motivational CQ through costly, adaptive engagement
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the respondent takes visible ownership of the extra effort under pressure—such as personally synthesizing comments, convening a focused problem-solving session, or doing follow-up to convert dispersed concerns into a narrowed decision set—rather than pushing the burden back onto local teams with 'please align internally and revert.' Friendly tone alone does not score.

rubric.point: Assigns roles and channels concretely
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer distinguishes the role of country heads, implementation leads, and junior/specialist contributors; uses an operational channel such as a targeted working session plus written issue log; and specifies what each group is asked to decide, confirm, or refine. Generic 'consult stakeholders' answers do not score high.

rubric.point: Maintains bounded momentum and risk control
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan sets a narrow window for input, defines what issues are in scope for the final decision, and preserves a Friday decision boundary while explaining how unresolved noncritical items will be parked for post-decision execution. Answers that equate cultural adaptation with delay, safety, or maximum consultation lose credit.

reference_outline: Infer from the pattern of detailed junior/specialist comments plus light senior-manager comments that the team is still doing substantive pre-decision alignment, not merely post-decision implementation polishing.

Do not treat country-head support as sufficient closure; the near-miss is to finalize immediately with senior managers because that fits a generic hierarchy-first decision model but would weaken later execution and adoption.

Use the single extra coordination block for a tightly scoped cross-level session with implementation leads and the key specialists who raised operational blockers, then bring country heads a narrowed final recommendation after issues are worked through.

Personally absorb the adaptation cost: synthesize comments into 3-5 decision items, separate critical blockers from nice-to-haves, and avoid sending the team back a broad request to 'align internally' on your behalf.

Give senior managers a clear role: validate tradeoffs and commit resources once the operational concerns are narrowed; give junior and specialist contributors a defined role in surfacing friction points that could derail rollout.

Set a firm timing boundary: issue triage on Thursday, final recommendation to country heads and VP after that block, go/no-go by Friday, with noncritical refinements logged into phase-two implementation rather than reopening the decision.
Explain that the aim is not endless inclusion but faster execution after decision by building enough real agreement before the announcement.

Include a repair/monitoring step: after final decision, track first-month adoption and be ready to address any ignored concern quickly, but do not use post-launch monitoring as an excuse to skip the pre-decision alignment that is still needed now.

scenario: A newcomer from a global sales team is in Stockholm for a first procurement meeting with a manufacturing client. Headquarters has already shipped premium welcome bags with the company logo for each attendee, and the regional VP expects a strong first impression. The local colleague is focused on getting the pilot discussion finished in one hour because the client has compliance staff joining for the opening minutes.

roles.newcomer: Daniel, newly assigned international sales lead

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The client added their procurement manager and someone from compliance for the first ten minutes. After that, it should just be the technical team and us.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Good to know. I saw the branded bags from HQ at each seat. I'm taking those out before they come in and keeping the table to the agenda, samples, and pricing sheets.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The VP was quite keen on making the visit feel premium. The bags have already been delivered to reception.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll explain it to him later. For a first meeting, I don't want anything personal waiting at their places. If they ask about the bags, I'll say we brought materials for the product trial and can leave the shared demo unit with the lab after the session.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Reception can still send the bags upstairs if you want. We only have a few minutes before they arrive.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: No, let's keep them downstairs. Please add the demo unit and the calibration guide to the sign-out sheet so there's a record of what stays on site.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. I’ll tell reception to hold the delivery and print one more copy of the pilot timeline.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Thanks. I'll open with the pilot milestones directly and keep the room setup simple.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer matches the seed-specific mechanism by avoiding personal or premium gifts at the start of a first-time negotiation in a Nordic setting, while using only modest, purposeful, transparent trial materials that are documented. The decisive axis is timing and purpose: no seat-by-seat welcome items for a first meeting, but a shared demo item left for the work task with a record.

scenario: A regional sales manager is closing a six-month industrial pilot with a German manufacturer. The account team wants to send a thank-you package to the procurement lead before quarter-end, and finance will reimburse up to €80 if the manager approves the route today. The team knows the recipient's company has a formal vendor code, but nobody has found the section on courtesy items yet.
question: Which approval line should the manager give?

options.A: Approve a small package now if it stays below the team's own €40 courtesy threshold and is entered in the CRM, letting the recipient decline or return it after delivery.
options.B: Approve only a modest token if the coordinator first confirms the recipient company's acceptance rule or limit; if that cannot be confirmed today, send written thanks and no parcel.
options.C: Approve a modest shared package addressed to the procurement department rather than the individual lead, with the value kept under €50 and the expense logged internally.
options.D: Approve the package and include a note saying the recipient may keep it personally or place it in a common area, with the amount recorded for compliance.

scenario: A software supplier is meeting a Malawian telecom company to finalize commercial terms before the supplier's regional pricing window closes that evening. The newcomer's team wants a signed term sheet quickly so production slots can be reserved, but the local company has hosted several relationship-building meetings and now sends a smaller working group to discuss the final draft.

roles.local: Procurement manager at the Malawian telecom company
roles.newcomer: Regional sales lead from the foreign supplier

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Thank you for joining us again. The team has reviewed your revised numbers, and the direction is encouraging. We should use this session well, since your pricing window closes today.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I appreciate that. To keep momentum, I brought a clean term sheet with only the service credits and rollout dates left open. If we can settle those now, I can leave a signed copy with your team before lunch.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That may help the process. On service credits, your latest proposal is lighter than we had hoped, though perhaps there is still room for comfort. On the dates, our side would want confidence before anything is settled.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll improve the credits slightly and move the second rollout milestone by two weeks. Since we're all here and broadly aligned, let's mark those changes in pen and have this group confirm the package today, then legal can polish the wording afterward.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: It is good that you are trying to make movement. Our managing director is not in this meeting, but we can certainly continue refining the package. If you wish, we can also arrange dinner this evening with two of our operations heads.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Dinner would be valuable, thank you. To avoid losing the factory slot, I'll email a final commercial version within the hour and note that your team has accepted the business points pending legal clean-up. That should hold the pricing while everyone keeps reviewing.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: You may send what you feel is helpful. We will study it carefully once it arrives.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Perfect. I'll keep the tone positive and say we have agreement in principle so headquarters can release capacity while we move the paperwork forward.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer miscalibrates indirect, relationship-based negotiation cues and the hierarchy signal. After hearing that the managing director is absent and that the package still needs confidence and study, the newcomer treats the working group's encouraging language as authorization to record provisional acceptance and push the deal forward. In this Malawi context, that overreads soft alignment and bypasses the expected top-level decision sequence.

scenario: A medical equipment firm is negotiating a distributor agreement in Lagos. Your product manager, who knows the technical bundle best, led the first meeting and came away with warm reactions and a request for another in-person discussion next week. The launch window closes in ten days, and your company can fund one additional trip. Your normal practice is to keep the same deal lead through signature.
question: Which staffing decision should you make for the next negotiation round?

options.A: Keep the product manager as sole lead for the next session and ask them to convert the positive meeting into a draft close while headquarters stays available by phone.
options.B: Replace the current lead with your regional vice president and have senior commercial staff handle the next session without the product manager, reserving technical clarifications for later emails.
options.C: Add a higher-ranking commercial sponsor to lead the next session, keep the product manager in the room for specifics, and use the visit to work toward internal alignment as well as terms.
options.D: Send only a higher-ranking executive for the next visit to focus on relationship building first, then return the product manager after that meeting once commercial approval looks settled.

scenario: You are a regional partnerships manager on a multicultural team preparing a distribution agreement for a new medical device line in Nigeria. Your team includes legal staff in Germany, a pricing lead in the UAE, and a commercial VP in the UK. A Lagos-based distributor has already attended two video calls and one in-person dinner with your team over the past month. The distributor's operations director has been warm, responsive, and detailed about market access, but each time your team tries to move to draft exclusivity terms, service penalties, or signature timing, the conversation shifts back to market history, mutual contacts, rollout ambitions, and who will support the relationship long term. After the last meeting, the operations director emailed: "Good discussion. We are aligned in principle. Next week we can continue with your team and include additional leadership on our side." Your UK VP reads this as near-closure and wants a marked-up contract sent within 24 hours so procurement can hit quarter-end targets. Legal supports sending the full draft now to create momentum and protect your position. Budget only allows one more in-person visit this month, and a competitor is rumored to be courting the same distributor. You must send your team a decision memo today on how to run the next 10 days of contact with the Nigerian partner.
question: Write the decision memo. Specify what you infer from the interaction so far, what assumption your internal team is most at risk of making, and your concrete plan for the next 10 days. Your memo must decide the sequence of meetings, who should attend from both sides if possible, when and how contract details should be introduced, what evidence would make you speed up or slow down, and how you will brief your UK VP and legal team without either overcommitting or stalling. Do not give a generic relationship-building plan; make clear execution choices under the deadline and competitor pressure.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden mechanism from the actual interaction pattern
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers from repeated topic shifts, prior personal contact, and mention of "additional leadership" that apparent principle-level alignment is not yet equivalent to deal readiness, and that trust-building plus senior-level involvement still materially affect the path to agreement. No credit for merely saying "culture matters" or naming relationships/hierarchy without linking them to these exact cues.

rubric.point: Identifies and bounds the tempting imported assumption
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly rejects the internal near-miss that a warm counterpart, prior discussions, and an "aligned in principle" email justify pushing a full draft and quarter-end close sequence immediately. Partial credit if the answer notices risk but treats it as only a generic communication issue rather than a misread of negotiation stage.

rubric.point: Makes a seed-specific sequence decision on the primary axis
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan sequences the next contact around relationship/trust consolidation and senior decision-maker engagement before or alongside limited contractual movement, rather than leading with a full marked-up contract as the main next step. Strong answers narrow the contract step to a lighter frame such as principles, agenda, or scoped issue list until the right people and trust threshold are in place. No full credit for delaying everything indefinitely or for sending the entire draft first and hoping discussion catches up later.

rubric.point: Uses metacognitive CQ through calibrated evidence handling
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer states what can be inferred now, what remains uncertain, and what evidence would change the plan, such as whether the newly included leaders are actual decision makers, whether the partner invites substantive term discussion once senior figures join, or whether responsiveness changes after a relationship-focused meeting. No full credit for overconfidence (treating the cultural hypothesis as certainty) or inert caution (saying only to ask more questions without deciding how to proceed).

rubric.point: Designs role-specific coordination across internal and external stakeholders
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer assigns concrete roles: for example, choosing a senior commercial representative or executive sponsor to attend the next interaction, limiting legal's direct front-stage role at the wrong moment, and using the Nigerian-side inclusion of additional leadership as a signal to match status appropriately. Partial credit for generic advice to "include stakeholders" without role or timing consequences.

rubric.point: Controls wording and channel risk under deadline pressure
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes a communication frame that preserves momentum without prematurely forcing closure, such as confirming strategic alignment, proposing the next discussion structure, and introducing selected commercial issues in a way that does not imply the relationship stage is complete. No full credit for either a purely social note with no business progression or a legalistic contract-forward email that enacts the near-miss.

rubric.point: Provides a realistic monitoring or repair path
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer includes a contingency for signs of miscalibration, such as if the partner continues deferring term discussion, if the added leaders do not appear, or if the team accidentally sends too formal a draft too early; the response must specify how to repair without treating the partner as non-serious. No credit for generic "follow up respectfully" language alone.

reference_outline: Infer that repeated personal interaction, warm engagement, and topic redirection away from detailed terms indicate the negotiation is still in a trust-and-relationship-building phase rather than true contract-close phase, even though interest appears real.

Treat the mention of "additional leadership" as operationally important evidence that senior authority may matter for commitment; plan the next meeting to include a status-matched senior representative from your side and aim to confirm who on their side shapes final approval.

Reject the attractive internal default of sending a full marked-up contract immediately as the main move; if any document is sent, keep it limited and stage-appropriate, such as a discussion framework, principles summary, or prioritized issue list tied to the next meeting.

Use the next 10 days to combine momentum with calibration: secure a meeting with the newly included leaders, continue trust-building through direct interaction, and only deepen into exclusivity, penalties, and signature timing after testing whether the conversation is ready for those specifics.

Brief the UK VP and legal team that current evidence supports real interest but not yet closeable readiness; explain what is known, what remains uncertain, and which signals would justify accelerating to full drafting versus slowing to more senior relationship work.

Specify evidence thresholds: accelerate if senior Nigerian stakeholders engage directly on substantive terms and decision route; slow or reframe if conversations stay principle-level, leaders remain absent, or responses suggest the relationship owner and formal approver are not yet aligned.

Include a repair path if someone sends a heavy contract package too early: re-anchor the exchange around shared goals, clarify that the document is exploratory rather than a closure demand, and quickly restore a higher-trust conversation with the right-level participants.

scenario: A newcomer from a regional procurement team is visiting Accra for a first meeting with a potential local distributor. Headquarters wants a draft launch timeline by the end of the day because a donor review is tomorrow morning. The meeting is warm and encouraging, and a commercial officer from the distributor handles most of the discussion, while the managing director joins only briefly before leaving for another appointment.

roles.local: Kojo, commercial officer at the Ghanaian distributor
roles.newcomer: Elena, regional procurement manager visiting for the first meeting

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Welcome, Elena. I hope your trip was not too tiring. How is your family back home, and have you settled in since arriving?

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Thank you, Kojo. The trip went smoothly, and my family is well. I arrived last night and I'm settling in fine. I hope everyone here is doing well too before we get into the numbers.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We are well, thank you. From what you've shown, the volumes and service levels look workable on our side. If things continue like this, I think we can do good business together.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: That's encouraging. I need to brief headquarters today, so I'll note that the discussion is positive and that the next step is to confirm the commercial points after your internal review. Could you tell me who should receive the draft summary and when I should expect the formal go-ahead?

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: You can send it to me first this afternoon. Our managing director was here earlier, but he has stepped out for another meeting. We usually tidy these things up once he has looked at them.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll send a short recap with the pricing options, proposed start window, and the open items, and I'll mark it as a discussion note rather than a final agreement. For the donor review, I'll say we had a strong first meeting and are awaiting your side's confirmation.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That is fine. If you send it before five, I can prepare it for review this evening.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Perfect. I'll keep the note concise and send it before five so your team can consider it tonight, then I'll hold the launch date as provisional until I hear back through the review process.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer matches the Ghana-specific mechanism by not treating a warm, promising first meeting with a junior commercial contact as final commitment. She updates her interpretation, preserves the relationship-focused opening, and seeks concrete evidence about authority, recipients, and timing while reporting the outcome only as provisional.

scenario: You are visiting Accra to secure a signature on a vendor shortlist before bids expire tomorrow evening. The director's assistant confirmed yesterday afternoon, and your local operations lead says the office often begins later than the diary suggests. You have one printed pack, a 9:00 meeting time, and another client call across town at 11:00.
question: Which sequence is the best way to handle the morning?

options.A: Arrive before 9:00, send a brief check-in that morning, wait without visible irritation if the start slips, then ask for the earliest same-day decision point before leaving.
options.B: Arrive before 9:00, wait quietly until someone calls you in, and if the meeting has not started by 10:00, leave the pack with reception and request feedback by email.
options.C: Send a short reconfirmation the previous evening, arrive before 9:00, and at 9:15 ask the assistant to move the meeting to another day with a firmer start time.
options.D: Arrive before 9:00, open with the printed pack at reception, and at 9:10 ask your operations lead to escalate the delay so the signature can be prioritised.

scenario: You are the regional program manager for a fintech rollout preparing a one-hour contract-finalization meeting in Nairobi for 9:00 a.m. tomorrow. The meeting determines whether the Kenyan distributor signs this week or pushes review into next month. Your team includes a London-based legal lead, a Nairobi-based operations manager, and a Johannesburg-based implementation lead. The distributor’s procurement manager has confirmed the agenda and asked for a tight meeting because their CEO may "join when free." In the last two calls, the procurement manager logged in a few minutes after the scheduled time, but the Nairobi operations manager has consistently delivered internal milestones exactly when promised and warned that your company will be judged on professionalism if your side appears disorganized. London wants to send a message tonight stating that the meeting will begin exactly at 9:00 with or without late participants, because legal counsel has another call at 9:40. Johannesburg argues that if senior people appear late, pushing ahead could embarrass the client side and damage trust. You cannot extend the meeting, and rescheduling would likely miss the quarter-end target. No one on your team has worked directly with this distributor before.
question: Write a brief decision memo to your team that sets the meeting plan. Your memo must specify: how you interpret the mixed signals in the case, what assumption you think your team is most likely to import incorrectly, the exact start-sequence you will use between 8:50 and 9:15, what you will communicate in advance and to whom, and what evidence during the first 15 minutes would cause you to continue, pause, or re-sequence the discussion. Make the plan concrete enough that the Nairobi operations manager, London legal lead, and client-facing host each know their role.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the mixed punctuality mechanism from the scenario rather than treating lateness as a single fixed norm.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that the team should be on time and visibly prepared, while also recognizing that actual start behavior may vary by stakeholder and status in this Nairobi business setting; no credit for answers that flatten the case into either 'everything starts late' or 'everyone must start exactly on time.'

rubric.point: Identifies and bounds the tempting imported assumption.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer names a plausible outsider overgeneralization and explains why using a single global punctuality rule would miscalibrate the plan here; partial credit if it notices a trap but does not show how it would distort execution.

rubric.point: Makes a seed-specific start-sequence decision on the primary timing axis.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer sets a concrete sequence such as arriving early, opening punctually with available working participants, using the first minutes for agenda framing or technical/working items, and reserving decision-sensitive items until enough authority is present; no credit for either waiting passively without structure or declaring that the core negotiation will proceed unchanged regardless of who has joined.

rubric.point: Allocates roles and channels by stakeholder instead of using one generic message.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan differentiates advance communication and live roles for the Nairobi operations manager, London legal lead, and meeting host, including how to signal professionalism without publicly challenging absent senior participants; partial credit for generic 'confirm with everyone' plans.

rubric.point: Applies metacognitive CQ through explicit monitoring and revision criteria.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer states what can be inferred now, what remains uncertain, and what specific early evidence would change the plan during the first 15 minutes; no credit for 'be flexible' or 'ask more questions' without decision thresholds.

rubric.point: Rejects polished near-miss plans that are careful but mis-scoped.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly rules out at least one attractive but wrong option, such as announcing that the meeting will proceed fully at 9:00 regardless of attendance, or delaying all substantive discussion until every invitee appears; partial credit if it implies this without explaining why the option is miscalibrated.

rubric.point: Balances deadline pressure and relationship risk with operational consequences.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan preserves quarter-end progress and legal time constraints while protecting client trust, using a narrower execution design rather than the longest, safest, or broadest consultation plan; no credit for answers that solve pressure only by rescheduling, extending indefinitely, or stripping the meeting to generic politeness.

reference_outline: State that your side should be fully punctual and prepared before 9:00 because professionalism will be judged, but do not assume every external participant will behave by the same exact clock.

Interpret the CEO's possible later arrival and prior slight delays as evidence that start-time behavior may be shaped by hierarchy as much as scheduling, while also weighting that this is a Nairobi professional business context where punctuality still carries signal value.
Reject the imported default of either hard global clock enforcement or blanket expectation of delay; name it as the key calibration risk.

Send an advance note that confirms the 9:00 agenda and readiness, but avoid wording like 'with or without late participants'; privately align internal roles so the host opens on time, the Nairobi manager reads attendance/status cues, and London counsel protects the 9:40 constraint.

Use the first minutes for welcome, agenda confirmation, introductions, and non-final working items if authority is incomplete; hold decision-closing or signature-critical segments until the relevant senior participant is present or clearly delegated.

Define update signals for 9:00-9:15: continue into substantive review if the empowered client participants are present or explicitly authorize proceeding; pause or re-sequence if only junior participants are present and status cues suggest waiting for a higher-ranking arrival; do not sit silently without structure.

Explain that the metacognitive task is to act on enough evidence now while keeping uncertainty visible: infer a likely hierarchy-linked timing pattern, but revise if the distributor explicitly signals strict punctuality or delegated authority.
Include a repair path if timing slips: summarize progress crisply, preserve respect for absent senior stakeholders, and secure a clear next commitment rather than framing the delay as noncompliance.

scenario: A regional sales director in London must approve the briefing for an account lead flying to Nairobi tomorrow to align on distributor terms with a Kenyan host company. Headquarters wants clear follow-up records for legal review, but the host team has described the first session as a chance to get acquainted before moving into the deal, and the venue booking shows only a start time.
question: Which briefing line is the most defensible for the director to approve?

options.A: Approve a full timed agenda and pre-numbered decision log, asking the host team to confirm the opening introductions block and the planned closing time before anyone travels.
options.B: Approve a light courtesy note only, with no agenda or record template for the first session, and wait until a later meeting to introduce formal follow-up documentation.
options.C: Approve a short issue list and ask the host team when they want business to begin, while also requesting their sign-off on a scheduled wrap-up point for the meeting record.
options.D: Approve a short issue list and internal note template, let the host side set when substantive topics start, and send the formal action memo only after the discussion lands naturally.

scenario:
You are coordinating a three-country product rollout for a telecom supplier. The final internal approval package must be completed in Ghana before a regional client review on Friday at 16:00. The Ghana-based approval group includes a finance manager, operations lead, and campus IT liaison who all need to sign off on the implementation window. Two earlier meetings this month started 20-30 minutes after the calendar time and pushed later decisions into the evening, which frustrated the German procurement lead and caused rework. However, for the last two weeks, the Ghana operations lead has been sending revised documents before deadline and has pushed back when others missed agreed turnaround times. 

Your Singapore-based director now wants a plan by tonight. She is pressing for a 'no-slippage' approach because brand risk is high if the client review moves. The German procurement lead wants every approval meeting to start exactly on the hour, with anyone absent after 10 minutes recorded as missed and the decision moved ahead without them. A UK legal reviewer prefers a broad safety buffer: schedule the Ghana sign-off session 90 minutes earlier than needed, assume delays, and tell the client only the final result. Budget does not allow a second formal workshop, and one missing signature will block release.

You have email access, Teams, and phone, but no local coordinator on the ground in Ghana. You must propose how the final 48-hour approval sequence should run.
question: Write a short decision memo that recommends the approval sequence for the Ghana sign-off. Your memo must: (1) diagnose what the mixed timing evidence suggests about this workplace context, (2) identify the most tempting but miscalibrated assumption in the proposals you received, (3) specify the meeting and pre-meeting sequence for the next 48 hours, including channels, timing checkpoints, and who must confirm what by when, and (4) explain how your plan reduces domino-effect delay risk without treating the Ghana team as either uniformly late or uniformly clock-driven.

rubric.point: Diagnoses contested time orientation from the evidence
rubric.score_rule: Awards credit only if the answer infers that this Ghana workplace shows mixed or contested scheduling norms from the scenario evidence and therefore requires explicit expectation-setting; no credit for simply saying 'Ghana is polychronic,' 'people are late,' or 'everyone should be punctual.'

rubric.point: Rejects the attractive imported assumption
rubric.score_rule: Awards credit only if the answer explicitly identifies a tempting but wrong frame such as imposing a strict global default meeting rule or padding the schedule on the assumption that delay is normal, and explains why either overgeneralizes the evidence in this specific Ghanaian work setting.

rubric.point: Makes a seed-specific timing and sequence decision
rubric.score_rule: Awards credit only if the plan uses concrete sequencing to clarify expectations before the formal sign-off meeting, such as pre-confirming attendance, document readiness, decision rights, and hard cut-off points, rather than relying on the workshop itself to reveal who is ready.

rubric.point: Controls domino-effect risk operationally
rubric.score_rule: Awards credit only if the answer translates delay risk into workflow controls tied to this case, for example staging approvals, locking document review windows, confirming signature dependencies, or setting escalation checkpoints before the final meeting; generic statements about 'planning ahead' or 'being flexible' do not score.

rubric.point: Applies cognitive CQ through correct evidence weighting
rubric.score_rule: Awards credit only if the answer distinguishes between stereotype, generic business process, and the actual mixed evidence in the case, and uses that distinction to justify the plan; no credit for broad consultation, generic empathy, or abstract cultural awareness language without execution consequences.

rubric.point: Assigns channels, roles, and wording appropriately
rubric.score_rule: Awards credit only if the memo specifies who gets email versus Teams versus phone contact, who must explicitly confirm time and readiness, and how the meeting invite or briefing should state expectations in a way that narrows ambiguity without punitive or culturally sweeping wording.

reference_outline: State that the evidence does not support a single fixed assumption about time behavior in this Ghanaian workplace: earlier delays matter, but recent deadline discipline and pushback on missed turnarounds show that some actors are operating with strong clock and dependency awareness.

Reject both polished near-misses: do not enforce a blanket 'start without anyone after 10 minutes' rule as if generic global SOP settles the issue, and do not simply add a large buffer on the assumption that delay is normal; both misread the mixed evidence and can create either relationship damage or hidden schedule drift.

Use a 48-hour sequence that front-loads clarity: send a written approval map today listing required signatories, decision scope, document version, start time, expected arrival or login confirmation, and what will happen if a dependency is not ready before the meeting.

Require explicit confirmations before the formal session: each Ghana-based approver confirms by a named checkpoint that they have the current file, know the decision required, and can attend or nominate the correct substitute if authorized; unresolved gaps trigger direct phone follow-up before the workshop rather than during it.

Run the formal sign-off meeting as a narrow closure step, not as the first moment of coordination: use Teams or phone reminders shortly before start, begin from pre-cleared items, and escalate only missing dependencies according to the preannounced sequence so one late start does not cascade across all approvals.

Use wording that is specific and non-stereotyping, such as confirming 'decision readiness' and 'required response times' rather than invoking lateness, local habits, or rigid disciplinary language; the plan should treat expectations as shared work mechanics, not cultural defects.

Monitor and repair through defined checkpoints: if one approver has not confirmed by the pre-meeting deadline, contact them directly, surface the dependency to the director early, and shift to alternative authorized sign-off or reordered agenda items only if that path was specified in advance.

scenario: A newcomer has just taken over a regional operations team in Accra and Kampala. A donor review is in two days, and the team needs one final rollout plan for a new field-reporting process. In the kickoff meeting, several senior and junior staff listened quietly while the country director said the draft still needed a final decision.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We need one version of the rollout note by tomorrow afternoon. After the meeting, the country director said the donor will want a clear approval trail, and the heads of programs and finance did not add much in the room.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll tighten the draft tonight and send it first to those heads. I'll keep coordinators to field-level implementation gaps so we don't blur roles.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That may help. The coordinators usually answer faster on operations, while the department heads often come in later on wording and risk.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: To keep this moving, I'll ask the heads for only any deal-breakers or policy conflicts. If they don't reopen the structure, I'll treat the direction as settled and fold in the coordinators' points before the director sees it.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The director said she wants something she can issue from her office in the morning.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Right, so I don't want another full round. If the heads send short notes or only minor edits, I'll package the near-final version as the agreed plan and have her release that copy.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. The donor mostly wants one implementation line and no confusion later about who approved what.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll add a note that comments were invited and no major changes were raised, so the approval path is easy to show.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer sounds orderly and respects roles, but the decisive error is narrowing senior input to objections only and then treating limited or absent pushback as substantive clearance. In this Uganda/Ghana hierarchy context, silence or brief replies are not reliable agreement, and the final decision is being inferred before explicit higher-level approval.

scenario: You are the regional program manager for a French manufacturing group rolling out a supplier-quality upgrade across a plant in Senegal, with commercial input from a procurement lead in Malawi and technical support from headquarters in France. In six weeks, a major client audit will decide whether the group keeps a high-margin contract. The Senegal plant director publicly endorsed the upgrade at kickoff, but the day-to-day implementation has been handled by a local quality coordinator who says the draft process changes are "ready to use" and asks you to launch sitewide training immediately so the audit timeline is protected. In three meetings, supervisors from production and maintenance were polite, took notes, and said they would "follow the guidance," but almost none of them volunteered questions or raised concerns. Afterward, several action items stalled. The Senegal quality coordinator keeps saying he is waiting for "internal alignment" before confirming dates. Meanwhile, the Malawi procurement lead wants the same package approved this week so she can tell suppliers the new requirements are final; she argues that if local coordinators are already running workshops, they clearly have enough authority to proceed. HQ in France is pressing for a visible rollout milestone by Friday and suggests that, if needed, you bypass slow internal loops by asking each function head for direct commitment in a working session. You have one chance tomorrow to send a decision memo and convene a 30-minute coordination call.
question: Write the decision memo you would send and outline the coordination plan for the next 10 days. Your answer must: (1) state what you think is happening and what evidence in the scenario supports that reading, (2) identify the most tempting but miscalibrated assumption another manager might make here, (3) decide exactly whose approval or commitment you need before training and supplier messaging become binding, and in what sequence, and (4) explain how you will test and update your interpretation without either freezing the rollout or treating tentative cooperation as final authorization.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that visible cooperation from coordinators and supervisors is not sufficient evidence of distributed decision authority.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers from the stalled follow-through, lack of volunteered participation, repeated references to 'internal alignment,' and pressure around formal launch that practical authority likely sits higher than the implementation staff or meeting attendees. No credit for merely saying 'there may be hierarchy' without tying it to execution consequences.

rubric.point: Rejects the tempting near-miss that the local quality coordinator or workshop participants can effectively greenlight rollout because they are already doing implementation work.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly bounds the attractive imported assumption that operational ownership equals approval power, and explains why acting on that assumption would misread the situation. Partial credit if the answer warns to 'double-check' but still treats coordinator-level readiness as enough to launch.

rubric.point: Makes a seed-specific approval sequence decision on the main execution axis.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan separates preparatory work from binding rollout, secures senior plant-level decision or explicit top-level signoff before sitewide training is announced as final, and delays supplier-facing finalization until that higher approval is obtained. Partial credit if the answer seeks broad consensus from many managers but does not identify the decisive approval route.

rubric.point: Uses metacognitive CQ by stating what can be inferred now, what remains uncertain, and what evidence would change the plan.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer distinguishes current working inference from certainty, names unresolved questions such as who can formally authorize the change and whether the plant director has already delegated that power, and proposes targeted checks that reduce the right uncertainty. No credit for generic caution, indefinite consultation, or asking everyone for more views without a decision focus.

rubric.point: Designs role-specific communication that protects progress under deadline without forcing premature public commitment.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo/call plan assigns concrete roles such as: coordinator prepares materials and implementation dependencies; senior plant leadership confirms authorization status and launch scope; procurement receives a provisional message rather than a final supplier mandate; HQ gets a milestone framed as 'pending executive confirmation' rather than falsely completed. Partial credit if communication is respectful but vague.

rubric.point: Avoids the opposite metacognitive error of becoming inert or overcorrecting into total delay.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer preserves momentum through nonbinding preparation steps, sets a short review checkpoint, and monitors for confirmation from the actual decision layer. No credit for plans that simply postpone everything, or that assume no one below the top executive can do anything useful.

reference_outline: State a working diagnosis: the Senegal coordinator and workshop participants appear able to prepare and comply, but the pattern of polite agreement plus stalled action suggests final authorization is centralized above them.

Name the near-miss: a global-SOP reading would treat implementation activity and meeting attendance as proof of delegated approval, then push immediate training and supplier messaging to satisfy audit pressure.

Set the execution-axis decision: split preparation from commitment; continue drafting materials, scheduling options, and gap analysis now, but do not treat the rollout as final until the relevant senior plant authority explicitly approves scope and timing.

Use a tight sequence: first confirm with the plant director or equivalent top decision-maker whether approval is granted and what remains pending; second align the coordinator on what is preparatory versus binding; third update HQ and Malawi procurement with a provisional status and date for final confirmation.

Apply metacognitive CQ explicitly: say what evidence currently supports the hierarchy inference, what ambiguity remains about delegated authority, and what specific signal would justify switching to full rollout.

Manage stakeholder messaging under pressure: tell HQ that a visible milestone will be a completed readiness package plus executive approval checkpoint, not a falsely finalized launch; tell Malawi procurement not to issue final supplier instructions until plant-level authorization is confirmed.

Include calibration and repair: if senior approval is delayed, escalate the risk transparently, preserve relationship trust by not exposing lower-level staff as blockers, and reset the timeline based on the actual approval path rather than blaming 'resistance' or forcing public commitments.

scenario: A regional manager is deciding whether to release vendor funds tonight for a Kampala rollout workshop. In the planning meeting, the country director arrived late; before that, several younger functional leads debated dates and staffing in detail. After the director joined, the room became more reserved, and the meeting ended without anyone restating a final decision. Later that afternoon, detailed follow-up notes came by email from multiple attendees, but none identified a final approver.
question: Which approval decision or briefing line is most defensible for the manager to use now?

options.A: Approve once the written notes show no objections from all attendees, and file the email trail as the meeting's collective authorization for the vendor release.
options.B: Approve once the country team's senior decision-maker gives explicit sign-off, and treat the earlier discussion plus email notes as input rather than final authorization.
options.C: Approve once the oldest attendee who contributed heavily before the director arrived confirms the plan, then copy the director on the release documentation.
options.D: Approve only after the director replies and each functional lead then reconfirms separately, using that second round to document agreement across the whole group.

scenario: A newcomer operations manager in Kampala is trying to finalize a distributor proposal before a regional deadline. The draft is technically ready, but the local team has been quiet in meetings, and the country director is traveling. The newcomer must decide how to move the file forward without losing a day.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The pricing sheet is complete, and the distributor wants our response today. In this morning's review, everyone said the draft was clear, but no one added much.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: If the room had no objections, I'll send the final version now and note that the team has aligned. We can keep momentum and avoid missing the window.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We can send something today, yes. The country director is still on the road, though, and Mr. Kato has not seen the revised cover page.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll circulate it to the managers and ask for any comments within thirty minutes so we still have a record before dispatch.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That would help the file. The sales team will probably stay quiet unless there is a specific issue.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then silence should be enough for us to proceed. I'll tell the distributor the branch team has cleared it, and if any manager replies later, we can fold that into the contract stage.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. The driver is leaving for the printer at four, so timing is tight.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll move it now with the circulation note attached, so we've been transparent and kept the deadline.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer misreads silence and broad team circulation as sufficient authorization. In this seed context, decision legitimacy is more vertically anchored, so the key execution error is treating non-objection from the wider team as approval instead of routing final clearance through the relevant senior decision-maker or title-bearing authority.

scenario: A newly arrived regional manager in Kampala is trying to finalize a supplier choice for a field rollout before a donor deadline. He has already reviewed written comments and wants the 2 p.m. meeting to produce a clear procurement direction, but the room will include a senior long-serving finance head, several unit leads, and one local operations coordinator.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The comparison pack is printed. Mr. Kato will come in once his budget call ends, and procurement wants our direction this evening.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Good. Since most comments came in already, I'll open with the two strongest options and the cost differences so we do not spend the whole meeting recapping.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That will help. A few leads said they still have concerns, especially on transport and payment terms.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then once Mr. Kato joins, I'll ask those leads to explain in the room what they would change in my ranking before he gives his view, so we hear the unresolved issues directly.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We can keep the figures on one page. People have been checking the same numbers several times.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Perfect. I do not want side conversations later, so if someone thinks option two should move ahead, I want them to say it at that point rather than after we leave.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. I will make sure the supplier sheet and payment schedule are both on the table.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Thanks. After that discussion, Mr. Kato can confirm the direction and procurement can act tonight.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: Daniel prepares well and keeps decision ownership with Mr. Kato, but the decisive behavioral mismatch is sequence and audience: he plans to have unit leads openly state how they would change his ranking in the main meeting before the senior authority gives direction. In this Uganda workplace context, using the shared meeting for junior or peer staff to voice direct challenge upward is miscalibrated; lower-risk input sequencing and clearer vertical decision flow would fit better.

scenario: You are the regional implementation lead for a donor-funded agricultural payment platform rolling out in Malawi. On Friday afternoon, your team must decide whether to launch a pilot on Monday with one large cooperative. The client sponsor in London wants a written go/no-go by 17:00 Malawi time because their board pack closes that night. The Malawi country team includes a local operations manager, two senior field supervisors, and a finance lead. In the last two meetings, the operations manager opened and closed the discussion, while the supervisors mainly added examples when invited. When you asked in the group meeting whether the pilot site was ready, one supervisor said, "It may be possible if a few remaining matters are looked at," and another said, "We can still talk about some details." No one directly said not to launch. After the meeting, the London sponsor messaged you: "Please get explicit confirmation from each local lead today so we can document alignment and move." You also know the operations manager will be traveling for three hours before the deadline, has weak connectivity, and dislikes public disagreement in written threads. If the launch slips, the client may cut budget for the second district. If the launch proceeds and fails at the cooperative, trust with local partners could be damaged for months.
question: Write a brief action memo for the next 4 hours that sets out exactly how you will get to a defensible go/no-go recommendation. Your memo must specify who you contact, in what order, through which channel, what you ask publicly versus privately, how you interpret the earlier responses, and how you will communicate the final recommendation to both the Malawi team and the London sponsor. In your plan, identify the most tempting but miscalibrated approach under the deadline pressure and explain why it is risky here.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that the earlier noncommittal answers cannot be treated as clear approval and may be signaling concern without open refusal.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires interpreting the supervisors' wording as ambiguous concern that needs careful follow-up, not as simple agreement or mere lack of detail. No credit if the answer assumes silence or soft wording equals consent.

rubric.point: Routes the decision sequence through the Malawi hierarchy rather than collecting parallel equal-signoff votes from everyone.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires centering the operations manager or top local decision owner in the final internal decision path while still gathering input from others. Partial credit for consulting everyone but leaving final authority diffuse. No credit for a flat consensus or majority-vote process.

rubric.point: Uses calibrated channel and audience choices to surface concerns without forcing public contradiction.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires a concrete split between private follow-up for unresolved concerns and a narrower public message for status coordination. Answers lose credit if they push for explicit yes/no replies in a group thread, force written public disagreement, or rely only on a meeting recap email.

rubric.point: Chooses wording and timing that reduce face threat while still moving the task forward under the deadline.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires specific behavior such as asking what conditions remain, what would need to be fixed before launch, or whether the site is ready enough to stand behind, with fast but non-confrontational follow-up before the sponsor deadline. No credit for generic 'be respectful' language without executable phrasing or timing.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the tempting imported approach of demanding explicit documented approval from each local lead for sponsor clarity.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires naming this as attractive under audit/KPI pressure but risky because it misreads indirect responses and pressures subordinates to contradict or commit publicly outside the local decision pattern. Partial credit if the answer notes it is impolite but does not connect the risk to execution quality.

rubric.point: Translates behavioural CQ into visible execution details rather than abstract cultural awareness.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires concrete action on wording, sequence, channel, audience, and follow-up rhythm. Partial credit for correct cultural explanation without operational behavior. No credit for answers that stay at the level of 'consult stakeholders carefully.'

rubric.point: Provides a defensible sponsor update that preserves task progress without overstating local commitment.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires a sponsor-facing message that reports conditional status, notes that final local confirmation is being closed through the country lead, and avoids claiming unanimous readiness before that step. No credit for telling London the team has approved when that has not been secured.

reference_outline: Treat the supervisors' earlier phrasing as a warning sign of unresolved concerns, not as a green light; assume the issue is readiness risk unless clarified.

First contact the Malawi operations manager as the key internal decision owner, ideally by direct call or voice note given travel/connectivity constraints, to frame the decision and ask what remaining matters could block launch.
Privately and quickly follow up with the two supervisors for concrete unresolved issues, using wording that invites risk disclosure without demanding a public yes/no contradiction.

Do not run a flat reply-all request for explicit signoff from each local lead; that is the polished near-miss because it satisfies sponsor documentation pressure but breaks the local decision and face-saving pattern.
Use a narrow public/team update only for coordination: summarize that readiness items are being confirmed through the country lead and that a final recommendation will follow by a set time.

Send London a calibrated update that distinguishes local input from final local authorization, explains whether launch is conditionally feasible or should pause, and avoids converting indirect concern into false approval.

If concerns remain unresolved before deadline, recommend no-go or conditional delay rather than forcing clarity by escalation in the group channel; protect long-term partner trust over same-day paperwork neatness.
If a public thread already asked for explicit approval, repair by moving sensitive follow-up into private channels and then restating the decision through the appropriate local authority.

scenario: Your company is finalizing a distributor agreement with a Malawian firm. A pricing window closes in six days, and flying in your regional vice president would be costly. So far, workshops with the counterpart's operations, finance, and commercial managers have been constructive, and your local team thinks one more round of technical alignment may be enough. Before deciding whether to keep working through the current group or bring in your regional vice president now, you want one observation that would most justify the extra effort.
question: Which observation would be most diagnostic?

options.A: Managers from several functions continue refining terms together and ask for another cross-department session before anyone summarizes the latest draft for internal review.
options.B: The counterpart's team says they prefer broad discussion first, then suggests collecting written agreement from each department head before scheduling any final meeting.
options.C: After resolving most clauses in group sessions, the team pauses commitment language and proposes a short meeting once their managing director is back, asking who from your side can attend at that level.
options.D: Mid-level managers handle detailed bargaining smoothly, while the most senior person joins only for the closing ceremony after both sides have finished the commercial terms.

scenario: You lead a multinational product team preparing a 10-day rollout decision for a mobile payment feature with a Kenyan distribution partner. Your company wants a signed go/no-go recommendation before the quarter closes. The Kenyan partner has already hosted two meetings. In both, the country director opened the discussion, several operational staff gave detailed concerns about agent training, fraud escalation, and customer messaging, and the country director closed by saying the team would 'align internally and revert.' After the second meeting, your headquarters asked why no decision has been locked if 'everyone already spoke.' Your regional finance lead is pushing you to get written sign-off from the operational managers directly so procurement can start. Budget only allows one in-person visit before launch, and your own vice president is reluctant to travel. At the same time, the partner has hinted that delay will affect trust because a rival vendor is also in discussion. You have team members from Germany and India proposing different approaches: one wants a workshop vote with all functions present to prove alignment, and another wants to keep circulating documents until every department explicitly agrees in writing. You must send a decision memo today on how your side will secure commitment and move the rollout forward without losing the relationship.
question: Write the decision memo you would send to your vice president. Specify the stakeholder sequence, who from your side must engage at each step, what commitment you will seek in each interaction, and what effort you will personally invest despite the time and status cost. Your memo must explain what hidden decision pattern you infer from the meeting history, why the most tempting imported assumption would misfire here, and how you will keep the project moving under deadline without either forcing a premature broad-consensus mechanism or retreating into indefinite waiting.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the decision pattern from the neutral evidence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that broad discussion is expected but final commitment is likely concentrated with the top leader, using the opening/closing pattern and 'align internally and revert' as evidence. No credit for merely saying 'hierarchy matters' or 'they value consensus' without linking both to the exact decision structure.

rubric.point: Chooses the correct stakeholder and approval sequence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan gathers operational input first or in parallel, then routes final commitment through the partner's senior decision-maker rather than treating staff agreement, a workshop vote, or department-by-department signatures as the decisive endpoint. Partial credit if senior engagement is mentioned but not made the actual approval route.
