Specify evidence weighting: do not treat a late join or extended discussion by itself as decisive; instead watch whether the necessary operational voices eventually participate, whether issues are clarified enough for risk assessment, whether substantive blockers remain unresolved, and whether a recommendation can be assembled by the synthesis cutoff.

Brief Sydney with a performance frame, not a cultural lecture: explain that you are adjusting the meeting architecture to improve reliability of the launch recommendation, not lowering standards; reject exclusion of late arrivals as the default because it would remove needed input from the decision path.

Brief Singapore on exactly when compliance input is needed in the sequence so compliance is not left waiting through open-ended discussion but is available for the consolidation step if operational questions affect launch conditions.

Brief the client account director with a concrete deliverable timeline: Thursday review, immediate internal consolidation, and Friday recommendation package; avoid language that frames the Fiji team as delaying and instead describe the process as ensuring a defensible recommendation.

State revision criteria: if key participants still have not engaged by the buffered midpoint, if core launch risks remain unresolved after the working session, or if the synthesis step cannot produce a recommendation, then escalate scope or recommendation status; otherwise proceed without overreacting to timing alone.

scenario: You are an Australia-based program manager coordinating a three-country rollout workshop in Nuku'alofa for a digital agriculture project funded by an Australian sponsor and co-delivered with a Tongan ministry and a Fiji-based implementation partner. The sponsor wants the workshop date, invitation list, and minute-by-minute agenda locked today so travel can be booked before fares rise and the next board pack can say the project is 'on schedule.' The ministry's deputy secretary has not objected to the proposed Wednesday morning slot, but has only replied, 'We will confirm once the full program and those to be received are settled.' A Tongan operations officer separately asks whether the agenda can be sent 'with the opening and acknowledgements placed properly' and whether the venue is the hotel conference room or the community hall that the ministry often uses for major gatherings. Your Fiji partner says to stop overthinking it: send calendar invites now, add a short welcome at the top, and adjust on the day if needed. The Australian sponsor is pressing for efficiency and warns that another date may delay the quarter's KPI. You have one afternoon to brief your team and decide what to lock, what to hold provisional, and whom to involve before invitations go out.
question: Write a decision memo to your team that sets the coordination plan for the next 24 hours. Your memo must: (1) diagnose what the ambiguous signals most likely mean for scheduling and agenda design, (2) identify the tempting but miscalibrated assumption in the Fiji partner's advice, (3) specify exactly what you will and will not lock today on the workshop timing/sequence axis, (4) name who must be consulted first and what evidence would change your plan, and (5) explain how you will keep sponsor pressure, travel risk, and local relationship risk under control without simply delaying everything.

rubric.point: Infers that the unresolved issue is not just attendance logistics but whether ceremony/protocol obligations affect the workshop date, venue, opening sequence, and acknowledgement order before the schedule can be finalized.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer translates the neutral cues into operational scheduling consequences; no credit for merely saying 'respect local customs' or mentioning prayer/ceremony without linking them to timeline locking.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the attractive near-miss plan of sending final invites now and 'adjusting on the day.'
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explains why a generic global scheduling default is risky here on this stage of the work; partial credit if it recommends checking later but still locks the full agenda prematurely.

rubric.point: Makes a concrete primary-axis decision about what remains provisional versus fixed in the next 24 hours.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer distinguishes between holding the final date/time/venue/opening sequence provisionally while still progressing on contingent bookings, draft materials, and internal prep; no credit for all-stop delay or for fully locking the workshop before protocol and calendar checks.

rubric.point: Uses metacognitive CQ by stating what can be inferred now, what remains uncertain, and what specific evidence or response would trigger a revision.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer shows calibrated reasoning under uncertainty rather than certainty or inertia, such as naming which cues are strong, which are ambiguous, and what confirmation is needed from whom.

rubric.point: Names the right stakeholder sequence and scope for confirmation.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer prioritizes the Tongan ministry/host side for confirmation of ceremonial calendar and protocol expectations before external finalization, rather than relying mainly on the Fiji partner, sponsor, or generic admin staff.

rubric.point: Designs role-specific communication that manages hierarchy and pressure without exposing the local side to unnecessary public correction or sponsor-driven escalation.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer uses a targeted coordination route such as a direct host-side clarification on program order, acknowledgements, and venue implications, plus a separate sponsor update framing the date as provisional for protocol clearance; generic 'communicate clearly with everyone' is insufficient.

rubric.point: Includes a practical risk-control plan that protects budget and schedule while preserving local legitimacy.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes bounded operational safeguards such as holding refundable travel windows, preparing two draft agenda versions, or reserving tentative slots without announcing a fixed final schedule; no credit for solving the problem only by broad consultation or indefinite postponement.

reference_outline: State that the ministry's wording about the full program, those to be received, venue choice, and proper placement of opening acknowledgements signals unresolved host-side protocol and possible ceremony-related scheduling constraints, not mere slow administration.

Treat the Fiji partner's suggestion as a plausible but miscalibrated imported default: it assumes the workshop can be finalized first and culturally adjusted later, when here the sequence may need host-side clearance before locking time, venue, and opening order.

For the next 24 hours, do not issue final external invites or a fixed minute-by-minute agenda; instead hold the proposed slot and travel options provisionally, draft the agenda, and mark date/venue/opening sequence as pending host confirmation.

Contact the Tongan ministry/host coordinator first to confirm whether any ceremonial calendar, opening/closing expectation, acknowledgement order, or venue protocol affects the proposed slot and participant order; use that evidence to decide whether Wednesday morning stands, shifts, or moves venue.

Send the Australian sponsor a progress update that the workshop remains on track but final confirmation depends on host-side program and protocol clearance, with a decision deadline and budget-mitigation steps already in place.

Show metacognitive calibration by separating strong inference from uncertainty: it is reasonable to infer that protocol may materially affect schedule design now, but not to assume exactly which ceremony or rule applies without host confirmation.

Prepare a repair/monitoring path: if the host confirms no conflict, release invites immediately; if a conflict emerges, revise the date/venue/opening sequence quickly using prebuilt alternatives rather than treating the change as a failure or escalating blame.

scenario: A newcomer project manager from New Zealand is in Suva to secure local sign-off on a community water upgrade before a donor deadline. The workshop is scheduled for 9:00 a.m., but several invitees are still arriving and a nearby community event is affecting the morning. The newcomer must keep the project moving without damaging local coordination.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The hall is open and the chair will come after he stops at the other program. We still need the supplier choice discussed today because the donor wants our note by tomorrow.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I’ll stay with the 9:00 start on our side and set the papers out now, but I won’t run the selection first thing. As people come in, I’ll use the time to hear each team’s concerns and map options on the board.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Some of the village reps are not here yet, and the engineer has to leave by eleven. We may not get everyone in the room at once.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: That’s fine. I’ll brief the engineer early, then keep the discussion open for the others instead of closing the recommendation before they arrive. If needed, I’ll capture the trade-offs clearly so the chair can weigh them once he has heard the room.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Procurement asked whether you can leave with one confirmed supplier name today. They said it would save time for head office.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I’m not going to force a show-of-hands decision just to send a neat update. I’ll send head office a short note this afternoon saying the options were discussed, who raised what, and that final confirmation will come from the chair after everyone has been included.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. When the chair arrives, he usually wants a quick recap rather than a restart. Keep it tight because he has another stop after this.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I’ll keep the recap brief, note where people already agree, and leave the final call with him once the discussion has settled.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer applies the Fiji-specific scheduling and decision pattern: being punctual personally, not treating late arrival as a failure, keeping discussion inclusive as people join, and preserving the senior person’s final decision after consensus-building instead of forcing an on-time, fully closed decision for donor efficiency.

scenario: A newcomer leading a regional software rollout in Fiji needs a local distributor to approve a pricing sheet before a donor reporting deadline that evening. In the review meeting, several team members comment quickly, while the oldest board member mostly listens and takes notes. The newcomer must decide what to treat as actual approval and what to do next without stalling the project.

roles.local: Mere, operations coordinator at the Fijian distributor
roles.newcomer: Jonas, newly assigned regional rollout manager

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We have twenty minutes before the drivers leave for the outer offices. If the pricing sheet is settled today, I can attach it to the donor packet tonight.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Great, I'll walk everyone through the last two changes and see if we can close it in one pass.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The sales lead likes the numbers, and Mr. Naqelevu said yes when he saw the draft this morning. He has not said much in the meeting yet.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll summarize the points aloud, hear the room, and then check what timing Mr. Naqelevu wants for a decision before I mark anything final.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: People will tell you now if a line item is awkward. They may still want the packet moving tonight.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I'll send the donor team a provisional packet with the pricing page flagged as pending confirmation, and in the room I'll ask whether there are any remaining concerns before I ask him how he wants us to proceed.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That would keep the dispatch schedule intact. We can print as soon as you finish the summary.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll do that now and keep the page editable until I hear his final direction after everyone has spoken.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer's behavior fits the Fijian decision pattern by not treating an earlier 'yes' as firm approval, allowing broader input first, and recognizing that the older senior participant may stay quiet while retaining final decision authority. The decisive axis is evidence calibration: provisional progress is made, but final approval is deferred until the senior person's post-discussion decision.

scenario: You are facilitating a supplier-selection meeting in Fiji for a donor-funded project. The local host asked you to keep the session participatory, but procurement needs a same-day note stating whether the shortlist is approved. During discussion, several team members speak at length, one older leader says little, and a few people give short verbal acknowledgements as points are summarized.
question: Which briefing line should you give your note-taker about when to mark the shortlist as approved?

options.A: Keep the discussion open to the full group, note emerging agreement, and mark approval only when the senior host closes the matter and signals the meeting can move on.
options.B: Mark approval once most attendees have voiced support during the open discussion, then circulate minutes that reflect the group's consensus as the meeting decision.
options.C: Hold the note until the oldest leader offers a view, then treat that statement as the approval point even if the wider discussion is still continuing.
options.D: Invite broad discussion, then ask the quiet senior leader directly for a clear public confirmation before recording approval and releasing the procurement note that afternoon.

scenario: A newcomer program manager in Fiji is running a meeting to choose one of two suppliers for a community internet rollout. A donor wants the shortlist by the end of the day, but the contract cannot move without local agreement. Several team members have spoken at length, while the oldest committee member has said very little and mostly watched the discussion.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We have both supplier quotes printed. The donor office keeps asking whether we can send a name before 5 p.m.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I will not force a vote yet. I will walk through the two options, hear everyone out, and then send the donor a brief note that the team is concluding today after this discussion.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That helps. Mere has strong views on installation speed, and Jope is worried about maintenance on the outer islands. Ratu Jone has mostly been listening.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I noticed. I will keep the comparison moving, but I will not treat the quietness as disinterest. After the others finish, I will ask whether there are any final concerns before we close on one direction here.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The donor also asked if we can show that the committee was aligned, not just efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I will summarize where the room seems to agree, note the remaining concern on servicing, and hold the email until the discussion is fully settled in the room rather than sending a provisional winner during the break.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. We are going back in now, and the finance officer is expecting something concise afterward.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I will keep the close short and practical, but I will let the room finish its sequence first and send finance the outcome once that is complete.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer's behavior fits the Fijian meeting pattern by recalibrating away from a fast egalitarian decision script: he does not read senior silence as lack of authority, lets broader discussion run first, seeks room-wide alignment, and waits for the meeting's internal decision sequence before sending the result.

scenario: In Suva, a partner meeting on vendor selection has just ended. Two younger managers led most of the technical discussion, while Mere, the oldest participant on the partner side, mostly listened and asked only a few brief questions. Headquarters needs your written status tonight, and you can make one short follow-up before people split off into side conversations and leave the room.
question: Which immediate move is most likely to let you record the right level of decision status without pushing the meeting into the wrong rhythm?

options.A: Catch one of the younger managers at the doorway and ask whether you should report the vendor they seemed to favor as the final choice.
options.B: Before anyone leaves, say to the partner group, "For tonight's note, should I record this as a final selection or as still under review?" and give them a moment to settle the answer among themselves.
options.C: Turn to Mere right away and ask, in front of the others, whether she wants you to name the vendor in tonight's update.
options.D: Tell the room you will send a draft saying the preferred vendor is selected, and they can correct you later by email if needed.

scenario: You are the regional operations lead for an NGO rolling out a mobile reporting tool for community health workers in Fiji. A donor requires a signed rollout decision and launch date by Friday. If you miss the date, the donor may reassign the funds next quarter. A local ministry unit has already hosted two planning meetings with your team, a municipal health manager, a provincial administrator, two clinic supervisors, and several community representatives. In both meetings, most people spoke at length, newer staff spoke only after being invited, and the oldest clinic supervisor was not interrupted even when the discussion drifted. At the end of the second meeting, several participants said versions of “yes, okay” when your draft pilot timeline was summarized, but no one explicitly stated who was authorizing the pilot. Afterward, your headquarters director asked you to send one email that confirms agreement, names the launch date, and assigns tasks immediately so the donor sees momentum. A Fijian team member has sent you the ministry office contact for formal coordination but has not interpreted the meeting for you. You also know that if the launch is announced too early and then shifts, local trust will be harder to rebuild than donor trust. You must produce a decision-and-coordination plan today.
question: Write a brief decision memo to your headquarters director that explains how you will secure a real rollout decision and coordinate the next 72 hours. Your memo must: (1) diagnose what the meeting evidence does and does not show, (2) identify the most tempting but miscalibrated imported assumption in this case, (3) specify the exact sequence, channel, audience, and wording of your next actions, and (4) show how you will keep donor momentum without falsely treating the current discussion as final approval. Be concrete about who you contact first, what you ask in each step, how you treat the verbal responses already given, and how you will know when you can announce the launch date.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that the prior meetings show discussion and surface understanding, not yet reliable final agreement or closure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer uses the meeting evidence operationally: broad discussion, delayed speaking, deference to older voices, and noncommittal verbal assent must lead to withholding final launch confirmation. No credit for simply saying 'be careful' or 'there may be ambiguity' without linking it to a decision consequence.

rubric.point: Routes closure through the appropriate senior decision path rather than treating group verbal responses as binding approval.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan explicitly seeks final confirmation from the senior authority after inclusive discussion, using the official ministry/local contact route already available. Partial credit if the answer mentions hierarchy or protocol but still treats the room's overall tone or a mass email reply as sufficient approval.

rubric.point: Designs a concrete behavioural sequence for the next 72 hours that fits the local interaction rhythm while still moving the project forward.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies visible execution details such as: first contacting the official local coordination point, then arranging targeted follow-up with the senior decision-maker and key participants, giving space for remaining views, especially older stakeholders' views, and separating provisional planning from final announcement. Generic advice to 'consult more people' or 'be respectful' does not score high.

rubric.point: Rejects the tempting imported assumption that a summarized meeting plus several verbal 'yes' responses equals consensus, approval, and immediate authorization to assign tasks publicly.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer names this as an attractive near-miss under donor pressure and explains why it would be efficient but miscalibrated. Partial credit if the answer criticizes rushing in general but does not identify the specific mistaken inference from the verbal responses and meeting close.

rubric.point: Uses behavioural CQ through calibrated wording, channel, timing, and audience choices rather than abstract cultural labels.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo includes concrete phrasing or communication design such as using provisional language, asking whether the timeline is understood versus approved, avoiding a public all-stakeholder launch message before formal closure, and choosing a channel that preserves relationship trust while clarifying authority. No credit for merely naming values, norms, or etiquette without visible action choices.

rubric.point: Balances donor pressure with trust protection by creating a two-track plan: donor-facing momentum now, public/local launch commitment only after confirmed decision.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer distinguishes between what can be reported upward immediately and what must wait locally, for example sending headquarters a status update on progress and next approval steps while withholding external launch claims until confirmed. Lower credit if the answer either freezes progress entirely or announces the launch prematurely.

reference_outline: State that the two meetings generated broad discussion and apparent understanding, but the evidence does not yet prove final agreement, final authorization, or a fixed launch date.

Treat the verbal 'yes/okay' responses as possible acknowledgment of the summary rather than confirmed commitment; do not use them as the basis for a public launch announcement or task assignment email framed as settled.

Use the official ministry/local coordination contact first to confirm the proper approval path and arrange a focused follow-up with the senior decision-maker, while also checking whether any key voices, especially older participants or quiet stakeholders, still need to be heard before closure.

Sequence actions behaviourally: first private/formal clarification through the official local channel, then targeted follow-up to confirm decision authority and outstanding concerns, then a narrower internal provisional task plan, and only then a broader launch communication after explicit closure.

Use calibrated wording such as 'confirming whether the proposed date is understood and acceptable for final approval' rather than 'as agreed, we will launch Friday'; visible wording choice is part of the score.

Name the near-miss plan directly: sending a single momentum email that treats meeting assent as final consensus and authorization would satisfy global efficiency logic but would misread the local decision process and create trust risk if the date later shifts.

Manage donor pressure with a parallel headquarters update that shows momentum through completed meetings, pending confirmation steps, and a short decision window, without claiming the launch is finalized before the senior approval route is completed.

Define the release condition for public commitment: explicit confirmation through the recognized senior authority, after inclusive consultation has run its course, not merely silence, polite assent, or lack of objections in the room.

scenario: A newcomer operations manager in Suva needs internal sign-off by the end of the week to confirm a hotel booking and transport for a regional client workshop. In a meeting with staff from several functions, the most senior director says little while others discuss practical concerns. The hotel is holding the rooms only until tomorrow afternoon, so the newcomer wants enough commitment to keep the booking alive without forcing a premature final decision.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The hotel needs an update tomorrow. In this meeting everyone will want to comment, and we still need something workable for transport and room numbers.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll run through the booking options quickly, hear each team's concerns, and then I'll send a same-day summary with the open points so we can keep the hold active.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That would help. Finance has one concern, field staff have another, and the director is here as well.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Great. Let's hear each group in turn. I'll note where views line up, and for the booking I can ask the hotel for a 24-hour extension instead of locking everything today.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We may still not have a final answer before the meeting ends.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: That's fine. I won't push for a vote in the room. Once I've captured the concerns, I'll send the options with the main areas of agreement and leave space for the final call after review.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. The client is asking for certainty, so we just need to keep progress visible.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll handle that. I'll tell the client we're confirming logistics in stages, keep the booking alive tonight, and circulate the summary to everyone after the meeting so the decision can close properly.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer's decisive behavior fits the Fijian meeting pattern by including broad discussion, not treating the senior person's relative silence as lack of authority, and avoiding pressure for an in-meeting vote while still doing extra follow-through to keep the work moving until the final decision is made after wider input.

scenario: Your team in Suva has to release a purchase order by noon tomorrow to keep a supplier hold. In a 70-minute meeting, operations staff, finance, and site supervisors all gave views on a vendor change. The oldest department head spoke only briefly, mostly listened, and closed by saying the group had heard the main points. You now have to approve the documentation route for the decision record tonight.
question: Which approval line should you sign off on for this decision record?

options.A: Circulate a short meeting summary tonight, note the areas of agreement, and release the order after a brief confirmation from the senior department head is added tomorrow morning.
options.B: Record the meeting outcome as agreed unless attendees object overnight, and let the order proceed on the strength of the discussion already held across the full group.
options.C: Pause the order until each attendee sends written confirmation, then file the record once the senior department head adds the final approval after those replies are collected.
options.D: Route the record first to the senior department head for decision, then send the finalized note to the wider meeting group after that approval is logged.

scenario: You are the regional program manager for a telecom company rolling out a small-business data bundle in Fiji. A launch recommendation must be sent by 5 p.m. tomorrow to a Pacific vice-president in Singapore, who wants a single clear option, owner, and date. The Fiji country team has already held one 70-minute meeting with representatives from sales, retail operations, customer support, finance, and field marketing. During that meeting, many people spoke, several concerns were surfaced, and the most senior Fiji-based executive in the room, the Head of Commercial, said very little except for two brief clarification questions near the end. After the meeting, three younger team leads emailed you detailed opinions and asked whether you want them to vote tonight so you can lock the recommendation early. A New Zealand colleague suggests using a fast follow-up survey and treating the majority view as the team decision, since 'everyone already had their say.' Meanwhile, the Fiji finance manager warns privately that if the recommendation is sent up and then reversed locally next week, trust with the country leadership team will take a hit and the launch may slip a full month. You have budget for only one more live coordination step before the deadline, and asking people to stay late will create friction because several staff are already covering weekend activation work.
question: Write a short decision-and-coordination plan for the next 24 hours. Specify what you think is happening in the Fiji meeting dynamic, what tempting assumption would lead you to mishandle it, and exactly how you will use your one remaining live coordination step. Your answer must include: who should be involved, who should speak when, what you will ask for, what you will not do, how you will keep the process moving under deadline, and what extra effort you personally will absorb to reduce the risk of a recommendation that looks agreed but is not actually settled.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden decision mechanism from the meeting evidence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that broad discussion does not by itself settle the decision and that the quiet senior Fiji-based leader may still be assessing and is likely central to final closure; no credit for merely saying 'respect hierarchy' or 'get consensus' without linking it to the observed silence, meeting stage, and final decision risk.

rubric.point: Identifies and rejects the polished near-miss plan
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly bounds the attractive but miscalibrated move of using a vote, survey majority, or email tally as the deciding mechanism because it converts inclusive discussion into the wrong closure route; partial credit if the answer objects vaguely to speed or says only to 'consult more.'

rubric.point: Uses the final live step on the correct execution axis
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan uses the one live coordination step to surface remaining views and then obtain or enable a final call from the senior Fiji decision-maker after hearing the group, rather than reopening unlimited debate or bypassing that person with a democratic shortcut; partial credit if the senior person is included but not positioned for final closure.

rubric.point: Designs concrete sequence, roles, and message framing
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies an operational sequence such as: circulate a brief options summary beforehand, invite concise input from the broader group, reserve space for the senior Fiji leader to conclude, and document the outcome as the country recommendation; low credit for generic advice like 'facilitate respectfully' or 'make sure everyone is heard.'

rubric.point: Shows motivational CQ through costly, targeted follow-through
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the respondent absorbs visible cost in time, comfort, or status to sustain adaptive engagement—for example, staying late to prepare a neutral summary, personally running the extra session, or taking on follow-up drafting so locals do not carry the adaptation burden—while still keeping boundaries and the deadline. No credit for friendliness without ownership, or for pushing all adaptation work back onto the Fiji team.

rubric.point: Balances task speed with relationship and trust protection
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explains how the plan preserves tomorrow's deadline while reducing the risk of sending a recommendation upward that later lacks local closure; partial credit if it chooses either pure speed or pure delay without a mechanism for both progress and trust protection.

rubric.point: Handles ambiguity and repair if closure is still incomplete
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer includes a bounded fallback such as escalating with a clearly labeled provisional recommendation only after the senior Fiji decision-maker has had a defined chance to conclude, and states how to communicate residual uncertainty without pretending a majority vote equals settlement; no credit for indefinite postponement or for sending a recommendation as final without that check.

reference_outline: Infer from the Fiji meeting pattern that open participation is part of the process, but not the same as the final decision; the quiet senior Head of Commercial may still be observing and is likely the person whose conclusion matters for real closure.

Reject the imported assumption that once everyone has spoken, a survey, vote, or email majority can stand in as the team decision; that is the tempting fast plan under deadline but it risks false closure and later reversal.

Use the one remaining live step as a tightly structured closure meeting or call: send a concise options memo first, invite short final comments from key functions, then explicitly create space for the senior Fiji leader to state or confirm the country recommendation after hearing the group.

Keep the participant scope narrow enough to meet the deadline but broad enough to preserve the inclusive discussion stage: include the senior Fiji decision-maker and the functions already involved, not a larger symbolic consultation round.

Personally absorb adaptation cost by preparing the summary, coordinating availability, and drafting the recommendation note yourself instead of asking the Fiji team to translate the process for you or do extra after-hours alignment work without support.

Frame the communication carefully: ask for remaining concerns and preferred option, but do not ask the group to vote as the deciding mechanism; document the outcome as the Fiji leadership recommendation once the senior local leader concludes.

If closure remains incomplete, use a bounded repair path: note that the recommendation is provisional pending final country confirmation, specify what is unresolved, and set a near-term check rather than either pretending consensus or delaying indefinitely.

scenario: A visiting telecom vendor from New Zealand has a 40-minute first meeting in Nuku'alofa with a local state-owned buyer about a pilot rollout. The team can fit a few small items in carry-on luggage, but the country manager wants one clear briefing line on how to handle them during the meeting opening.
question: Which direction should guide the team?

options.A: Bring small items from the home market and hand them over as soon as greetings end, before any broader conversation, then move straight into the rollout plan while the gesture is still fresh.
options.B: Bring small items from the home market and offer them once the opening conversation is underway, then let the meeting settle before turning the group toward the pilot proposal.
options.C: Bring small items from the home market and save them for the last few minutes, after the commercial discussion, framing them as a closing thank-you once the main points are covered.
options.D: Leave out any items and keep the opening fully businesslike, using informal conversation alone to build rapport while avoiding anything that could be read as influencing the buyer.

scenario: A visiting procurement manager from New Zealand is meeting a Tongan partner organization to finalize a supply pilot before a donor reporting deadline. At the start of the meeting, the local team presents the visitor with a woven item and a box of local snacks. The newcomer has also brought small branded treats from home for the trip, and the meeting agenda is already running late.

roles.local: Sione, operations lead at the Tongan partner organization

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Before we get into the delivery numbers, our team wanted you to have these from us. We still need to lock the pilot dates today because the donor note goes out this afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Thank you, I really appreciate that. I'll keep these with me, and I'll send photos to my team later. I did bring a few small things from Auckland, but let's finish the dates first so we don't lose the slot.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. We can cover the warehouse sequence now, then the signing page after that.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Good. I marked two pages with the shipping changes, and I can stay concise so we still finish on time.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That works. Once we settle the page numbers, the drivers can be briefed this evening.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then let's confirm those first. After we close, I'd like to leave the Auckland items with your office for the team, along with a note from our side.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We can do that. The admin desk is still open after the meeting.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Perfect. I'll hand them over then and keep today's meeting focused on the pilot so we can submit on time.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer accepts the local gift and does not reciprocate immediately in the same exchange; instead, she delays giving her own items until after the meeting. That timing fits the Tongan reciprocity rhythm, where instant return-giving can signal closing off indebtedness rather than valuing the relationship.

scenario: You are the global mobility lead on a Tokyo-based product launch team with members in the U.S., Germany, and Singapore. A newly promoted Japanese engineer, Kenji Mori, must transfer from Nagoya to Tokyo in six weeks to lead the client integration workstream. The client kickoff date cannot move, the CFO has frozen any increase to housing allowances this quarter, and your VP wants all three pending transfers processed through one standardized family-relocation workflow by Friday. Kenji is getting married next month. In email, he has not objected to the move, but he has asked four unusual operational questions: whether the company can issue a residence-support letter addressed to 'household members' rather than only to an employee and spouse; whether a storage and furniture shipment can be split between two addresses; whether the temporary housing can be placed near a rail line that also serves his parents' district rather than near the office; and whether the reimbursement form can list costs for a larger shared kitchen even if no children are involved. His HR file shows he is the older of two sons. Your U.S. operations manager argues this is probably just personal preference and says the team should book the standard one-bedroom newlywed apartment near the office now to avoid delay. A German finance partner agrees because policy is written around employee, spouse, and children, and any broader interpretation may trigger audit questions. No one on the Japan team has directly explained the pattern behind Kenji's requests, and you do not have time for an open-ended culture workshop.
question: Write a short decision memo for your project team that sets the evidence-use plan and stakeholder sequence for finalizing Kenji's relocation package this week. Your memo must: diagnose the most relevant hidden family-structure mechanism suggested by the facts; identify the tempting but miscalibrated assumption in the standard workflow; specify what you would confirm, with whom, and in what order before booking housing; and explain how your plan protects both delivery deadlines and relationship risk without turning into a broad delay or generic consultation exercise.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the likely household pattern from the exact clues, not from generic 'family-oriented culture' language.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that a married son in Japan may be expected to live with or organize housing around his husband's-side parental household, especially when he is the older son, and ties that inference to the specific clues in the scenario. Partial credit for noticing non-nuclear possibilities without connecting them to the actor and likely direction of co-residence.

rubric.point: Rejects the attractive near-miss of defaulting to a nuclear-family relocation package.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly identifies the imported assumption that a newly married employee will automatically set up an independent two-person household near the office, and explains why that assumption is plausible under time and policy pressure but operationally risky here. No full credit for answers that merely say 'don't stereotype' or 'ask more questions' without bounding the standard-package mistake.

rubric.point: Makes a concrete execution choice on the primary axis: evidence weighting and stakeholder sequence before booking housing.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer prioritizes confirming actual intended household composition and residence arrangement before locking apartment type/location, rather than booking first and fixing later. It must specify a tight sequence such as: direct mobility call with Kenji, confirm who will live together and whether proximity/co-residence with parents is part of the move, then align HR/finance on policy treatment, then book housing. Answers that gather broad opinions from many stakeholders first, or delay until after kickoff, do not earn full credit.

rubric.point: Applies cognitive CQ by separating culture-specific interpretation from process, personality, and generic efficiency explanations.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer distinguishes this case from explanations like personal taste, commute preference, or budget opportunism, and shows why the combination of clues changes the interpretation. The answer should use the cultural logic to refine, not replace, evidence gathering. Generic claims such as 'Japan values family' or 'he might just be shy' are insufficient.

rubric.point: Translates the diagnosis into role-specific coordination and wording.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo specifies who says what to Kenji, HR, and finance—for example, using neutral wording about 'intended household arrangement at destination' or 'residence configuration' rather than forcing a spouse-children template—and shows how to preserve dignity while obtaining decision-critical facts. Answers that name the pattern but do not change forms, wording, or routing do not earn full credit.

rubric.point: Designs a bounded risk-control plan under deadline pressure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes a narrow, fast control such as a temporary hold on final housing type, a provisional booking with changeable terms, or a documented exception-review path tied to confirmed household facts. No full credit for the longest or safest plan, such as pausing the whole transfer, escalating everything immediately to executives, or launching a general regional policy review.

reference_outline: State that the clues point to a possible patrilocal or husband's-family-centered post-marriage household arrangement in Japan, with the older-son detail increasing the relevance; therefore a standard newlywed nuclear-household assumption is unsafe.
Name the near-miss: treating the case as a routine employee-plus-spouse relocation near the office because the deadline, policy wording, and audit pressure make that feel efficient.

Use a tight evidence sequence: speak directly with Kenji first to confirm intended household composition, whether parents are part of the living arrangement or location constraint, and whether split shipment / larger kitchen / household-member wording reflect actual co-residence needs; only then classify the package.

Coordinate second with Japan HR and finance using confirmed facts, asking for a narrow policy interpretation or exception path based on destination household configuration rather than a broad family-benefit expansion.

Keep wording operational and neutral: ask about 'who will be living in the destination household' and 'residential setup required for the transfer,' not broad cultural questions or assumptions about parents.

Protect delivery by using a reversible short-term housing hold or temporary accommodation while the household configuration is confirmed, instead of locking a one-bedroom unit that may damage trust and require rework.

Show cognitive CQ by explaining why the answer is not just 'be respectful' or 'consult more': the key is correctly mapping the clues to the likely family-structure logic and using that interpretation to change the booking sequence and evidence threshold.

scenario: A newcomer at a Seoul consumer-finance company is finalizing participant logistics for next-day evening interviews about household budgeting. The stipend rules require one transfer per participant by 6 p.m., and the legal team wants the consent file to match the account holder receiving payment. One participant, Minseo, is listed on the screener as a married office worker in a two-bedroom apartment with her spouse and one child. Her intake form says she is financially independent and employed full time, but the callback number that keeps answering scheduling questions belongs to an older family member at the same address block. The local coordinator is overloaded and only gives fragmentary operational cues.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We still need Minseo's stipend details before legal closes the file. She works full time and marked herself as a separate household unit, but the person who keeps answering about the time slot is Mrs. Han from the neighboring building number. We have to lock the transfer recipient today.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Got it. Since Minseo is an employed adult with her own family, I'll avoid assuming the older contact manages things. I'll call Minseo directly, confirm whether she wants the transfer in her own name, and keep Mrs. Han only on timing messages if Minseo asks.

dialogue.speaker: Local

scenario:
You are an operations lead on a multicultural HR-tech team preparing a pilot in rural southern China for a benefits platform that helps factory workers request short-term leave and caregiving support. The China sales director wants a draft rollout memo by tomorrow because a county-level manufacturing client is deciding this week. The platform needs one default triage rule for urgent eldercare requests before the pilot starts, because supervisors will only see one recommended household contact path in the first release.

The current draft from headquarters treats married employees' eldercare obligations as symmetrical across both sides of the family: if a worker reports competing requests from a spouse's parents and their own parents, the system flags both as equal-priority immediate family and routes the case to the same approval channel. Legal says this is defensible and simple. Product likes it because it keeps one global standard. The China client, however, has pushed back indirectly in two meetings. They did not dispute the leave policy itself, but kept asking who in a married couple's household would usually be expected to take the first call when the husband's father needs help, and why the app's household map lets a married woman list her own mother before her husband's parents in the default order. No one on the client side has explained further, and they are also under pressure because dormitory staffing is thin during harvest season.

Your team includes a German compliance manager who argues that changing the default order would look biased and create documentation risk, and a Singapore-based product manager who suggests solving it by making every family field fully customizable and leaving the default untouched for launch. You have budget for only one localized workflow change before the deadline. If the client loses confidence now, the pilot may be postponed for six months.
question: Write a decision memo for your team that recommends the single workflow change you would make before launch. Your memo must: (1) diagnose the hidden family-structure mechanism behind the client's questions using the evidence in the scenario, (2) identify the most tempting but miscalibrated imported assumption in the current draft, (3) specify the exact default contact/approval sequence the system should use for married women and married men in urgent eldercare cases, including where you would allow exceptions, and (4) explain how you would brief compliance, product, and the client so the change is narrow, defensible, and testable rather than a broad cultural rewrite.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the client's concern as a household-responsibility logic, not just a preference for traditional wording.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that the client is reacting to who is expected to carry primary elder-support obligations within a married household and ties this to the specific clues about the husband's father, married women's ordering, and household call routing. No credit for vague statements about respect for elders, family values, or collectivism without operational implications.

rubric.point: Rejects or sharply bounds the equal-obligation default as the key near-miss.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly identifies the global-symmetry assumption as attractive but wrong for this case and explains why a generic 'both sides are equal immediate family' workflow misreads the local responsibility structure. Partial credit if the answer notices the default is risky but treats the issue as mere personalization or optics.

rubric.point: Sets the correct execution-axis decision on default sequence.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer recommends that urgent eldercare defaults for a married son's household prioritize his parents, and for a married woman in that household prioritize parents-in-law before natal parents in the initial contact/approval path, while recognizing that the burden is carried through the son's household rather than through an abstract equal-family model. rubric.point: Builds in negotiated exceptions without collapsing the default.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer preserves the local default but adds a narrow override based on actual living arrangement, caregiving reality, or work/eldercare negotiation evidence, such as co-residence, current caregiver role, or documented dependency. No credit for answers that either rigidly freeze one traditional path with no exception logic or make everything fully open-ended so the diagnostic default disappears.

rubric.point: Uses cognitive CQ by mapping evidence to category, boundary, and exception.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer separates the core norm from its boundary conditions: it must show that the respondent understands both the default family-structure logic and why modern work and care pressures can alter implementation through negotiated arrangements. Generic advice to 'ask locals' or 'be flexible' does not earn this point.

rubric.point: Designs role-specific messaging for compliance, product, and client.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer gives distinct briefings: to compliance, frame the change as a localized default with documented override criteria; to product, frame it as one constrained workflow adjustment rather than full customization; to the client, frame it as aligning first-route logic with expected household responsibility while allowing real household exceptions. No credit for one-size-fits-all communication.

rubric.point: Defines a narrow test and repair plan under deadline pressure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes a practical pilot check tied to this exact default sequence, such as monitoring override frequency, disputed routing cases, or client feedback on first-contact fit, and states how to revise if evidence shows a different caregiving arrangement. reference_outline: Infer from the client's repeated questions that the issue is not eldercare in general but who in a married household is expected to assume first-line obligation for an older parent, especially when the parent is on the husband's side.

Name the near-miss clearly: the headquarters default assumes symmetrical obligations to both sides of the family and treats that as neutral, but in this context that imported standard misroutes responsibility.

Change the workflow at the default-sequence level: for married men, route urgent eldercare involving their parents through their household as primary; for married women, place parents-in-law ahead of natal parents in the default urgent-contact and approval path because her married household is expected to support that side first.

Keep the localization narrow by adding exception triggers tied to actual living arrangement or caregiving facts, such as separate residence, current primary caregiver status, or documented dependency, rather than opening unlimited customization from the start.

Brief compliance that the system is not declaring human worth or legal entitlements; it is using a locale-specific default sequence with auditable overrides to improve routing accuracy in urgent cases.

Brief product that full customization is the wrong immediate fix because it removes the needed local default and shifts the burden to users under time pressure; one localized sequence plus override logic is the smaller high-value change.

Brief the client that the pilot will reflect expected household responsibility in first-contact logic while still allowing staff to record cases where work patterns or caregiving realities require a different route.

Monitor pilot performance through override rate, cases disputed by supervisors, and whether the client sees fewer mismatches between app routing and expected household response; repair by tightening or broadening override criteria, not by reverting to equal-family default without evidence.

scenario: A health insurer is building a claims-review prompt for home-recovery cases in Bangkok and Ho Chi Minh City. options.C: Use no default relationship, because once a system is bilateral, any gender-based first guess would misrepresent the culture.
options.D: Default to "youngest child," because the most relevant household clue in Thailand is birth order rather than whether the child is a son or daughter.

reference_outline: State that the Bangkok pilot should not inherit a son-centered regional default; the evidence suggests Thailand's household care expectations may center on daughters as well, with a meaningful signal around the youngest daughter in these cases.

Recommend two country-specific designation logics: in India, a son-centered default may be a reasonable starting hypothesis if locally supported; in Thailand, intake should provisionally map the likely live-in caregiver from the family member handling care logistics and explicitly test for daughter-based co-residence rather than defaulting to a son.

Add a repair boundary: if the provisional Thai caregiver cannot attend or the family corrects the assignment, allow one pre-visit reassignment through the coordinator without restarting legal approval, while flagging repeated mismatches as evidence to refine the intake script.

scenario: A newcomer account manager at a home-interiors firm is finalizing a wardrobe and storage plan for a bedroom in an Indian joint-family home before the younger son's wedding. The room sits inside the parents' house, where the family has already reassigned storage between rooms, and the carpenter needs a stable cut list tonight. The newcomer must decide how to sequence a short evening review and how to introduce any last-minute preferences while still locking the vendor brief.

roles.newcomer: Daniel, a newly transferred account manager

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We only have one short review slot tonight. The room is inside the parents' house, two cupboards were already redistributed across rooms, and I need a vendor-ready sheet before 9.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Okay. I'll keep the built-in measurements anchored to the revised room plan so the carpenter can move. I also want to check privately with the bride in case she has non-negotiables on hanging space or shelves before everyone joins.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That works for collecting details. The mother has been mapping where linens and wedding gifts will sit, and the younger son may only join near the end of the call.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I'll send you the fixed measurements first and keep her notes off the vendor sheet for now. On the call, I'll open with a slide showing her preferred wardrobe split as the reference version, then we can see what the room setup needs to change around it.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: If the call runs short, I still need to know what is truly locked and what can wait. The older brother may dial in too, since his room lost one storage unit when this room was adjusted.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll mark carcass sizes as closed and keep handles, shelf count, and drawer mix flexible. But I still want discussion to start from her layout, so any compromises happen after her side is clearly on the table rather than being folded in later.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Fine, send me the carpenter version separately from the review deck so I can release one even if the call ends abruptly.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Will do. I'll keep the production sheet clean, and in the family review I'll present the household plan plus a first-slide overlay built from her requests so that becomes the opening frame for sign-off.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer is competent on vendor timing, but the decisive behavioural mismatch is sequence and framing: he privately gathers the incoming bride's wishes and makes them the opening reference for the household's final review. In this Indian patrilocal joint-family setting, that imports a generic equal-voice script by centering the daughter-in-law's preferences at the initial lock stage instead of introducing them within the husband's household's existing arrangement.

options.A: Approve provisionally and have HR confirm the household receiving the parent after discharge, then send the first documents there while keeping other sibling contacts active in case care shifts after review.

options.C: Approve provisionally and have HR route the first documents through the older brother, since the sibling paying bills and coordinating with hospital staff is the safest lead contact.
options.D: Approve provisionally and have HR keep the employee as the sole contact for now, then wait for the family to nominate one household later before sending any home-care documents.

scenario: A newcomer at a home-care nonprofit in Japan is preparing a same-day family briefing before a municipal funding cutoff. The elderly client's chart lists the mother, one married son's household address from an older registration, a nearby daughter's mobile number, and notes that family living arrangements changed recently. The newcomer must decide how to structure the briefing invitation and action sheet without delaying the case.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The city office wants the family plan submitted by five. The file is old: the mother is now alone, one son is in Saitama, a daughter lives twenty minutes away, and another household may join online if they can.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll make it simple and invite every adult child to the briefing, then we can divide tasks evenly based on who lives closest and who answers fastest.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That would move things quickly. Just so you know, the landline messages have mostly been returned by the daughter, but the paperwork history is tied to that son's household. We have not sorted out what that means now.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I'll avoid presuming anything from the old paperwork. I'll send one neutral agenda to all siblings and ask each person to state directly what support they can offer this month.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The online participant may only join for ten minutes, and the mother usually answers briefly when family matters come up. We mainly need one workable contact path today.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Right, so I'll keep the call efficient: first I’ll ask the mother which child she prefers us to coordinate with, then I’ll confirm a rotation with the others so no one feels singled out.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Please send me the final template before noon. I may need to print it without revisions if the driver leaves early.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I will. The form will list all children side by side, with equal action boxes, and a blank line for the mother to choose the main family contact during the meeting.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer applies a generic equal-siblings/default individual-choice model instead of calibrating to the Japanese family-care pattern in which a married son's household has often been the expected care-responsibility anchor, even if weakened today. The execution error is the planning axis: structuring the briefing and contact path around equal distribution and the mother's live selection, rather than provisionally centering the historically relevant son's household while keeping recent changes open to confirmation.

scenario: You are coordinating a regional VP’s Seoul stopover. A Korean team lead, Minho, invites the company to his Saturday wedding hall ceremony.
