rubric.point: Balances burden risk without overcorrecting into a one-size-fits-all family-care script.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer preserves a real pathway for cases where an older woman expresses not wanting to burden children, or where family caregiving capacity is failing, but keeps that pathway as a calibrated secondary route rather than the visible front door. No credit if the answer erases the variation or treats all cases as identical.

rubric.point: Designs a workable launch memo under operational constraints.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer translates the cultural read into a launchable workflow: primary track, optional referral track, triggers/escalation, and language choices that satisfy sponsor measurability and director risk concerns. No credit for broad delay, open-ended consultation, or a maximalist multi-track design that ignores the budget limit.

reference_outline: Set the primary pilot track around supporting care within the family first, because the case evidence shows that this is the expected default and early residential framing risks resistance and reputational damage.

Make residential-care referral an optional secondary track introduced only after assessing caregiver load, family capacity, and the older adult's own concern about burdening children; do not present it as the opening menu item.

Open first meetings by addressing the family care arrangement and current caregiving realities, then identify who is doing day-to-day care work, with explicit attention to women relatives who may already be carrying most of the load.

Assign the Mexico-based social worker to lead the first conversation and wording calibration, have operations document measurable burden/risk triggers, and have finance keep the optional referral track narrow and criteria-based for launch.

Use wording in the workflow such as supporting the family in caring for the older adult at home first; avoid language that suggests the hospital is moving directly toward placement or treating residential care as the standard efficient solution.

Explain that the tempting near-miss is a generic scalable autonomy/choice script: it seems sponsor-friendly and burden-reducing, but in this context it introduces the wrong option too early and to the wrong audience frame.

Preserve a defined repair/escalation path: if caregiver strain is severe or an older woman explicitly raises concern about burdening children, move to a later, more private and carefully framed discussion of residential options rather than forcing the topic in the opening encounter.
Show behavioural CQ by specifying visible sequence, speaking order, wording, and follow-up cadence, not merely by citing cultural labels or recommending more consultation.

scenario: A care-navigation company is preparing a phone script for a pilot in Mexico. The first calls will be with middle-aged daughters arranging support for an older parent, but the product team also wants one short module for older callers planning their own later years. Training time is limited, and operations wants one simple briefing line for both modules before launch this week.
question: Which briefing line should guide the script team?

options.A: Use the same opening assumption in both modules: present residential care early as a normal independence-focused option, then let each caller say whether family involvement matters.
options.B: Frame residential care mainly as a relief option when adult children sound stretched, and carry that emphasis into the self-planning module for older callers as well.
options.C: Keep family-based support as the default frame for current-parent calls, but in self-planning module allow a careful branch for older callers who raise not burdening their children.
options.D: Avoid any residential-care branch in either module at launch, and add it only after a broader local advisory review confirms that families want staff to discuss it directly.

scenario: A museum team is helping coordinate printed materials and seating for an Osage wedding celebration that will be held after visiting hours. The newcomer is covering two jobs at once because the lead designer is out sick: finalizing the program insert and arranging where several wrapped bundles from both sides should be placed before families arrive. The print deadline is in forty minutes, and the venue manager wants a clean, minimal floor plan with as few extra tables as possible.

roles.local: Osage community liaison working with the venue
roles.newcomer: New event coordinator from outside the community

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We need the insert to the printer soon. Also, both households are sending more wrapped bundles than the floor plan expected, and the venue manager keeps asking whether we can combine things onto one display near the couple's table.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I can still make the print cutoff. For the room, I won't fold those bundles into one decorative station. I'll add two small labeled tables by household names, even if the layout looks less streamlined, and I'll cut one photo easel instead.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That means reworking the entrance path, and the manager will ask why we're adding furniture this late.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll handle that pushback myself and stay to reset it. On the insert, I'm also changing the inside page so it doesn't read like only a spotlight on the pair; I'm giving a little more space to the family lines and removing the oversized couple quote.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The photographer already liked that quote because it matched the engagement photos. We also still need someone at the loading door when relatives start arriving.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll cover the loading door too. If more bundles come in, I'll keep them with the same household grouping instead of sending them straight to the sweetheart area, even if it slows setup a bit.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. I can text the manager that the room plan is being revised. The print runner leaves in twenty minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Send that, and I'll eat the extra design time. I'll deliver the file myself once the family sections and table labels are locked.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer's decisive behavior aligns with the Osage wedding mechanism by treating the event as linking extended families rather than as a purely couple-centered display. The key execution axis is scope and placement: they preserve separate household-linked gift grouping and revise materials to represent family connections, even at visible cost in time, layout simplicity, and venue convenience.

scenario: A museum team in North America is finalizing a 90-second educational video about a historic Arapaho wedding for a school platform. The editor wants one clear narrative focus so the clip feels easy to follow, and legal has asked the team not to imply facts the source material does not support.
question: Which production brief should the curator approve for the shortened wedding segment?

options.A: Frame the wedding mainly around the couple’s mutual choice and private exchange, then show relatives and elders joining later so students first recognize the marriage as a personal bond.
options.B: Frame the wedding mainly as an agreement between the two households, keep reciprocal contributions and elder instruction visible, and retain that the bride could still decline within that arrangement.
options.C: Frame the wedding mainly as an agreement between the two households, keep reciprocal contributions and elder instruction visible, and leave the bride’s own decision unstated to preserve the ceremony’s formality.
options.D: Frame the wedding mainly around the groom’s family bringing goods and elders guiding the union, with the bride’s household shown hosting afterward rather than matching the exchange in the shortened cut.

scenario:
You are operations lead for a hospital-community partnership in Saskatchewan. A staff member from a First Nations family has died unexpectedly, and the hospital has offered its auditorium, shuttle support, and catering budget for a memorial gathering that must be confirmed by 3 p.m. today so facilities, security, and food vendors can be booked. Your supervisor wants a single run sheet by noon because local media may attend and the CEO plans to acknowledge the death publicly if the family agrees.

The team is multicultural: a communications manager from Toronto wants to send one standard condolence package and publish a draft agenda with opening remarks, music, and refreshments so "people know what to expect"; a logistics coordinator from Germany wants a fixed checklist and one point of approval for fire-code and food-safety reasons; a community liaison has only said by text, "Please wait before posting anything. Marla is speaking for the family right now." In the message thread, different relatives have separately mentioned an Elder, a wake, food after the burial, and items that "should go out later," but no one has explained who decides what. Marla has not replied for two hours. The auditorium booking will lapse if you do not act soon, and your supervisor is pressing you not to look disorganized or indecisive.
question: Write a decision memo to your supervisor that explains how you will move the project forward in the next 3 hours. Your memo must: (1) identify the key uncertainty you can and cannot resolve yet from the evidence; (2) name the most tempting but miscalibrated planning assumption in this situation; (3) set the stakeholder sequence, approval route, and what you will and will not pre-build before hearing back; and (4) show how you will update the plan if Marla confirms only some details before the noon deadline. Be concrete about timing, channels, and what information you would treat as provisional versus family-controlled.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the real coordination mechanism from the scenario evidence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that authority over ceremony design is family- and community-specific and is likely being coordinated through the named family contact, rather than assuming the hospital or a generic bereavement template should define the event. Partial credit for noting uncertainty without identifying where decision authority probably sits.

rubric.point: Distinguishes actionable evidence from unresolved unknowns
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer separates what can be acted on now (hold flexible space, reserve budget, prepare support options, pause public messaging) from what remains unknown and must not be fixed yet (order of events, ceremonial elements, who else must be contacted, whether an Elder is involved, timing of food or distribution of items). Low credit for broad delay or for locking details despite ambiguity.

rubric.point: Rejects the polished near-miss assumption
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly rejects or tightly bounds the attractive default of issuing a standard memorial agenda/condolence package and collecting generic approvals first. It must explain why a polished global SOP, brand-safe schedule, or fixed checklist would misfire here even if well-intended. Low credit if the answer merely says 'be respectful' or 'consult widely' without naming the mistaken assumption.

rubric.point: Sets the correct stakeholder sequence and approval route on the primary axis
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer routes content decisions first through the family-designated contact and treats other institutional approvals as enabling constraints around that channel, not as the source of ceremonial decisions. It should specify who gets contacted now, what is asked, what is deferred, and how internal teams are told to prepare flexible support rather than a fixed program.

rubric.point: Applies metacognitive CQ through calibrated updating
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer shows a working hypothesis, names what evidence would confirm or change it, and describes how to revise without overcorrecting. It should avoid both premature certainty ('we know the ceremony format') and inert caution ('do nothing until everything is clear'). Low credit for generic humility or asking questions that do not reduce the key uncertainty.

rubric.point: Designs concrete communications and controls under deadline pressure
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer includes operational moves for the next 3 hours: hold the venue provisionally, pause external publication, prepare modular logistics options, use a direct channel to the family contact, document provisional status internally, and create a fallback if only partial confirmation arrives. Low credit for vague plans, overlong consultation trees, or public-facing wording that implies the institution is defining the ceremony.

reference_outline: State the diagnosis: the mixed references to an Elder, wake, food, and later distribution do not justify choosing a standard funeral format; the strongest evidence is that Marla is currently the family speaking point, so planning should center on that authority while recognizing community-specific variation.

Make the primary execution decision on sequence: immediately hold space, shuttle capacity, and catering budget in a flexible way, but do not publish an agenda, ceremonial order, or public statement beyond a holding line until the family contact confirms what the hospital is being asked to support.

Set role-specific coordination: call or text Marla directly with a narrow decision menu about what needs confirmation now (space hold, privacy level, whether public acknowledgment is welcome, who else the hospital should coordinate with), while telling communications to stop drafting a public program and telling logistics to prepare configurable support options rather than a single checklist-driven schedule.

Handle the near-miss explicitly: explain to the supervisor that the tempting efficient move is to impose a standard memorial package with institutional approvals first, but that this would wrongly convert the hospital into the ceremony designer and could clash with family/community-led steps.

Show metacognitive CQ: identify the current inference as provisional, note which signals matter most, discount weaker cues that do not settle authority, and specify what new evidence would trigger revision, such as Marla naming another family coordinator or asking the hospital to contact an Elder through a family route.

Provide a noon-deadline fallback: if only partial confirmation arrives, submit a run sheet that marks venue, transport, privacy, and budget as confirmed supports, labels ceremony content as family-controlled and pending, and limits the CEO/public message to a non-programmatic acknowledgment only if the family has approved that scope.

Include repair and monitoring: if internal teams already drafted or circulated a fixed agenda, retract it quickly, clarify that details were provisional, and re-anchor all further planning through the family contact so the hospital supports rather than leads the process.

scenario: A newcomer working for a regional health nonprofit is helping coordinate a memorial week in a Oneida community after a family's second loss in one year. The immediate task is to finalize the meal rota, transportation list, and the printed schedule before the printer's 4 p.m. cutoff. The local liaison has given names, but not a formal decision chart.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The printer needs the schedule by four, and the kitchen volunteers want one final list for rides, overnight help, and who is covering the house tomorrow.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Got it. Since there have been two recent losses in the same family, I'll keep this tight and ask Leonard and his two adult sons for one clean approval so we don't burden everyone else with another round.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: I can text you the names already moving supplies and staying late. A few people have been handling the house since yesterday, and the aunties asked about the order of the visits.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Please send them. I'll list those women as support leads, but for decisions I'll still route the final draft to Leonard's side first, then copy the others once the family spokesman confirms.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The meal list, condolence table, and car seats are all tied together, so if one part shifts the rest may move with it.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. To reduce confusion, I'll separate logistics from family matters: volunteers can keep updating tasks, but the authority line on timing and names should stay with the husband and sons for today.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. We just need something people can use before folks start arriving from out of town.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll send the proof in the next twenty minutes with Leonard and the sons as the approving contacts, and the rest of the relatives listed underneath by work area.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer politely applies a generic next-of-kin or male-spokesperson model, but the seed-specific mechanism is that mourning here functions as community infrastructure and, after repeated deaths, caretaking and decision authority can shift through women in the maternal line. The miscalibration is the execution axis of who holds final coordinating authority over labor, timing, and household arrangements.

scenario: At a Prairie hospital in North America, a unit manager must approve a same-day charting route for a patient whose relatives have begun discussing ceremony-related preparations. One adult daughter has been coordinating calls and asks staff to speak about planning indirectly. The night team needs a clear note before shift change, and the manager wants a route staff can follow without taking over arrangements.
question: Which approval decision is most defensible for the chart and staff briefing?

options.A: Approve a note naming the daughter as first contact, record planning in indirect terms, and have staff confirm through her whether any additional protocol contacts should be involved next.
options.B: Approve a note listing all next of kin for parallel outreach, record the discussion under the standard end-of-life planning heading, and let the first available clinician coordinate the calls.
options.C: Approve a note directing staff to contact local Elders before relatives, record planning in indirect terms, and update the daughter afterward on the steps already underway.
options.D: Approve a note to hold documentation until a wider relatives meeting confirms the ceremony path, keep planning language indirect, and ask day staff to revisit the chart after consensus.

scenario: You manage a multicultural project team at a Canadian nonprofit that is co-delivering a printed guide, registration workflow, and event-day operations plan for a North American Indigenous community's youth transition ceremony. The event is in 10 days. A funder wants the materials finalized tomorrow because press time is fixed, and your director is pushing for a single standardized youth-safeguarding protocol across all programs. The current draft treats the event as a 'teen milestone weekend' and assigns staff by availability. In the message history, one community committee member asked whether the boys' lodging and supervision list had been confirmed with the men's side, while another separately asked when the girls' room supplies would be reviewed with the women organizing preparations. A third note asked that the final printed guide clearly support how youth return to family and community after the ceremony. Your team is split: a US colleague argues for mixed-gender staffing and one unified prep schedule to avoid exclusion complaints; a Germany-based operations lead wants one parent briefing, one check-in desk, and one youth handbook because it is cleaner and easier to audit. Budget only allows one on-site project manager from your side, and a sponsor representative will attend the public portion.
question: Write a short decision memo for your director that sets the operational plan. Your memo must: (1) diagnose what the message history suggests about how this ceremony functions socially, (2) identify the most tempting but miscalibrated imported assumption in your team's current draft, (3) make concrete choices on one primary execution axis for staffing and workflow from preparation through the public portion, and (4) explain how you will justify those choices to the director and sponsor without turning the plan into a vague 'consult more' answer. Be specific about roles, sequence, documentation, and what you will and will not standardize.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the ceremony as a community-recognized status transition rather than a generic age-based youth event.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers from the separate preparation requests and the return-to-community note that the event changes recognized social standing and responsibilities; no credit for merely calling it 'important,' 'traditional,' or 'sensitive.'

rubric.point: Maps the hidden logic to the correct stage and actors in the workflow.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer applies the distinction to preparation and reintroduction stages, with male caregivers/organizers aligned to boys and female caregivers/organizers aligned to girls during preparation, and treats the public return as a community-facing status moment; partial credit if the answer notices role separation but applies it only to seating, symbolism, or general staffing.

rubric.point: Rejects the attractive near-miss plan in operational terms.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly identifies unified mixed staffing, a single undifferentiated prep track, or a purely age/biology/safeguarding frame as the tempting imported assumption and explains why it would misread the event; low credit if it only says 'don't use global defaults' without naming the execution mistake.

rubric.point: Makes a concrete staffing and sequence decision on the primary execution axis.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies separate preparation chains, role-specific supervision/briefing ownership, and a controlled handoff into the public reintroduction, while limiting what remains shared; no full credit for generic 'coordinate with community leaders' or for the broadest possible consultation plan.

rubric.point: Applies cognitive CQ by separating cultural mechanism from generic policy, personality, or efficiency explanations.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer shows why the evidence points to a cultural logic about social identity and role transition, not just preference, modesty, logistics, sponsor optics, or individual organizer style; partial credit if it uses correct facts but does not distinguish them from noncultural explanations.

rubric.point: Designs bounded standardization, documentation, and risk control under deadline pressure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer preserves shared safety/compliance elements where appropriate while documenting a justified exception or tailored protocol for role assignment and sequence; low credit if it solves pressure by delaying, over-expanding review, or replacing the ceremony logic with a one-size-fits-all compliance template.

reference_outline: State that the evidence suggests the ceremony is not just a teen program milestone but a socially recognized transition in which community and family acknowledge changed status and responsibilities.

Use the separate requests about boys with men and girls with women as diagnostic evidence for how preparation should be staffed and supervised, rather than treating those notes as incidental preferences.

Set the primary workflow decision: separate preparation tracks with role-aligned caregivers/organizers, then a planned reintroduction/public portion that reflects return to family and community in new standing.

Reject the polished near-miss of one unified youth protocol, mixed prep staffing, and one generic handbook because it misreads the event as neutral age-group programming and collapses the stage distinction.

Tell the director that standardization should apply to baseline safety, escalation, and documentation, but not erase the culturally required role assignment and sequence; document this as a scoped operational adaptation, not an ad hoc exception.

Specify who does what: your on-site manager coordinates logistics and compliance, while community-designated men and women own the respective preparation streams; sponsor-facing materials should describe the public portion carefully without flattening the social meaning into generic youth language.

Include a monitoring/repair step: confirm the printed guide, check-in flow, and staff roster all preserve the preparation split and the return-to-community sequence before press deadline, and correct any wording that frames the event as only age or biology based.

scenario: In Santiago, a newcomer from an international housing nonprofit is trying to finalize a rental-support package for a recently married employee who must relocate within two days after a factory transfer. If the paperwork is not settled by tomorrow afternoon, the subsidy slot may go to someone else. The local HR coordinator has already mentioned that the couple has been hard to pin down because evenings fill up quickly and several relatives have been involved in move-related errands.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: I finally reached Tomás. He said tonight is the only open window before the subsidy cutoff, but he was vague about who would be around.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll make it work. I'll stay late, bring the forms to their apartment, and keep the meeting focused so the two of them can decide without extra noise.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That would certainly save time. Just so you know, his mother has already asked twice about the storage dates, and his wife's father came by the office this morning about the school route.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Good to know. I'll prepare a short summary for the relatives afterward, but for the actual choices I'll ask everyone else to step out so the couple can settle it privately and we don't lose the slot.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The landlord also wants one clear answer tonight on whether the smaller unit is acceptable for the first month.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I'll simplify it: I'll present only the two apartment options, get the spouses' signatures, and leave the parking, child pickup, and furniture rotation for family follow-up once the lease is secured.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right, send me whatever you collect before 9 so I can upload it before the portal closes.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Will do. I'm heading over now, and I'll keep the decision with the newlyweds so we can move fast.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer makes real effort and absorbs time pressure, but the decisive mistake is assuming the married couple should function as a separate decision unit and pushing older relatives into an after-the-fact role. In this Chile-specific seed, support and decision involvement may still run across generations, so excluding active parents from the live housing discussion misapplies a nuclear-family default.

scenario: Your company is piloting a two-year engineering rotation in Santiago, and the regional director wants one Chilean finalist, Tomás, to sign by Monday because a backup candidate in Peru is ready. You lead the rollout team from headquarters. Tomás is 26, lives in Santiago, has strong interview scores, and said in the final panel, "I like the role, but I need this weekend before I can confirm." He has already asked twice whether the housing stipend can support staying near his current neighborhood, and after receiving the written offer he replied with one question about whether the start date could shift by two weeks. A Chilean HR coordinator notes only that he is "serious, not shopping around," while the finance lead warns that holding the slot past Monday risks losing budget approval for this quarter. The regional director wants a fast close and suggests sending a firm message: either sign now or release the offer. Your team also includes a U.S. recruiter pushing for candidate autonomy and a German operations manager pushing for clean deadlines and equal treatment across markets. You must send a same-day coordination plan and candidate-communication approach that will be judged on whether it closes the hire without damaging trust or creating an avoidable miss in Chile.
question: Write a brief action memo for your team that specifies exactly how you will handle Tomás's weekend request. Your memo must: (1) diagnose what hidden decision process is likely affecting the delay based on the facts given; (2) identify the most tempting but miscalibrated assumption your team might import; (3) choose a concrete sequence, channel, timing, and wording for communication with Tomás between now and Monday; and (4) explain how you will protect deadline pressure without pushing the process in a way that makes the offer more likely to fail. Be specific about who contacts whom, what is said, what is not said, and what checkpoint you will use on Monday.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that the decision is likely not purely individual and that close family consultation may be part of the acceptance process.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers a family-involved decision path from the scenario evidence and translates that into execution consequences; no credit for merely saying Tomás is 'hesitant' or 'needs time.'

rubric.point: Uses the correct execution axis: communication timing and sequence must preserve the weekend consultation window rather than forcing immediate closure on Friday.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan deliberately avoids a Friday ultimatum and builds a paced sequence such as Friday acknowledgment plus a Monday checkpoint; partial credit if the answer slows down but without a defined sequence.

rubric.point: Rejects the attractive near-miss assumption that a good process should treat this as an entirely autonomous individual decision under a universal fast-offer SOP.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly bounds the imported assumption and explains why a clean, equal, deadline-driven sign-now-or-release message is miscalibrated here; no credit for generic 'be flexible' language.

rubric.point: Chooses calibrated visible behavior: right channel, wording, and audience.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies a direct private contact to Tomás, acknowledges his request without naming or probing his family, confirms the timeline, and avoids public escalation or copying broad stakeholders on pressure messages.

rubric.point: Balances task progress with relationship management through a concrete Monday checkpoint and contingency.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan defines what happens Monday, such as a specific check-in time and decision window, plus an internal hold/backup trigger; no credit for open-ended waiting or indefinite consultation.

rubric.point: Applies behavioural CQ through exact phrasing and interaction rhythm, not generic respect.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer includes operational wording or message framing that gives room for consultation while keeping ownership of the hiring process; answers that stay abstract about 'sensitivity' or 'respect' do not score highly.

rubric.point: Avoids wrong-scope application of cultural knowledge.
rubric.score_rule: No full credit if the answer tells the team to contact parents, ask explicitly whether his family approves, broaden the decision to extended relatives without evidence, or transfer authority away from Tomás; the answer must adjust the process around him, not bypass him.

reference_outline: Infer from the weekend request, housing-location concern, and minor start-date question that Tomás is likely aligning the offer with family expectations or consultation, not simply negotiating for leverage.

Do not send a Friday sign-now-or-lose-it ultimatum; instead send a private Friday message acknowledging that he asked for the weekend, confirming that the team will reconnect Monday, and keeping the offer active through that checkpoint.
Use one accountable owner, ideally the recruiter or hiring lead, for a direct one-to-one call or message to Tomás; avoid broad cc's, public pressure, or mixed signals from finance and headquarters.

Frame the message around decision support and clarity: confirm enthusiasm, answer any final practical questions, state the Monday check-in time, and invite him to come prepared with any remaining concerns; do not mention family directly and do not force him to justify the delay.

Explain internally that the tempting imported assumption is to read the delay through an individual-autonomy or equal-deadline lens and treat fast closure as neutral, when here that behavior risks breaking trust and reducing acceptance odds.

Protect the business side by setting a Monday morning or midday checkpoint, reserving the slot until then, and preparing an internal backup release rule only after that checkpoint rather than before it.

Show behavioural CQ by choosing wording, timing, and rhythm that cost some speed but fit the likely decision process: space over the weekend, clear follow-through on Monday, and pressure contained inside the team rather than pushed onto the candidate.

If Monday still brings uncertainty, use a narrow repair step such as one more same-day clarifying conversation with Tomás before releasing the offer, rather than escalating immediately with a blunt final warning.

scenario: At a microfinance office in Quito, a newcomer branch supervisor is finalizing Saturday staffing for a client workshop with an auditor attending. A local employee asks for part of the afternoon off for a family event, but the relationship described is not a nuclear-family one, and the branch is already short-staffed.

roles.local: Marisol, senior loan officer at the branch

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Daniel, I need to leave after the second session on Saturday. The workshop matters, so I can finish the intake forms before lunch if that helps.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Saturday is tight with the auditor coming, so I need to understand what can and cannot move. Is this something you need to be physically present for, or mainly a visit afterward?

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: I need to be there during the ceremony and stay a while with the family. I also have to bring the envelope myself. My husband can cover our kids, but not this part.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I’ll keep you on the morning client block, move Javier to the afternoon tables, and tell the auditor now that our floor lead changes after lunch.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: If it becomes impossible, I could still arrive late there. I know it’s not my household and I don’t want to create trouble on your first audit weekend.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: No, don’t plan around that. Send me the handoff notes by Friday evening, and I’ll brief Javier myself so we don’t build the schedule on you missing the important part.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right, I’ll leave the notes and the cashbox count separated before lunch. I appreciate the quick decision.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Good. Keep the morning as promised, then go straight from here. I’ll explain the switch to the room when we open so we don’t lose time later.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer calibrates away from a nuclear-household default and treats the obligation as a legitimate family duty extending beyond spouse and children, adjusting staffing once the role and timing become clear instead of downgrading it as optional. The decisive axis is scope of family responsibility in scheduling, not tone.

scenario: A manufacturer in Bolivia is updating a supervisor briefing line for short-notice ceremonial leave before peak production week. Recent requests included travel for a baptism sponsor, a funeral of a relative living elsewhere, and a marriage-related obligation involving two households. HR wants one sentence supervisors can use consistently without opening unlimited leave.
question: Which briefing line should HR approve?

options.A: Approve leave when the person is part of the employee's current household or immediate legal family; for other ties, offer shift swaps or personal days through the standard exception process.
options.B: Do not use shared address or nuclear-family labels as the first test; ask whether the person holds an ongoing family obligation in the employee's network, then decide within the existing leave limits.
options.C: Treat ceremonies tied to sponsors or marriage obligations as eligible when the employee is directly named in that ritual role, while keeping funerals limited to parents, partners, children, and siblings.
options.D: Allow ceremonial leave for relatives outside the home and for sponsor relationships whenever the employee identifies a continuing family duty, with documentation handled after travel if needed.

scenario: You are the regional implementation lead for a nonprofit launching a 6-week pilot in a South American city. The pilot gives emergency after-school transport and meal vouchers to low-income families so children can keep attending school during a transit strike. Your team includes a finance manager in Germany, a safeguarding officer in Canada, and two local field coordinators. The donor requires a defensible enrollment method within 72 hours because media coverage has already announced the pilot. Finance wants one household file per address, one primary caregiver signature, and one emergency contact listed inside that household record to reduce fraud and speed reimbursement. The local coordinators' intake notes are messy: several mothers list the same apartment but different sleeping arrangements across the week; some children are picked up by an aunt or grandmother who lives elsewhere; one mother says she 'has help every few days' and another says a child's meals are handled by relatives 'not here' when work shifts change. No one has explicitly objected to finance's plan, but the field team keeps asking whether the form can capture 'who actually covers what' without delaying launch. The donor also warns that any visible enrollment confusion in week 1 could damage renewal chances. You need to send a rollout memo today that tells the team exactly how to enroll families, who to contact, what evidence to collect, and how to control fraud and child-safety risk without missing the deadline.
question: Write the rollout memo you would send. Your memo must: (1) diagnose what the intake notes imply about how care is organized, (2) identify the most tempting but miscalibrated assumption in finance's proposed approach, (3) set a concrete enrollment workflow on one clear decision axis: who counts as part of the case and must be mapped before services start, and (4) show how you will sustain team effort under time pressure without turning the process into open-ended consultation. Be specific about contact scope, sequencing, documentation, ownership, and what you will do when the reported caregiver network extends beyond one address or one daily caregiver.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that the operational care network cannot be inferred from co-residence or a single address record.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer translates the intake clues into an execution consequence: enrollment must map who actually provides transport, meal, supervision, or pickup support even when those people do not live in the same household or participate daily. No credit for merely saying 'family structures differ' or 'be culturally sensitive.'

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the attractive near-miss of treating one household file, one resident caregiver, and one in-home emergency contact as the full service unit.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer names this as a tempting efficiency/compliance shortcut and explains why it would miss key responsibility holders, create pickup/safeguarding failures, or misjudge who can activate support. Partial credit if it adds extra contacts but still keeps the address boundary as the decisive scope.

rubric.point: Makes a seed-specific stakeholder-scope decision before launch.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer requires a bounded pre-service mapping of the active care network for each child or case, including nonresident or non-daily caregivers with defined roles, rather than deferring all clarification until after enrollment or expanding to a vague unlimited family census. Must specify who must be captured before vouchers start and who can be added later.

rubric.point: Designs a concrete workflow with roles, sequence, and evidence rules.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer assigns ownership (for example, local coordinators collect network role data, safeguarding reviews authorization, finance receives a simplified case structure), specifies sequence, and distinguishes evidence for service role authorization from evidence for reimbursement or fraud control. Generic calls to 'consult locals' or 'use a flexible form' do not score high.

rubric.point: Shows motivational CQ through costly but bounded adaptive effort.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer commits to visible extra effort under discomfort or time pressure—such as additional follow-up calls, flexible contact windows, re-contacting families when roles are unclear, or taking on temporary documentation burden centrally—while keeping the process finite. No credit for warm language without follow-through, for withdrawing to avoid ambiguity, or for shifting the burden onto families to reorganize themselves to fit the form.

rubric.point: Balances deadline, donor, fraud, and safeguarding pressure without defaulting to the broadest or safest plan.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes a narrow risk-control boundary that still fits the wider care network: for example, role-based authorization and verification for actual pickup/meal/transport actors, with exceptions/escalation for unclear cases. Low credit if the answer delays launch broadly, demands exhaustive proof from all relatives, or uses generic caution to avoid deciding.

rubric.point: Includes a repair and monitoring loop tied to the same scope decision.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies how week-1 discrepancies will be checked and updated when the lived care network does not match the initial form, without collapsing back into a household-only model. Partial credit for generic monitoring language without a trigger or owner.

reference_outline: State that the notes suggest care responsibilities are distributed across people who may live elsewhere and may not provide care every day, so the service case cannot be defined only by shared address or one resident caregiver.

Set the primary execution-axis decision: enroll by child-centered active care network, not by household boundary alone; require mapping of the people currently responsible for pickup, meals, transport coordination, and emergency decisions before service starts.

Bound the scope operationally: capture essential role-holders first (primary applicant, actual pickup/transport adults, meal-responsible adult if different, backup decision-maker), while allowing nonessential extended contacts to be added later if needed.

Explain that finance's one-address/one-signature default is attractive for speed and fraud control but miscalibrated here because it would omit the very adults who operationally enable or authorize the child's daily support.

Assign workflow: local coordinators run short structured intake calls; safeguarding checks authorization and pickup permissions; finance receives a standardized summary that preserves reimbursement control without forcing the care network into a single-resident template.

Show motivational CQ by taking on extra effort explicitly: add a second contact pass for unclear cases, allow after-hours calling windows, and centralize the documentation cleanup burden on the project team rather than expecting families to fit the imported form immediately.

Use bounded risk control: verify role-specific authority and contactability for service use, separate from broader kinship proof, and escalate only ambiguous or conflicting cases instead of demanding exhaustive family documentation from everyone.

Add a week-1 repair loop: compare actual pickup/use patterns to enrolled role-holders, update authorized contacts quickly when mismatches appear, and track whether household-only assumptions are causing missed handoffs or voucher failures.

scenario: At a partner school in Ayacucho, a newcomer from an education NGO is finalizing emergency transport stipends before a donor deadline that night. One student listed her mother's village address, but weekdays she sleeps at her madrina's home near town and helps an older relative there in the evenings. The stipend file allows only one short justification note and one primary household contact, so the newcomer must decide how to complete the case while keeping the batch moving.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: I have one more file before we send the stipend list. Rosa studies here during the week, and the contact numbers on her form belong to different homes, so the donor portal flagged it.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll stay and clean it up. If the portal wants one household, I'll rewrite the note around the registered address and mark the town stay as temporary so finance doesn't hold the whole batch.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The town address is where she sleeps most school nights. Her mother is outside the city, and the older woman there depends on having someone in the house after dark.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. To keep it defensible, I'll call Rosa now and ask which reason should appear officially: school convenience or helping the older woman. Mixing both can look inconsistent in an audit.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: She is still in class, and we need to upload in an hour. Her madrina can answer quickly if you need confirmation.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll call, but I should still narrow it to one category and one real household head. Otherwise it reads like an informal arrangement instead of a stable residence.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right, send me whatever wording you use before you submit.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Will do. I'll note the village home as primary, list the madrina only as a temporary host, and keep the justification focused on study access so the case looks straightforward.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer invests real effort, but misplaces it by forcing the case into a single nuclear-household and single-motive frame. This conflicts with the Peruvian care-network mechanism where co-residing with a madrina or older relative can be a legitimate kin-based care arrangement and can simultaneously support caregiving and schooling.

scenario: A social-enterprise team in Ecuador is finalizing next-day home visits for a clean-cookstove pilot. Visit notes show that in the city route both spouses are usually home in the early evening, while in the highland route the wife is often the household member handling sales income and daytime decisions. Vans leave at noon, so the team needs one field sequence now.
question: Which field sequence best fits these visits?

options.A: Open the first conversation with the husband on both routes, confirm household-use details with the wife afterward, and close repayment timing jointly if both spouses remain present.
options.B: Open the first conversation with both spouses together on both routes, ask who wants to take the lead, and then finalize timing and repayment with that person.
options.C: Open with the husband in the city route, then confirm household-use details with the wife; in the highland route, begin with the wife and close terms with both spouses if available.
options.D: Open the first conversation with the wife on both routes, settle repayment timing with her first, and then bring the husband in later for installation scheduling if present.

scenario:
You lead a multicultural product team launching a paid after-school learning app in Lima through employer partnerships. A Peruvian HR director has agreed to circulate the final enrollment packet to 40 employees by Friday so payroll deductions can start this month. Missing Friday means the pilot slips by four weeks and your regional VP has already promised the date to investors. Your team has one last decision: how to structure the family-facing enrollment workflow for employees with school-age children.

Current facts are mixed. In user interviews, several fathers asked first about contract length, cancellation, and whether the app would affect household budget planning. In separate onboarding calls, several mothers asked detailed questions about homework routines, screen-time limits, who will monitor progress, and how monthly charges appear in household spending. In two households, fathers stayed quiet during the child-use discussion but later emailed follow-up questions about the annual commitment. In three others, mothers completed most of the form but said they needed to "review it at home tonight" before authorizing the deduction. Your Mexico-based operations manager argues for a fast global workflow: one legally complete consent form signed by the employee who receives the benefit, plus a child-use guide sent only after payment setup. Your Germany-based compliance lead wants one strict decision-maker recorded for audit clarity. Budget only allows one live briefing session, one follow-up message, and one form redesign before Friday.

You need a plan that your VP will judge on conversion rate, low reversal risk after signup, and whether local partners feel you understood how family decisions are actually made.
question: Write a short decision memo for your team that specifies the enrollment workflow you would use in Peru. Your memo must: (1) diagnose what pattern in the evidence should drive the workflow, (2) identify the most tempting but miscalibrated assumption in the current team debate, (3) choose a concrete stakeholder sequence for the live briefing, follow-up message, and form design, and (4) explain how your plan reduces reversals without turning into a generic "consult everyone" process. Be explicit about whose concerns are addressed at which stage and why.

rubric.point: Diagnoses differentiated household influence rather than a single universal family decision-maker.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers from the evidence that major commitment and provider-risk questions tend to require consultation with the man, while child-use and household-spending details are strongly shaped by the mother; no credit for treating the household as either fully male-dominated or fully individual-autonomy by default.

rubric.point: Applies the diagnosis to the exact execution axis: stakeholder sequence.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan deliberately sequences budget/commitment issues and child-use/household-management issues to the relevant actors and stages; partial credit if both topics are mentioned but not assigned to a clear sequence, actor, or stage.

rubric.point: Rejects or bounds the attractive near-miss plan.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly identifies a tempting imported assumption such as 'the employee-beneficiary alone should decide' or 'one official decision-maker is enough for audit and speed' and explains why that would create sign-up reversals or missed buy-in in this Peru case; no credit for merely saying 'avoid stereotypes' or 'be respectful.'

rubric.point: Designs an operational workflow using the actual constraints.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer uses the single live briefing, one follow-up message, and one form redesign in a concrete way—for example, structuring the briefing, splitting message content by concern type, and building a form or packet that supports at-home review without reopening the whole process; partial credit for generic consultation steps that ignore the Friday deadline.

rubric.point: Shows cognitive CQ by separating cultural logic from generic process, legal, or personality explanations.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explains why the observed pattern is not best handled as mere legal compliance, personal preference, or broad family inclusiveness, and instead maps the evidence to who influences which kind of decision in this context; no credit for repeating cultural labels without execution consequences.

rubric.point: Controls reversal risk with a narrow, not maximal, coordination design.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes a bounded process that targets the likely household decision points without turning into unlimited extra approvals or delay-for-more-info; partial credit if the answer simply broadens outreach to every family member or recommends postponing launch.

reference_outline: Infer from the evidence that household decisions are differentiated by domain: fathers are likely to be consulted on major financial commitment and provider-related risk, while mothers strongly shape childrearing use and day-to-day household spending implications.

Choose the primary sequence accordingly: use the live briefing to cover both the commitment case and the child-use case in one household-ready presentation, but order or frame it so major financial commitment is addressed early and child routine/monitoring and spending details are made concrete before asking for enrollment completion.

Redesign the form or packet so the employee can take home a concise enrollment set that visibly includes both commitment terms and child-use/household-management details, rather than a single employee-only consent flow followed later by a usage guide.

Use the one follow-up message as a household review prompt that summarizes cancellation, payroll effect, term length, supervision/progress features, and spending visibility, so the employee can review it with the relevant family members that evening before final authorization.

Explicitly reject the near-miss assumption that one official beneficiary or one recorded decision-maker is enough for this market; explain that this may satisfy a global SOP or audit preference but will raise post-signup reversals because it ignores who actually influences different parts of the decision.

Keep the process narrow: do not require signatures from multiple family members or indefinite consultation, but do build one deliberate at-home review step before final authorization to align with likely household decision structure under the Friday deadline.

Show cognitive CQ by distinguishing the Peru-specific influence pattern from generic patriarchy, generic egalitarian autonomy, or generic family-inclusion policy, and by translating that distinction into actor-stage-topic matching rather than abstract cultural commentary.

scenario: A newcomer from an international nonprofit is helping prepare a same-day community briefing in an Andean village for a small irrigation repair grant. The donor wants a short video and a practical work list by evening. A local coordinator has arranged for several households to gather in the school courtyard, including older residents and school-age family members who came with tools and notebooks.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We only have this afternoon before people head back uphill. For the donor clip, families are already gathering in the courtyard, and Don Mateo brought the old canal sketch from his house.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Great, I’ll keep it organized. For safeguarding and a cleaner message, I’ll film only adults for the clip and ask the younger ones to stay off camera near the supplies table.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. We also need the work list fast, because tomorrow's truck space depends on the numbers we send tonight.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I’ll split the discussion: first a quick adults-only planning circle, and later I can give the children a separate drawing activity so they still feel included without carrying meeting pressure.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Don Mateo has been pointing to the upper bend since he arrived, and two of the boys who came with him were measuring something with string.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I saw that. To avoid putting too much weight on one family’s version, I’ll use the engineer’s form for the main decisions and keep Don Mateo’s story as background context.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We should start in five minutes. The municipal officer may stop by before sunset, so whatever we record needs to look orderly.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I’ll open with the formal agenda, seat the older people in front for courtesy, and keep the actual planning with the adult heads of household so we can move quickly.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer's decisive misstep is treating elders mainly as symbolic figures and younger family members as people to protect from real responsibility, instead of recognizing elders as substantive knowledge holders and younger members as expected contributors to practical work and decision-making.

scenario: Your Bogotá field team is closing a home-delivery pilot with a 29-year-old pharmacy owner. The first shipment window closes tomorrow, and headquarters wants one documented approval route for similar small-family businesses.
question: Which manager briefing line is most defensible for the approval record on this deal?

options.A: Approve the pilot once the owner signs the deal memo, and document family views separately as relationship context rather than part of the approval record.
options.B: Approve the pilot after the owner signs, but require a second recorded confirmation from his mother before dispatching stock for the first delivery cycle.
options.C: Approve the pilot with the owner as signer, and require the team to document whether another senior family figure also needs confirming before the first shipment is released.
options.D: Approve the pilot only after the owner signs and the team attaches confirmations from the household’s senior relatives to the launch approval record.

scenario: You are the regional implementation lead for a multinational employer that is launching a caregiver-support pilot in São Paulo within 10 days. The pilot budget is fixed, the global HR VP wants a clean metric story for the board, and the Brazil country manager wants to avoid a rollout that looks out of touch with local employees. A draft designed by headquarters assumes elder care is mainly arranged through external providers and proposes three benefits only: a provider-directory app, a short emergency leave policy, and a reimbursement cap for professional home-care services. In two internal listening sessions, several Brazil-based employees did not directly criticize the draft, but they kept returning to examples such as rotating weekend visits, sending money to parents in another city, rearranging schedules to accompany parents to appointments, and stress from siblings arguing over who is 'showing up enough.' One manager also noted that some staff may not use formal services even when they are exhausted, and another warned that employees may avoid a program that seems to judge their family choices. At the same time, finance is pushing to keep the pilot narrow and measurable, and legal says the company should not imply responsibility for employees' relatives' medical care. Your project team includes a US benefits analyst, a German operations manager, and the Brazil HR lead. You must send a decision memo tomorrow morning that recommends the first-wave pilot design, what evidence you are relying on, and how the team should brief managers.
question: Write the decision memo recommendation. Specify which parts of the headquarters draft you would keep, change, or defer in the first wave; what hidden pattern you think explains the employee signals; which tempting assumption in the current draft you would explicitly reject or bound; how you would brief the US, German, and Brazil teammates so they execute consistently; and what evidence or feedback in the first month would make you revise your approach. Your answer should make concrete choices on scope and sequence rather than giving a generic 'consult more' plan.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the operative mechanism behind the Brazil employee signals
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires inferring from the scenario that elder-care burden is being experienced through family obligation to be personally present, provide support, visit, and help financially, not just through outsourcing gaps. Low credit if the answer only says 'family is important' or names a cultural label without changing execution.

rubric.point: Makes the first-wave design fit that mechanism on the scope/sequence axis
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires changing the first wave so it supports family-based caregiving realities operationally, such as including schedule flexibility, manager guidance around accompaniment/visitation, emotional-support or navigation resources, and/or recognition of financial strain, while not making formal provider reimbursement the sole centerpiece. Low credit if the answer simply adds more vendor options or delays everything for more research.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the attractive near-miss assumption in the headquarters draft
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires explicitly identifying the tempting imported assumption that elder care can be treated mainly as a market-service access problem and explaining why that would misread the Brazil evidence under current constraints. Low credit if the answer accepts the global default and merely suggests communicating it more sensitively.

rubric.point: Uses metacognitive CQ rather than certainty or inertia
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires stating what can be inferred now from the listening-session evidence, what remains uncertain at household level, and what first-month signals would justify recalibration. Low credit if the answer is overconfident about every Brazilian family, or if it avoids a decision by hiding behind generic caution and endless consultation.

rubric.point: Coordinates role-specific execution across the multinational team
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires assigning concrete briefing implications to the US analyst, German operations manager, and Brazil HR lead on the same execution axis: what not to over-weight, what to measure, and how to present the pilot so managers do not frame it as only a vendor benefit. Low credit if the answer gives broad teamwork advice without role-specific adjustments.

rubric.point: Controls trust, legal, and budget risk without erasing the cultural mechanism
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires preserving legal boundaries and budget discipline while still designing a credible pilot that does not imply employees should simply institutionalize care or prove severity through formal service use. Low credit if the answer solves risk by making the plan so narrow, safest, or generic that the core Brazil need disappears.

rubric.point: Provides an operational manager-briefing and repair approach
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires concrete wording or briefing guidance for managers, including how to discuss caregiver strain without judging family arrangements and how to handle early signs that employees see the program as misframed. Low credit if the answer only says 'train managers to be respectful' with no execution detail.

reference_outline: Recommend a first wave that keeps only limited elements of the provider directory and legal-safe leave structure, but re-centers the pilot around support for employees who are directly carrying family elder-care duties through presence, accompaniment, visits, emotional labor, and often money.

State the diagnosis from the neutral evidence: repeated references to weekend visits, schedule rearrangement, sibling pressure about who is showing up, remittances, and reluctance to use formal services indicate the draft is misframing the burden if it assumes external providers are the main solution.

Name and reject the near-miss: a competent global HR default would treat elder care as primarily a purchasable service-access problem; bound that assumption by saying it may help a subset of cases but is too narrow for the Brazil first wave.

On scope and sequence, prioritize manager-approved flexibility, appointment accompaniment norms, caregiver counseling or navigation, and optional financial-planning/support resources before expanding heavy reimbursement mechanisms; defer broader vendor spending until usage patterns show it fits actual employee behavior.

Brief the US analyst to stop using vendor uptake as the main proxy for relevance, brief the German operations manager to design process consistency around flexible-use cases rather than formal-service claims only, and brief the Brazil HR lead to shape language that validates family-based caregiving without implying a single expected family model.

Apply metacognitive CQ by writing what is known now, what remains uncertain across income levels and households, and what evidence in month one would trigger revision: who uses flexibility, whether employees avoid the benefit because it feels misframed, whether financial-strain requests surface, and whether managers interpret the policy too narrowly.

Include a manager script or guidance frame that recognizes elder-care obligations can involve being present, coordinating family care, and handling costs, while staying within legal limits by offering workplace support rather than assuming responsibility for relatives' treatment.

Add a repair plan: if employees treat the pilot as irrelevant or judgmental, quickly reframe materials, adjust intake categories beyond formal service use, and use Brazil HR to collect pattern-level feedback without turning the response into indefinite delay.

scenario: At a municipal health post in Várzea Grande, a newcomer coordinator is helping arrange same-day support for an older patient after a minor procedure. The clinic must confirm who will check on her that evening before the transport van leaves, but the chart is incomplete and the senior nurse is in another appointment.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Dona Celina is ready to go in about forty minutes. We still need to note who will make sure she eats and takes the evening tablets after the van drops her off.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I’ll call her family first and put a relative down before we release the van slot. It’s safer if we confirm someone from the family can take over tonight.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: There’s a son listed, but the number often goes to voicemail. She usually comes here by herself, and the pharmacy slips in her bag have two other names written on them from her street.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I’d still rather not rely on people from the street for post-procedure care. I’ll keep trying the son and ask the driver to wait a bit longer.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The van cannot stay long; it has two more pickups. Dona Celina is already asking whether she can tell the women near her gate when she gets back.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Let’s not make the plan informal. If no relative answers, I can note that we advised family follow-up and send her with printed instructions.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Alright, I just need something entered before transport closes the list.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Please enter the son as primary contact for tonight, and I’ll continue calling him after she leaves.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer stays polite and procedural, but miscalibrates the key uncertainty: cues suggest the elder likely manages daily life alone and looks to nearby non-family contacts, yet the newcomer keeps forcing a generic family-first discharge plan. For this seed, expected support depends on living arrangement, and for elders living alone, neighbors or friends are often the relevant helpers.

scenario: You are finalizing the opening script for a municipal wedding event in northern Ecuador. The mayor wants the first minute to feel locally grounded, but the printed program must go to press tonight. Your current draft opens by celebrating each pair's love story before naming any other people. This afternoon you can review notes from two recent ceremonies in the same area.
question: Which observation would be the most diagnostic reason to revise that opening script before sending it to print?

options.A: In both ceremonies, relatives coordinated clothing, transport, and meal logistics, while the couples themselves handled the legal paperwork and signed the register without much extra ceremony.
options.B: In both ceremonies, the first public acknowledgments placed each pair within their two families and the gathered community before the couple spoke about themselves as a new household.
options.C: In both ceremonies, older relatives were seated prominently and thanked by name near the end, after the couple had exchanged vows and the emcee had already introduced them.
options.D: In both ceremonies, the most photographed moments were the couple-only portraits, and guests formed long lines afterward to congratulate them one pair at a time.

scenario:
You manage field rollout for a regional livelihoods project. A donor wants a rapid pilot in one Otavalo Kichwa community in Ecuador, with a possible second phase in a highland Bolivia site that works with Aymara- and Quechua-speaking families. Your multinational team must finalize, within 10 days, who will serve as the first local co-facilitators for household budgeting workshops and who should be invited to the community planning meeting that will approve the pilot calendar. The donor prefers younger, bilingual participants who can travel and submit reports quickly. Your operations director in Madrid wants a simple individual-selection process that can be reused in both countries. 

The local shortlist includes: (1) an unmarried 27-year-old woman with strong Spanish, mobile access, and previous NGO experience; (2) a 24-year-old man who recently moved to his wife's family area and is now being copied on messages about communal work and meeting logistics; (3) a recently married couple whose names now appear together in invitations from several households, and whose families keep referring to future obligations tied to the project if they accept; and (4) two older men suggested by one neighborhood leader but described by others as hard to coordinate. 

Message history is ambiguous. Several local contacts respond slowly to direct requests for individual CVs but quickly to invitations framed around households, compadres, and who will 'stand behind' the work. One email from the Bolivia partner warns only that in their site, selecting people too quickly as if they were free-standing volunteers caused follow-through problems after the kickoff event, because people who seemed available at first were later said not to be in the right position to carry obligations. No one explains this further. 

You have budget for one extra in-person visit before decisions are locked. If you miss the donor deadline, the pilot may lose funding. If you choose the wrong local structure, the first public meeting may look successful but later attendance and community decisions may stall.
question: Write a decision memo for your team that sets the selection and rollout mechanism for the co-facilitators and planning meeting. Your memo must: (1) diagnose what hidden social mechanism is shaping who can credibly carry this work, based only on the evidence in the case; (2) identify the most tempting imported assumption your director is making and why it is risky here; (3) choose a concrete stakeholder sequence for the next 10 days, including how you will use the one extra visit, who must be engaged first, and which candidates you would treat as lead, support, or not-yet-appropriate choices; and (4) explain what adaptive effort you personally will absorb to keep the project moving without forcing locals to do all the interpretive work for you.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that local legitimacy for this work is tied to community-recognized adult household status and obligation-bearing standing, not just age, education, or individual availability.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers an earned social status linked to marriage completion and resulting rights/obligations in community life; partial credit if it vaguely mentions family importance or respect; no credit if it treats the issue as simple seniority, language skill, or generic stakeholder buy-in.

rubric.point: Applies the mechanism to the exact selection decision by distinguishing who can credibly carry community-facing obligations now versus who may be useful only in a supporting role.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer operationalizes the evidence around the recently married couple and/or newly repositioned married man as more plausible obligation-bearers for community-facing roles, while bounding the unmarried experienced candidate as potentially valuable but not automatically the right lead; no credit for picking solely on CV strength or donor-friendly reporting capacity.

rubric.point: Rejects the tempting near-miss of using a reusable individual volunteer-selection template and explains the execution failure it would create.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if it identifies the attractive imported assumption as treating candidates as free-standing individuals who can be appointed quickly and then perform on their own; the answer must explain likely downstream failure in follow-through, decision legitimacy, or reciprocal commitment rather than just saying 'it may be culturally insensitive.'

rubric.point: Sets a seed-specific stakeholder sequence on the primary axis of approval and role scope.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan prioritizes confirming the household/family-backed and community-recognized basis of the role before locking titles, public invitations, or reporting expectations; partial credit for broad consultation without sequence; no credit for announcing individuals first and repairing later.

rubric.point: Shows motivational CQ by taking on visible adaptive cost instead of shifting the burden to locals or hiding behind delay.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the respondent commits to costly but bounded engagement such as using the extra visit to test role legitimacy, revising the donor-friendly template, absorbing schedule inconvenience, and doing follow-up coordination personally; no credit for generic patience, indefinite waiting, or asking locals to send a full explanation before the team changes course.

rubric.point: Builds a risk-control and repair plan that fits the hidden mechanism under deadline pressure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer includes a narrow safeguard such as provisional role framing, a two-step confirmation before public designation, or separate support/reporting functions from community-obligation functions; no credit for maximal delay, overly broad consultation, or generic respectful communication without operational controls.

reference_outline: State that the evidence suggests community-facing responsibility depends on recognized transition into full social adulthood with obligations and standing, not merely competence or enthusiasm as an individual.

Name the main trap: the director's portable NGO logic assumes the team can appoint the strongest bilingual individual as a standalone volunteer and then scale that template across Ecuador and Bolivia.

Use the extra visit to verify which candidates are publicly recognized as able to carry obligations, who is expected to act through a household or affinal network, and whose acceptance would bind wider reciprocal relationships.

Recommend not locking the unmarried NGO-experienced candidate as sole lead; instead place such a person in a support, translation, logistics, or reporting role unless local confirmation shows broader standing for the community-facing function.

Give priority to candidates whose recent status change is reflected in meeting inclusion, family-backed invitations, and references to future obligations, while checking whether the role should be held by an individual, a couple, or a household-linked pair rather than one free-standing person.

Show motivational CQ by absorbing the extra coordination cost personally: revise the template, explain to the donor why a fast individual appointment creates implementation risk, make the extra visit, and keep momentum with a bounded provisional schedule rather than withdrawing or demanding that locals fully decode the system for you.

Sequence the next 10 days operationally: first test legitimacy and obligation-bearing scope, then confirm role design, then issue planning-meeting invitations through the validated social channels, then assign reporting/admin tasks separately if needed.

Include a repair/control move: if donor timing forces early action, present initial roles as provisional until community confirmation, avoid public over-appointment of the wrong person, and monitor whether attendance, backing, and follow-through come from the wider relationship network rather than from the selected individual's résumé.

scenario: In Ecuador, you accompany a Chachi coworker to his aunt's overnight wake in a river community. Your team must leave by boat at dawn, and the fuel key is with the person informally managing the wake, someone you have only met once. When you arrive, the closest relatives stay beside the coffin while other attendees move between seated groups and ritual games. You need a sequence for your first part of the night that keeps the departure on track without mishandling the gathering.
question: Which sequence best fits this situation?

options.A: Offer condolences to the family, remain near the coffin for most of the night, and wait until morning to ask about the fuel key after the wake has ended.
options.B: Offer condolences to the family, ask one of the closest relatives who is guiding the night, join a game soon after, then return to stay beside the coffin.
options.C: Find the informal wake leader early, confirm the fuel key right away, spend most of the evening in the games with other attendees, and leave before dawn without another check-in.
