options.D: Offer condolences briefly, identify the acquaintance coordinating the night, spend time with the attendees joining the games, and later make a short dawn-departure check through that organizer.

scenario: You are the regional community-relations lead for a multinational food company opening a small training center near Otavalo, Ecuador. The center launch is scheduled for 3 November, and the country manager wants a same-day social post and a short on-site tribute because a respected local facilities coordinator, Don Luis, died earlier this year and his relatives still work with your team. A global brand director in Miami has already drafted a safe template: flowers, a black ribbon, a framed photo, and a line about 'honoring all who are no longer with us.' The local operations supervisor has only sent fragmented notes: several relatives plan to arrive very early, some team members mentioned bringing cleaning supplies to the cemetery before coming to the site, and one niece asked whether the company would 'leave space on the table for what he liked.' No one has explicitly asked the company to attend the family observance. Budget is tight, legal wants to avoid appearing to sponsor religion, and the country manager insists the launch cannot be postponed because municipal officials and press are confirmed. Your team includes an HR partner in Spain who prefers a uniform condolence protocol and an Ecuador sales lead who says only that 'if we do something, the details matter more than the speech.' You must send a decision memo tonight and coordinate the morning execution.
question: Write a concrete execution memo for the team. Specify what you will and will not place at the training center, who should communicate with which stakeholders tonight and tomorrow morning, what timing and sequence you will use around the launch, and how you will handle the global template. Your memo must explain what cultural mechanism you think is operating from the available clues, what tempting assumption could lead the team wrong, and how your visible actions, wording, and interaction rhythm reduce relationship risk while still delivering the event.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden mourning mechanism from the clues
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that remembrance should be anchored in offerings linked to the deceased person's personal identity and family participation, rather than a generic memorial display; partial credit if it mentions family or food vaguely without tying them to the deceased person and the observed clues.

rubric.point: Makes the primary execution-axis decision on material placement and sequence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan rejects a generic flowers-photo-black-ribbon centerpiece as the main act and instead creates limited, family-calibrated space for personally relevant offerings at the right moment and scale, with the launch proceeding but not competing with the family's early observance; no full credit for generic tribute tables or broad memorial décor.

rubric.point: Uses behavioural CQ in wording, timing, and channels
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if it specifies visible behaviors such as a private check-in tonight with the relatives, careful wording that asks about appropriate items tied to Don Luis rather than offering a standard package, and a morning sequence that avoids public improvisation; generic statements like 'be respectful' or 'consult locals' do not score high.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the attractive near-miss plan
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if it identifies the global condolence template or other generic default as tempting but miscalibrated, and explains the operational risk: it is brand-safe and efficient yet misses the locally meaningful form of remembrance; answers that simply add the template alongside everything else without boundary lose credit.

rubric.point: Assigns roles and stakeholder scope precisely
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if it names who contacts the family-facing employees, who informs legal/brand, who briefs municipal-facing staff, and who controls on-site setup so the act stays appropriately scoped; answers that spread responsibility diffusely or rely on a broad committee approach do not receive full credit.

rubric.point: Balances launch pressure with relationship maintenance
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan preserves the launch under constraint while adjusting rhythm, acknowledgment length, and placement to avoid overshadowing family observance; answers that solve the issue only by cancelling, delaying everything, or making the tribute larger and safer than necessary lose credit.

rubric.point: Builds monitoring and repair into the morning execution
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if it includes a real-time check before setup is finalized and a repair path if relatives signal the display is off-target, such as scaling back public elements and shifting to a quieter family-facing acknowledgment; no full credit for one-time planning with no adjustment mechanism.

reference_outline: Infer from 'leave space on the table for what he liked,' the early cemetery visit, cleaning supplies, and family arrival timing that the meaningful act is not a generic memorial object but remembrance expressed through family-linked offerings connected to Don Luis specifically.

Decide that the company should not lead with the global flowers-and-ribbon template as the core tribute; instead, privately confirm with the niece or another family representative whether a small space with items reflecting his favorite foods is welcome and how visible it should be.

Sequence the morning so family-related observance is not interrupted: brief staff tonight, make a private family-facing contact first, keep any site acknowledgment short and later, and avoid forcing a public ceremonial moment before relatives have completed their early routine.

Assign roles tightly: Ecuador sales lead or local supervisor handles family-facing calls, community-relations lead manages the final decision and on-site boundaries, legal/brand is told the company is supporting a family-calibrated remembrance rather than staging a generic memorial activation, and municipal/press-facing staff receive a minimal script.

Use behavioural CQ through concrete wording and channel choice: ask privately, specifically, and in action terms what would be appropriate to place or not place; do not send a mass message, do not overexplain culture, and do not improvise a public speech as a substitute for the right material action.

Bound the near-miss explicitly: the global template is efficient, neutral, and brand-safe, but applying it unchanged would import a generic mourning default and miss the locally meaningful mechanism; if brand insists on some standard element, keep it secondary and not the centerpiece.

Monitor and repair on the day: check again before setup is finalized, watch whether relatives engage with the space comfortably, and if the arrangement feels too public or too generic, reduce it quickly and shift emphasis to quiet family acknowledgment while preserving the launch schedule.

scenario: A newcomer working for a mobile health program is finalizing next month's family register in a Wayãpi area before the supply boat leaves. The register affects food allotments and where a starter housing kit will be delivered. A local liaison is helping review names, but the donor also wants a clean list of newly formed households by tonight.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: I marked Iara and Poti with the new families. They have been spending time between both sides lately, and everyone already knows they are together.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Great, then I'll put them in tomorrow's public signing block with the other new couples so the file is consistent before the boat goes.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Tomorrow is busy, and for them the sleeping place is still shifting. Her mother mentioned one thing, his uncle another.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I can keep it short. I'll just ask both families to stand with them when I read the names, then I'll lock one delivery point so the housing kit doesn't get split.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The materials team only needs to know where to unload first. They can come to me later if the list needs adjusting.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. To avoid confusion, I'll enter them now as one completed household under his side, and if they want a different long-term place we can amend it next quarter.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right, I still need to finish the canoe manifests before dark.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll send the finalized register tonight and note that the families were present when I confirmed the entry.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer applies a generic marriage-administration script by creating a public formal confirmation step and fixing the couple to one permanent household line under the husband's side. For this seed, marriage formation does not hinge on a special ceremony, and residence is not permanently fixed because the husband may later build near either his parents or his in-laws.

scenario: A museum archive is standardizing metadata for two Wayãpi clips before publication. For each clip, the catalog requires a `social unit changed` field and a `change completed when...` field. One clip shows a girl's emergence from seclusion with women marking the occasion. The other shows repeated reciprocal deliveries between two households before a young woman begins living with her intended's family.
question: Which metadata entry is the most culturally accurate?

options.A: Seclusion clip: `social unit changed = alliance between families`; `change completed when = the girl's seclusion ends`. Delivery clip: `social unit changed = future couple`; `change completed when = the first exchange is made`.
options.B: Seclusion clip: `social unit changed = girl's life stage`; `change completed when = the seclusion rite concludes`. Delivery clip: `social unit changed = marriage formation between households`; `change completed when = she moves to her parents-in-law's house`.
options.C: Seclusion clip: `social unit changed = girl's readiness for marriage`; `change completed when = parents approve the match`. Delivery clip: `social unit changed = marriage formation between households`; `change completed when = the exchange period ends after years of deliveries, regardless of residence`.
options.D: Seclusion clip: `social unit changed = girl's procreative status`; `change completed when = she later enters the exchange relationship`. Delivery clip: `social unit changed = union between kin groups`; `change completed when = the young man has supplied fish and game to her family`.

scenario: A newcomer at a housing nonprofit in Papeete is preparing next-day home visits for a rental assistance program. The agency usually schedules one interview slot per household to confirm occupancy, income pooling, and who can receive follow-up documents. A local colleague has already warned that the team is overbooked and drivers can only make one stop per address this week, so the newcomer must decide how to handle an application file that lists a young couple at the same address as an older relative, with several contact names attached and no time for multiple separate visits.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Tomorrow's route is packed. For the Teva file, the address note has three adults tied to the same place, but we only have one visit slot and one printed packet.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I saw that. Instead of splitting them into separate appointments, I'll keep the one stop, bring extra copies, and ask whoever is there to gather the people who handle the household decisions so we can review it together.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That could mean a longer visit, and the regional office wants the forms back by tomorrow afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll start there first, even if it slows my morning. If the younger pair aren't the only ones managing the place, I don't want to make them chase signatures across town after we leave.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The file also mentions a cousin who sometimes answers the phone. We don't know who will actually be home.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: That's fine. I'll call ahead, say I'm bringing one packet for the household at that address, and ask them to have the people involved in the living arrangement present if possible.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. Just keep the visit moving; the driver has another pickup at noon.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll keep it tight, but I'll still work from the address group first and sort individual details inside the visit rather than treating the younger couple as a stand-alone case.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer invests extra time and logistical effort to handle the address as a shared multigenerational household unit rather than imposing a nuclear-family default. The decisive execution detail is keeping one household-centered visit and inviting the relevant co-resident decision-makers into the process, which matches the seed's pattern of complex households and strong kin-based shared housing obligations.

scenario: You are preparing first-home visits for a budgeting-app pilot in Suva. Each visit includes shared-expense mapping and printed forms for everyone in the home who may use the app. You have limited car space for materials, visits start tomorrow morning, and the local coordinator can share mobile numbers but cannot contact households for you tonight.
question: Which preparation sequence is the best fit for tonight?

options.A: Call each household yourself tonight to confirm the visit, ask who currently lives there and who plans to join, pack to that number, and carry a small backup set tomorrow.
options.B: Plan each Suva visit around a smaller household, pack lean sets first, and let households request extra forms later if more people want to join.
options.C: Prepare the same medium-size bundle for every home, confirm only the visit times tonight, and adjust on site if the number of participants is different.
options.D: Text each household tonight asking who lives there and who expects to join, pack to the replies you get, and leave unclear cases for the coordinator to sort out tomorrow.

scenario:
You are the regional community-relations manager for a renewable-energy company. A mixed project team based in Port Vila, Auckland, and Singapore must finalize a compensation and access-use proposal for a small solar microgrid near Big Bay, Vanuatu. The draft must be sent in 48 hours because the donor board wants evidence of local agreement before releasing equipment. A senior operations director in Auckland is pushing for a fast sign-off path: meet the village chief and the most vocal adult sons from the affected households, confirm who can authorize access, then issue a clean memorandum listing payment recipients and a grievance contact. 

Your Ni-Vanuatu field officer has sent neutral notes from two visits: in one household discussion, younger women spoke confidently about who should be present before any boundary discussion moved forward; an older woman interrupted when one man tried to settle the order of speakers; several people asked whether the proposal protected the 'next holders' if an elder died; and one family said a cash-only payment to the current male representative would be 'easy now but difficult later.' No one directly refused the project. The land strip needed for poles is narrow, but the route touches family land connected to status and inheritance, not just temporary use. 

The legal team says the company only needs a documented signature set and can defend a standard process. The donor, however, will react badly if agreement appears rushed or later disputed. Budget allows one more in-person session, not a long consultation cycle. You must tell the team today how to structure the next meeting, who must be in the room first, what draft to circulate, and how to close without losing the deadline.
question: Write a decision memo for your project team that specifies the meeting sequence, audience, speaking order, draft-handling approach, and close-out steps for the next 48 hours. Your memo must: (1) diagnose the hidden family-authority mechanism suggested by the field notes; (2) identify the tempting imported assumption in the Auckland director's plan; (3) choose one concrete execution sequence for the final consultation and signature path; and (4) show how your wording, channel, timing, and follow-up reduce both deadline risk and later legitimacy disputes.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that authority over this land-access decision cannot be treated as resting primarily with current male household representatives or a generic chief-plus-sons shortcut.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers from the notes that maternal-line continuity and women with lineage standing must shape the decision because the issue touches inheritance/status, not mere temporary logistics. No credit for vague statements like 'include women too' without tying them to authority, succession, or the land-related decision.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the attractive near-miss plan of using a fast, globally familiar sign-off path focused on male spokespeople and legal sufficiency.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explains why a chief/sons/current-male-representative route is appealing under time pressure yet miscalibrated here, and limits legal-minimum documentation from becoming the actual decision mechanism. Partial credit if it adds more people to the same shortcut without changing who validates authority.

rubric.point: Chooses the correct primary execution sequence for the final session.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan visibly sequences the consultation so lineage-relevant women/maternal-side authority are engaged before or at the decisive stage of boundary/payment/inheritance confirmation, rather than after a near-final draft is already socially committed. No credit if the answer consults them only as a courtesy after signatures are essentially settled.

rubric.point: Translates behavioural CQ into concrete meeting design rather than abstract respect language.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies visible actions such as who receives the pre-read, whether the first discussion is a smaller validation meeting or a full forum, who presents the draft, who is asked to confirm beneficiary logic, when signatures occur, and what not to announce publicly too early. Generic advice like 'communicate sensitively' or 'be inclusive' does not score.

rubric.point: Uses wording and draft control that keep the proposal provisional until the right actors confirm the authority logic.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer recommends language such as 'working draft' or equivalent, avoids framing the recipient list as already decided, and reserves final naming/payment allocation until the legitimacy of the maternal-line authority path is confirmed. No credit if the plan circulates a fixed memo with named recipients before that step.

rubric.point: Balances deadline pressure with legitimacy risk through a narrow, operationally efficient process.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer avoids both extremes: neither the fastest legal-signature shortcut nor an open-ended broad consultation. It should propose one extra targeted session, a tightly defined attendee set, and a same-day or next-day documentation path once the correct authority is confirmed.

rubric.point: Designs close-out and repair steps for downstream dispute prevention.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer includes a concrete record of how authority and beneficiary logic were confirmed, identifies a follow-up channel for corrections before funds/access are finalized, and treats later objections as a legitimacy signal rather than mere resistance. Partial credit for generic grievance channels without linking them to the authority question.

reference_outline: State that the field notes indicate a matrilineal authority/inheritance mechanism: the decision affects land, title continuity, and future holders, so maternal-line women are not optional attendees but part of the valid decision path.

Flag the Auckland near-miss as a plausible but wrong imported default: chief plus adult sons plus current male representative may satisfy speed and legal optics, yet it risks invalidating the agreement because it mislocates who must shape land/inheritance decisions.

Use one additional in-person session with a deliberately sequenced structure: first validate authority and beneficiary logic with the lineage-relevant women/maternal-side actors and other necessary family figures, then move to the broader confirmation/signature stage once that core logic is settled.

Circulate only a provisional draft before the meeting, with route, compensation categories, and unresolved recipient/allocation fields clearly marked pending family confirmation rather than pre-filled as final.

In the meeting, have the facilitator explicitly ask who must confirm future-holder and lineage implications before any signature is taken, and avoid public pressure for immediate closure until that authority path is acknowledged.

Take signatures only after the attendee group aligned with the inheritance logic has confirmed the access and compensation structure; document not just names but how the family authority basis for agreement was established.

Use behavioural CQ through concrete visible choices: controlled audience, delayed public finalization, careful wording of the draft, timing signatures after the right stage, and a narrow correction window for legitimacy-related amendments before donor submission.

Close within 48 hours by sending the donor a finalized memorandum only after the targeted session, plus an internal note explaining why this narrower sequence is faster overall than defending a disputed agreement later.

scenario: At a logistics company in Port Moresby, a warehouse team is preparing a donor shipment that must leave by Friday. One forklift operator, Daniel, has asked for three days away and an early partial pay release because people from several places are gathering in his home area this week. The newcomer operations manager must respond quickly without delaying the shipment or damaging team trust.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Daniel handed in a leave form this morning. We are already thin for the Friday dispatch, and he also asked whether payroll can release part of next week's pay today.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I can act fast. I'll approve one day, move his shift earlier tomorrow, and ask payroll for a small advance if he signs the deduction form.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That would help the roster, but he wrote that people are coming in from other places and that he needs to be there before the main day.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll keep the advance, and I'll tell him we support him joining the main day in person. For the days before that, he can stay reachable by phone so the team still sees flexibility.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: He is one of the steadiest operators, and the others will notice whatever we decide. We still need the containers loaded by Thursday night.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I'll make the decision myself today and be consistent: one day of leave, cash early, and no extra discussion in the team meeting. I don't want this turning into an open-ended family exception.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. I can prepare the paperwork and line up a casual driver for Thursday if needed.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Please do that. I'll speak with Daniel directly and explain that we're backing him financially, but operationally we have to limit time away to the actual ceremony day.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer sounds fair and supportive, but the decisive behavior is culturally miscalibrated: he treats attendance as limited to the single main event and frames earlier participation as optional remote availability. In Papua New Guinea, extended family duty commonly includes being physically present to contribute across the surrounding clan process, not just attending the central day, and support often involves both time and resources.

scenario: You manage field rollout for a nonprofit pilot in a Polynesian community in Oceania. The pilot must launch in 10 days and includes a monthly food-support and home-check schedule for elders who live without a spouse or resident children. Your regional director wants a defensible beneficiary list within 48 hours because a donor report and shipping order depend on household counts. A finance officer in Australia insists the list must be tied to stable household units to prevent duplicate benefits. A local school administrator has sent you a spreadsheet with elders' sleeping addresses, emergency contacts, and who usually brings meals, water, or medicine. The pattern is messy: several elders listed as 'alone' receive daily help from younger adults registered at other homes; one older man has no children at his address but two middle-aged women from different homes alternate care; one older woman is marked 'no co-residents' yet a teenage boy stays with her on school nights and is registered elsewhere on weekends. Another case shows three brothers in different dwellings contributing jointly to one elder's care, while the legal next-of-kin column names a nephew working off-island. The school administrator also notes that some children have spent years moving between relatives' homes. Your team includes a logistics lead from New Zealand who proposes assigning support strictly by sleeping address plus legal next-of-kin, and a safeguarding officer from Singapore who proposes asking each elder to nominate a single primary caregiver for the file. If you miss the donor deadline, the shipment may be delayed a month; if you classify care networks badly, community trust may drop and the pilot may be seen as bypassing the people who actually carry day-to-day responsibility.
question: Write a short decision memo for your team that sets the rule for building the first-round beneficiary and caregiver map. Your memo must: (1) diagnose what the address-based and single-primary-caregiver proposals are assuming, (2) specify exactly how you will identify the relevant care unit for this rollout, (3) decide what evidence counts most when records conflict, (4) assign roles for verification and donor documentation, and (5) explain how you will control duplicate-support risk without forcing the wrong family structure into the file. Be concrete about sequence, scope, and what you would document in the first 48 hours versus what you would refine after launch.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden kinship mechanism from scenario evidence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that the operative care unit is not limited to co-residence or a single nuclear/legal household, and ties that inference to the specific evidence in the case such as daily contributors sleeping elsewhere, fostered or mobile children, and care obligations spread across kin/personal ties. No credit for merely saying 'family is broader' without operational consequences.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the tempting imported assumption
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly identifies the flaw in using sleeping address, legal next-of-kin, or a forced single caregiver as the primary mapping rule, while still preserving them as secondary documentation fields if needed. Partial credit if it notices one flaw but still makes address or legal kin the decisive unit.

rubric.point: Sets a seed-specific first-round mapping rule
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan defines the first-round care unit around the actual support network responsible for daily elder care, including non-resident contributors and relevant kin/personal ties, rather than around a fixed dwelling. The answer must state how this applies to cases with alternating carers, fosterage-linked ties, or distributed sibling support. Answers that are generic, overly broad, or simply say 'consult the community' do not earn full credit.

rubric.point: Weights evidence correctly under ambiguity
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer ranks recurring day-to-day caregiving evidence above formal residence or legal labels when those conflict, while still capturing legal/administrative data separately for audit. Partial credit if it mixes evidence without a clear hierarchy. No credit if it defaults to the most standardized record source.

rubric.point: Applies cognitive CQ through exact category mapping
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer shows it understands who counts in the relevant social unit, where its boundary is, and why a global default category misclassifies the cases. This must appear as a judgment about the local logic of care responsibility, not as etiquette, empathy, or generic caution.

rubric.point: Designs a concrete workflow with role assignment and timing
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer gives a workable 48-hour sequence such as: provisional network map, quick verification against observed care patterns, donor-facing aggregation rule, and post-launch refinement; and assigns distinct roles to field verification, finance documentation, and logistics. Vague statements about teamwork or communication are insufficient.

rubric.point: Controls duplicate-support risk without collapsing the care network
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes a mechanism such as one elder-centered case file linked to multiple contributors, cross-referenced network IDs, or a separate benefit-delivery unit versus care-network record, so duplicate shipments are prevented without erasing shared obligations. No credit if duplicate control is handled by reducing the record to one household or one caregiver.

reference_outline: State that the scenario evidence points to a fluid care network: people who sleep elsewhere may still belong to the operative support unit, and children or younger relatives moving between homes can be part of the care structure rather than noise in the data.

Name the near-miss assumption: the New Zealand and Singapore proposals import a stable co-resident household or single-accountable-caregiver model that is administratively neat but misreads who actually carries responsibility.

Set the primary execution-axis decision on stakeholder scope: build each elder's first-round file around the active care network responsible for regular support, not around a fixed address; keep sleeping address and legal next-of-kin as secondary fields for compliance and contact purposes.

Define evidence weighting: repeated daily provisioning, accompaniment, medicine/water delivery, and recognized contribution patterns outrank residence labels when identifying the care unit; conflicting records trigger a quick targeted verification, not automatic reversion to the legal or address field.

Assign roles operationally: field staff map contributors and care frequency, finance keeps the donor-compatible audit trail, and logistics delivers against one elder-centered case ID while recording linked contributors to avoid duplicate material allocation.

Handle the first 48 hours versus later refinement: create a provisional network map now for shipment decisions, flag ambiguous ties for post-launch update, and avoid delaying the rollout just to force complete certainty.

Explain duplicate-risk control as a separate administrative layer: one support entitlement per elder or approved elder case, cross-linked to multiple carers, so risk control does not overwrite the local care logic.

Show cognitive CQ by correctly separating local responsibility categories from global default household categories, and by explaining why using the wrong category would damage both accuracy and trust.

scenario: On Sikaiana, a relief team is assigning one of the last two home-care supply kits after a storm. The kit requires a same-day support plan naming who will check on an older resident, refill water, and coordinate clinic transport over the next month. The local coordinator is under pressure because the boat leaves at sunset and the donor form has space for only a few names.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We can still put Mereana's name forward today, but the form needs a short care plan before the boat goes. She lives alone now, and the form only has three lines for household support.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll make the three lines the people who actually rotate through her place. Not just whoever is listed as closest on paper. Can you bring in the woman sleeping there this week, the man who handles her fishing share, and the younger one who usually takes her to clinic?

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: They're not all from the same roof, and one of them has been staying with another family lately. We also need this done fast.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: That's fine. I only need ten minutes with the people she leans on now. I'll draft the plan from the current pattern and keep it to three names for the donor sheet.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Mereana's brother's son is away on the outer reef, and her married daughter is on Honiara this month. If you want, I can just put the daughter's name first so the paperwork looks clean.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Let's not anchor it to absent children if others are already carrying the daily load. I'll note the daughter separately and put the regular helpers on the working plan so the kit matches who will actually maintain it.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. I'll call them over from the shade house now. The carpenter is waiting for the final signature.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Great—once they agree on the rotation, I'll sign immediately and post the refill days by the doorway before the carpenter starts.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer correctly treats elder care as organized through broader kin and fosterage-based reciprocity networks rather than defaulting to biological children or a single nuclear household. The decisive execution detail is choosing current practical caregivers across households for the care plan, even under a formal form and time pressure.

scenario: Your team is preparing a same-week pilot in Sikaiana that will issue household cooking vouchers. A draft recipient list is due tonight for budget approval, but the local roster mixes descent-group information with notes on where people have recently been staying. Several young adults married in the past year, and a few children are listed in one home while regularly eating in another. You need one working rule for the first draft that can still be tightened tomorrow.
question: Which mapping should guide the draft list now?

options.A: Group people first under the male descent line that controls family resources, then place wives, children, and attached relatives within that line for the voucher list.
options.B: Treat each sleeping location as the primary unit for the draft, assigning adults and children to the dwelling where they stayed most recently and reconciling kin ties later.
options.C: Build the draft around each married pair's home as the working unit, count newly married adults separately from their natal homes, and flag children who move between homes for review.
options.D: Keep newly married adults under their natal family entries until tomorrow's review, then split them into separate homes only after confirming which relatives continue sharing food and supplies.

scenario: A public-health NGO in Samoa is finalizing tomorrow's community briefing. The event will be held in the courtyard of the family where Lina lives after marriage. Lina is respected locally, chairs parts of the meeting logistics, and her brothers from another nearby household are helping mobilize volunteers. Headquarters requires one documented family approval route today before the country manager signs off the briefing pack.
question: Which approval route should the country manager authorize for the briefing pack?

options.A: Approve Lina as the sole family signatory, noting that a senior local woman coordinating the event can represent the household hosting it for documentation purposes.
options.B: Approve a route led by Lina and one of her brothers, using her standing with her birth family to document consent for the courtyard and meeting setup.
options.C: Approve a route signed by Lina and the village women's committee lead, treating the committee relationship as the clearest community-backed basis for household authorization.
options.D: Approve a route that documents consent through Lina's husband's family for use of the courtyard, while listing Lina's own relatives as supporting participants rather than household authorizers.

scenario: A newcomer coordinating a school support shipment on a small island has one afternoon to hand out bedding rolls and enrollment packets before the cargo boat leaves at dawn. The roster is messy: several children are listed under different homes, and the donor office wants a clean count by household tonight.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The boat agent wants our final numbers by sunset. A few names on the student list may look repeated, but the supplies still need to go out today.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I started making one pack per child's main home so the count stays clean, but I can still adjust the handout method before we print the pickup sheet.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: At lunch, three adults asked about the same Year 6 boy. One said he sleeps near the clinic this week, another said she keeps his uniforms, and an older uncle said he'll be stopping by several houses tonight anyway.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I won't force one household line for collection. I'll group the packs by the related homes on each route, note who is carrying what, and let the linked families sort the handoff this evening while I keep the donor count separate.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That will look untidy on the pickup table. The donor rep also asked whether each child has a single receiving adult on the form.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll keep one reporting name in the spreadsheet for the donor, but on the ground I'll brief the runners and leave the packets with the connected households that are already sharing the evening visits. We can add any missing signatures tomorrow.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. I'll tell the boat agent the count is coming, and I'll have the runners wait by the office at four.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Good. I'll call people over together, hand out the grouped bundles quickly in front of everyone, and mark the follow-up names afterward so the boat paperwork still goes out tonight.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer updates away from a nuclear-household default and works through kin-linked sharing and visiting patterns: the decisive axis is distribution scope and reporting sequence. They keep a clean donor record, but the actual handoff follows fluid household and kin-network obligations rather than forcing each child into one exclusive home.

scenario: You are a program manager for a New Zealand-based nonprofit coordinating a youth scholarship celebration in Nuku'alofa with a local Tongan partner school. The event is in 5 days, the donor's office wants the printed program approved tomorrow, and the school principal has asked your team to avoid last-minute changes because seating, speaking order, and family acknowledgments affect attendance. The scholarship recipient is a 17-year-old girl. Her father has been emailing your team in English and has quickly approved most logistics. A male field officer from your team proposed doing a short home visit tomorrow evening to finalize the student's bio, collect a family photo, and rehearse the student's entrance with her and two same-age cousins. He suggested going alone because the budget is tight and he already has a good rapport with the family. Separately, the draft program lists the father as the family representative for the ceremonial presentation, and the donor wants the agenda locked tonight so social media graphics can be designed. In the message thread, a senior female relative has not written much, but several family members keep asking whether the printed order and acknowledgments are 'set' yet. No one has explicitly objected to the current plan.
question: Write a concrete coordination plan for the next 24 hours that you would send to your team and partner school. Your plan must specify who should contact whom, in what sequence, through which channel, and what should change in the visit and program draft. Explain what hidden cultural mechanism you think is shaping the risk here, what tempting imported assumption could lead a competent outsider astray, and how your execution choices reduce relationship damage while still meeting the deadline.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden mechanism from the scenario evidence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit identifies both relevant risks operationally: the home-visit plan creates a problem if a post-puberty male is alone with the student or her female cousins, and the ceremonial program may be misassigned if the father's line is treated as the only authority path. Partial credit mentions family hierarchy or respect in general without tying it to these exact decisions.

rubric.point: Changes the visit design on the decisive execution axis
rubric.score_rule: Full credit explicitly stops the solo male visit and replaces it with a visibly different arrangement such as adding an appropriate female colleague, moving the interaction to a broader family setting, or using a channel that avoids secluded one-on-one coordination with the girl and girl cousins. Partial credit only says to 'check if the family is comfortable' or to 'be careful' without redesigning who is present.

rubric.point: Corrects stakeholder sequence for the ceremonial program
rubric.score_rule: Full credit revises the approval route so the team does not finalize the family ceremonial role only through the father, and instead confirms the proper senior female family role before locking the printed order. Partial credit suggests broad family consultation or generic consensus-building without identifying the specific side and level of family authority relevant to the ceremony.

rubric.point: Rejects the polished near-miss plan
rubric.score_rule: Full credit names the tempting outsider assumption: using the fastest globally normal plan of 'the father already approved, the male staffer has rapport, so proceed unless someone objects' and explains why that would be courteous but miscalibrated here. Partial credit criticizes the plan only as risky, sensitive, or insufficiently inclusive.

rubric.point: Applies behavioural CQ through visible wording, channel, and timing
rubric.score_rule: Full credit gives concrete behavioural moves: a same-day private confirmation path before public printing, careful wording that asks how the family wants ceremonial roles handled rather than announcing them, and a channel choice that preserves dignity while meeting the deadline. Partial credit gives abstract advice about respect or cultural awareness without message timing or audience design.

rubric.point: Balances deadline pressure with narrow, seed-specific control
rubric.score_rule: Full credit proposes a narrow 24-hour workflow that still protects the deadline, such as freezing all non-family elements, marking the family-role line as pending, and assigning one person to secure the correct family confirmation today. Partial credit defaults to delaying the whole event, launching a broad consultation, or collecting more information without a deadline-preserving structure.

reference_outline: Infer two linked cultural risks from neutral clues: the proposed solo evening visit by a male staffer to work privately with a 17-year-old girl and female cousins is not just a safeguarding optics issue; the family-ceremony draft also likely misreads who must be recognized or cleared on the father's side.

Immediate sequence: pause the solo visit, tell the team no one confirms the rehearsal in that format, and switch to either a female-led contact, a joint visit with an appropriate additional person present, or a family-group setting that avoids private male-female coordination.

Program workflow: do not lock the ceremonial family representative line through the father's email alone; ask the partner school to help confirm the correct senior family role for the brother's child ceremony before printing that section.

Use behavioural CQ in the message design: contact privately first, use wording like 'we want to make sure the family acknowledgments and visit arrangement are set in the right way before printing,' and avoid public correction or donor-facing announcements until the family-side confirmation is secured.

Bound the near-miss: reject the efficient default of proceeding because no one objected, because silence plus prior father approval is not enough evidence for either the visit format or ceremonial placement.

Deadline control: keep donor graphics moving on everything else, mark the family acknowledgment block as temporarily pending, assign one owner for same-day confirmation, and prepare a fast repair path if the printed order must change after tonight.

scenario:
You manage implementation for a regional health NGO. Next week, your team must pilot a home-support intake process for older adults on Sikaiana, then present the process to a donor on Friday. The pilot has to show that the NGO can identify who should be involved in care planning without creating family conflict or delaying service start. Your team includes a program officer from New Zealand, a compliance lead from Australia, and a community liaison based in Honiara. Budget allows only one in-person family meeting per elder, and the donor wants evidence that the process can scale.

One pilot case is a 78-year-old widow, Malia, who has limited mobility. In case notes, different people appear across earlier contacts: a woman described as the person who cooks for Malia most days, a man on another island who sends store goods, an older fostered relative who is spoken of as having obligations to her, and two younger kin who joined a church fundraising visit but have not been present during recent clinic transport. In a phone call, one contact says, 'Our family will take responsibility,' but when your liaison asks who can accompany Malia to weekly appointments, the answer becomes less specific. Separately, the compliance lead wants a clean rule: either collect consent and care commitments only from the closest biological descendants, or require all named relatives to be listed as active carers before services begin. The New Zealand program officer prefers a broad family meeting and a shared rota because it looks inclusive and reduces reputational risk if someone later says they were left out.

You have 48 hours to send the team a one-page operating memo for this pilot. If the first intake goes badly, village trust may drop and the donor may block expansion. If the process is too heavy, the pilot will miss Friday's review.
question: Write the core of that operating memo. Explain what you infer from the case, what assumption the team is most at risk of importing, and exactly how you would structure the first intake around family involvement. Your memo must specify: who should be treated as relevant stakeholders versus likely day-to-day carers at this stage; what evidence you would gather now versus later; how you would brief the Australia and New Zealand teammates so they do not force the wrong process; and what contingency you would use if the broader family verbally supports care but only one or two people can actually perform it. Be concrete about sequence, role assignment, and what would make you revise your initial read after the first meeting.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the family-care mechanism in operational terms
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that care responsibility is socially framed across a wider kin network, potentially including foster ties, while practical daily care may still rest with a small number of relatives; no credit for treating care as only nuclear-family business or assuming every named relative will provide hands-on help.

rubric.point: Distinguishes stakeholder scope from hands-on care scope
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan separates who should be acknowledged or consulted in the intake from who must be confirmed for actual day-to-day tasks such as transport, meals, medication, or accompaniment; partial credit if both groups are mentioned but not operationally separated.

rubric.point: Rejects the tempting imported near-miss
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo explicitly bounds at least one attractive but miscalibrated plan: either limiting involvement to biological descendants or requiring all named relatives to be committed active carers before service start; low credit if the answer adopts a broad inclusive meeting/rota as the default solution without testing who can actually do daily care.

rubric.point: Uses metacognitive calibration under uncertainty
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer states what can be inferred now, what remains uncertain, and what specific evidence would change the care-assignment decision after the first meeting; low credit for generic 'ask more questions' or indefinite delay without identifying the key uncertainty.

rubric.point: Designs a concrete first-intake sequence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer gives a practical sequence such as: acknowledge wider kin responsibility, map all relevant kin and obligations, then pin down one or two realistic daily carers and backup functions before service start; low credit for abstract principles without workflow.

rubric.point: Briefs teammates to avoid process distortion
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo gives role-specific guidance to the Australia and New Zealand teammates on why a biologically narrow consent model or a donor-friendly all-family rota would misread this case; partial credit if teammate concerns are mentioned but not translated into process instructions.

rubric.point: Includes a viable contingency and repair path
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies how service can begin when broad verbal support exists but only one or two people can deliver care, including backup communication, follow-up checks, or escalation if the named practical carers fail; low credit for saying only 'consult more' or 'pause the pilot.'

reference_outline: Infer from the mixed case notes that family obligation should be mapped broadly, including foster-linked obligation, but do not treat every listed relative as an equal probable daily carer.

Use stakeholder scope as the primary execution axis: recognize wider kin in the intake conversation, while separately identifying the one or two people who can reliably handle routine assistance in the next two weeks.

Run the first meeting in two passes: first document who is recognized as having responsibility or standing; second test concrete task capacity for transport, meals, medication reminders, and clinic accompaniment.

Tell the compliance lead not to reduce the case to biological descendants only, because that can miss socially binding obligations; also reject a rule that services wait for all named relatives to become active carers.
Tell the New Zealand program officer not to use a broad shared rota as the default success marker; visible inclusion is not the same as realistic care capacity.
Record current evidence as provisional: broad kin backing appears likely, but the operational unknown is which one or two people are actually able and willing to provide everyday help now.
Assign the liaison to test commitment with task-specific questions rather than general promises, and use the memo to distinguish verbal family endorsement from confirmed daily-care capacity.

If only one or two carers can be confirmed, start the pilot with them plus named secondary contacts for non-daily support, then review after the first week and revise if attendance, transport, or meal support fails.

scenario: An inter-island care program must finalize today’s boat manifest for post-discharge supplies for an older woman who will need dressing changes, meals, and transport for review visits. Her intake form lists no spouse and no children. The shipping template requires either naming one receiving coordinator or marking the case as having no standing receiver. In the chart, three different adults appear: one signed a home-care arrangement during an earlier recovery, one has been bringing meals during this admission, and one arranged transport on two past visits. A ward clerk says the case should count as unsupported unless a clear next of kin can be identified. A village aide adds that the person who keeps things organized is not always the most visible visitor, but says she has not dealt with this household recently. The coordinator has time for one same-day call before filing.
question: What is the best next move?

options.A: Call the adult who signed the earlier home-care arrangement, ask whether they still handle the case, and list them unless they clearly decline.
options.B: Call the village aide to identify who is currently expected to organize support for this woman, enter that person if she can name one, and use the unsupported code only if she cannot identify any standing coordinator.
options.C: File the case as unsupported because no spouse or children are listed, then ask the island team after delivery whether a broader support contact should be added next time.
options.D: Hold the manifest until the local team can confirm how all three adults are related to the woman, then choose a coordinator once the family network is documented.

scenario: You are helping coordinate a Rotuman wedding in Oceania. The venue requires one written handling plan for ceremonial presents before tomorrow, and the couple wants donor records kept for thank-you notes. Both families have already divided wedding duties among relatives, and several senior participants will be present during the ceremony.
question: Which gift-handling decision should the coordinator put in the final plan?

options.A: Use one shared reception table, record each donor there, and release the presents straight to the couple after the ceremony so neither family appears to control the process.
options.B: Use one recorded intake point, then place the presents under the bride’s side for sorting and onward transfer within the family process rather than releasing them directly to the couple.
options.C: Use one recorded intake point, then place the presents under the groom’s side for sorting and onward transfer within the family process before any remainder is passed across.
options.D: Use two family intake areas, record each side separately, and leave the presents with their original side until the later family redistribution stage is completed after the ceremony.

scenario:
You are the regional partnerships manager for a Pacific cultural tourism nonprofit. A Rotuman staff member in Suva is getting married in three weeks, and your team has been asked to help coordinate a short filmed family-approval segment for a community exhibit opening. The exhibit sponsor wants a confirmed shooting plan by tomorrow because travel and catering funds expire at noon the next day. The groom's cousins, who live partly in Fiji and partly overseas, keep pushing for a fast solution: one cousin suggests the groom and bride should simply visit the bride's parents that evening with an engagement ring, flowers, and a printed budget so everyone can lock the wedding size and filming permissions in one meeting. Another teammate from Australia supports that approach because it is efficient, private, and easier for the sponsor's paperwork. A New Zealand-based producer warns only that the family is 'particular about how these things start' but gives no details. In the message history, the bride's uncle has not objected to filming, but he has repeatedly asked who will be coming, what they will bring, and whether the discussion is meant to settle dates immediately. You cannot miss the funding deadline, but a visible misstep could damage the family's trust and the nonprofit's standing with local communities.

You need to send a coordination note tonight telling the team exactly how to structure the first approach to the bride's family, who should attend, what should happen before any discussion of filming or wedding scale, and how to keep the sponsor satisfied if the first visit does not produce immediate clarity.
question: Write the coordination plan you would send. Your answer must: (1) diagnose what hidden mechanism is shaping the family's questions, using the evidence in the scenario; (2) identify the tempting but miscalibrated assumption in the cousins' and Australian teammate's plan; (3) specify the first-approach sequence in concrete behavioural terms, including timing, attendees, what is brought, entry/arrival protocol, and when wedding size or filming details should and should not be discussed; and (4) explain how you would phrase the sponsor update and contingency plan so the project still moves forward without forcing the wrong kind of first meeting.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the family's questions as signaling a formal, rank- and kin-structured initiation that must be enacted before substantive negotiation.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers from 'who is coming,' 'what they will bring,' and uncertainty about settling dates that the first contact must be a family delegation with protocol and ceremonial seriousness, not just a casual visit; no credit for vague statements like 'be respectful of tradition' without operational consequences.

rubric.point: Rejects the attractive near-miss plan of sending the couple alone for an efficient private decision meeting.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly bounds the ring/flowers/budget-meeting approach as a plausible imported default that misreads actor scope and meeting purpose; partial credit if it says not to rush but does not explain why the proposed attendees and meeting frame are wrong.

rubric.point: Gets the primary execution axis right: the first approach must be sequenced as an early, formal delegation before discussion of scale, dates, or filming permissions.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan specifies an early-morning first visit, family representation on the groom's side rather than the groom acting alone, and postpones or subordinates wedding-size/production details until after the formal approach is enacted; no full credit if correct cultural elements are mentioned but applied at the wrong stage or treated as optional add-ons after a business discussion.

rubric.point: Specifies concrete visible behaviours for attendees, materials, and protocol.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer names appropriate representatives such as parents/elders/titled men or chiefs, includes serious ceremonial offerings rather than generic gifts, and addresses protocol-sensitive arrival/entry behaviour; partial credit for mentioning 'elders' or 'gifts' without the representational or ceremonial function.

rubric.point: Uses behavioural CQ by translating inference into calibrated wording, timing, channel, and interaction rhythm.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer gives actionable phrasing for the coordination note or first contact, shows how to ask/confirm attendance and purpose without flattening the ritual into logistics, and preserves the right sequence even under deadline pressure; no credit for answers that remain at the principle level.

rubric.point: Designs a sponsor-facing contingency that protects task progress without forcing premature closure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes a bounded update such as confirming that a formal family approach is being conducted first, giving a staged timeline for later filming/date details, and protecting funds or decisions through a two-step plan; no full credit for indefinite delay, generic consultation, or forcing immediate answers to satisfy paperwork.

rubric.point: Avoids common scoring traps.
rubric.score_rule: Responses lose credit if they rely mainly on generic politeness, broaden the stakeholder list indefinitely, propose asking 'a local person' to decide everything, or apply accurate knowledge to the wrong actor, timing, or purpose—for example, treating ceremonial items as props for the film shoot rather than part of the initiation itself.

reference_outline: Interpret the uncle's questions as evidence that the issue is not only permission but the correct form of initiation: the bride's side expects to know the representing party, the seriousness of the overture, and whether this first visit is for formal approach rather than immediate bargaining.

Do not send the couple alone with a ring, flowers, and budget sheet as the main first meeting; that efficient private model is the near-miss because it collapses family representation, ceremonial exchange, and negotiation into one imported script.

Structure the first move as an early-morning formal visit by the groom's family side, including appropriate senior representatives and, where available, titled/rank-relevant figures, with ceremonial offerings that signal seriousness before any attempt to settle logistics.

Treat protocol-sensitive arrival and entry behaviour as part of execution, not decoration; the delegation should follow the expected route and order rather than improvising for convenience, and the meeting should open with the formal overture before dates, guest counts, or filming permissions are pressed.

Sequence discussion so that, after the formal approach is accepted and hospitality begins, timing and wedding scale can be discussed in the family's rhythm; filming and sponsor requirements should come later or be framed as dependent on the family's process, not as the reason for the visit.

Write the team note in concrete behavioural terms: who attends, what they carry, when they arrive, what not to raise at the start, and how to brief overseas cousins and the producer so nobody turns the visit into a budget-closing session.

Send the sponsor a staged update: confirm that the first family approach is being completed tonight/tomorrow morning, explain that substantive production details will follow that step, and offer a follow-up checkpoint rather than a forced final answer by the first encounter.

Include a repair boundary in case teammates have already signaled the wrong format: quickly restate that the first meeting is representational and ceremonial, not a direct negotiation by the couple, and adjust expectations before anyone arrives with the wrong gifts or agenda.

scenario: A community liaison in Auckland is helping coordinate support after a Samoan staff member's father dies in Samoa. Flights are being booked quickly, the church hall schedule must be confirmed by noon, and the company wants to send food and a condolence contribution without causing confusion. The newcomer has to decide how to organize workplace support and who should be included first.

roles.local: Sina, Samoan HR coordinator in Auckland
roles.newcomer: Mark, recently transferred operations manager from New Zealand headquarters

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Tui just left to be with family. We need the church-hall numbers by noon, and people here are already asking how to help.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I can steady this. I'll keep it tidy: one condolence note from leadership, a meal roster for the next two days, and I'll ask staff not to contact Tui directly so the immediate family gets space.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Thanks. There are also cousins, church people, and village contacts calling different team leads, so the questions won't stay in one place for long.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. To avoid mixed messages, I'll have everything routed through me and send one update saying support should go only through the household list we've already got.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The finance team also asked whether the company contribution should wait until next week, once we know final numbers.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'd rather hold the contribution until then and keep today's response practical. A smaller, immediate circle is usually easier on grieving families than lots of separate obligations.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Alright, I still need a headcount for the hall and names for who may attend from our side.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Send me the names from our office only, and I'll finalize a compact group this morning so the family isn't overwhelmed.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer's decisive behavior applies a generic bereavement model of protecting the immediate family through tight privacy, centralizing contact, limiting attendance scope, and delaying reciprocal support. For this seed, mourning commonly involves wider family and church gathering, observable honoring patterns, and timely reciprocation of honour within family/church/village structures.

scenario: In Auckland, a hospital bereavement coordinator must send one final text before 1 p.m. about releasing a deceased patient to a funeral director. A niece who lives in another city has handled most calls so far, but an uncle at the bedside said this morning that several relatives are still talking and sorting responsibilities. The transfer can happen today if the family confirms by 3 p.m.; otherwise the next slot is tomorrow.
question: Which text should the coordinator approve?

options.A: Please ask the legal next of kin to confirm the transfer decision by 3 p.m.; once that person replies, we will arrange today’s release with the funeral director.
options.B: Please let us know by 3 p.m. who is speaking for the family on today’s transfer and whether you expect to confirm today; if needed, we can hold the later slot.
options.C: Please reply by 3 p.m. with agreement from the wider family group on today’s transfer; once everyone is aligned, we will proceed with the funeral director booking.
options.D: Please ask the relative at the hospital to confirm today’s transfer by 3 p.m.; after that bedside contact replies, we will arrange the release with the funeral director.

scenario: A newcomer coordinating logistics for a Rotuman community wedding is under pressure from an overseas sponsor to lock the budget and print the program this week. The local contact is juggling family expectations, village coordination, and visiting relatives, but has not given a final headcount or sequence yet.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The sponsor wants the program file tomorrow, but people here are still talking through who is handling what. If we print now, at least the visitors will have something in hand.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I can hold the print run and take the heat from the sponsor. Instead of forcing one final version tomorrow, I'll draft a working schedule and leave the ceremonial sections open until the right people confirm them.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That may push costs up. Also, both families keep adding tasks, and I'm getting messages from different houses, not one list.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I won't ask you to compress it into one quick checklist. I'll come back tonight and again this weekend, and I'll build the budget around separate work crews, food, transport, and hosting from both sides rather than a one-day event package.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Some relatives overseas are asking why we cannot just name one coordinator and settle the order on a video call.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: For the livestream pieces, yes, but not for everything. Before I lock sequence or announcements, I want the elder handling the formal knowledge, the village ceremony lead, and the chiefs' side reflected properly in the plan, even if that means more calls and another version.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That is a lot more work than the sponsor expected, and they'll ask why the file is still marked draft.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll explain that myself and keep the draft label on it for now. I'd rather spend the extra week and staff time aligning the families' roles than save money by flattening the whole thing into a standard weekend program.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer's behavior fits the Rotuman mechanism by sustaining costly engagement over time, planning for major labour and resource mobilisation from both sides, and preserving defined ceremonial roles and etiquette instead of collapsing the wedding into a generic quick, single-coordinator event.

scenario: You are the regional operations lead for a nonprofit that is co-sponsoring a community wedding on Rotuma as part of a family-support initiative. The event is in 16 days. Your Fiji-based finance manager wants a simple grant transfer to the couple so they can make their own arrangements and close the file quickly. Your Australia-based communications manager wants to publish a short story framing the support as "helping a young couple start independent married life" and needs a final plan in 48 hours for donor approval. On the ground, your Rotuma field assistant has sent a spreadsheet with dozens of names, separate work groups, ceremonial items, transport needs, and several lines marked only with titles rather than job descriptions. The assistant also notes that some people "should be present" even if they are not doing logistics, and that changing the order of conversations could create offense, but does not explain further. Budget is tight, headquarters dislikes open-ended commitments, and the bride's family has already asked whether your team understands what it is agreeing to support. You cannot add more funding, and you will be judged on whether the collaboration plan protects trust while still getting a workable approval package through headquarters.
question: Write a decision memo for your team that sets the coordination plan for the next 72 hours. Your memo must: (1) diagnose what the spreadsheet and message history imply about how this wedding support actually functions; (2) identify the most tempting but miscalibrated plan your non-Rotuman teammates are likely to push; (3) choose a concrete stakeholder and sequencing plan for approvals, budget framing, and communications; and (4) show what extra effort you personally will invest to keep the project moving without dumping the adaptation burden onto the Rotuma side. Be specific about who is contacted first, what is and is not packaged for headquarters, how you handle the unnamed titled roles, and what you do if headquarters resists the broader coordination structure.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the wedding as a coordinated kin-and-community ceremony rather than a couple-centered purchase
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers from the spreadsheet, titled roles, presence expectations, and ordering sensitivity that support must cover a structured social process with distributed obligations and protocol; no credit for generic statements about 'family involvement' or 'important tradition' without execution consequences.

rubric.point: Sets the primary execution axis correctly: stakeholder scope and sequence before finalizing budget and messaging
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan avoids treating the couple as the sole approving unit and instead sequences outreach to the relevant ceremonial and status-bearing actors before locking the grant structure or public story; partial credit if additional stakeholders are mentioned but contacted too late or only as courtesy checks.

rubric.point: Rejects the attractive near-miss of a fast direct transfer plus independence-framed communications
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly identifies why a tidy donor-compliant plan centered on couple autonomy, reimbursement simplicity, or generic wedding normalcy is tempting yet miscalibrated here; low credit if the answer merely says to 'consult more' or 'be respectful' without bounding this imported assumption.

rubric.point: Uses seed-specific role handling rather than collapsing unnamed titles into ordinary volunteers
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer preserves the distinct significance of the titled or presence-marked people in planning, treats some roles as guiding or dignifying the ceremony rather than interchangeable labor, and adjusts workflow accordingly; no full credit if roles are reduced to line items or assigned only by operational efficiency.

rubric.point: Shows motivational CQ through costly, targeted ownership
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the respondent takes on visible effort such as rearranging their schedule, drafting multiple approval versions, staying up for time-zone calls, or doing iterative follow-up to understand and represent the coordination structure accurately, while not pressuring locals to educate headquarters for free; no full credit for warm tone, patience, or generic willingness alone.

rubric.point: Designs a bounded headquarters package that protects trust without asking for unlimited resources
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer translates the broader ceremony logic into a workable internal frame such as categorized support, conditional approvals, or phased commitments that fit the fixed budget while preserving the necessary structure; low credit for either open-ended spending promises or a rigid one-line grant that strips out the core coordination need.

rubric.point: Provides a repair path if headquarters resists
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes a concrete repair move such as narrowing scope while preserving protocol-bearing roles and sequence, revising communications language, or escalating with a risk explanation tied to trust and project credibility; no full credit for default delay, cancellation threats, or sending the burden back to the local family to justify themselves.

reference_outline: Infer from the spreadsheet details that the event is a layered communal ceremony requiring organized labour, status presence, and guided stages, not a private couple event that can be supported through a simple cash handoff.

In the first 24 hours, contact the Rotuma field assistant to map the titled participants and decision sequence into functional categories for internal use, then verify which actors must be approached or recognized before budget and messaging are finalized.

Do not let finance or communications lock a direct-to-couple transfer model or an independence-focused donor story before the broader ceremonial structure is represented; explicitly flag that this default is efficient but risks misframing the event and damaging trust.

Package the budget for headquarters as a bounded coordination-support plan with named categories and approval gates, preserving key protocol-bearing roles and required labour groups even if some discretionary items must be narrowed.

Personally absorb adaptation cost by owning the extra calls, redrafting, and internal advocacy needed to translate the structure for headquarters instead of asking local counterparts to repeatedly defend why the ceremony cannot be treated like a standard private wedding grant.

Revise communications language away from a private-couple success narrative toward a community-supported marriage event without overexplaining cultural doctrine; keep the message accurate to the support structure being funded.

If headquarters resists, propose a narrowed but still protocol-respecting version that keeps the required sequence and status-related participation intact, and explain that stripping those out is a trust and execution risk, not just a cultural nicety.

scenario: A university in Shanghai is piloting a case-based accounting module written by a visiting curriculum team. After two trial classes, the visitors note that students seldom challenge the instructor during explanation segments and are considering rewriting the next session to rely much more on peer-led debate. They have time to review one more classroom observation before deciding.
question: Which observation would most strongly justify revising that initial interpretation?

options.A: During lecture segments, students write continuously, avoid interrupting, and bring most questions to the instructor after class rather than raising them while the explanation is still underway.
options.B: When the instructor pauses to invite explanations of a worked example, several students respond with detailed reasoning, build on one another's points, and ask follow-up questions about the method.
options.C: Even when a spreadsheet result appears inconsistent, students wait for the instructor to revisit it instead of openly correcting the explanation in front of the full class.
options.D: In breakout discussions without the instructor at the front, students speak much more freely, rotate speakers quickly, and generate more alternative answers than during plenary discussion.

scenario: At a Seoul elementary school, a visiting science curriculum specialist is helping with a short model lesson that will be observed by the vice principal and filmed for a district workshop. The lesson needs visible student participation, but the class schedule is tight and the homeroom teacher remains responsible for the room.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The camera crew will only have fifteen minutes once we start. The vice principal asked if the clip can show students thinking, not just me talking.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I can make the activity sharper so we still get student voices without slowing the lesson.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Yesterday, when I previewed the experiment, they watched very carefully but did not add much on their own. I still need to finish the unit objective before lunch.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I won't turn it into an open debate. After your setup, I'll show the second tray, pause, and have you choose one or two students to describe what they noticed before I explain the result.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That would keep us on time. The district trainer also likes to see students explain evidence, not just repeat terms.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
