dialogue.text: Good. If an answer differs from the setup, I'll ask what they observed in the tray and build from that, rather than asking the class to challenge the first explanation.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. We start as soon as the crew finishes placing the back microphone.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll keep my part brief and visible, and I'll hand the floor back to you each time before a student speaks.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer fits the Korean high-authority classroom mechanism by preserving teacher control of turn-taking and avoiding direct student contradiction of the teacher; the decisive axis is who allocates speaking turns and whether student participation is framed as observation-sharing rather than open challenge.

scenario:
You are the learning design lead on a multicultural university project team preparing a 2-week pilot module for a joint China-based undergraduate business program. The pilot starts in 9 days and will be reviewed by the China campus dean, a UK partner-school quality manager, and a corporate sponsor that wants visible student engagement in the recorded class. The dean has already warned that the module cannot look passive, because the sponsor may cut next year's funding if the pilot appears weak. The UK quality manager has pushed for a participation score in the first live session, based largely on how many students volunteer questions or comments in the full class. 

Your team includes a curriculum specialist in Shanghai, an assessment manager in London, and a facilitation trainer in Singapore. In the last three online trial classes with Chinese undergraduates, students submitted strong written prep, completed the reading quiz accurately, and gave detailed answers when called on in small groups, but whole-class discussion stayed quiet. After one session, the London manager wrote that the class seemed underprepared or disengaged and suggested requiring spontaneous public comments from each student for grading in the first session. The sponsor also wants short video clips showing 'active participation' by day 3. 

You must send a one-page implementation memo today deciding how the first live session will be run, what evidence will count as participation for the review group, and how the team will explain the design to stakeholders without weakening confidence in the pilot.
question: Write the implementation memo. Your memo must: (1) diagnose the most likely interaction mechanism behind the trial-class pattern using the available evidence; (2) identify the tempting but miscalibrated assumption in the current team discussion; (3) decide the participation design for the first live session, especially how and when students will be expected to speak; (4) assign roles for the Shanghai, London, and Singapore teammates on the first-session workflow and stakeholder briefing; and (5) explain how you will show credible engagement to the dean and sponsor by day 3 without using a plan that is likely to distort student participation in this setting.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the classroom-specific participation mechanism from the evidence pattern
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires inferring that quiet whole-class response should not be read directly as low preparation or low interest because the evidence shows strong preparation and stronger response under more structured or lower-exposure conditions; partial credit for noting only 'different communication styles' without linking to classroom hierarchy, public exposure, or the contrast between whole-class and structured participation.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the imported near-miss assumption
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires explicitly identifying the attractive but flawed assumption that visible, spontaneous full-class speaking is the cleanest universal indicator of engagement, and explaining why making it an immediate graded requirement is likely to misread the local classroom mechanism; partial credit for saying the metric is 'too harsh' or 'not inclusive' without showing why it is specifically miscalibrated here.

rubric.point: Makes the correct execution choice on the primary axis of participation sequence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires designing the first session so oral participation is elicited through structured formats before or instead of broad open-floor volunteering, such as paired discussion, named small-group reporting, prepared prompts, written-to-oral progression, or teacher-facilitated turn allocation; no full credit if the answer mainly keeps the global SOP of immediate whole-class spontaneous commenting and only adds encouragement or extra wait time.

rubric.point: Applies the cultural logic to the right stage, actor, and evidence type
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires matching the intervention to the first live session and the evaluation method by shifting what counts as participation evidence for the review group, not just coaching students privately or training faculty to 'be warmer'; partial credit if the answer contains accurate cultural knowledge but applies it only to later weeks, to individual office hours, or to generic relationship-building rather than the classroom design and review metric.

rubric.point: Uses cognitive CQ rather than stereotype or generic caution
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires distinguishing among plausible explanations and using scenario evidence to justify one interpretation over alternatives such as poor preparation, low confidence in English, or simple introversion alone; partial credit for naming cultural labels or saying 'in China students are quiet' without evidence-based mapping to this exact case.

rubric.point: Assigns concrete roles and channels across the team
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires an operational division such as Shanghai teammate shaping prompts and instructor briefing for structured discussion, Singapore teammate scripting facilitation moves and transition timing, and London teammate revising the evidence rubric and stakeholder language; partial credit for saying the team should 'align' or 'coordinate' without role-specific workflow.

rubric.point: Designs stakeholder-proof evidence and messaging under deadline pressure
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires offering credible day-3 evidence of engagement that fits the mechanism, such as small-group outputs, short designated spokesperson clips, response cards, structured polling linked to discussion, or sampled oral reports, and framing these as valid indicators for the dean and sponsor; no full credit for solving pressure only by delaying measurement, collecting broad extra feedback, or maximizing visible random volunteering.

reference_outline: State that the trial evidence points away from disinterest: students prepared well in writing and quizzes, and they responded better in smaller or more structured settings than in open whole-class discussion.

Identify the key risk in the London proposal: treating spontaneous public comments in the full class as a universal early-session engagement metric would misread the local classroom logic and may suppress rather than reveal participation.

Set the first-session sequence to move from low-exposure structure to visible oral output: individual written prompt, paired or small-group discussion, designated group spokespersons or teacher-invited reports, then limited full-class synthesis rather than open volunteering first.

Revise what counts as participation evidence for the dean and sponsor: include quality of written prep, group outputs, prompted oral reports, and structured discussion clips instead of relying mainly on unsolicited whole-class comments.

Assign roles operationally: Shanghai teammate adapts prompts and instructor notes to the local classroom setting; Singapore teammate designs facilitation timing and reporting mechanics; London teammate rewrites the evaluation memo and sponsor-facing definition of engagement.

Explain the cognitive judgment explicitly: the answer should separate this case from generic assumptions about passivity, personality, or weak English by weighing the contrast between strong preparation and low open-floor speaking.

Control risk under deadline by briefing stakeholders in advance that the pilot uses a structured participation design to produce reliable engagement evidence early, while monitoring whether oral participation expands once the format reduces public exposure and ambiguity.

scenario: A visiting lecturer is teaching a master's class at a university in China. Students completed a written case worksheet before class, and the lecturer has just given them 45 seconds to mark which recommendation they would support. When the lecturer opens the debrief to the room, no one speaks. There are four minutes left before the class must commit to one option and move on.
question: What should the lecturer do next?

options.A: Ask for volunteers to read one line from their worksheet, and if no one starts after a short pause, then name a student to respond.
options.B: Ask two named students to give one brief recommendation each from their worksheet, then invite one short build or contrast from the room before deciding.
options.C: Have students compare choices with a neighbor for a minute, then ask for any pair to report its main recommendation to the whole class.
options.D: Ask students to show which option they chose by hand signal, summarize the pattern aloud, and only call on someone if extra time remains.

scenario: At a South Korean high school, an exchange student is helping finalize a graded team presentation for a model class that will be observed by senior staff the next morning. During rehearsal, the teacher stops the group, revises one slide's explanation, and moves on quickly because there are still four teams to review. The newcomer notices the teacher's version may weaken one comparison on the slide, but the class is still in the middle of the formal run-through.

roles.local: Minji, a local student leading the team
roles.newcomer: Leo, an exchange student on the team

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We only get this last rehearsal tonight. When the teacher reaches our slide, please keep your section short so we can finish the full run.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Got it. I'll keep to the script and note anything I want to revisit after the run instead of stopping the flow.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: He changed the comparison line on slide six just now. I thought you might want to say something, but he already moved to the next team.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I saw it. I'll use his version in rehearsal and mark the source note on my printout so I can ask when he opens questions or after class if there's time.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: After our turn, he usually gives fast comments and expects the next group to be ready immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I won't jump in during the lineup change. If he comments on my section, I'll just adjust it first and keep us moving.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Okay. We still need the final file uploaded before 9 p.m., so I need to know whether to lock that slide.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Lock his wording for tonight's file. If there's an opening later, I'll ask briefly with the data sheet in hand, but I won't turn the rehearsal into a back-and-forth.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer aligns with the seed-specific mechanism by deferring to teacher authority during the formal class run, accepting correction for the immediate task, and saving any substantive challenge for an invited or later moment rather than openly debating the teacher in front of the class.

scenario: You are the product lead on a multicultural team building a post-exam intervention flow for a private secondary-school math program in Seoul. The pilot starts in 10 days, and the school director wants a draft script and workflow by tomorrow because midterm mock-exam results just came in. The current prototype, written by a U.S. content manager, sends students who scored below 60 a private app message that says they should reflect on whether advanced math is still the right fit, choose between three next-step paths, and book an optional wellbeing call if they feel discouraged. The Korean school partner did not reject the draft, but in comments they changed several top scores downward, added notes about "unfinished basics" and "insufficient effort pattern," and asked why the message lets students decide on level changes before teacher review. A Thailand-based operations colleague is pushing to keep the student-choice flow because it reduces parent complaints and call-center volume. The Seoul school director also wants any outreach to look serious enough for parents, but does not want a public shaming incident or a high dropout rate from math electives. You have one homeroom teacher, one math teacher, the app, and one parent message slot available in the first 48 hours after results are released.
question: Write a short decision memo that specifies the first-48-hour intervention design for low-scoring students. Your memo must: (1) diagnose what the Korean partner is signaling from the available evidence; (2) identify the most tempting but miscalibrated assumption in the current draft; (3) choose the exact wording frame, actor sequence, and channel timing for student and parent communication; and (4) explain how your plan maintains performance pressure without triggering unnecessary withdrawal or reputational risk. Be concrete about who says what first, what is delayed, what is not offered yet, and how you would handle students who ask to move out of advanced math immediately.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden mechanism behind the partner's edits
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that post-failure communication should combine reassurance with role- or duty-framed advice to continue effort in math, rather than treating the low score mainly as a cue for immediate self-directed path switching. Mere statements like 'Korea is competitive' or 'teachers are strict' are insufficient.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the autonomy-first near-miss
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly identifies the current draft's attractive mistake: inviting low scorers to choose level changes or opt out before teacher intervention. Answers that keep broad student-choice language, present easier-track switching as an early equal option, or solve the issue only by adding softer wording do not earn full credit.

rubric.point: Sets the correct first-48-hour sequence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan gives the math teacher an early, active role after results, with student messaging first framed around responsibility, effort, next steps, and improvement work before any level-change discussion. High-scoring answers delay track-change decisions until after teacher review and follow-up evidence. Wrong-stage use of correct knowledge loses credit.

rubric.point: Uses behavioural CQ through calibrated wording, channel, and audience
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies visible execution details: a private but serious teacher-to-student message or meeting, concrete improvement tasks, parent communication that signals structure and commitment without public embarrassment, and wording that is firm and encouraging rather than purely therapeutic or purely punitive. Generic advice to 'communicate respectfully' does not score.

rubric.point: Designs a role-specific coordination plan under pressure
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo assigns distinct roles to the homeroom teacher, math teacher, app, and parent message slot, and shows why this division helps both retention and credibility under the deadline. Answers that rely on a single generic app notification or broad consultation with everyone score lower.

rubric.point: Handles immediate withdrawal requests without making them the default path
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer creates a bounded review path for students requesting to leave advanced math: acknowledge concern, require teacher follow-up and diagnostic review, and avoid same-day self-service switching. Answers that instantly approve exits or simply block all discussion of switching without review do not earn full credit.

rubric.point: Controls trust and reputational risk without overcorrecting into softness
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer prevents public shame and parent confusion while preserving demanding expectations and visible improvement monitoring. Plans that maximize safety by delaying action, replacing performance talk with wellbeing-only support, or using the longest most consultative process receive limited credit.

reference_outline: Infer from the partner edits that low scores are being treated as evidence for more guided, responsibility-laden teacher intervention focused on persistence and improvement, not as a neutral branching point for student preference.

State the main near-miss clearly: a globally familiar autonomy-first script that asks discouraged students to decide early whether advanced math still suits them, which risks signaling acceptable exit before teacher obligation and effort guidance occur.

Set the primary execution axis as first-48-hour sequence: results release -> private teacher message or meeting to student with firm encouragement and concrete study obligations -> parent note emphasizing structured follow-up and improvement plan -> only later, after review, discuss any level change.

Specify visible behavioural details: the math teacher should name the weak areas, assign immediate corrective work, and communicate that the score is a setback to work through rather than a cue to step away; wording should comfort and direct at the same time.

Use the homeroom teacher for reinforcement or scheduling, not for replacing the math teacher's authority; use the app to support teacher-directed next steps, not to offer equal-choice pathways upfront.

If a student asks to leave advanced math immediately, acknowledge the concern but route it into a teacher review with evidence from recent work, effort pattern, and remedial response before any track decision is finalized.

Protect reputation by keeping intervention private, avoiding public ranking or public correction, and giving parents a serious but non-alarmist message that the school has identified gaps and started a structured response.

Explain the tradeoff: this plan is less frictionless than the app-choice draft and may create more follow-up work, but it fits the local expectation that teachers actively push students to improve after failure and helps reduce premature disengagement from math.

scenario: A university team is finalizing a one-paragraph facilitator brief for a two-session problem-solving pilot in Vietnam. The activities must start on the first day, room assignments are locked, and the local department wants the brief today so visiting instructors can prepare materials tonight. The draft needs one line telling facilitators how to form student groups at the start.
question: Which line should be approved for the brief?

options.A: Before class, collect short partner preferences if available, place students into socially comfortable teams, and name one student in each team to coordinate the first task and report back.
options.B: At the start, let students choose any teammates freely, then invite each team to decide for itself who will coordinate discussion and share results with the class.
options.C: Before class, assign mixed teams alphabetically for fairness, then name one student in each team to coordinate the first task and report back.
options.D: Ask the local department to suggest how teams should be formed after session one, while facilitators begin with open collaboration and rotate the coordinating student during activities.

scenario:
You are the regional learning-design manager for an edtech company piloting a 6-week collaborative science module in a Vietnamese upper-secondary school. The school principal approved the pilot on the condition that the first observed lesson shows visible student participation and no parent complaints about unfair grouping. Your company’s global template, used successfully in Canada and Singapore, assigns students to mixed-ability teams based on diagnostic scores and rotates facilitation so that no student is formally designated as group leader. 

Three days before launch, the Vietnamese teaching team sends you a class list, friendship notes collected from homeroom teachers, and a brief message that several students became quiet during last term’s mixed-team activities when they were placed with classmates they did not usually work with. Your supervisor in headquarters insists that score-balanced grouping is important for the pilot report because the client wants measurable peer-learning gains, and changing the template now will require extra justification. The local school also wants printed team lists by tomorrow so parents can see the class setup in advance. Budget is too tight for a second pilot class, and the principal will observe only one lesson before deciding whether to continue.

You are leading a multicultural implementation team: a Vietnamese teacher, a product analyst in Germany who wants clean comparison data, and a curriculum lead in the US who argues that rotating roles is more inclusive and avoids hierarchy inside groups. No one explicitly tells you what to do. You must send the final implementation note tonight.
question: Write the implementation note you would send to your team and supervisor. Specify how you will form groups, whether and how you will assign in-group roles, what extra effort you will personally take on before launch, and how you will justify the design under the deadline and reporting pressure. Your note must identify the most tempting but miscalibrated default plan in this case, explain why it is attractive, and show how you will keep the pilot credible without simply postponing, broadening consultation indefinitely, or using a generic ‘be respectful and flexible’ response.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden classroom mechanism from the scenario evidence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires inferring from the Vietnamese class context, the friendship notes, and prior quiet participation that team effectiveness depends on social relationship structure inside groups and on a stabilizing internal lead, not just on balanced skill distribution or abstract inclusion. Little or no credit if the answer only says to 'adapt to local culture' or names relationships vaguely without execution consequences.

rubric.point: Makes the correct role-assignment decision on the main execution axis
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires explicitly choosing non-rotating or initially fixed group leadership for the pilot lesson, with a designated student lead in each group selected for interpersonal coordination capacity rather than only top academic performance. Partial credit if a leader is assigned but treated as purely academic or only for teacher convenience. Low credit if the answer preserves role rotation or avoids naming any lead.

rubric.point: Makes the correct group-composition decision despite KPI pressure
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires forming groups around existing friendship ties or other clearly positive social relationships rather than primarily by cognitive-level balancing, while still documenting a bounded way to monitor academic spread. Low credit if the answer keeps the global mixed-ability template as the main structure, merely adds icebreakers, or treats friendship as a minor preference after score balancing.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the attractive imported default
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires identifying the tempting near-miss as the global default of score-balanced groups with rotating facilitation, explaining why it appeals under fairness, data-comparison, and inclusion pressure, and then limiting it rather than fully adopting it. Low credit if the answer attacks the default as obviously bad, or accepts it with generic mitigation such as extra teacher check-ins.

rubric.point: Shows motivational CQ through costly adaptive follow-through
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires the respondent to take visible ownership of the inconvenience: reworking group lists tonight, defending the deviation upward, absorbing reporting burden personally, and investing relational effort with the local school rather than shifting adaptation burden to them. Low credit if the answer sounds supportive but mainly asks locals to solve the issue, waits for more certainty, or chooses the easier headquarters template to avoid friction.

rubric.point: Designs a concrete coordination and justification plan for stakeholders
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires role-specific communication: one explanation to headquarters about why the pilot design changes, one operational instruction to the Vietnamese teacher about leader selection and group setup, and one way to preserve evaluation credibility such as documenting the rationale, tracking participation patterns, or treating this run as a locally adapted baseline. Low credit for broad statements about alignment without stakeholder-specific actions.

rubric.point: Includes calibration and repair under constraint
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires a bounded monitoring or repair plan for the first lesson, such as checking whether designated leaders actually draw out quieter members, adjusting only a small number of groups after observation, and avoiding wholesale mid-lesson restructuring. Low credit if the answer proposes maximal consultation, indefinite delay, or a full redesign after launch without a practical trigger.

reference_outline: State that the pilot should not use the global default as-is: in this Vietnamese upper-secondary setting, the evidence points to group functioning depending on existing positive peer relationships and a clear internal coordinator.

Form groups primarily around friendship or other known positive social ties from the homeroom notes, then check for extreme academic imbalance only as a secondary constraint rather than the main grouping rule.

Assign one student leader per group before the first lesson and choose for interpersonal steadiness or ability to keep peers engaged, not simply highest test score; avoid rotating facilitation in the observed launch lesson.

Own the extra work personally: rebuild the team lists tonight, write the justification for headquarters yourself, and confirm the local teacher’s input on which students can coordinate peers effectively without asking the school to redesign the whole pilot for you.

Tell headquarters that the tempting mixed-ability plus rotating-role model is attractive for fairness, comparability, and inclusion reporting, but it risks weak participation in this class and would undermine the pilot’s actual objective if transferred unchanged.

Preserve credibility by documenting the local adaptation explicitly, tracking participation and collaboration quality in the first lesson, and noting academic distribution as a monitored variable rather than the organizing principle.

Give the Vietnamese teacher concrete instructions on leader briefing and printed group lists, and give the principal a stable first-lesson structure rather than an experimental rotation that may suppress participation.

Set a repair rule: review after the observed lesson, adjust only groups showing clear non-functioning, and reconsider broader role rotation only after the class demonstrates stable collaboration under the initial structure.

scenario: An American curriculum coordinator has joined an international middle school in Shanghai. Midterm math results dropped, and the grade-level team must send a recovery plan to families by tonight before a district review tomorrow morning. The local homeroom lead mentions that many parents have already been asking what they should do at home, while the coordinator is also under pressure to avoid creating a long translation burden for teachers.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We need one message out tonight about the math dip. Some families have already contacted us, and the district will ask what support plan we started.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I can draft it now. Rather than only explaining the new lessons, I want to include a short home routine for the next two weeks and a place for families to note what the student corrected each night.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That would move fast, but it adds work. We also have mixed income levels, so we should be careful about what we ask for.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I’ll keep it low-cost and specific: fifteen minutes, one checked problem set, and one line on where the student fixed an error. I’ll stay late and make the bilingual version myself so teachers are not chasing replies one by one.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Parents may ask whether this means the students are falling behind badly. We do not want the note to sound alarmist.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I’ll keep the tone calm, but I won’t make it vague. I’ll say steady effort at home matters now, and we’ll review common mistakes in class so families know exactly what to reinforce.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. Send me the draft before 8, and I’ll release it through the class channel.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: You’ll have it by 7:30. I’m also adding a simple return slip for tomorrow so we can see which homes want extra practice sheets right away.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer's effort is culturally aligned because they actively build structured home involvement and high follow-through into the recovery plan, and they frame support around effort and correcting mistakes rather than leaving remediation mainly to student independence or optional school-side help.

scenario: An edtech team is finalizing the homework setup for an elementary math pilot in Shanghai, Tokyo, and Seattle. They may change only one market-specific default before launch, and after launch they will get just one short readout. In the prep week, Shanghai had the highest share of sessions in which an adult-linked account opened the child’s work before the next homework attempt, but those classes had also been told to bring a family member to setup night. In Tokyo, fewer adult-linked accounts opened work between assignments, yet teachers consistently reported that families wanted to stay informed and caregiver message response rates were the highest of the three sites. In Seattle, several families asked for more account visibility during setup, but once homework began most activity stayed on student screens. Product wants a launch choice that acts on the most likely market difference without treating every positive family signal as the same kind of evidence.
question: Which launch plan best fits the evidence right now?

options.A: Keep the student-first homework flow in all three markets at launch, and use the readout to see whether any market shows enough adult-linked activity to justify a later change.
options.B: Move caregiver linking and work-review prompts earlier in both Shanghai and Tokyo, while keeping Seattle student-first, because both cities show stronger signs of family follow-up than Seattle.
options.C: Move caregiver linking and work-review prompts earlier in Shanghai, keep Tokyo and Seattle student-first, and use the readout to compare whether adult-linked review before the next homework attempt persists outside setup week.
options.D: Move caregiver linking and work-review prompts earlier only in Tokyo, because its teacher reports and caregiver response rates are less distorted by setup-night instructions than Shanghai’s prep-week behavior.

scenario: Your edtech company is piloting a live online math tutoring program in Tokyo for students preparing for selective entrance exams. The teaching team includes veteran tutors recruited from local after-school programs in Tokyo, while product managers and parent-success staff are based in the United States. After two weeks, U.S. dashboards show lower student satisfaction scores than in the company’s U.S. program, and several parents have written that tutors 'rarely say excellent' and spend much of each session marking weak steps, asking students to redo problems, and having them explain where their reasoning broke down. At the same time, attendance is steady, homework completion is high, and students who stay in the pilot are attempting harder problem sets by week 2. The Japan country manager needs a recommendation by tomorrow morning before a board update. The U.S. VP wants to protect retention metrics and proposes an immediate global-style intervention: require tutors to start each session with praise, cap the number of corrections per problem, and avoid giving low weekly performance ratings. Local tutors have not pushed back directly, but in meeting notes they keep asking whether the goal of the pilot is 'confidence maintenance' or 'exam preparation accuracy.' You lead the cross-border pilot review and must propose the operating plan.
question: Write a decision memo for the country manager recommending how the pilot should handle tutor feedback and weekly ratings for the next four weeks. Your memo must: (1) diagnose what is most likely driving the Tokyo pattern from the limited evidence; (2) identify the most tempting but miscalibrated assumption in the VP’s proposal; (3) specify the execution plan on one primary axis—how feedback and ratings should be handled now versus what, if anything, should be monitored or adjusted later; and (4) explain how you will brief U.S. leadership, parent-success staff, and Tokyo tutors so the team acts consistently without either overcorrecting or freezing for more data.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the likely mechanism behind the Tokyo tutoring pattern from the scenario evidence.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that demanding correction, restrained praise, low ratings, and asking students to redo or explain errors are likely being used as part of serious exam-preparation discipline and weakness-finding for improvement, not simply poor teaching quality or tutor insensitivity. Partial credit if it notices the pattern but frames it only as 'different style' without linking it to examination preparation and error-based improvement.

rubric.point: Identifies and bounds the attractive near-miss in the U.S. VP’s proposal.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly rejects or narrows the imported assumption that lower satisfaction and fewer affirming comments automatically mean feedback should be softened, ratings inflated, or corrections capped. Partial credit if it calls for 'balance' but still adopts the VP’s core intervention without showing why that would misread the local teaching signal.

rubric.point: Makes a seed-specific decision on the primary execution axis: how feedback and weekly ratings should be handled now.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer recommends preserving demanding, error-focused feedback and non-inflated ratings for the pilot rather than immediately standardizing to the U.S. encouragement template, while setting narrow monitoring or translation supports instead of broad softening. No full credit for answers that mainly delay, broaden consultation, or redesign the whole system without a clear immediate operating decision.

rubric.point: Uses metacognitive CQ by separating what can be inferred now from what remains uncertain and what evidence would change the plan.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer states a calibrated working interpretation, names remaining uncertainties such as whether some parents misunderstand the program goal versus whether some tutors are truly overcorrecting, and proposes evidence that would discriminate between those possibilities. Partial credit if it merely says 'get more data' or 'do not assume' without specifying which uncertainty matters.

rubric.point: Designs role-specific coordination for U.S. leadership, parent-success staff, and Tokyo tutors.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer gives concrete, different instructions by role—for example, briefing U.S. leaders not to read low praise frequency through a U.S. retention lens alone, giving parent-success staff a clear explanation of the program’s learning approach, and aligning Tokyo tutors on when to maintain rigor versus when to flag outlier cases. Partial credit for generic communication advice.

rubric.point: Builds a constrained monitoring or repair plan that does not default to the safest or broadest response.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes a narrow follow-up mechanism such as reviewing a sample of sessions, separating complaints about tone from complaints about academic rigor, or tracking whether correction-heavy sessions correlate with persistence and progress, without suspending the approach wholesale. No full credit for blanket caution, indefinite delay, or a maximal consult-everyone plan.

reference_outline: State a provisional diagnosis: the Tokyo tutors’ pattern of restrained praise, visible correction, low ratings, and asking students to redo or explain errors most likely reflects an exam-focused improvement model in which weaknesses are surfaced and worked on directly.
Name the misleading imported assumption: treating satisfaction dips and fewer affirming comments as enough evidence that the program must switch to a U.S.-style confidence-first feedback template.

Make the execution decision now: do not cap corrections, force inflated ratings, or require generic praise scripts across the pilot; keep rigorous error-focused tutoring in place for the next four weeks because changing it immediately would distort the pilot’s core instructional method.

Add bounded safeguards rather than a full redesign: review session samples for outlier tutor behavior, distinguish rigorous academic correction from genuinely unproductive tone, and create a short parent-facing explanation of the program’s exam-preparation approach.

Show metacognitive calibration: specify what is known now, what is still unclear, and which evidence matters most—for example, whether complaints cluster among families expecting a different goal, whether progress is improving despite lower satisfaction, and whether any tutors differ sharply from the rest.

Coordinate by stakeholder: brief the U.S. VP that retention metrics alone are insufficient to interpret this pilot; equip parent-success staff with a consistent explanation of why mistakes are being surfaced; instruct Tokyo tutors to maintain rigor while flagging cases where correction intensity may exceed the student’s level or the pilot’s stated goals.

scenario: At a Chinese private after-school academy preparing students for entrance exams, a newly arrived learning-support coordinator is asked to finalize tonight's follow-up plan for a high-performing student who abruptly dropped on two mock tests. The academy director needs a same-day action plan because the family has already asked whether extra sessions should be added before next month's exam, and teachers are worried the student has been staying late every night.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We need a plan before 6. Mina's scores fell twice this week, but she still asked for the advanced worksheet pack. Her mother called again this afternoon, and the math teacher wants guidance before evening study hall.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I don't want to overread two tests. I'll meet Mina when she arrives, check whether sleep or burnout is driving this, and give the teacher a lighter plan for tonight rather than adding more drills immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That could help. She came in early again today and apologized before anyone said anything. Her mother's question was mainly whether the academy thinks extra sessions are necessary this month.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I'll keep tonight focused on evidence. I'll ask Mina first how much load she can realistically carry, and I won't answer the family's extra-session question until I hear her view directly.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Alright. The teacher also said Mina corrected every missed problem after class on her own, so it doesn't look like she has checked out. If there is any schedule change, the family usually responds fast.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Good to know. I'll send the family only a brief holding message that we're reviewing fatigue and won't recommend changes yet. For tonight, I'll tell the teacher to skip any talk about adding sessions or expectations until after my one-to-one with Mina.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Send me the final note before you leave so I can attach it to her file.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Will do. I'll frame it as a temporary pause on parent-side decisions so we can keep the next step between staff and student until Mina decides what workload feels manageable.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer sounds measured and evidence-based, but updates on the wrong uncertainty: after cues that the family is actively seeking the academy's guidance and the student remains highly effortful, the newcomer narrows the immediate plan to private student preference and delays substantive family involvement. In this exam-pressure context, the miscalibration is the stakeholder scope and sequence of the follow-up, not generic caring or caution.

scenario: A UK university is rewriting the first-line guidance tutors use after mock-exam reviews on a foundation programme with many students from mainland China. In one cluster of cases, students had attended workshops, completed practice tasks, and could describe what they would change next time, yet some still became intensely upset after failing one paper. A few avoided group spaces, said they had "not done what they were supposed to do this year," or worried that they had not justified the sacrifices behind studying abroad. The director wants a single instruction that helps tutors decide how to record the case at the meeting itself, before any later referral decisions.
question: Which instruction should the director put in the guidance?

options.A: If the student has clearly been trying, record the distress mainly as a wellbeing reaction and keep the academic note to technical revision points unless there is immediate safety risk.
options.B: If the student describes the failed paper in terms of not having done what they should have done, record that within the academic follow-up note and address it with the next study plan in the same meeting.
options.C: If the student refers to sacrifices made for study abroad, treat that as a family-context issue rather than an academic one, and only add it to the record if the student wants home contacted.
options.D: If the student reacts strongly after a single failed paper despite steady effort, avoid obligation-related wording in the academic record until a repeated pattern shows the concern is not just temporary embarrassment.

scenario: A multinational edtech company is piloting a middle-school math tutoring product in Shanghai and Seattle. You lead a four-person launch team: a U.S. product manager, a China-based curriculum lead, a Taiwanese teacher trainer, and a data analyst in Singapore. In two weeks, you must present one unified 'error-response script' for live tutors to the VP of Learning, who wants a single global framework to simplify QA and branding. The U.S. product manager proposes a student-facing script for wrong answers that starts with reassurance such as 'That’s okay—math isn’t everyone’s strength yet,' then quickly offers the correct method to protect confidence and keep session times down. The China curriculum lead has pushed back on earlier drafts, saying the current version may make students disengage after mistakes, but has not offered a full rewrite. In pilot clips from Shanghai, some local tutors spend more time after wrong answers asking students what went wrong or having them try again before moving on; QA flagged this as inefficient and inconsistent. In Seattle, shorter corrective exchanges tested well with parents who value smooth tutor affect. The VP is pressuring you to lock the script this week because marketing already needs screenshots, and legal has warned against language that could be interpreted as shaming students. You need to submit a concrete rollout memo that covers the Shanghai launch first, while still explaining how the framework can remain globally governable.
question: Write the core of your rollout memo for the Shanghai launch. Specify the hidden learning mechanism you think is operating, the tempting imported assumption you would reject or tightly bound, and the exact tutor-response sequence you would require after a student gives a wrong math answer. Your memo must include: (1) the wording/frame tutors should use first, (2) what they should ask the student to do next, (3) what not to say even if it sounds supportive, (4) how you would explain this choice to the VP and QA under the time/legal pressure, and (5) one safeguard for adapting the framework later in Seattle without flattening the Shanghai logic into a generic global script.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the specific learning mechanism behind the Shanghai evidence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer identifies that after error, the response should sustain persistence by framing the setback around responsibility/continued effort on the task and by eliciting student correction or explanation; no credit for vague claims about 'saving face,' 'being respectful,' or generic growth mindset without the error-response mechanism.

rubric.point: Sets the correct tutor-response sequence on the main execution axis
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the sequence clearly places task-directed comforting/advising first and follow-up correction/explanation immediately after the error, before simply supplying the solution or moving on. Partial credit if both elements appear but in the wrong order or as optional add-ons.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the attractive near-miss script
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if it explicitly warns against ability-comforting reassurance such as implying the student may not be naturally strong at math, or against rapidly rescuing with the correct answer to preserve affect/efficiency. Partial credit if the answer rejects generic U.S. default language but does not explain why it is miscalibrated here.

rubric.point: Applies cognitive CQ rather than stereotype or generic caution
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer separates the seed-specific educational logic from process pressure, brand pressure, and personality explanations, and uses scenario evidence to justify why the Shanghai script should differ. No credit for answers that rely on broad consultation, delaying the decision, or country generalizations without operational consequences.

rubric.point: Provides concrete wording or tutor moves with actor and stage specificity
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if it gives usable tutor language or moves for the moment immediately after a wrong answer, such as brief duty-oriented encouragement plus a prompt to correct/explain. Partial credit for abstract advice like 'encourage resilience' or 'ask reflective questions' without specifying actor, timing, or stage.

rubric.point: Handles VP, QA, and legal constraints without erasing the mechanism
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if it proposes a narrow risk control that preserves the mechanism—for example, approved wording that avoids shame while still directing renewed effort and student self-correction, plus QA criteria that score persistence-oriented follow-up rather than speed alone. No credit if the answer solves the pressure by reverting to one bland global script.

rubric.point: Designs a bounded cross-market adaptation path
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if it preserves the Shanghai mechanism as locally necessary while proposing later testing or modular adaptation for Seattle, rather than assuming one market's preferred supportive style should govern both. Partial credit if it mentions localization but gives no rule for what must remain distinct.

reference_outline: State that the Shanghai clips likely reflect a persistence-oriented error logic: after failure, tutors should keep the student engaged in the task through obligation/continued-effort framing rather than cushioning the mistake as evidence of limited ability.

Require a post-error sequence for Shanghai: brief task-directed comfort or advice first, then immediately ask the student to correct, retry, or explain the mistake before the tutor supplies the method.
Ban or tightly restrict ability-comforting language such as 'maybe math isn’t your strength' or other reassurance that can imply low ability, even if it sounds kind and brand-safe.

Explain to the VP and QA that the local issue is not tutor warmth alone but what kind of meaning is attached to the error; therefore QA should score whether tutors prompt student repair/explanation and sustain persistence, not just whether sessions stay short.

Address legal pressure by scripting approved non-shaming wording that still points the student back to the work, for example a brief 'let’s work through where this went off and fix it' style frame rather than identity-based praise or consolation.

Name the imported assumption as a generic global/default support script that protects confidence by soothing and quickly rescuing; explain why that is attractive under brand and efficiency pressure but miscalibrated for the Shanghai launch.

Create a bounded global governance rule: keep a common framework at the level of tutor goals, but allow market-specific error-response modules; for Seattle, test alternatives later rather than flattening Shanghai into the same short reassurance-and-answer pattern.

scenario: At an international school in Bangkok, a newly arrived university counselor is finalizing tomorrow's parent briefing for Grade 12 families. The school director wants the deck tonight because several families have invited relatives and an alum donor will attend. The local counselor has sent last year's material, which lists university destinations and entry routes very prominently. The newcomer wants the event to feel less status-driven and more focused on student fit.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The director wants the final slides by 7 p.m. I've put last year's file in the folder, including the destination page and the parent Q&A notes.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Got it. I’m tightening the deck and making it less like a scoreboard. I’ll move the destination page to the appendix and open with how students chose courses, internships, and personal projects.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Tomorrow's audience is mostly families of seniors, plus a few grandparents. They usually stay for the comparison questions at the end.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: That’s fine. I’ll answer questions if they come, but I’d rather not put school names and entry bands front and center. It can pressure the students who are still waiting on results.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We also have the donor joining for the first twenty minutes, and the director asked for a short opening section before the student videos.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I’ll use that opening to explain our advising process and show three student profiles without labeling which campus each one entered. It keeps the message fair and avoids turning the room into a ranking exercise.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. Please send me the final order once you've locked the opening.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Will do. I’m keeping the outcomes list in a handout at the back, but the main presentation will stay centered on learning fit rather than headline placements.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer politely reframes the event around learning fit and individual development, but misreads the local meaning of exam-linked placements. In this context, institution gained through exam results is a core status signal tied to family pride, future pathways, and the school's standing, so pushing destination prestige and entry-route evidence out of the main briefing is the wrong audience-and-sequence choice.

scenario: A Finnish university is revising a one-page orientation note for incoming exchange students. The dean wants the note finalized today, after several students last term said they felt unsettled when seminar leaders introduced themselves by first name, joked easily, and spoke to students in a very relaxed way during the first week. The note should help students interpret those early interactions without overexplaining local culture.
question: Which sentence is the best one to add now?

options.A: Faculty may seem easygoing at first, but students should rely mainly on formal course documents rather than read much into conversational style during the opening classes.
options.B: If a seminar leader sounds relaxed and uses first names, students can usually take that as a sign of a less hierarchical classroom and address staff the same way immediately.
options.C: Even when instructors are friendly in the first meeting, students should begin with formal address until the relationship is clarified and the instructor explicitly sets the tone.
options.D: A relaxed first meeting does not by itself signal low expectations, so students should watch how feedback, deadlines, and discussion norms are handled before deciding what the classroom style means.

scenario: A newly arrived secondary-school teacher is covering a mixed-ability lesson in England for a visiting department head who needs to see a clear learning segment before the bell. The class has already fallen behind because the projector failed, and the newcomer must decide how to run the final ten minutes of a problem-solving activity.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The head will step in for the last ten minutes. We still need something she can observe, and the board is all we have now.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I'll drop the slides and put one problem on the board. I'll ask a few students to talk me through how they start, even if it takes a minute longer.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Some of them freeze when they're put on the spot, especially after a disruption like this.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: If they get stuck, I won't rescue it with a full explanation straight away. I'll give a prompt, ask what they noticed first, and build from that.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We also need to show pace. The head dislikes lessons that drift.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll keep it tight and call on three students in sequence rather than opening a long whole-class debate. I may cut in quickly to sharpen an answer, but I'll keep their reasoning visible.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Alright, I'll settle the back row and leave you to it.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Great. Once the first method is out, I'll contrast it with another route and use short cues if someone loses the thread.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer aligns with the seed-specific participation mechanism by making students explain their thinking aloud and by responding in real time with prompts and cues instead of reverting to a teacher-dominated explanation. The decisive execution axis is live classroom sequence under time pressure: brief, direct steering is acceptable because the teacher still works with student contributions rather than bypassing them.

scenario:
You are the new module coordinator for a postgraduate business course at a university in the United Kingdom. The class has 34 students, including home students and international students from China, India, Nigeria, and Germany. A senior dean will observe one seminar in 10 days because NSS-style engagement scores in the department have dropped. The previous coordinator left a note saying, "Seminars look flat unless students speak early and often." The course leader wants a visible improvement before the observation, and the faculty learning team has offered to print a one-page participation policy if you submit it tomorrow.

You review three weeks of records. In whole-class discussion, four students speak frequently. Six students rarely speak unless directly invited. However, in the online forum and weekly reading annotations, two of the quieter students submit some of the most analytically detailed comments in the cohort, and one quiet student has written two strong critiques of classmates' arguments but almost never speaks in class. In small-group worksheets, the seminar tutor's notes say several quiet students "appear engaged" but "hard to read in plenary." One tutor suggests adding cold-calling and a participation mark tied to speaking turns so the dean can see activity. Another suggests waiting until after the observation and just asking quiet students privately whether they are confused.

You need to send a decision memo tonight to the seminar tutor team and the course leader. The memo must set a participation approach for next week's seminar, define what evidence tutors should use during and after class, and explain how they should respond if the dean later asks why some students still spoke less than others.
question: Write the core of that decision memo. Your plan must diagnose what is and is not safe to infer from the current evidence, identify the tempting but miscalibrated assumption in the two suggestions you received, and specify the seminar design, tutor briefing, and evidence-use sequence for next week. Be concrete about what tutors should do before class, during whole-class and small-group phases, what they should record as participation evidence, and how they should explain the approach upward if pressured for a more visibly vocal room. Do not give a generic inclusion statement; make a specific execution plan under the deadline.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden participation mechanism from mixed evidence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer treats quietness as ambiguous rather than as evidence of low interest or weak thinking, and uses the scenario evidence to separate speaking frequency from other forms of engagement. No credit if it assumes silence mainly signals confusion, passivity, or lack of preparation.

rubric.point: Rejects the attractive near-miss on the correct execution axis
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly bounds both tempting suggestions: it rejects tying participation quality mainly to visible speaking/cold-calling for the observation, and rejects postponing action into purely private checking after the observation. Partial credit if it criticizes one but still centers the plan on making students visibly talk more for optics.

rubric.point: Sets a concrete seminar sequence that does not equate participation with plenary speech
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer redesigns the next seminar with multiple channels of contribution in a defined sequence (for example pre-class annotation, pair/small-group processing, targeted reporting, written or digital prompts, then selective whole-class discussion) so tutors can evaluate engagement without forcing uniform vocality. Generic calls for 'encouraging everyone to join in' do not score.

rubric.point: Uses metacognitive CQ by calibrating claims and evidence thresholds
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer states what can be inferred now, what remains uncertain, and what specific evidence next week's seminar should gather to revise the reading of quieter students. No credit for answers that sound careful but only say 'ask more questions' or 'be culturally sensitive' without defining what uncertainty matters and how evidence would change the plan.

rubric.point: Briefs tutors on actor-specific observation and recording
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer tells tutors what to watch for in small groups and written tasks, what not to over-interpret in plenary silence, and how to record participation using more than speaking turns alone. Partial credit if the answer mentions observation broadly but gives no operational criteria.

rubric.point: Manages hierarchy and observation pressure without surrendering to optics
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer gives a credible explanation for the course leader/dean that defends a broader evidence base for participation under the imminent observation, rather than optimizing only for a noisier room. No credit if the answer simply escalates, delays, or adopts the most dean-visible method because of pressure.

rubric.point: Avoids wrong-scope application of accurate knowledge
rubric.score_rule: No full credit if the answer romanticizes all silence as automatically positive, treats every quiet student as intentionally agentic, or removes any effort to create opportunities to contribute. High-scoring answers must preserve active teaching and monitoring while refusing premature negative inference.

reference_outline: State that current evidence does not justify reading quiet students as disengaged or weak thinkers because some of the least vocal students already show high analytical engagement in annotations, forums, and written critique.

Identify the main near-miss assumption: importing a participation model that treats visible speaking frequency as the primary valid proof of engagement, especially under dean-observation pressure; also note that delaying everything into private follow-up leaves the wrong classroom metric intact for next week.

Set next week's seminar sequence to generate multiple legitimate participation traces: require brief pre-class written response, begin with pair or triad processing, collect short written or digital positions before plenary, then invite selected summaries/challenges rather than relying only on spontaneous whole-class talk.

Brief tutors to observe and record evidence across channels: quality of annotations, written response, small-group contribution, evidence of listening and uptake, and whether a student's later written or reported contribution engages critically with peers' ideas; do not code silence in plenary by itself as disinterest.

Use metacognitive calibration explicitly: note what remains uncertain about each quiet student's reasons for not speaking, define what next week's structured tasks are meant to test, and say what new evidence would justify changing the interpretation or adding follow-up support.

Provide an upward explanation for the course leader and dean: the seminar is designed to improve participation quality and visibility through multiple contribution routes, not to force identical speaking behaviour; explain that engagement is being evidenced through structured outputs and observed interaction, not just airtime.

Include a repair path under constraint: if some students remain quiet across all channels, then follow up after class with targeted support or check-in based on that broader pattern, rather than on plenary silence alone.

scenario: At a primary school in Spain, a visiting curriculum lead is helping set up a 40-minute lesson built around small mixed tables of five students, each with one adult volunteer. One student at a table usually receives learning support, and another is still building Spanish fluency. The principal wants the lesson plan finalized today, and the volunteers need one clear instruction for how to run the table work.
question: Which direction should the curriculum lead give the volunteers?

options.A: Use tiered worksheets within each table so every student can contribute at an appropriate level, with the volunteer helping the lower-attaining students complete the simpler version.
options.B: Keep one common worksheet at each table, with the volunteer rewording and reducing parts of it during the activity for students who are struggling while others continue ahead.
options.C: Keep one common worksheet at each table, but have the volunteer take students needing extra support aside during table time for a shortened version before rejoining the group.
options.D: Keep one common worksheet at each table, arrange any extra preparation before the lesson for students who need it, and use the volunteer during table time to balance turns and peer help.

scenario: An American teaching assistant has joined an Italian secondary school for a joint science project week. On the morning of the parent open class, student lab posters are being checked before they are displayed in the corridor. One group has a visible calculation error on its main chart, and the posters must go to print within twenty minutes because the copy room slot is fixed.

roles.local: Italian science teacher coordinating the class display
roles.newcomer: American teaching assistant supporting the project week

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The red group finished first, but their chart has one wrong total in the center panel. Printing closes in twenty minutes, and parents will pass this corridor before lunch.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I saw it. I'll pull the four students aside at the back table and have them fix the number quietly so they don't feel singled out before the open class.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: They are still setting out the boards now, and the other groups are watching what goes up. We also need the corrected file before the copy room takes the next department.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll keep it efficient: I'll ask the group to step out for two minutes, tell them the standard has to stay encouraging in front of everyone, and get the revised slide sent immediately.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. The class monitor has the USB, and the math teacher will walk through in a few minutes to review the displays.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Good, then I'll avoid making it a scene. I'll speak with just the group, have them explain the correction themselves, and return the updated version before the review starts.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Please make sure the board order stays the same once it's reprinted.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Yes, I'll keep the lineup unchanged and handle the revision with the group privately right now.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer's decisive choice is to move error correction into a private side conversation and preserve a supportive public front. For this Italy-anchored classroom mechanism, the key issue is the handling of mistakes in front of the class and teacher authority; the newcomer sticks to a U.S.-leaning default about shielding students from open disappointment instead of recalibrating the correction setting.

scenario: You lead a four-week design sprint for an NGO that is helping one lower-secondary school in Barcelona and one in Bergen launch the same family-engagement pilot before next term. Your team includes a Spanish school coordinator, a Norwegian data analyst, and a Brussels-based program manager who wants one dashboard and one communication template for both schools. The funder wants early evidence of impact within six weeks, and the principals want something lightweight because staff time is already stretched. Current facts are mixed: the Barcelona school reports low turnout at formal parent sessions but strong informal concern about students' long-term prospects; the Bergen school reports decent digital response rates but uneven follow-through for families with fewer resources. Message history shows that previous school-family contact in both sites has mostly been one-way updates about assignments, attendance, and deadlines. The Brussels manager proposes a simple common plan: define parental involvement as homework support plus attendance at parent nights, push one translated email/SMS campaign, and track portal logins, meeting turnout, and homework-completion pledges as the pilot's main KPIs. You are told not to expand the budget, not to miss the launch date, and not to create a plan that schools see as 'extra consultation with no delivery.'
question: Write a decision memo for your team that recommends how the pilot should be structured across the two schools. Your memo must identify the most tempting but miscalibrated assumption in the Brussels proposal, explain what hidden mechanism in the situation changes the design, and give a concrete rollout plan for the first six weeks. Be specific about which forms of family involvement you will prioritize, how you will split roles and communication channels, what evidence you will count early, and where you will personally invest extra effort when participation is slow or ambiguous. Also explain what you will not do, even though it looks efficient or brand-safe under deadline pressure.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that family involvement in this case cannot be treated as a single behavior and must distinguish support tied to current schooling from involvement expressed through future educational expectations and school-input spaces.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer translates this distinction into design consequences for the pilot; no credit for merely saying 'parents engage differently' or naming culture in generic terms.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the attractive near-miss plan of using one common involvement definition centered on homework help, portal use, and parent-night attendance.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explains why that dashboard would systematically miss relevant involvement and misread low-resource or low-response families; partial credit if it questions the KPI set without replacing it operationally.

rubric.point: Makes a seed-specific execution choice on stakeholder scope by building at least two involvement tracks and assigning them to the right stage, channel, or artifact.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if one track covers current-schooling support and another covers future-oriented expectations and/or parent voice into school practice, with concrete channels such as meeting spaces, structured input, or different outreach formats; no credit for one broad engagement stream.

rubric.point: Uses motivational CQ by taking visible ownership of costly follow-through when early participation is weak, instead of shifting the adaptation burden to schools or families.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer includes bounded but real extra effort such as iterative outreach, revised formats, personal follow-up, or reworked meeting access under constraints; no credit for warm language without follow-through, or for simply telling local staff to 'consult more.'

rubric.point: Designs role-specific coordination across the multicultural team without letting standardization pressure erase the hidden mechanism.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo assigns distinct responsibilities such as local adaptation, evidence review, and dashboard interpretation while preserving one comparable frame; partial credit if roles are named but the common template still enforces the wrong scope.

rubric.point: Selects evidence that can detect involvement forms that are easy to overlook under deadline pressure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if early evidence includes more than turnout and homework metrics, such as expressed aspirations, quality of parent input, response by resource-constrained families, or uptake of dialogue spaces; no credit for adding more volume metrics alone.

rubric.point: Sets boundaries against generic 'safest' answers such as delaying launch, expanding consultation indefinitely, or making the broadest possible inclusion plan.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer preserves launch timing and budget while narrowing to the culturally relevant mechanism; no credit for solving uncertainty by postponement, maximal consultation, or abstract respect statements.

reference_outline: State that the Brussels proposal collapses distinct forms of parental involvement into a single visible-compliance model and would undercount families whose engagement appears through future expectations or through wanting meaningful voice rather than more homework monitoring.

Recommend a two-track pilot: one stream for current-school support needs and one stream for future-oriented expectations plus structured parent input into school practice, with both schools using the same frame but not the same narrow KPI definition.

Keep a shared dashboard, but split indicators by involvement type: current-school indicators can include assignment support or follow-up contact, while the second track captures aspiration-related conversations, use of parent meeting spaces, and concrete parent input that reaches school decisions or routines.

Assign the Spanish coordinator and school leads to adapt outreach formats locally, the Norwegian analyst to protect comparability without forcing one proxy, and the Brussels manager to report a dual-metric model rather than a single attendance-based success story.

Invest personal effort in the costly middle: when participation is low, do another outreach cycle, reframe invitations, offer lower-friction channels, and create bounded meeting/input opportunities rather than concluding that families are disengaged or telling schools to wait for parents to adapt.

Explicitly decline the efficient near-miss of one translated campaign plus attendance/homework KPIs as the main definition of success, because it rewards only the most visible and school-shaped form of involvement.

Use six-week monitoring to compare which involvement forms are appearing in each site, watch whether lower-resource families are only being detected in one channel, and repair quickly by shifting format or contact route rather than broadening into endless consultation.

scenario:
You lead a multilingual pilot for a dropout-prevention initiative serving lower-secondary schools in northern France and francophone Belgium. Your team includes a French school principal, a Belgian municipal youth-services coordinator, a data analyst from the Netherlands, and a foundation program director in London who wants a visible launch in three weeks. The deliverable is a family-engagement rollout for 60 students with rising absenteeism. The director wants a fast, measurable start: one school-based evening forum, a digital survey sent through the school app, and a slide showing that 'parents were consulted before implementation.' 

The principal is supportive but notes that turnout at school meetings is usually low for the target families. The Belgian coordinator says municipal mediators and neighborhood centers already know many of these families, but using them will take more coordination and will make the launch look less centralized. Budget allows either one large school event plus survey translation, or several smaller outreach sessions in community locations with staff time for follow-up, but not both. There is also reputational pressure: the foundation does not want to be seen as imposing a program without family input, and the schools do not want a process that becomes symbolic participation with no practical influence on next steps.

You need to send a decision memo today that sets the first two weeks of execution, assigns roles, and specifies how parent input will be gathered and used before the public launch materials are finalized.
question: Write the decision memo you would send to the team. Your memo must do four things: (1) infer the main participation risk from the facts given, (2) identify the tempting but miscalibrated plan that many international teams would choose here, (3) set a concrete first-two-week sequence for outreach, channels, roles, and follow-up, and (4) explain how your visible actions, wording, and timing make parent participation credible rather than symbolic while still meeting the deadline pressure.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the core mechanism as credibility and accessibility of parent participation channels, not merely lack of information.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer links likely low engagement to where and how families are invited to participate, and to whether their input can realistically shape action. No credit for answers that only mention 'be respectful,' 'communicate clearly,' or 'increase attendance' without identifying the participation-channel problem.

rubric.point: Rejects or clearly bounds the attractive near-miss of a school-based consultation package presented as sufficient parent voice.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly identifies the tempting default plan—central school meeting plus app survey plus consultation claim—as attractive under deadline/visibility pressure but inadequate or tokenistic for this target group. Partial credit if the plan is criticized vaguely without showing why it fails in this context.

rubric.point: Chooses the correct execution sequence on the main axis of channel and timing.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the first move is to use community- or family-comfortable outreach channels before finalizing launch messaging, with concrete early sessions or contacts outside the school building and a delayed or secondary role for any school event or survey. No full credit if the answer keeps the school event or digital survey as the main initial mechanism and merely adds optional outreach later.

rubric.point: Assigns specific roles that make participation structurally credible.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer gives operational roles such as municipal mediators/community staff conducting or hosting first contact, school leadership attending in a listening/responding role, and someone responsible for capturing issues and converting them into program changes. Generic calls to 'involve stakeholders' do not score highly.

rubric.point: Shows behavioural CQ through concrete wording, audience choice, and follow-up rhythm.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo specifies visible execution details: who invites whom, through which channel, with what framing, in what order, and how feedback is acknowledged and closed back to families. Answers must show that the respondent can translate the diagnosis into action, not just strategy language.

rubric.point: Builds a non-tokenistic feedback loop with observable consequences.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan states how parent input will be summarized, what decisions it can affect before launch, and how families will be told what changed because of their input. No full credit for one-way listening exercises, broad promises to 'take feedback into account,' or metrics that only count attendance/survey responses.

rubric.point: Balances deadline and reputational pressure without using the broadest or safest possible delay.
