rubric.point: Chooses the correct primary scope for week-one outreach on the stakeholder axis.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if week one includes selective engagement with community referral actors already likely to send people onward, alongside biomedical staff, instead of launching a purely biomedical pathway first; partial credit if community actors are mentioned vaguely but not built into the first-week mechanism; no credit for delaying all non-biomedical links to phase two by default.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the tempting imported assumption.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly identifies the attractive near-miss plan as overgeneralizing a generic formal-system default such as 'only formal biomedical actors should be in the referral design at launch' and explains why that would misread local referral realities and power dynamics; no credit for generic statements about being respectful or open-minded.

rubric.point: Applies metacognitive CQ through calibrated provisional judgment.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer states what can be inferred now, what remains uncertain, and what specific evidence in week one would change the plan; no credit for false certainty, generic 'ask more questions,' or indefinite delay pending perfect data.

rubric.point: Designs an operational referral and documentation workflow that fits both collaboration and risk constraints.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer gives a concrete mechanism such as limited-scope reciprocal referral intake, named documentation boundaries, triage criteria, and a non-endorsement safeguard for risky practices; no credit for abstract collaboration language without workflow consequences.

rubric.point: Addresses power and trust risks in message framing and role assignment.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the hospital is not positioned as replacing or absorbing all other care roles and if communications are framed around earlier identification and onward referral rather than institutional supremacy; no credit for messages that centralize authority in a way that predictably undermines cooperation.

rubric.point: Uses monitoring and repair that are narrow enough to preserve launch timing.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes a fast feedback loop tied to referral-source tracking, early partner response, or missed-case patterns during the first week, with a predefined adjustment path; no credit for broad consultation rounds, blanket pauses, or the longest safest plan.

reference_outline: State a working diagnosis: in this Uganda setting, mental-health help-seeking is likely pluralistic, so existing community-based actors are not noise but part of the actual referral ecology.

Make the execution-axis decision: week one should not be hospital-only; include a limited first-wave set of community actors already likely to refer onward, plus biomedical staff, because the key opportunity is to strengthen and document two-way coordination rather than wait for phase two.

Define a bounded workflow: create a simple intake field for source of referral, allow hospital staff to record incoming referrals from community and faith/traditional channels, specify which symptoms or crisis signs require immediate biomedical escalation, and prohibit any language that certifies outside treatment quality beyond referral collaboration.

Handle the near-miss directly: reject the polished compliance-style plan that starts with only formal biomedical channels because it imports a default system map, ignores asymmetric existing referral behavior, and risks missing where patients actually enter care.

Apply metacognitive CQ: distinguish between what is inferred now (multiple coexisting care routes; outside actors may already refer) and what is still uncertain (which actors are safest, most active, and most trusted locally), then name the exact week-one evidence that would trigger expansion, narrowing, or repair.

Assign communication roles: have the clinical lead brief hospital staff on triage and documentation, while outreach staff invite selected community referral actors into a narrow referral-focused meeting framed as earlier identification and safe onward transfer, not subordination to the hospital.

Build a fast repair loop under deadline: review first-week referral-source data, no-show patterns, and partner response quality; if outside actors are not referring or risky practices emerge, tighten the collaboration scope rather than abandoning the entire mixed-channel model.

scenario: A tribal-serving clinic in the United States is revising its intake workflow after chart reviews showed that some patients denied using anything beyond prescribed medicines on the written form, but later mentioned other sources of health support only after a treatment change was underway. The nurse may add one spoken follow-up line immediately after the standard medication list. The team wants a line that improves safety-relevant disclosure at that moment without making the visit feel like a challenge to the patient’s choices.
question: Which follow-up line should the nurse add?

options.A: Besides the medicines on this list, what other kinds of help, treatments, or guidance are part of how you’re managing this right now?
options.B: Many patients combine clinic care with community or traditional support; is there a healer, elder, or family advisor whose advice I should record before today’s orders are finalized?
options.C: If you would rather keep non-clinic approaches separate, I can note that preference and come back to them after today’s medication changes.
options.D: To avoid confusion, tell me only about things you actually take into your body today, and we can leave practices or outside advice out of this review.

scenario: At a tribally serving clinic near the U.S.-Canada border, a newcomer physician is preparing for a same-day treatment discussion with an Indigenous patient who left a previous hospital visit feeling dismissed. The patient needs to choose between two medication plans before transport leaves at noon. A local care coordinator and the newcomer quickly align on how the visit will be run.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: She made it clear on the phone that last time she felt talked over, and we only have one ride back after noon. She brought a family member and a small pouch she keeps with her.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I’ll keep the plan clear and not rush the paperwork, but to stay efficient I’ll open with the two medication options, explain the side effects in plain language, and get her preference before we drift too far.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: She usually listens carefully at first. If something does not sit right, she can go quiet rather than interrupt.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I’ll pause often and ask her to repeat back what she heard. I’ll also ask whether she wants her family member involved in the decision so she has support in the room.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The pharmacy needs the order by 11:40 if she is leaving with medicine today.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I can work within that. After she chooses, I’ll ask what else she uses at home so I can note any teas, ceremonies, or over-the-counter items in the chart and check for interactions before printing the final instructions.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right, I’ll bring them in once the room is ready.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Thanks. I’ll keep the explanation simple, give her space to ask questions, and make sure we leave with one concrete treatment choice today.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer sounds respectful and uses plain language, pauses, and family inclusion, but the decisive sequence is wrong for this context: he plans to secure the biomedical choice first and only afterward ask about home practices and worldview-linked care. For Indigenous patient trust in North America, engagement improves when worldview acceptance and reciprocal respect are established as part of shared decision making, not treated as a post-choice safety check.

scenario: At a hospital in northern Canada, a physician is preparing a portal message for an Indigenous patient who has an abnormal scan and a biopsy slot tomorrow morning. The patient previously answered the medication checklist very briefly, asked whether decisions had to be made tonight, and said she wanted to speak with people at home before anything invasive. If tomorrow's slot is released, the next opening is in three weeks.
question: Which message should the physician send now?

options.A: To keep your biopsy on schedule, please reply tonight with a complete list of any remedies, supplements, or non-clinic treatments you use so the team can confirm safety before proceeding.
options.B: I can hold tomorrow's biopsy slot until 8 p.m. if you want time to speak with people you rely on, and we can also talk tonight about any healing practices you want considered in the plan.
options.C: If you need to meet with a traditional healer before the biopsy, we should release tomorrow's slot now and arrange a new date after that conversation is finished.
options.D: You are welcome to bring family members and a traditional healer tomorrow so everyone can hear the consent discussion together before you decide whether to go ahead.

scenario: In a hospital in northern Canada, a newcomer palliative-care physician needs to sort out overnight planning for an Indigenous patient whose breathing has worsened. The chart notes that the daughter has been helping with communication. A CT slot may still be available, several relatives are arriving at different times, and the team needs a note that is clinically usable for the night shift.

roles.local: Ward nurse who has worked on the unit for years

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: CT can still hold a slot for a bit, but they need to know whether to keep it. Her daughter has been answering some questions, and two more relatives are expected soon.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I won't force a final treatment choice right this minute. I'll first see who is already part of these conversations and make sure the night note only covers what we can responsibly clarify.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: When respiratory therapy asked earlier about doing more, the daughter looked down, said she'd talk first, and then went quiet. He glanced at her but didn't really answer them either.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: That sounds like the earlier question may have been too abrupt. I'll speak with her beside the room, explain the prognosis carefully, and ask her to go over it with him in Ojibwe so he hears it once in a familiar voice before I write the note.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: She just asked whether we could wait until her sister gets in from the highway. Her aunt is already here, though, and they haven't asked for anyone from language services.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I can leave the scan decision open for now, but I still need one workable account tonight. I'll ask the daughter to tell me what he understands and what the family is leaning toward, then I can document that provisionally and revisit with the others after they arrive.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. They're both still in the room, and the aunt is near the window if you need space.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Thanks. I'll start with the daughter and use her translation of his response so I have a clean summary for the chart before I circle back.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer sounds measured and even avoids forcing an immediate final decision, but he calibrates the wrong uncertainty. After cues about hesitation, absent relatives, and the daughter's mediating role, he still channels serious information and the patient's response through the daughter as interpreter and provisional decision source, instead of reassessing how decisions are being handled and avoiding reliance on family translation for this discussion.

scenario: You are the acting unit manager at a regional hospital in Canada. By 5 p.m. you must send a concrete overnight coordination plan to the ICU attending, charge nurse, palliative consultant, security desk, and patient-relations office for a critically ill Indigenous patient who may die within 12 hours. The patient has so far answered treatment questions briefly and has not volunteered much beyond saying that several relatives are driving in. Earlier today, a niece asked whether 'someone from home' could come tonight and whether the room could stay available for family if the patient's condition worsens. A resident replied that any non-staff visitor would need standard daytime approval and suggested discussing spiritual needs after the morning ethics round. The family did not argue, but since then they have become less responsive to staff questions. Bed pressure is high, infection-control rules limit room crowding, and the ICU attending wants a clean, uniform process that does not assume anything about 'Indigenous customs' without evidence. At the same time, patient-relations warns that a refusal handled badly could trigger a serious trust complaint. You need to propose an action plan that can be executed tonight by staff who do not know the family well.
question: Write the overnight coordination memo. Explain what hidden cultural mechanism you think is most relevant from the available evidence, what tempting but miscalibrated assumption staff are at risk of following, and the exact sequence of actions, wording, audience, and fallback options you would use tonight. Your plan must specify who should speak to whom first, what should be asked and not assumed, how requests involving family and non-staff spiritual support should be handled under time pressure, and how you would protect both care delivery and trust if the family remains guarded.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the likely mechanism as a trust-sensitive need to actively make space for family and possible traditional or spiritual support near dying, without assuming all Indigenous patients want the same practice.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires inferring both parts: staff should not wait for spontaneous disclosure, and they should not generalize a single pan-Indigenous script. Partial credit for naming only family involvement or only spiritual support without the trust/disclosure dimension.

rubric.point: Rejects the attractive near-miss of applying a uniform default process that postpones or narrowly routes the request until routine daytime approval.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires explicitly identifying why a generic 'treat everyone the same, verify later' approach is tempting under bed, hierarchy, and compliance pressure but miscalibrated here because delay or denial can damage trust at the critical stage. No full credit if the answer merely says to 'be respectful' or 'follow policy carefully.'

rubric.point: Chooses the correct execution sequence for tonight rather than a broad future consultation plan.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires an actionable order such as: immediate bedside/private check-in with patient and/or designated family contact, prompt clarification of who should be involved, rapid exploration of whether a spiritual or traditional support person is wanted tonight, then expedited operational coordination with charge nurse/security/attending. Answers that lead with committee review, morning ethics, or a general cultural consult score low even if well-intentioned.

rubric.point: Uses behavioural CQ through calibrated wording, channel, timing, and audience.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires concrete visible behaviour: private rather than public questioning, non-leading but explicit invitation to mention family or spiritual needs, avoiding dismissive wording such as 'not allowed until approved,' and assigning a specific staff member to close the loop tonight. Generic statements about empathy or listening are insufficient.

rubric.point: Applies the mechanism to the correct scope and actor.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires making room for requests involving the patient's chosen family/spiritual network at the end-of-life stage while still checking this patient's wishes rather than imposing a template. Penalize answers that either ignore family/spiritual coordination entirely or presume a specific ceremony or leader without asking.

rubric.point: Designs an operational workaround under real constraints instead of the broadest or safest plan.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires concrete constraint management such as limited bedside numbers with rotation, expedited access instructions, infection-control boundaries communicated without shutting down the request, and contingency if the support person arrives late. Answers that simply delay everything, allow unlimited access, or escalate vaguely for more consultation do not earn full credit.

rubric.point: Includes a trust-repair move if earlier staff wording has already chilled disclosure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires a brief repair step acknowledging that staff may not have understood what was being asked, reopening the conversation tonight, and inviting clarification without forcing disclosure. No full credit for ignoring the prior interaction or for making the repair purely legalistic.

reference_outline: State that the key issue is not a generic need for sensitivity but a likely trust-fragile situation in which important traditional/spiritual or family-at-dying needs may not be volunteered unless staff actively and carefully reopen the door.

Note the evidence: guarded communication, family driving in, request for 'someone from home,' deterioration toward death, and reduced responsiveness after a procedural reply all point to a risk that delay or refusal will be heard as dismissal.

Do not assume one Indigenous template; assign a bedside clinician or charge nurse to ask privately tonight which people the patient wants involved, whether there is someone outside hospital staff they want contacted now, and what room/access arrangements matter most.

Sequence the plan operationally: immediate private check-in, identify decision/contact person, clarify desired family and spiritual involvement, notify attending and security of an expedited exception pathway, then document the agreed limits and handoff for overnight staff.

Use calibrated wording such as an explicit invitation that some patients want family or a spiritual/traditional support person involved and staff can try to arrange that tonight if desired, instead of waiting for the family to raise it again or hiding behind daytime approval language.

Bound the near-miss: do not rely on a uniform 'wait until morning / do not assume customs' process, because the correct response is not stereotype-driven accommodation but timely, case-specific opening and coordination.

Manage constraints concretely: permit limited numbers at bedside with rotation if needed, explain infection-control and security boundaries as logistics to solve rather than reasons to refuse, and set a named staff owner for arrivals after hours.

Include repair and monitoring: acknowledge earlier communication may have been too procedural, invite the family to restate what they need, document unresolved items for the next shift, and watch whether the family re-engages as a signal that trust is stabilizing.

scenario: At a hospital in Montana, a palliative-care team needs an opening line for a same-day goals-of-care meeting before discharge planning is finalized. The patient is alert, several relatives have arrived together, and the chart notes that the family asked to be included in serious updates.
question: Which opening line should the team approve for the clinician to use first?

options.A: Before we get into the medical updates, how would you like us to handle this conversation today: begin with everyone together, or start with you and then bring your relatives in?
options.B: I need to review the diagnosis and likely course directly with you first, and after that we can invite your relatives in to discuss decisions and next steps together.
options.C: Since your relatives came together for this meeting, I'll begin with them first outside the room, then come back and go over the medical updates with you afterward.
options.D: Let's bring everyone in now, and I'll walk through the diagnosis, likely course, and next decisions together so nobody is left out of the full discussion.

scenario: At an Indian Health Service clinic serving Blackfeet patients, a visiting physician needs to speak with an older patient whose scan shows the cancer is no longer treatable. The patient's daughter is parked outside trying to get off work, the inpatient bed team wants a decision before noon, and the newcomer is trying to avoid being blunt or disrespectful while still documenting the discussion today.

roles.local: Blackfeet clinic nurse coordinating the visit

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Mr. Heavy Runner is in room 3. He asked for a little time after vitals, and his daughter said she may come if she can leave work. The bed office keeps calling about today's plan.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I don't want to corner him with a full prognosis alone, so I'll give a brief medical update now, keep the language general, and tell him we can go into the bigger picture later with support.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: He's awake and asking when the doctor will come by. Transport can move him upstairs in about forty minutes if the note is in.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll see him right away, explain that the treatment isn't working and that time may be short, then let him know his daughter can join afterward if he wants help with next steps.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. His daughter just texted the desk that she's still twenty minutes out. He hasn't used the call button.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I won't delay the core conversation. I'll keep my voice calm, ask if he'd like me to repeat anything when she arrives, and avoid making him wait in uncertainty.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Okay, I can print the transfer packet once your note is done.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Thanks. I'll document the discussion now and circle back with the daughter after I've already reviewed the prognosis with him.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer politely avoids harshness, but the decisive execution is miscalibrated: he proceeds with prognosis disclosure before first asking permission to have that conversation and before checking whether the patient wants family present as part of the conversation process.

scenario:
You are a program manager on a multicultural hospital team in western Canada redesigning the first-visit workflow for a regional cancer clinic that serves urban patients and fly-in patients from several Indigenous communities. The team includes a Canadian oncologist, a Mexican operations lead, a legal/compliance manager, and a patient-education vendor. Your deliverable is a one-page implementation memo due by 4 p.m. today for the medical director.

The proposed workflow is meant to reduce no-shows and speed treatment starts: diagnosis review, risk explanation, consent signing, patient-education video, and booking of the first infusion all on the same day. The medical director wants the new workflow piloted next week because wait-time metrics are under scrutiny. Legal says the script must show that the physician offered options clearly and obtained timely consent. The operations lead argues that the safest approach is to keep one standard sequence for all patients and avoid adding extra actors unless the patient formally refuses treatment.

In the last two months, staff notes from several missed-start cases show a repeating pattern: patients were polite in the appointment, signed forms, and said they understood the plan, but later stopped responding or postponed treatment after returning home. In two chart notes, family members had asked whether a community knowledge holder could be included before finalizing the plan. In another case, a nurse documented that the patient became quieter after being told the clinic could not pause the schedule for a separate discussion because the infusion slot might be lost. A patient-experience summary also shows that some patients describe the clinic as 'not hearing how we make decisions' even when translation and printed materials were provided.

You are not being asked to write a cultural training guide. You must recommend an operational workflow that can be judged as work performance by the director next week.
question: Write the core of the implementation memo: what workflow should the clinic pilot, what specific stage should change, which people must be included or not included at that stage, and how should the team explain the change internally? Your answer must identify the hidden mechanism suggested by the case evidence, name the tempting but miscalibrated assumption behind the standard same-day workflow, and show how your design balances treatment-speed pressure with relationship and trust risk.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the mechanism from the case evidence, not just from generic patient-centered care language.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that engagement is being damaged by a mismatch between Western clinical decision flow and patients' decision process, including trust/worldview acceptance and power imbalance signals in the notes; partial credit for generic mentions of family preference, autonomy, or communication barriers without linking them to why patients sign then disengage later.

rubric.point: Changes the workflow at the decisive stage rather than adding broad optional consultation everywhere.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer modifies the point before final commitment to treatment (for example, before same-day consent is treated as final and before booking proceeds as if agreement is settled); lower credit if it adds a general cultural check-in after consent, at discharge only, or as a nonbinding courtesy once the plan is already locked.

rubric.point: Sets the correct stakeholder scope for that stage.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer makes room for the patient to involve the person or people they identify for that decision stage, including non-biomedical knowledge holders if requested, without making that involvement mandatory for all cases; lower credit if it limits participation to nuclear family only, requires formal refusal before inclusion, or expands to a vague 'consult everyone' model that is operationally unworkable.

rubric.point: Rejects the polished near-miss behind the standard workflow.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly bounds the attractive assumption that a legally clean same-day script and a uniform sequence are sufficient evidence of informed acceptance; lower credit if it merely says 'be flexible' or 'be respectful' without identifying why the standardization logic is specifically misleading here.

rubric.point: Applies cognitive CQ by separating culture-specific interpretation from generic process explanations.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer uses the mixed evidence to distinguish this case from simpler explanations such as poor literacy, generic noncompliance, translation alone, or ordinary scheduling friction, and then turns that interpretation into an operational design choice; lower credit if it names culture in the abstract or treats all missed starts as the same problem.

rubric.point: Provides concrete coordination and wording for internal rollout under deadline pressure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies who does what (for example, scheduler, physician, nurse navigator), what internal message frame to use, and what boundary protects both care progress and trust (for example, provisional hold, follow-up pathway, documentation of requested inclusion); lower credit for broad consultation, indefinite delay, or a plan with no role assignment.

reference_outline: Interpret the repeated pattern of polite in-clinic agreement followed by later disengagement as evidence that the clinic is overreading signed same-day consent as true decision completion; the issue is not solved by information delivery alone.

Change the workflow before final commitment: treat the initial oncology visit as diagnosis and option explanation plus an explicit decision-point check, with a structured path to pause final consent/booking when the patient wants additional decision participants involved.

Allow the patient to bring in the relevant decision participants they identify, including community-based knowledge holders if requested, rather than restricting the decision stage to physician-patient exchange or nuclear family only.

Explain internally that the tempting standardization logic is miscalibrated: a uniform same-day sequence may protect throughput and documentation on paper while increasing hidden treatment drop-off when patients perceive their way of deciding is not accepted.

Assign roles operationally: physician introduces options and asks whether others need to be included before finalizing; nurse navigator arranges the follow-up decision conversation quickly; scheduler places a short provisional hold instead of forcing immediate loss-or-sign pressure; charting distinguishes explanation completed from decision finalized.

Use cognitive CQ by weighing the evidence pattern carefully: translation and printed materials were already present, yet mistrust signals and requests for additional decision participants still predicted disengagement, so the workflow must respond to worldview acceptance and power imbalance rather than to language alone.

Control risk under time pressure with a bounded pathway: define a short turnaround for the follow-up decision conversation, document the patient's requested participants, and monitor whether this reduces signed-then-disengaged cases rather than simply slowing every case.

scenario: At a hospital in the southwestern United States, a patient from a nearby Indigenous community is deciding today whether to proceed with a biopsy tomorrow or delay a week. During the consult, the patient says they want to speak with a ceremonial practitioner their family trusts before choosing. The attending has one open slot left this afternoon, interpreters are available, and the charge nurse is revising a brief chart message for the team.
question: Which message should the charge nurse enter?

options.A: Patient requests time with a trusted ceremonial practitioner; provide the treatment explanation, document the request, and ask the patient to reconnect once they have consulted and are ready to decide.
options.B: Patient wants input from a trusted ceremonial practitioner; ask whether they want us to arrange a brief joint discussion today with that person and the care team before the decision.
options.C: Patient wants input from a trusted ceremonial practitioner; complete today’s consent discussion, then invite that person into follow-up planning so the treatment team can answer questions after the choice.
options.D: Patient wants input from a trusted ceremonial practitioner; hold the decision discussion until family identifies who should join, then reopen the visit when the outside conversation is complete.

scenario:
You are the operations lead on a multicultural care-improvement team at a tertiary hospital in Ontario. The team must deliver, by 5 p.m. today, a one-page escalation plan for a real case that the Chief Medical Officer will review at 6 p.m. before tomorrow morning’s procedure block. A Cree-speaking patient from a remote community was transferred in overnight for a limb-salvage decision with significant risk either way. The attending surgeon, trained in the United States, wants formal consent completed by noon so the OR slot is not lost. The risk manager is worried about allowing any non-employed practitioner into pre-op discussions because documentation, liability, and infection-control rules are already under scrutiny after a recent audit. A nurse notes that the patient has become less communicative since the surgical options were explained and keeps saying they need to speak with someone from home before deciding. The family has asked whether a community healing person can be involved, but no one has said exactly how. The Indigenous patient navigator is off-site covering another hospital and can only join by phone for 20 minutes. Budget rules make last-minute travel difficult, and the surgeon has told your team that ‘we should not delay evidence-based care for side conversations.’

Your team includes a Canadian quality manager, the U.S.-trained surgeon, and a UK-trained risk specialist. They all agree the plan must protect safety, preserve the OR option if possible, and avoid a complaint about disrespect or coercion. The CMO will judge your plan as a work product, not as a values statement.
question: Write the decision memo your team should send to the CMO. Specify the mechanism you think is driving the patient’s disengagement, the tempting but miscalibrated plan your teammates may default to, and the exact stakeholder sequence for the next 6 hours. Your memo must make concrete choices about who should be brought into the decision process, when, through what channel, and what the surgeon should and should not try to complete before that happens. Also explain what effort your team should be willing to absorb under time, hierarchy, and compliance pressure to keep the case moving without shifting the adaptation burden entirely onto the patient and family.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that the issue is not mere hesitation but a decision-making breakdown caused by lack of trusted, culturally legitimate participation and accepted knowledge translation.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers from the facts that engagement depends on involving a trusted community/traditional healing figure and demonstrating that the patient’s worldview is accepted in the care discussion; no credit for generic claims about language barriers, anxiety, low health literacy, or 'needing family support' without this operational consequence.

rubric.point: Chooses the correct execution sequence: pause pressure for immediate final consent and first create a bounded collaborative discussion among patient, relevant traditional/community healing support, and clinical team.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan explicitly avoids locking in definitive consent before that discussion occurs, while still preserving a time-bounded clinical pathway; partial credit if it mentions consultation but still has the surgeon finish formal consent first or relegates the outside figure to after the decision.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the attractive near-miss plan of following generic hospital consent/compliance workflow and offering supportive services later.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer identifies why a brand-safe, legally tidy plan such as 'complete standard consent now, document concerns, and allow spiritual support later' is miscalibrated here; no credit for answers that simply add chaplaincy, social work, or a later courtesy call without changing decision-process scope.

rubric.point: Designs concrete stakeholder roles and channels for the next 6 hours.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer assigns operational roles such as who contacts the patient navigator, who explores whether remote participation from the requested community/traditional healer is acceptable, who briefs risk/infection control on a bounded exception or remote option, and who reframes the clinical conversation with the surgeon; no credit for vague 'consult stakeholders' language.

rubric.point: Shows motivational CQ through costly but targeted follow-through rather than friendliness or delay.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan absorbs visible effort or status cost—such as the team lead pushing back on the surgeon’s timing, arranging rapid phone/video coordination, staying engaged through ambiguity, or doing extra documentation work—while keeping momentum; no credit for polite withdrawal, indefinite postponement, or placing the burden on the family to organize everything alone.

rubric.point: Translates respect into execution consequences for trust, autonomy, and safe care.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer links acceptance of Indigenous worldviews and reciprocal respect to better engagement in the actual medical decision, not just to bedside manner; no credit for naming autonomy, inclusion, or cultural sensitivity without specifying how the decision pathway changes.

rubric.point: Provides calibration and risk control under operational constraints.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer includes bounded safeguards such as a time-boxed case conference, documenting the rationale for involving the requested support, clarifying what medical safety information must still be covered, and identifying a fallback if the requested person cannot join quickly; no credit for the longest or broadest plan unless it preserves the urgent clinical window.

reference_outline: State that the patient’s withdrawal likely reflects a loss of trust and legitimacy in the decision process because the current discussion excludes a form of knowledge/authority the patient sees as relevant to deciding, not just a need for more biomedical explanation.

Recommend an immediate time-boxed pause on obtaining final procedure consent and convene a collaborative discussion before noon involving the patient, available family contact, the Indigenous patient navigator by phone, and a feasible route to the requested community/traditional healing support, preferably by phone or video if travel is unrealistic.

Instruct the surgeon to keep urgent clinical options open, explain medical risks plainly, and avoid pressing for a definitive signature until the bounded collaborative step occurs; the surgeon should not frame the request as irrelevant, private-only, or something to handle after consent.

Assign the team lead to own the adaptation cost: coordinate the navigator call, obtain rapid risk-management approval for remote or controlled participation, document why this is part of decision quality rather than an optional courtesy, and preserve the OR option where medically possible.

Explicitly reject the near-miss plan of completing standard consent first and adding spiritual or supportive services later, because that preserves compliance optics while failing the actual decision mechanism and can be experienced as disrespectful or coercive.

Show motivational CQ by accepting inconvenience, hierarchy friction, and extra coordination work to sustain engagement rather than withdrawing behind policy, and by not shifting all organizing work to the patient or family.

Include a fallback: if the requested person cannot join in time, use the navigator to co-design the closest acceptable interim discussion, explain what decisions truly cannot wait, and schedule the next contact point so the team continues relational repair rather than treating the missed connection as refusal.

scenario: At a regional hospital in western Canada, a newcomer resident is helping prepare a same-day consent discussion for an urgent but non-immediate biopsy slot that may be lost if it is not used by late afternoon. The patient has been quiet during rounds, and an aunt who usually comes with her is still driving in from another community. The unit is busy, the attending wants the slot decision documented before lunch, and interpreter support is limited.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The biopsy team needs an answer before lunch if we want to keep today's slot. She has not signed yet and keeps saying she wants a little more time.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll go back now, explain the risks and benefits again in plain language, and make sure she knows the slot may disappear. If her aunt arrives later, I can update her afterward.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Her aunt is usually part of these conversations, but the schedule is tight and the attending wants the chart closed before noon.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I understand. To avoid pressure, I'll keep the room calm and give her space to decide on her own. If she agrees, I'll complete the form and ask spiritual care to stop by after, so she still has support.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: She asked this morning whether someone from home could come before anything invasive happens. We do not know if that can be arranged quickly.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll make a few calls, but I do not want the decision to drift. I'll ask her directly whether she personally consents today, and if she does, I'll secure the slot while we keep trying to reach people.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Alright, the porter will come in about twenty minutes if the paperwork is ready.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I'll document the discussion clearly, keep the choice with her, and move the paperwork once she says yes, even if the others are still on the way.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer makes a polished informed-consent effort but misplaces it in an individual, time-pressured consent model. For this seed, the key is not just clearer explanation or private choice; it is allowing trusted family/traditional support to be part of the decision process before an invasive step, rather than obtaining consent first and treating that support as aftercare.

scenario: A physician in the United States is preparing for a 20-minute first preventive visit with a new patient whose registration notes enrollment in a tribal nation. The clinic uses a standard screening checklist and wants to keep the visit on schedule without rewriting the whole intake process.
question: Which direction should guide the physician's approach in this visit?

options.A: At the start, ask the accompanying relative which home-based or community healing approaches the family wants folded into today's screening discussion and any later care decisions.
options.B: Early in the visit, ask the patient whether they want any home, community, or family-based health preferences considered while discussing screening choices and possible follow-up plans.
options.C: Use the regular preventive checklist first, then ask the patient about home, community, or family-based health preferences only if the visit later turns to treatment decisions.
options.D: Use the same preventive script given to other new patients, and reserve questions about home, community, or family-based health preferences for a separate follow-up appointment.

scenario: At a river clinic in Peru, a newcomer clinician is helping with triage during a crowded morning after a delayed boat arrival. A local nurse needs the line to keep moving because one child may need transfer before noon. An adult patient with fever has arrived late, and a relative mentions home treatments were tried first. The newcomer must decide how to handle intake and whether to frame treatment as compatible or mutually exclusive while still moving the case forward.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We need to sort this line quickly. The man with fever came by canoe this morning, and his sister says they already tried some things at home. If he worsens, we may need to arrange transport before the river rises.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll keep it brief and respectful. I'll tell him we're ready to treat him here, but I need him to stop the home remedies now so he doesn't mix approaches and delay proper care.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Please make sure we know what he has taken already. His sister is answering part of the history, and he looks tired.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Yes, I'll note what he used and ask the sister for timing and doses. Then I'll explain that for this visit we should stick to one system so he can show commitment to the treatment plan.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: He has been quiet with the registration volunteer too. We still need a fast decision on tests and whether family can stay nearby.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll bring the sister in, ask a few direct questions, and keep my language simple. If there was confusion earlier, I'll reassure them. But I want to be clear that once we start, they shouldn't continue anything from home.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right, the room is free now. I just need the chart and next step soon.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll do the exam now, record what was taken, and present biomedicine as the single path for this illness so we can move without mixed messages.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer does several reasonable things, including asking what remedies were used, involving family, and checking for communication problems, but the decisive behavior is miscalibrated: they treat prior traditional treatment as something that must be stopped to prove commitment and frame care as one system only. The seed-specific mechanism is plural health-seeking, where traditional remedy use does not automatically mean rejection of biomedical treatment.

scenario:
You are the regional implementation lead for a multinational public-health NGO piloting a snakebite referral protocol in northern Brazil. The pilot will be judged next month by a Brazilian state health sponsor, your Europe-based medical director, and a donor that wants a clean increase in time-to-antivenom compliance. A local hospital has agreed to test a discharge workflow for caregivers of child snakebite patients. 

A draft workflow written by headquarters says: (1) screen caregivers for 'alternative-treatment reliance' at intake, (2) if any home remedies were used, trigger a counseling script focused on why unverified practices can delay lifesaving care, and (3) at discharge, give a standard handout that says recovery depends on following hospital instructions only and avoiding non-prescribed practices. 

In the past two weeks, three Brazilian field notes describe a similar pattern: caregivers often report actions taken at home before travel, ask detailed questions about when the child can return to normal routines, and mention additional care practices for the days after discharge. In all three notes, the child still arrived for antivenom, and one caregiver praised the speed of the hospital treatment while also insisting that recovery was 'not finished' at discharge. 

Your operations manager argues the draft should stay because it is safer, legally cleaner, and easier to measure: anyone using home remedies is a likely risk for treatment refusal or nonadherence, so the team should separate those cases early and deliver one firm message. The Brazilian hospital administrator is mainly worried about crowding and wants the discharge step to stay short. You have budget for only one revision cycle and one 20-minute staff briefing before launch.
question: Write a decision memo for the launch team that redesigns the intake-to-discharge workflow. Your memo must identify the hidden interpretation problem in the headquarters draft, name the tempting imported assumption behind it, and specify one concrete sequence for intake, in-hospital communication, and discharge. Explain which staff role says what, what should and should not be documented as a risk flag, and how you will handle recovery guidance without undermining biomedical treatment or expanding the workflow beyond the time limit.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that reported traditional care does not, by itself, indicate refusal of antivenom or opposition to hospital treatment.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly distinguishes coexistence from refusal and uses the scenario evidence that caregivers still brought children for antivenom and treated recovery as continuing after discharge. No credit for simply saying 'respect beliefs' or 'avoid stereotypes.'

rubric.point: Rejects the headquarters near-miss of using traditional-care disclosure as an automatic early risk category.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer identifies the draft's mistaken inference and limits risk escalation to actual indicators of delayed arrival, refusal, interruption, or unsafe post-discharge conflict with treatment. Partial credit if the answer softens the script but still keeps traditional remedy use as a presumptive refusal flag.

rubric.point: Sets the primary execution sequence across intake, treatment, and discharge.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the workflow keeps intake focused on urgent clinical facts and barriers to prompt antivenom, avoids a binary 'alternative-treatment reliance' branch, and treats discharge as a place to align hospital recovery instructions with the caregiver's expectation that care continues after leaving. No credit for answers that move all discussion to a vague later consultation or that use a one-stage warning message.

rubric.point: Applies cognitive CQ by mapping the exact local logic to the right stage and scope.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer shows the respondent understands that the cultural issue is not generic mistrust of biomedicine but a broader recovery-care model spanning before, during, and after hospitalization, and then translates that into stage-specific workflow choices. Partial credit for naming coexistence correctly but applying it only to intake or only to discharge.

rubric.point: Designs role-specific communication that protects biomedical adherence without creating a false opposition.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo assigns concrete wording or functions to staff roles, such as triage collecting timing/exposure facts, clinician reinforcing antivenom and hospital instructions, and discharge staff asking about planned home recovery practices in order to identify specific conflicts rather than ban everything categorically. No credit for generic 'the team should communicate clearly.'

rubric.point: Handles documentation and measurement under sponsor and legal pressure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes a documentation route that records clinically relevant delays, refusals, or conflicting recovery practices rather than coding any traditional-care mention as noncompliance, while still preserving a measurable workflow for the donor. Partial credit if it proposes broad narrative notes without a usable operational marker.

rubric.point: Calibrates the discharge step to the 20-minute briefing and crowding constraint.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer gives a narrow, operational discharge revision that fits a short briefing and brief encounter, such as a short question set and an escalation trigger for specific post-discharge conflicts. No credit for answers whose main solution is extensive extra counseling, broad community outreach, or delaying launch.

reference_outline: State that the draft wrongly treats home or traditional care reports as evidence of biomedical refusal; the field notes instead show support for antivenom alongside an expanded view of care continuing through recovery.

Replace the intake flag with a clinically focused intake: capture bite timing, what was done before arrival only insofar as it affects urgent care, travel delay, and any explicit hesitation about antivenom; do not classify traditional remedy use alone as refusal risk.

Keep in-hospital communication pro-antivenom and collaborative: the clinician confirms hospital treatment as essential, while not framing the conversation as a forced choice between hospital care and all other caregiver practices.

Use discharge to address the real decision point: ask what the caregiver plans to do during recovery, compare those plans against hospital restrictions, and intervene only where a specific planned practice conflicts with recovery or relapse-prevention instructions.

Document measurable risk in narrow categories such as delayed presentation, explicit refusal, interrupted treatment, or identified post-discharge practice conflict; avoid using 'alternative treatment used' as a compliance proxy.

Name the imported assumption as a generic global default that equates traditional medicine use with rejection of biomedical care; explain why that shortcut is attractive under KPI, legal, and workflow pressure but misreads the Brazilian evidence in this case.

Fit the redesign to constraints by giving a short role-based script for triage, clinician, and discharge staff, plus one escalation path for conflicting recovery plans rather than a broad new counseling program.

scenario: At a public clinic in highland Ecuador, missed postpartum follow-up visits remain concentrated in one catchment area even after transport vouchers and fee waivers were added. Several women who do return bring family members, keep their hospital papers carefully, and ask whether home remedies they received locally can continue alongside clinic treatment. The director wants a pilot plan within a week and will approve only one extra briefing meeting.
question: Which group should you include in that one briefing meeting first?

options.A: Bring in the transport coordinator and billing clerk serving that catchment area first, and review whether hidden costs or route problems are still disrupting return visits.
options.B: Bring together a physician and recognized local healers from that catchment area first, and leave discharge nurses for a later meeting once treatment questions are clarified.
options.C: Bring together a physician, a discharge nurse, and a recognized local healer from that catchment area first, and compare how follow-up care is being explained across settings.
options.D: Bring together physicians, nurses, registration staff, transport staff, family representatives, and local healers in one broad forum first, before narrowing the pilot to any single interaction point.

scenario: You lead a multicultural implementation team for a nonprofit hospital network piloting a mental-health referral pathway in Loreto, Peru. The pilot must launch in 12 days because a regional donor visit has already been announced. The Lima medical director wants a one-page operating note by tomorrow that shows a credible collaboration model but does not expose the network to accusations of endorsing unsafe or unscientific practice. A Peruvian field coordinator has sent you three facts from recent meetings: families in two river communities asked whether people with persistent fear, agitation, or hearing distressing voices could continue seeing a named local specialist while also attending the clinic; community attendance improved when outreach staff stopped describing existing local care as 'informal support'; and one clinic physician wrote that collaboration should be limited to post-treatment counseling because 'ceremonial elements are not part of medicine.' A compliance manager in Bogotá suggests the safest route is to keep local practitioners outside the care pathway and mention them only under 'community beliefs' in the briefing. Meanwhile, the local clinic team says they need a process that can actually work next month with current staff and cannot afford a long consultation round. No one in the message thread explicitly states what model of care should be recognized, and the donor will ask whether the network is reducing stigma while maintaining clinical standards.
question: Draft the core of your decision memo for the next 30 days of the pilot. Explain what hidden mechanism you infer from the evidence, what tempting assumption you would reject or tightly bound, and the exact referral-and-communication sequence you would implement now. Your answer must specify: which actors are recognized in the pathway, at what stage they appear, what the clinic should and should not say publicly, what evidence is strong enough to act on immediately versus what remains uncertain, and how you would monitor and revise the plan after launch without defaulting to indefinite delay.

rubric.point: Infers a complementary care mechanism rather than treating local mental-health care as merely symbolic, informal, or automatically incompatible with clinic care.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer reads the scenario evidence as supporting a workable parallel or coordinated role for the named local specialist within mental-health care; no credit for answers that classify the local role only as belief management, outreach decoration, or post-clinic counseling.

rubric.point: Makes the primary execution-axis decision on stakeholder scope and stage of inclusion.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer places the traditional healer within the operational pathway early enough to matter for referral or coordination, rather than excluding them from the pathway or adding them only after biomedical treatment is complete; partial credit if inclusion is mentioned but not tied to exact stage, actor, or workflow.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the attractive near-miss plan of relegating Indigenous care to a brand-safe 'community beliefs' note or keeping it outside the formal pathway.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explains why that cautious-seeming plan would reproduce stigma, misread the local care system, and likely weaken trust or uptake; little or no credit for generic statements about being respectful without naming the operational harm of the near-miss.

rubric.point: Uses metacognitive CQ by separating what can be inferred now from what remains uncertain and naming what evidence would trigger revision.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer commits to a provisional design now, identifies remaining unknowns such as case boundaries, documentation limits, or escalation criteria, and specifies what launch-period evidence would confirm or change the model; no credit for either overconfident certainty or open-ended delay for more consultation.

rubric.point: Designs a concrete referral and communication workflow with role-specific actions.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer gives an operational sequence such as intake language, consent or disclosure step, referral options, clinician recognition of concurrent care, escalation route for acute risk, and who records what; partial credit for broad collaboration language without executable roles or sequence.

rubric.point: Calibrates public and internal wording to avoid stigma while preserving clinical boundaries.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer avoids dismissive framing like 'beliefs' or 'informal support' and instead uses wording that recognizes organized local treatment without collapsing all standards or claiming equivalence where not yet established; no credit for answers that simply say 'use respectful language' without showing what changes.

rubric.point: Builds a narrow monitoring-and-repair loop suited to deadline pressure rather than the safest or broadest possible process.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes a time-bounded review using concrete signals such as referral uptake, drop-off, patient/family disclosure comfort, clinician resistance, or adverse coordination issues, with a defined adjustment point inside the 30-day pilot; partial credit for broad monitoring promises with no trigger or timebox.

reference_outline: Diagnose from the evidence that, in this Peruvian Amazon context, local mental-health treatment may be structured and clinically framed within its own system, so the working assumption should be complementarity with biomedicine rather than symbolic add-on status.

Decide on stakeholder scope now: recognize the traditional healer as a legitimate actor in the referral ecosystem at intake and care-planning stage, not only after biomedical treatment or only in community messaging.

State the near-miss explicitly and bound it: do not hide the healer under 'community beliefs' or exclude them from the pathway just because that looks safer to donors or compliance, because that would encode stigma and misread why families are asking for coordination.

Implement a concrete workflow: intake asks whether the patient is currently seeing any local specialist for these symptoms; clinician acknowledges concurrent care; patient can choose clinic-only, healer-only disclosure, or coordinated referral discussion; acute-risk cases follow clinic escalation while still documenting concurrent local care.

Use calibrated wording in the memo and outreach materials: describe local care as an existing treatment system used by families in the area, avoid language that trivializes it, and avoid claiming blanket equivalence or making unverified safety claims.

Apply metacognitive CQ by naming what is known enough to act on now and what is not: act on the evidence that recognition and non-stigmatizing integration matter, while flagging uncertainties such as documentation format, case categories for coordination, and limits of shared decision protocols.

Set a 30-day review loop with specific triggers: track whether patients disclose concurrent care, whether referrals are accepted, where clinician resistance appears, whether attendance improves, and whether any case requires tightening boundaries or changing the coordination script.

Define repair if the first framing misfires: if staff revert to dismissive wording or families stop disclosing, revise the script and briefing immediately rather than broadening consultation indefinitely or reverting to exclusion.

scenario: At a small river clinic in the Peruvian Amazon, a newcomer physician and a local health technician are preparing a same-day referral for a boy whose fever has worsened after two days at home. The boat to the district hospital leaves soon, and the referral note must include what has already been tried and who will accompany him.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The boatman wants the referral packet in about half an hour. The mother is inside with the boy, and some relatives came with them but are waiting near the steps.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll examine him now and start the transfer note. After that, I want a quick rundown of what was given at home so we don't delay the boat.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. The mother has answered only a little so far. The grandfather has been speaking more, and the aunt brought a bundle and a thermos.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then let's not do the history one person at a time. Please bring them to the doorway while I finish listening to his chest, and I'll ask together what they used, when the fever changed, and who is traveling with him.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We can do that. The pharmacy runner is also waiting to know whether to pack only the clinic medicines for the trip.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Pack the clinic medicines for the transfer, but don't clear away what they brought. I need the names and timing in the note so the hospital team sees the full picture.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Understood. The boatman is calling again, so we should keep this brief.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Good. I'll explain the referral in front of them all, confirm who agrees on the plan, and send the note with both the treatment already tried and what we are starting here.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer updates from an individual-only intake frame to a household-level care discussion and treats home treatment plus clinic referral as complementary rather than mutually exclusive. The decisive execution detail is gathering the accompanying relatives into the medical briefing and documenting prior remedies while still moving quickly toward biomedical transfer.

scenario: A hospital team in Iquitos is updating its intake brief for outreach referrals from river communities. The medical director wants one clear line clinicians can use in first-contact conversations so triage stays fast, charting stays consistent, and patients are less likely to stop coming after the first visit.
question: Which direction should guide that first-contact brief?

options.A: Acknowledge home-based healing early, but keep it outside the initial care conversation until the clinician has completed tests and explained the treatment plan.
options.B: Keep the intake brief centered on hospital treatment alone, and invite patients to raise any other practices later if they want them noted separately.
options.C: Present home-based healing and hospital treatment as care that can be discussed together, without asking patients to choose one side before the visit proceeds.
options.D: Frame home-based healing as part of care, but address it first through the family’s recognized local healer before discussing it directly with the patient.

scenario:
You manage implementation for a nonprofit health pilot in Loreto, Peru. In 10 days, your team must launch a referral workflow linking a river community outreach campaign, a regional clinic, and a donor-facing monitoring dashboard. The donor requires a measurable increase in same-week clinic follow-up for adults flagged during outreach visits. Your medical director in Lima wants one standard script so outreach workers can explain symptoms, consent, and referral steps consistently and avoid "mixed messages." A legal reviewer also insists that any mention of non-clinic care must not look like the organization is endorsing unsafe treatment. 

The local field team reports a pattern from recent visits: some households accept screening but do not complete clinic follow-up after the first conversation, even when transport support is offered. In debrief notes, outreach staff wrote that some families asked who else should be present before discussing the illness, some wanted to "continue what they already started" before deciding on the clinic, and some reacted badly when workers corrected local explanations too early. A few families later did come to the clinic after a second contact, but not always through the original outreach worker. The regional operations lead is pushing you to freeze the script today because printing, training, and dashboard configuration all depend on it. Budget only allows one extra coordination step before launch.
question: Write a decision memo for the launch team. Specify the one extra coordination step you would add before launch, how you would change the referral workflow and message sequence, which roles should carry each part, and how you would explain this choice to the Lima medical director and donor. Your memo must identify the most tempting but miscalibrated plan in this situation, show why it is attractive under current pressures, and explain what adaptive effort you are personally willing to invest to make your plan work without derailing the deadline.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that the barrier is not just low health literacy or transport, but a different trust-and-treatment frame around illness that affects who can discuss care, how clinic care is evaluated, and whether clinic referral is treated as exclusive or complementary.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers from the scenario that some patients may not accept a biomedical-only framing and may evaluate clinic care alongside other trusted treatment pathways; no credit for generic statements about "respecting beliefs" without linking this to referral uptake and disclosure behavior.

rubric.point: Chooses the primary execution move on the message-frame and sequence axis: do not lock a single biomedical script as the first and only pathway; instead add a pre-launch step that redesigns wording and handoff so referral can be presented without forcing an either-or choice at first contact.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer makes a concrete sequence change before launch, such as revising first-contact language and escalation flow so outreach does not prematurely close off other care frames; partial credit if it suggests later flexibility but still centers the rollout on one standardized biomedical script.

rubric.point: Assigns roles narrowly and operationally, including who does first contact, who handles follow-up, and who is authorized to continue the conversation when the original worker is not the trusted channel.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies actor-stage matching, for example allowing outreach staff to identify hesitation and route follow-up through a locally credible intermediary or second contact rather than insisting the first worker complete the disclosure and referral alone; no credit for broad "engage the community" wording.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the tempting near-miss plan of using one legally safe, donor-efficient, biomedical standard script plus generic transport support and expecting better compliance through consistency alone.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer names why this imported default is appealing under deadline, legal, and dashboard pressure, yet shows how it misfires by enacting the wrong assumption about how people frame illness and treatment decisions; partial credit if it criticizes standardization in general without identifying the specific miscalibration.

rubric.point: Shows motivational CQ through visible, bounded adaptive effort rather than symbolic openness: the respondent takes on extra work, status cost, or timeline pressure to sustain the culturally targeted adjustment.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer commits to a concrete cost such as owning an extra field debrief, reworking training materials overnight, defending a narrower KPI interpretation to the donor, or adding a second-contact protocol despite operational inconvenience; no credit for low-cost statements like "stay open-minded" or "be patient."

rubric.point: Explains how to satisfy legal and donor constraints without collapsing back into the near-miss plan.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer preserves non-endorsement and measurement needs while still allowing referral language that does not stigmatize or negate other trusted care routes; no credit for answers that solve the cultural issue by removing measurement, postponing launch, or offering unlimited consultation.

rubric.point: Builds calibration and repair into the rollout with a specific monitoring signal tied to the hidden mechanism.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes a targeted check such as tracking whether second-contact referrals convert better, whether refusals cluster after corrective wording, or whether different messengers change follow-up uptake; partial credit for generic monitoring like "collect feedback" without a seed-specific hypothesis.

reference_outline: State that the outreach problem likely reflects an intercultural interpretation of illness and treatment, where clinic care may be judged in relation to existing trusted treatment paths rather than as the sole legitimate option.

Use the one extra coordination step for a rapid redesign session with field staff to rewrite first-contact wording and referral logic before printing, so the opening script does not force a biomedical-only disclosure and decision frame.

Sequence the workflow so first contact screens and opens referral non-exclusively, a follow-up contact handles deeper discussion when hesitation appears, and the case can move through a different trusted channel instead of requiring the original outreach worker to close the referral.

Tell the Lima medical director that consistency should apply to risk boundaries and referral eligibility, not to a single explanatory frame that suppresses uptake; the standardized element is the handoff protocol, not a rigid illness narrative.

Tell the donor that this design protects same-week follow-up by addressing the actual dropout mechanism; propose reporting conversion by first-contact versus second-contact referral so the adjustment remains measurable.

Bound the near-miss plan explicitly: a legally clean, efficient, one-script workflow is attractive under time and dashboard pressure, but it wrongly assumes that more biomedical clarity at first contact will improve compliance.

Show motivational CQ by taking ownership of the extra burden yourself: absorb the late redesign, defend the adaptation upward, and keep the launch date by narrowing the added step to the highest-leverage workflow change rather than expanding into indefinite consultation.

Monitor for repair through operational signals tied to the mechanism, such as whether referrals improve when first-contact staff avoid early correction, whether alternate follow-up messengers convert better, and whether families who delayed still attend when clinic care is framed as compatible with what they already trust.

scenario: A mobile clinic in Loreto is assigning its last afternoon boat slot after a river community screening. A newcomer physician must decide how to handle follow-up for a man with recurring stomach pain while the local health promoter manages the boat schedule, referral paperwork, and messages coming back from the household about the treatment already started there.

roles.local: Local health promoter coordinating the river community follow-up
roles.newcomer: New physician from outside the region leading the clinic schedule

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We can still hold one boat place for Don Mateo this afternoon. His people sent word that the pain returned, and they want to know what to bring from home.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Keep the place for him. Ask them to bring anything he has already taken or prepared so I can record it and avoid a bad interaction.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. They also said they already turned to someone upriver before asking us, and they are waiting for the note on whether today's visit changes that plan.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then send back a clear message with the boat time: once I examine him, today's treatment should be the active plan, and the other one should be set aside until we finish the course.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: I still need the referral notes by sunset. If I send that wording now, they will likely arrive expecting a decision already made.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: That's fine. I would rather avoid mixed instructions on the dock, so I'll draft the referral in advance and mark the start for today unless I find a contraindication.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Understood. I can radio upriver before noon so they know whether to take the boat.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Please tell them to come ready to follow the clinic regimen first; I can document the rest during the visit.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer appears careful by asking about prior treatment and interaction risks, but the decisive error is how he uses that information: he sends advance instructions that make the clinic plan the sole active authority and asks the household to set aside the existing care path before any articulation with it. In this Peru context, health-seeking often works through ongoing local treatment relationships and household decision processes, so replacing that path in advance is culturally miscalibrated.

scenario: A regional health team in Loreto is launching a three-day river visit to a Shawi community in Peru after several adults reported a recurring illness. The district office wants at least some patients referred onward before the boat leaves, and the team has funding for one interpreter for only part of the first day. Community members have previously used local treatment first, and the nurse notes that earlier outreach visits drew little follow-up when consultations felt rushed.
question: Which sequence is the strongest way to handle the first day?

options.A: Begin with referral screening while the interpreter is available, then invite local healers to discuss supportive home care after the priority cases have already been identified.
options.B: Use the interpreter first to meet patients and local healers together, sort which complaints still lack a workable local response, then move those cases into same-day biomedical referral decisions.
options.C: Open by inviting local healers to review all cases with the team, wait to discuss referral until the second day, and use the interpreter mainly for discharge instructions before departure.
options.D: Start with standard biomedical triage for everyone, log unresolved cases for district approval, then return later with an interpreter if patients still want a clinic referral.

scenario:
You are coordinating a multicultural public-health pilot for a regional NGO in Peru. The pilot must raise completed Pap test appointments in three rural communities outside Cusco before the funder review in 6 weeks. The NGO's headquarters wants a fast, low-cost campaign and has already drafted an SMS/WhatsApp reminder sequence translated into Spanish and Quechua. The Lima medical director supports the draft because it is easy to track and compare across sites. A donor representative has also asked for a visible outreach launch this week.

Your local clinic partners report mixed signals. Appointment slots are available, but women who previously said they were interested often do not attend. In recent notes from community visits, staff mention that some women stop the conversation when the topic becomes specific, several ask whether the exam is dangerous or only needed when symptoms appear, and turnout was better after one physician spoke informally with residents than after a poster-and-text push. One nurse also noted that in one village, several husbands asked questions first when household health visits were discussed, but no one framed this as a formal objection. Budget allows only one extra field day per village, and the medical director will reject any plan that looks like an indefinite listening exercise.

Your team includes a program analyst from the US pushing for measurable reminder compliance, a communications lead from Chile who wants a strong women-only privacy message in mass media, and Peruvian clinic staff who can free up one physician for limited outreach time if used carefully. No one on the team is openly opposing the SMS plan; the issue is how to redesign the rollout without missing the donor deadline or creating brand risk.
question: Write a brief rollout memo for your team that specifies the outreach sequence for the next 2 weeks. Your memo must identify the hidden participation mechanism you think is driving the missed appointments, name the most tempting but miscalibrated default plan, and give concrete decisions about who should communicate, through which channel, to whom, in what order, and with what follow-up. Include how you would handle household-level influence without turning the campaign into a broad community consultation, and how you would monitor and repair the plan if the first village response is weak.
