Brief the emcee and country director to use the verified order exactly, avoid improvising a generic egalitarian thank-you list on stage, and keep the wording formal enough for the radio-recorded opening.
Tell donor-facing staff that 'neutrality' here should mean not making the event preachy or lengthy, not stripping out expected opening/closing forms that organize public interaction and respect.

Use a narrow confirmation channel under time pressure: contact the host-side coordinator or equivalent protocol owner for exact ordering and ceremonial expectations, rather than sending a broad email asking everyone for preferences.

Protect schedule by inserting brief, planned openings/closures and a finalized script now, while preparing a repair move if uncertainty remains: pause printing of the acknowledgment paragraph until verified, but not the whole event.

scenario: A newcomer from an overseas university is coordinating a partnership signing on a marae in New Zealand. A donor delegation has arrived early, the photographer wants everyone in position fast, and several guests are carrying takeaway coffees and pastry boxes because the next event starts immediately after the visit.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The delegation is here twenty minutes early, and the photographer keeps asking if we can move people closer so we don't lose light.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll keep everyone by the bus for now and do the briefing there, even if it looks a bit rigid. I'll also ask them to leave the coffees and pastry boxes in the van until we're through the welcome.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That may slow the run sheet. The deputy vice-chancellor wants to get inside quickly to review the speaking order.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll handle the speaking order outside on paper and keep it short. If anyone asks why we're pausing, I'll just say we're waiting for the hosts to start us properly.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: One of the guests is tired and has already set her tote on a side table near the doorway while checking her phone.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll move the tote off the table myself and ask her to keep everything with the group for now. We can sort bags and refreshments once this stage is finished.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The photographer is pushing again and says a quick pre-shot on the forecourt would save time before everyone settles.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: He can shoot from where we are, but I'm not moving the group forward early just to tidy the schedule. We'll enter when the sequence begins and make up time later.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer's decisive behavior matches the marae protocol sequence and tapu/noa boundaries: he keeps visitors from moving in early before the formal start, keeps kai and related items out at that stage, and removes belongings from a table rather than treating it as an ordinary surface.

scenario: A newcomer from an international NGO is helping host a provincial donor after-hours visit in Vanuatu. The donor needs one authentic-looking still image and a very short thank-you clip for a report due before dawn. At the venue, seating and the order of receiving the guest are still being arranged, and the donor has said she does not want anything that looks staged.

roles.local: Mele, a Vanuatu program officer hosting the visit
roles.newcomer: Jon, a recently arrived NGO communications manager

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The driver wants to leave as soon as the greeting is done. Once we go over, the host there will place everyone, and I'm still lining up who receives the donor first.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Got it. I won't stage anyone at the entrance. I'll take one arrival shot outside, then keep the rest natural so the donor doesn't have to redo anything.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: She also asked whether we could avoid pulling people out one by one. Some health staff are already there, and I need to stay focused on the handover order.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: That actually helps. If I stay seated once we're in, I can work with what's already happening instead of moving people around.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We only need something brief for the report—just enough to show participation tonight. If timing slips, we may only have a minute before the car leaves.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I'll skip the light and long lens. I'll get a still from where I am, and when things settle I'll record a ten-second donor line there so we don't create another stop outside.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. I'll bring her across once the elder arrives. If you have what you need quickly, we can go straight to the road.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Perfect. I'll keep it discreet—one still, then a very soft voice clip from inside while everyone's already in place.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: Jon makes several reasonable production choices, but his decisive plan is still miscalibrated: he treats the inside setting as the best place for a whispered spoken recording because it is efficient and looks natural. In Vanuatu, the relevant mechanism is that the nakamal carries expectations of quietness and local procedure inside that space, so using the interior moment itself for ad hoc voice capture is the wrong execution choice.

scenario: You are finalizing a two-page visit brief for an outside engineering team traveling to Lihir, Papua New Guinea. HQ wants one standardized "local heritage" stop in every site visit pack by tonight. In the draft schedule, Ailaya appears beside a cemetery access note and a separate land meeting later that week, but no one has commented on the wording. You need to decide how broadly the brief should treat Ailaya in the standard itinerary.
question: Which decision best sets the scope for the brief now?

options.A: Keep Ailaya in the standard heritage stop, but describe it as a quiet place for reflection and remind visitors to avoid casual sightseeing behavior during that portion of the tour.
options.B: Keep Ailaya out of the standard heritage stop, but include it in a special section for visits connected to funerals or family mourning, with the regular itinerary unchanged otherwise.
options.C: Leave Ailaya in the brief only as an optional stop that can proceed when local landholders approve the route, while adding a short note that some visitors may find it spiritually significant.
options.D: Remove Ailaya from the standard heritage stop and handle any visit or mention through a separate purpose-specific discussion with the relevant local counterparts before the pack is issued.

scenario: You are the regional partnerships manager for a public-health nonprofit preparing a two-day community launch in Port Vila, Vanuatu, for a donor-funded maternal health project. question: Write a decision memo for your team that sets the opening-session protocol and the evening-gathering conduct plan. Your memo must: (1) infer the most likely local mechanism shaping these interactions from the evidence given; (2) identify the tempting imported assumption in the current proposal and why it is risky here; (3) make concrete choices about sequence, who is acknowledged when, whether and how opening/closing elements are handled, and what the film crew should and should not do in the evening setting; and (4) show how you will keep the project moving despite budget, donor, and hierarchy pressure without shifting the adaptation burden onto local attendees.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden protocol mechanism from scenario evidence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that the launch is shaped by formal public protocol around stakeholder acknowledgment and meeting participation, plus different expectations for the evening kava setting, and ties this to the named actor mix and event structure; no credit for vague claims like 'be respectful of religion' or 'Pacific cultures value ceremony.'

rubric.point: Sets the opening sequence with seed-specific actor order
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan explicitly places acknowledgments in the correct order for this setting—government officials first, then traditional leaders, then religious leaders—and applies that order to the actual attendees before or around speaking remarks; partial credit if the answer mentions the groups but not the order or misapplies the order to the wrong stage.

rubric.point: Handles opening and closing meeting elements with bounded execution
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer chooses to include appropriate opening and closing prayer or devotional elements as normal meeting protocol in this context, while bounding them operationally rather than turning them into a generic theology discussion; no credit for omitting them in the name of generic neutrality or for recommending an open-ended interfaith segment.

rubric.point: Rejects the polished near-miss plan
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer identifies the attractive imported assumption—using a global neutral, efficiency-first launch format and treating the evening kava gathering as a normal networking opportunity—and explains why that would mis-handle this case even though it seems donor-safe, budget-efficient, and brand-consistent.

rubric.point: Designs evening-gathering conduct for the specific setting
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer states that the evening kava venue should be treated as a quiet or silent setting, meaning the team should not plan open mixer-style conversation there and should tightly limit or exclude film capture, prompting, and candid interviews in that space; partial credit if the answer merely says 'be discreet' without changing the crew plan.

rubric.point: Shows motivational CQ through costly but targeted follow-through
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan accepts a real cost—such as revising the run-of-show late, re-briefing senior staff, narrowing what the film crew captures, or moving relationship-building interviews to a different time/channel—while keeping momentum and not withdrawing behind 'we need more consultation'; no credit for friendly language without ownership of these costs.

rubric.point: Assigns roles and risk controls without over-delegating adaptation locally
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies who updates the briefing note, who re-briefs the ministry-facing MC and communications team, how the crew gets a clear do/don't list, and how success will be monitored on the day; no credit for plans that simply tell local attendees to correct the team in real time or that solve risk only by delaying the event.

reference_outline: Infer from the attendee mix and event structure that this is not just a neutral content launch; it requires formal ceremonial protocol in the opening and a different participation mode in the later kava gathering.

Revise the opening so acknowledgments and/or introductions follow the order of government officials, then traditional leaders, then religious leaders, and make sure the MC and speakers are briefed to preserve that sequence before substantive project remarks.

Include brief opening and closing prayer as normal meeting protocol for this context, handled as bounded ceremonial elements rather than as a broad interfaith discussion or something omitted for generic secular branding.

Reject the global-default near-miss: do not start with a generic video-first sequence, do not let ministry rank alone determine the entire protocol logic, and do not treat the evening kava venue as a normal chatter-heavy networking opportunity.

Instruct the film crew not to seek candid interviews or active soundbites in the evening kava setting; either exclude that space from capture or limit recording to pre-cleared visuals outside the quiet interaction itself, and move interviews to another time.

Demonstrate motivational CQ by taking on the inconvenience of late agenda changes, crew re-briefing, and donor-expectation management instead of choosing the cheaper but miscalibrated plan or passively waiting for locals to fix the format.

Assign concrete ownership: partnerships manager issues revised memo, MC gets a speaking-order brief, communications lead receives filming boundaries, finance is told why overtime risk is preferable to relational/protocol damage, and on-site monitoring checks whether the opening sequence and evening conduct stay within plan.
Build a bounded repair path under pressure: if timing slips, shorten video or project remarks rather than removing ceremonial elements or turning the evening setting into a backup interview site.

scenario: Your operations manager is clearing a one-page field brief for a two-day client workshop in Tokyo. Several visiting engineers smoke, the host venue has multiple floors and a roof terrace, and the local team can get a floor map by tomorrow but not a legal review. The brief must tell attendees what documentation they need before taking smoking breaks during the program.
question: Which approval decision and briefing line is the strongest to sign off?

options.A: Approve the brief if it tells attendees to step outside the building perimeter for any smoking break, with host reception confirming the nearest outdoor spot when the group checks in.
options.B: Approve the brief if it states that smoking is acceptable during breaks when the host contact or floor captain points visitors to a convenient place, with no added venue documentation.
options.C: Approve the brief once the coordinator attaches the venue’s posted smoking-location information and floor map, and instructs attendees to use only those designated places during workshop breaks.
options.D: Approve the brief only after HR adds the company’s standard smoke-free travel note, asking attendees to avoid smoking throughout the visit unless they make a personal arrangement offsite.

scenario: You are the regional operations lead on a multicultural workplace-services team. Your team is preparing a Friday night refresh of a rental flat in Singapore that will be used from Monday morning to host a visiting client delegation. The flat is in an HDB block. The vendor says the fastest way to finish is to do wall drilling, furniture assembly, and sound checks across Friday evening and part of Saturday. Your Singapore colleague has sent you a draft note saying, "We should keep it reasonable for neighbours and avoid late-night disturbance." Your Australia-based procurement manager is pushing for a single global rule: notify the whole building by email, finish the loud work by 11:00pm, and escalate to building management only if anyone complains. Your Japan-based project coordinator wants a conservative plan because the client visit cannot slip, but budget cannot absorb an extra hotel night for the crew. You also discover that next week includes a major public holiday, and the client sponsor has asked for a written assurance tonight that the setup plan is compliant, low-risk, and unlikely to damage local relationships. You have partial facts: the crew has not yet delivered any written neighbour notice, the vendor assumes Saturday daytime drilling is fine, and no one on the team is certain which noises are treated as a hard rule versus something managed informally.
question: Write the decision memo you would send tonight to your team and sponsor. It must specify: (1) what you will and will not authorize this weekend, (2) what assumptions you think the team may be importing from other markets, (3) what evidence is already strong enough to act on now versus what still needs checking, and (4) the sequence of neighbour-facing, team-facing, and escalation steps you will use if noise concerns arise. Make your plan concrete enough that teammates could execute it without another meeting.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the mixed mechanism correctly
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer distinguishes between harder procedural constraints for certain renovation noise and softer neighbourhood expectations for ordinary volume, rather than treating all noise as one generic after-hours issue.

rubric.point: Makes the primary timing-and-scope decision correctly
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo stops or reschedules noisy renovation work that should not be authorized under the scenario facts, instead of merely capping volume late at night or allowing weekend drilling with extra courtesy notice.

rubric.point: Uses evidence with calibrated confidence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer states what is actionable now from available facts, what remains uncertain, and what specific missing facts would change the plan; no credit for either blanket delay or overconfident approval.

rubric.point: Rejects the attractive imported near-miss
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly bounds the global-default plan of broad building notice plus complaint-based escalation, showing why that is miscalibrated here even though it sounds efficient and considerate.

rubric.point: Designs the correct neighbour and escalation sequence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan starts with direct neighbour-facing consideration at the appropriate scope, then uses the relevant community escalation path if needed, rather than jumping first to building management, mass messaging, legal threat, or passive waiting.

rubric.point: Applies procedural detail to the right actors and radius
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer assigns written notice and compliance checks to the neighbours and work types that require them, instead of notifying too broadly, too late, or only after complaints.

rubric.point: Shows metacognitive CQ in execution
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo monitors the team's assumptions across markets, separates hard-rule confidence from debated or informal norms, and revises the work plan accordingly without hiding behind generic caution.

reference_outline: State that the plan cannot treat all sound issues as a single global quiet-hours problem; distinguish regulated noisy renovation activity from ordinary neighbour-noise expectations.

Do not authorize heavy drilling or similar noisy renovation work on the proposed weekend schedule; reschedule those tasks into the permitted weekday window and account for the holiday-related constraint before promising completion.
Flag that the crew lacks required written neighbour notice for the relevant nearby units, so the team cannot cure this by sending a same-night mass email to the whole building.

Use what is already knowable now to act: the current schedule and notice status are enough to stop the loud renovation plan tonight, while finer questions about acceptable low-level evening activity can be handled through calibrated limits and monitoring.
Tell the team to make a direct, considerate neighbour-facing contact first for any residual ordinary setup noise, with a narrower scope and different tone than a formal compliance notice.
If concerns persist, route escalation through the appropriate community-based channels rather than defaulting first to building management or a generic corporate complaint workflow.

Name the imported assumption explicitly: other-market logic of 'finish by 11pm, notify everyone, act only if someone complains' is attractive under deadline pressure but misreads both the procedural and relational expectations in this context.

Include a sponsor-facing assurance that separates compliant rescheduling of restricted work from voluntary volume reduction after 10pm for non-restricted activity, showing monitoring and repair steps if neighbours raise issues.

scenario: A newcomer on a museum partnerships team is helping with a same-day VIP visit in Hong Kong. The group will arrive by minibus, and the museum manager wants everyone checked in smoothly because a donor is joining and the slot cannot be delayed. While the driver sorts parking, the newcomer notices one guest step into the painted boarding area near the drop-off point to finish a cigarette before the group walks over.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The donor is already inside, so if we miss the entry window the curator has to reshuffle staff. Our guests can wait by the marked pickup bay for a minute while the minibus circles.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I’ll keep the group together and move the check-in fast once the vehicle comes back.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: One guest has stepped back toward the painted bay lines. He says he’s not boarding yet, just finishing quickly before we head in.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I’m going over now. I’ll ask him to leave that marked area immediately and finish elsewhere if he needs to, even if it slows us by a minute.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: He may think that’s a bit abrupt in front of the others. We also have the membership cards to hand out.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I’ll keep it brief and matter-of-fact, then I’ll distribute the cards while he rejoins us. I’d rather absorb the awkward moment than risk a problem at the bay.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Alright, the minibus will swing back in about two minutes. The driver is asking whether everyone should already stand inside the marked point.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Tell him to hold a little farther up while I pull the group just outside the markings first, then we’ll step in together when it’s time.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer aligns with the Hong Kong rule by treating the delineated boarding point itself as the decisive boundary and moving the smoker and group out of that marked area, rather than using a generic assumption that smoking is only a problem when an actual line is actively boarding.

scenario: Your team is sending a same-day confirmation email for a client briefing at a Tokyo office tower. The landlord has building notices about smoking, one outdoor area is marked for it, and security asked tenants to keep visitor instructions aligned with posted site rules. The event manager wants one short English line that also works in Japanese translation.
question: Which line should be approved for the email?

options.A: If you smoke, please do so with consideration for nearby guests and use outdoor spaces where your smoke will not affect other people.
options.B: If you wish to smoke, staff can direct you to a ventilated place during breaks, including outdoor spots that are separated from the main entrance flow.
options.C: If you plan to smoke, please use the marked smoking area on site; if it is closed or full during your visit, please wait until you leave the property.
options.D: Guests who choose to smoke may step outside during breaks and use any open-air location that is away from the entrance and from other attendees.

scenario: You are the regional compliance lead for a multinational medical-device company. A Shanghai-based public hospital is expected to issue a technical clarification in 10 days that will strongly affect whether your bid remains eligible for a large procurement. Your China sales director says the hospital procurement office will not answer formal written questions before the clarification is posted, but a long-time distributor has offered to 'help smooth communication' by inviting the deputy procurement director, two surgeons, and your team to a private dinner this week. The distributor says no tender discussion will appear on the agenda; instead, the dinner would celebrate a recent training partnership and give your team a chance to 'show sincerity' before the clarification is finalized. He also suggests that after dinner your company could sponsor a study visit for one surgeon's department and send a premium baby gift because the deputy director recently became a grandparent. Your global legal head in Germany wants a simple rule: either ban all informal contact and send only a formal letter, or allow the dinner as ordinary relationship-building because no one is asking for cash and competitors are likely doing the same. Your China country manager warns that refusing all social contact this week may damage access with the distributor and hospital stakeholders just before bid review, but the board has already flagged this tender as high reputation risk. A US-based product VP is pressing for speed because missing this procurement would likely kill the quarter in Asia. You need to brief the cross-border team within 24 hours with a concrete plan for how to proceed.
question: Write the decision memo you would send to the Germany legal head, the China country manager, and the US product VP. Your memo must: (1) diagnose what mechanism is potentially operating in this situation based on the available facts, (2) identify the most tempting but miscalibrated imported assumption, (3) decide exactly what forms of contact, if any, are allowed in the next 10 days and in what sequence, and (4) explain how your plan preserves legitimate relationship management without creating obligation, special access, or bid-related influence risk. Be specific about stakeholder scope, timing, channels, approvals, and what evidence would make you tighten or relax the plan.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the risk as socially packaged influence rather than only obvious bribery or ordinary networking.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers from the dinner, distributor mediation, gift suggestions, and study-visit offer that the concern is reciprocal obligation and special access around a public-facing decision; no credit for answers that merely say 'possible corruption' or 'relationship culture' without operational implications.

rubric.point: Identifies and rejects the tempting imported near-miss assumption.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer names a plausible but wrong frame such as 'no cash means harmless networking' or 'formal channels only solves everything' and explains why that frame misreads this context; partial credit if it rejects only one side without showing why the other is attractive under deadline and KPI pressure.

rubric.point: Makes the correct execution-axis decision on timing and scope of contact before the clarification.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer narrows or suspends social contact that could create obligation or privileged access during the live procurement window, while allowing tightly bounded non-influence communications through documented, role-appropriate channels; lower scores if it either bans all relationship maintenance indefinitely or permits the dinner/gifts/study-visit during the decision window.

rubric.point: Separates legitimate relationship management from bid-linked favors with actor- and stage-specific controls.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer distinguishes what may be acceptable after the procurement stage or outside decision-making actors from what is unacceptable now, and applies that distinction to the distributor, surgeons, procurement office, and company leaders; no full credit for generic statements like 'follow policy' or 'be respectful.'

rubric.point: Uses cognitive CQ by mapping evidence to the local causal logic rather than to stereotype or global SOP.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer shows why the combination of social setting, introductions, gift-like exchanges, and public decision timing matters in this China context, while also avoiding the stereotype that all relationship-building is corrupt; partial credit for accurate facts applied at the wrong stage or wrong stakeholder.

rubric.point: Designs a concrete coordination workflow with approvals, messaging, and documentation.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies who communicates the boundary to the distributor, who may contact the hospital, what must be documented, and what wording/frame should be used to decline or redirect offers without insulting counterparts; lower scores for broad consultation or undefined 'check with compliance' plans.

rubric.point: Defines evidence thresholds for recalibration and repair.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer states what new facts would justify tightening controls further or resuming lower-risk relationship activity later, and includes a repair path if stakeholders perceive the boundary as a relationship slight; no full credit for indefinite delay or one-way prohibition without monitoring.

reference_outline: State that the key risk is not only overt bribery but a reciprocal-access mechanism embedded in social hospitality, introductions, and gift-like favors during a live public procurement decision.

Reject both polished near-misses: allowing the dinner because it is framed socially and contains no explicit tender talk, and banning every informal interaction as if all relationship maintenance were corrupt; explain why each misses the actual boundary.

Set the primary timing decision: during the 10-day clarification window, no private dinner with decision-relevant hospital actors, no celebratory gifts, no department study-visit sponsorship, and no distributor-facilitated social exchange tied to the tender context.

Allow only narrowly scoped contact through documented, role-appropriate channels such as a formal clarification request, compliance-approved procedural questions, or routine non-promotional logistics that do not seek privileged access or create personal obligation.

Assign roles operationally: compliance drafts the boundary and approval rules, the China country manager or sales director communicates them to the distributor in relationship-preserving language, and only designated authorized staff may contact hospital counterparts through logged channels.

Use wording that preserves face and relationship while redirecting the interaction, for example by thanking the distributor for support, citing company procurement-period rules, and proposing to revisit appropriate educational or partnership activities after the clarification and bid stage ends.

Show cognitive CQ by explaining why the social packaging itself changes risk interpretation here: the issue is the implied obligation and particularistic access surrounding a public decision, not a simplistic ban on all local relationship-building.

Define recalibration triggers: tighten further if the distributor pushes for off-record introductions, insists that attendance is necessary for access, or links future cooperation to responsiveness; relax only after the procurement stage closes and only with fresh review of actor roles, benefit type, and business purpose.

Include a repair path if the boundary strains relationships: offer a post-tender institutional meeting, transparent technical education open to appropriate participants, or a standard partnership review with documented agenda and approvals.

scenario: A French newcomer is helping a Japanese nonprofit deliver signed permit documents to a ward office before the counter closes. They leave the subway one block away, carrying a stamped folder and a camera battery the office also requested. At a broad intersection near the office, a few pedestrians begin moving before the signal changes, and the office closes in minutes.

roles.newcomer: Thomas, newly transferred staff member from France

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: If we miss the counter, they will only log the permit tomorrow. The signed originals have to reach them today.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I have the folder and the spare battery. We should still make it if we keep moving.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The office is just across this intersection and then half a block. A few people are already heading over.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Let's stop here for a moment. As soon as it changes, we'll go straight through and I'll jog the last stretch if needed.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. I'll message the clerk that we're arriving now so they know we're close.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Good idea. I'll get the papers ready while we wait so there is no delay at the desk.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: There it is.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Go ahead—directly to counter three. I'll hand over the permit first and the battery right after.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The decisive behavior is that the newcomer does not treat other pedestrians moving early as a cue to step off the curb. In this Japan-specific norm, rule-respect overrides crowd-following at the crossing, so waiting for the signal is the culturally calibrated choice even under time pressure.

scenario: Your team is drafting a one-line incident-responsibility statement for station staff, call-center agents, and a customer handout before a remotely monitored Level 4 shuttle pilot launches in Japan. The service company owns the route, sells the rides, and has contracted a separate remote operations vendor. A local filing for the pilot is due tonight, and the wording needs to stay consistent across all materials.
question: Which direction should the draft use for who is treated as the responsible operating party if the shuttle is involved in an injury incident?

options.A: Name the remote operations vendor as the responsible operating party, with the shuttle company listed as the customer-facing contact for follow-up and claims handling.
options.B: Treat the passenger who started the trip as the operating party, while the shuttle company coordinates reporting and helps route any compensation requests.
options.C: Assign responsibility to whichever entity is listed on the local pilot authorization for that route, whether that is the shuttle company or its monitoring vendor.
options.D: Identify the transport company running the passenger service as the responsible operating party, even when remote monitoring is contracted out and no rider is driving.

scenario: You manage a multicultural content team preparing a 36-hour turnaround launch package for a global travel client. The package needs six social posts and one hero image from a Kyoto shoot already completed by a junior producer. The producer sent 140 street photos from Japan, including several close shots of identifiable passersby and a cluster of images taken in a narrow lane in Gion where small warning signs appear in the background but are not fully readable in the thumbnails. The client’s regional VP wants 'authentic local faces' because similar campaigns performed well in other markets, and your brand lead says cropping is acceptable if the final composition looks editorial. Your Tokyo-based vendor can still request replacements before noon tomorrow, but only if you give specific instructions tonight. Legal has not reviewed the images yet and says they can only do a fast check on the final shortlist, not the full set. Your team includes a US social strategist pushing for speed and a Singapore-based operations manager urging you to keep the existing shoot because reshoots will exceed budget. No one on the thread explicitly objects to the current images.
question: Write the action memo you would send tonight to your team and vendor. Your memo must specify which images can move forward now, which cannot, what exact instructions the vendor should follow for any replacement shots, how you would handle the client pressure for 'authentic local faces,' and what visible behavior you want from team members if they need new shots involving people on the street. Be concrete about wording, sequencing, and risk boundaries, and explain which attractive but miscalibrated assumption you are rejecting.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden mechanism from the scenario evidence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that the main risk is not generic taste or broad privacy caution but using identifiable people without explicit permission, with heightened caution for the Gion images; partial credit if it mentions 'privacy' or 'be careful' without tying it to identifiable subjects and location-specific strictness.

rubric.point: Sets the correct image-selection boundary
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if it permits wide atmospheric images that do not single out identifiable people while excluding close or focal images of identifiable passersby unless permission was obtained; no full credit for blanket bans on all street photography or for approving close shots with editing-only fixes such as cropping or blur as the default solution.

rubric.point: Rejects the tempting imported near-miss plan
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if it explicitly bounds a plausible default such as 'we already shot in public so use the images unless someone complains,' 'crop later,' or 'legal can clear the shortlist,' and explains why that efficient global-market logic is miscalibrated here; low credit if it merely says to 'check with legal' or 'be respectful.'

rubric.point: Gives behaviorally calibrated replacement instructions
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if it instructs the vendor or team to either capture non-identifying atmospheric scenes or ask permission before photographing identifiable people, including usable street-level wording such as asking first before shooting; partial credit if it says 'get consent' without specifying timing or visible action.

rubric.point: Uses the selected CQ through wording, timing, and sequence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan translates understanding into visible execution: tonight shortlist boundaries, immediate vendor brief, exact do/do-not-shoot guidance, and a requirement that permission be sought before the camera is used on identifiable individuals; no full credit for abstract principles without sequencing.

rubric.point: Handles stakeholder pressure without losing the cultural boundary
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if it offers a concrete client-safe alternative such as atmosphere, backs-of-people, crowd distance, or clearly permission-based portraits while preserving deadline and budget as much as possible; low credit if it solves pressure only by delaying the campaign or escalating everything indefinitely.

rubric.point: Includes operational controls and repair steps
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if it assigns checks such as tagging images by 'identifiable person / permission status / restricted-location concern,' removes Gion images from default use pending replacement or proof, and defines what to do if uncertain images remain; partial credit for generic review language without operational categories.

reference_outline: State that the current shortlist must exclude close or clearly identifiable street portraits unless permission was explicitly obtained, and treat the Gion lane images as especially unsuitable for default use because the location signals stricter photography enforcement.
Approve only wide atmospheric shots that do not single out identifiable people, plus any people images that are clearly permission-based and documented.

Send the vendor an immediate replacement brief: prioritize Kyoto atmosphere, architecture, movement, backs/silhouettes, or distance shots; if a person will be identifiable, ask first before shooting using simple permission wording rather than relying on later cropping or postproduction fixes.

Reject the attractive shortcut that public-space photography is automatically usable if legally unobstructed elsewhere, or that final legal review/cropping can substitute for the correct capture-stage behavior.

Tell the client and internal team that 'authentic local faces' can be delivered only through permission-based portraits or non-identifying street atmosphere, not by defaulting to candid identifiable images from this shoot.

Create an overnight workflow tag for each image: non-identifying usable, identifiable with verified permission, or hold/remove; require the Tokyo vendor to confirm permission status for any people-centered replacement image.

If time pressure leaves gaps, ship the package with atmosphere-led creative rather than stretching the boundary, and note that the narrow fix is a content-format adjustment, not a broad campaign delay.

scenario: A newcomer helping organize move-in prep for a research apartment building in Germany needs to get a sponsor-ready video walkthrough by Monday morning. On Sunday, a wall-mounted shelf in the unit comes loose. The local colleague is off-site coordinating arrivals, and the newcomer must decide how to handle the repair timing while keeping the apartment usable and avoiding trouble with residents in the building.

roles.local: Mara, a German program coordinator managing tenant arrivals
roles.newcomer: Ethan, a recently arrived operations manager

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The sponsor wants the apartment video first thing Monday. One shelf is hanging forward in the study, and the room looks unfinished on camera. The building is full this weekend, so I can't come over.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I can still solve it today. I'll go over now, measure it, tape it safely in place so nothing drops, and send the video with that wall out of frame. Then I'll book the drilling and mounting crew for tomorrow morning.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Tomorrow before noon would help. The next tenant checks in late afternoon, and the landlord is strict when residents complain about building issues.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I won't start any cutting or drilling today. I'll message the handyman now for the earliest Monday slot and ask the tenant to leave the desk area clear.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Good. The sponsor may ask why the room angle is so tight if they notice.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll be direct and say we're finishing a minor fixture adjustment first thing tomorrow, so they get a clean final setup instead of a noisy rush job today.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. Please keep me copied if the handyman proposes a later time, because arrivals start stacking up after lunch.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Will do. I’m sending the booking note now and heading over only for the quiet safety check and video.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The decisive behavior fits the German noise-control mechanism: on Sunday the newcomer avoids noisy repair work such as drilling and shifts the loud task to Monday, while still progressing the job through a quiet inspection, temporary safety step, and scheduling follow-up.

scenario: A Brussels hotel is finalizing a one-page briefing for banquet staff before a reception. The floor plan includes a separately enclosed guest area where smoking is permitted, and the client expects smooth drinks service throughout the venue. The operations lead wants one short line clarifying how staff should handle that enclosed area without delaying sign-off.
question: Which briefing line should be approved?

options.A: Guests may use the enclosed smoking area, but orders and drink pickup stay at the doorway or main bar rather than being served inside that room.
options.B: Guests may use the enclosed smoking area, and staff may enter briefly to deliver drinks there if they avoid clearing tables or treating it like regular seating.
options.C: Guests may use the enclosed smoking area, and staff should direct all drink delivery there through one assigned runner instead of rotating servers through the room.
options.D: Guests may use the enclosed smoking area, and service may continue there under the same hospitality standards used anywhere smoking is legally permitted indoors.

scenario: You manage rollout for a travel-tech company launching a single 'station and shuttle boarding' signage pack for four pilot markets: Spain, Ireland, Greece, and Malta. The pack covers indoor waiting areas, enclosed shuttle bays, staff break rooms inside terminals, and a few optional outdoor queue zones. The design team in London wants one reusable template by tomorrow because the CEO will review screenshots at 09:00, and legal has asked you to avoid market-specific over-customization unless clearly justified. A Greek operations lead says only that 'travellers hate mixed signals, especially when drivers improvise.' An Irish facilities manager asks whether the indoor icons should match the bus decals exactly. A Malta commercial lead wants the message to feel welcoming and not 'anti-customer.' The current draft, based on a non-EU template used in several other regions, says: 'Please use designated smoking corners where provided' and places the same icon set in all boarding areas, with smaller text near indoor doors explaining that rules may vary by site. You have one chance tonight to send a decision memo and markup instructions to design, legal, and local operations. You cannot call a country-by-country meeting before the deadline, but you can request two targeted confirmations if needed.
question: Write the decision memo you would send tonight. Your memo must: (1) infer the most likely hidden rule pattern from the scenario evidence, (2) identify the tempting imported assumption in the current draft, (3) make a concrete choice about what must be standardized now versus what can remain locally confirmed later, and (4) explain how you will brief design, legal, and local operations so the rollout stays on schedule without creating the wrong behavioural signal in the four markets.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that the likely baseline for these named markets is a strict smoke-free approach in enclosed public places and transport-related indoor spaces, so the default rollout should not treat indoor smoking as ordinarily accommodated.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer converts the country pattern into an operational default for indoor waiting areas, enclosed shuttle bays, and indoor staff/public spaces; no credit for merely saying 'Europe is strict' or discussing smoking abstractly.

rubric.point: Rejects the imported near-miss assumption that a globally reusable template should default to directing people toward indoor or quasi-indoor designated smoking corners unless a site opts out.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly identifies the current draft's accommodation logic as the risky assumption and bounds it; partial credit if it notices ambiguity but still preserves the template's indoor 'use designated smoking corners' message.

rubric.point: Makes the primary execution-axis decision on evidence weighting and timing: standardize a no-smoking-in-enclosed-areas message now, while limiting follow-up checks to narrow exception handling rather than reopening the whole baseline.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer acts on sufficient evidence now and keeps later confirmation targeted to permitted exceptions or outdoor placement details; low credit for broad delay, full-country revalidation, or waiting for a meeting before changing the draft.

rubric.point: Translates the diagnosis into concrete design instructions about placement and wording.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer removes or replaces indoor accommodation wording, separates enclosed areas from any optional clearly defined allowed smoking areas, and avoids ambiguous 'rules may vary by site' language that weakens the indoor prohibition; partial credit for generic 'make it clearer' wording.

rubric.point: Shows metacognitive CQ by distinguishing what is known, what remains uncertain, and what specific evidence would justify any exception.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer states a calibrated working read (strict enclosed-space baseline), names the remaining uncertainty (whether any site has lawful, clearly defined allowed smoking area outside the enclosed spaces), and limits confirmation requests to that uncertainty; no credit for either overclaiming certainty about every site detail or asking broad questions that do not reduce the real uncertainty.

rubric.point: Assigns role-specific coordination to design, legal, and local operations in a way that protects schedule and behaviour.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer tells design what to change immediately, tells legal what narrow review is needed, and tells local operations what site-specific confirmation to provide; low credit for generic 'consult stakeholders' without division of responsibilities.

rubric.point: Controls the risk of mixed signals for travellers and frontline staff across markets.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explains that ambiguous or accommodation-framed indoor signage can cue staff improvisation and public misunderstanding, and therefore the baseline must be behaviourally unambiguous; partial credit for mentioning reputation or compliance risk without linking it to execution.

reference_outline: State that Spain, Ireland, Greece, and Malta should be treated as strict-enforcement markets for enclosed public places and transport-related indoor environments, so the default pack must prohibit smoking in those enclosed spaces rather than route users to indoor smoking corners.

Replace the current template's core indoor line with a clear no-smoking message for enclosed waiting, boarding, and workplace areas; if smoking is allowed anywhere, confine that reference to separately marked, clearly defined allowed areas outside the enclosed-space baseline.

Do not hold the whole rollout for generic local consultation; instead send two narrow confirmation requests: whether any site has a lawful, clearly defined permitted smoking area, and where any outdoor-only directional sign would physically sit so it does not appear to authorize indoor smoking.

Tell design tonight to remove the small 'rules may vary by site' qualifier from indoor assets, split indoor and outdoor signage logic, and keep bus decals and indoor icons aligned around a no-smoking baseline to avoid mixed cues.
Tell legal to review only the exception boundary and wording for any optional outdoor directional panel, not to reconsider the enclosed-space default across all four markets.

Tell local operations to confirm site-specific exception facts and placement constraints, while instructing frontline teams not to improvise customer-facing smoking directions inside enclosed boarding or waiting spaces.

Show metacognitive calibration by writing what is inferred now from the market pattern, what is still unknown at site level, and what evidence would change only the exception signage, not the baseline indoor pack.

scenario: In Vilnius, a newcomer helping a farm coalition prepare a next-day protest briefing must finalize the movement plan before the municipality closes its evening review window. The coalition wants strong visibility, several tractors are already en route, and journalists have asked where to film the action.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We have the approved gathering points and a short statement slot tomorrow morning. Media keeps asking whether the tractors will be seen from the main route out of the city, and I need the final briefing in twenty minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: For visibility, I can draft it as a slow procession past the city exit for half an hour, then back to the gathering area. It would be controlled and easy for cameras to follow.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The traffic center already mapped the lay-bys and service roads for us. Patrol units asked for the vehicle count again this afternoon, and some drivers keep saying they want to be noticed, not tucked away.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I should not imply a moving pass on the main route as if that is already covered. I will keep the public note to the approved stopping areas only and separate any wider idea into a request, not tomorrow's plan.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The farmers may think that sounds too restrained. Journalists also prefer one clear shot instead of scattered arrivals.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll solve that by setting one press position at the approved roadside turnout and tightening the arrival window. It is less dramatic, but it keeps the briefing consistent with what has actually been cleared.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Fine. Send me wording I can forward to drivers and the city desk before they log off.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Sending now: fixed locations, timed arrivals, no route language, and a separate note that any expansion needs fresh coordination first.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer updates away from a generic free-expression visibility plan and aligns with the Lithuania-specific mechanism: authorized demonstration arrangements do not automatically extend to near-total obstruction or expansion onto major traffic routes, so they keep activity within cleared locations and treat any broader roadway use as requiring new approval.

scenario: Your team needs a municipal operating permit in Athens to open a temporary service site in 10 days. A local coordinator handling the filing writes: "There is a lot of pressure on these offices right now. If speed matters, there are ways people sometimes get a file moved up. Otherwise we can wait and see." You need to reply now. The project can survive a delay, but canceling the opening would be costly and your regional director expects you to stay closely engaged.
question: Which reply is the best next step?

options.A: Thanks. Please use only the official route and standard fees, and avoid any side arrangements. Keep us posted if the office contacts you with a decision or document request.
options.B: Thanks. If files are often advanced through personal channels, please identify a reputable contact who can help ours move earlier, using whatever customary facilitation cost is normally expected.
options.C: Thanks. We cannot seek special placement or add unofficial payments, but please keep pursuing the ordinary route actively and tell us the earliest lawful step that can move this file forward.
options.D: Thanks. If others are likely trying to move ahead through relationships, please ask our local board member to contact the office so our application is not left behind in the queue.

scenario:
You lead market entry operations for a medical-device company opening a small service hub in Greece. The hub cannot start billing hospitals until three linked public steps are completed in sequence within six weeks: municipal occupancy sign-off, fire inspection, and final operating registration. A regional VP in Germany has already announced the launch date to investors, and a Greek hospital group says it will move to a competitor if the launch slips more than one month. Your local facilities vendor says the paperwork is technically complete but warns that files like yours often 'sit for a long time unless someone helps move them along.' In the last two email threads, two different intermediaries separately suggested using a retired municipal consultant who 'knows how to unblock queues' and charges a large cash retainer with no itemized deliverables. The vendor also says that if you refuse this route, no one will openly object, but your file may be pushed behind later submissions at multiple stages. 

Your team is multicultural: a German finance manager wants a written zero-exception rule and says any further contact should go only through formal submissions; a Greek commercial manager argues that if headquarters will not use the consultant, headquarters must at least commit people and budget for repeated in-person follow-up because the file will not advance on its own; a UK compliance lawyer says any ambiguous side arrangement must be blocked, documented, and escalated immediately. You have budget for temporary staff travel and overtime, but not for missing the launch. You have no proof of an explicit illegal request, only a pattern of hints, unusual payment structure, and the fact that the process is sequential, so one delay compounds the next.
question: Write a decision memo for your VP that sets the operating plan for the next six weeks. Your memo must: (1) diagnose what mechanism is most likely shaping the risk in this case from the available evidence, (2) identify the most tempting but miscalibrated imported assumption, (3) specify exactly how you will progress the file without using the consultant, including who does what at each stage and how much effort headquarters must absorb, and (4) explain how you will keep the team engaged and aligned when progress is slow, costly, and ambiguous rather than withdrawing into either passive compliance or aggressive pressure.

rubric.point: Diagnoses a queue-advancement corruption risk in a sequential public process rather than treating the case as a generic ethics issue only.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires inferring that the main risk is pressure to pay for faster placement or movement through linked administrative stages, where delay itself is the leverage; partial credit for noting corruption risk without tying it to sequential compounding delays; no credit for discussing only abstract compliance culture.

rubric.point: Rejects the polished near-miss that formal filing plus waiting is the safest sufficient response.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires explicitly bounding the imported assumption that once documents are correct, the company should minimize contact and let the process run; high-scoring answers explain why that plan misreads the likely mechanism and effectively cedes queue position; no credit if the answer relies mainly on broad consultation, delay, or 'follow standard process and monitor.'

rubric.point: Sets a seed-specific execution plan on the primary axis of timing and sequence.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires an active no-bribe progression plan tied to each linked stage: immediate lawful follow-up after submission, repeated checkpointing before stall points harden, stage-by-stage tracking, and preparation for the next office before the prior approval lands to reduce compounding delay; partial credit for generic follow-up without a sequential cadence; no credit for a one-time escalation plan or undifferentiated relationship advice.

rubric.point: Assigns concrete roles and channels that absorb effort centrally instead of shifting the burden entirely to locals.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires specifying who handles documentation, who conducts lawful in-person or phone follow-up, who records interactions, who approves escalation, and how headquarters funds travel/overtime or executive availability to sustain the plan; partial credit if roles are named but not operationalized; no credit if the answer says only 'ask the Greek team to manage it' or 'let compliance handle it.'

rubric.point: Shows motivational CQ through costly, bounded persistence under discomfort and ambiguity.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires visible willingness to spend time, status, and resources on sustained lawful engagement despite slow progress, without becoming intrusive or disengaged; the answer must keep ownership with the respondent's team rather than retreating behind policy language or pushing adaptation costs onto local staff alone; no credit for friendly tone without follow-through.

rubric.point: Designs compliance and evidence controls that fit ambiguous signals without waiting for an explicit demand.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires blocking the cash consultant route, documenting hints and payment irregularities, predefining escalation triggers, and preserving a lawful audit trail while still continuing active process management; partial credit for blocking the consultant without a monitoring plan; no credit for waiting for explicit proof before acting.

rubric.point: Maintains team alignment across competing work norms and pressures.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires integrating the German, Greek, and UK perspectives into one actionable plan: formal documentation remains intact, local reality of slow movement is addressed through lawful persistence, and compliance boundaries stay clear; no credit for simply siding with one stakeholder or proposing the broadest, slowest, or most risk-averse option.

reference_outline: State that the likely mechanism is not random bureaucracy alone but pressure around moving earlier through a queue-like, multi-step administrative chain, where each unresolved stage can delay the next and where paid 'unblocking' is a warning sign even without an explicit ask.
Name the tempting near-miss: treating this as a standard mature-market filing process in which complete paperwork and non-contact are enough, or assuming the only choices are pay or passively wait.

Choose the execution axis of timing and sequence: begin immediate lawful follow-up at the first stage, maintain a fixed contact cadence, log status after each touchpoint, and prepare downstream submissions in parallel so one delay does not create avoidable dead time.

Block the retired-consultant cash arrangement, route any third-party help through transparent contracted services only, and record why the proposed payment structure is unacceptable even if no direct illegal request has been made.

Assign roles operationally: local team or vetted vendor conducts scheduled in-person and phone follow-up; finance/compliance maintains records and approves any escalation; headquarters commits travel budget, overtime, and executive availability so refusal to shortcut does not translate into neglect.

Show motivational CQ by absorbing the inconvenience of repeated lawful engagement, uncertainty, and slower progress rather than withdrawing behind policy, blaming the local team, or overreacting with hostile pressure on officials.

Set escalation and repair triggers: if a file misses expected movement windows, escalate through formal supervisory channels, industry association routes, or documented legal review while continuing the base follow-up plan instead of freezing action.

Brief the VP that success depends on disciplined persistence with boundaries: the company avoids illicit acceleration, but it must invest visible effort to keep the process moving and protect relationships, timeline, and auditability under pressure.

scenario: In Berlin, a local coordinator and a newly arrived project officer are carrying a signed permit packet to a district office that stops accepting same-day filings at noon. Construction has fenced off their usual corner, adding a short detour, and the originals cannot be submitted digitally.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The works barrier pushes us to the next pedestrian light. If we miss noon, the filing rolls to tomorrow.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll take the folder and call ahead while we walk so they know we're close. If we move cleanly, we may still get the number ticket.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The office door is already in sight, but this crossing cycle can take a while.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I'll go across the tram island now with the originals and get the queue ticket started. You can come around with the barrier gap.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: There are still bikes filtering through that side lane, and I need to hand over the cover letter with the stamps attached.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll keep the packet flat and only cut over the last stretch where it's open, then wait by the machine so we don't lose more time.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We also have to submit the packet together at the window.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Fine, I'll get us as far ahead as I can and meet you inside.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer invests real effort and takes ownership, but places that effort in a cross-street shortcut with the originals, relying on a generic 'if the path looks open, advance anyway' assumption rather than adapting to Germany-specific pedestrian rule enforcement and norm compliance.

scenario: Your team is finalizing a one-paragraph arrival brief for conference guests staying in Rhodes and walking three minutes from the hotel to the venue. Legal wants the note to stay accurate, operations wants it short, and several guests will be from northern Europe.
question: Which direction should guide the pedestrian-safety line in the brief?

options.A: Tell guests to use marked crossings and pedestrian signals when they are nearby, while treating a crossing as a place to verify traffic has actually yielded before stepping out.
options.B: Tell guests to favor marked crossings and pedestrian signals when they are nearby, and to proceed there on the assumption that drivers will normally defer once the crossing is clear.
options.C: Tell guests that local driving flow can be unpredictable, so they should choose the shortest visible gap in traffic even if a marked crossing or signal is close by.
options.D: Tell guests to head for marked crossings and pedestrian signals when nearby, but to wait for a completely empty roadway before crossing rather than relying on the crossing itself.

scenario: You lead a multinational content team preparing a 90-second promo video for a nonprofit arts client launching in Rome. The final edit is due in 36 hours, and the client’s sponsor has already approved a teaser line promising “authentic Roman interior footage.” A freelancer on your team shot stills and short clips inside three churches on the same afternoon. In the shared folder, some files show tourists milling around; other clips clearly include a service in progress, candles lit near the front, and worshippers’ faces visible from the side. The freelancer’s note says, “No one stopped me, so it should be fine; these are public-facing interiors.” Your legal teammate in Berlin says to blur identifiable faces if needed and keep moving because the budget will not support a reshoot. Your brand manager in New York wants the strongest interior shots kept because outdoor footage looks generic. No one on the Rome side has yet reviewed the material, and the churches’ websites are inconsistent: one has visitor guidance, one has no obvious media policy online, and one site is temporarily down. You must send a same-day recommendation to your director on which footage can be used now, what must be checked first, and how the team should proceed without missing the deadline.
question: Write a decision memo to your director that sets the footage-use plan and the coordination sequence for the next 12 hours. Your memo must: diagnose the key local mechanism from the available evidence; identify the tempting but flawed assumption in the freelancer/legal/brand push; decide exactly which footage categories can move forward immediately versus which require a different approval route; and specify who should check what, through which channel, and in what order. Justify your plan in a way that shows why your decision is not just generic privacy caution or generic production efficiency.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden Rome-specific decision rule from scenario evidence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires inferring that interior church photography in Rome cannot be treated as automatically permissible based on public access or lack of immediate objection, with special weight on clips taken during a liturgical event; low credit if the answer only says 'be respectful' or 'watch privacy laws' without tying the rule to churches and service context.

rubric.point: Distinguishes footage by stage and setting rather than using one blanket rule
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires separating at least two categories, such as non-service interiors that may proceed only after checking posted rules or staff guidance, versus clips shot during Mass or comparable liturgical activity that should be held back pending direct verification or removed from immediate use; low credit for treating all church footage as equally usable or equally blocked.

rubric.point: Rejects the attractive near-miss that public visibility or face blurring solves the problem
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires explicitly bounding the idea that 'public place means free to shoot/use' and showing why blurring faces alone does not resolve the core issue; partial credit if the answer mentions privacy concerns but still treats the church footage as basically cleared once identities are obscured.

rubric.point: Applies cognitive CQ through exact evidence weighting and local category mapping
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires using the concrete clues in the case—interior churches, active service indicators, visible worshippers, inconsistent websites, no Rome review yet—to map which evidence matters most and which generic business/legal heuristics are misapplied; low credit if the answer relies on abstract cross-cultural principles without interpreting these clues.

rubric.point: Designs a concrete approval and coordination sequence on the primary axis
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires an operational next-12-hours sequence with role assignment, such as immediate internal hold/tagging of service footage, rapid review of any posted rules captured in images or site guidance, direct contact with church staff for unresolved interiors, and parallel editing of safer alternatives; low credit for vague advice to 'ask locals' or 'consult stakeholders' without order, owner, or channel.

rubric.point: Balances deadline pressure without turning delay into the whole answer
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires preserving progress by advancing lower-risk assets or alternate cuts while targeted checks happen, rather than halting the entire promo or defaulting to the most expansive review possible; low credit if the plan is simply to postpone everything or, conversely, to publish first and fix later.

rubric.point: Specifies communication framing to director and teammates
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires wording that explains the decision as a narrower use-condition issue tied to venue rules and context, not as a broad claim that all public photography in Europe is forbidden; low credit if the memo overstates the law, cites labels without operational consequences, or gives only generic compliance language.

reference_outline: State that the decisive issue is not whether the church was open to the public or whether no one intervened, but whether interior image capture and use in that venue and moment required checking posted rules and staff guidance, especially where a liturgical service appears to be underway.

Classify the assets into operational buckets: exterior/public street footage can proceed under normal review; church interior footage with no worship activity is conditionally usable only after rule/staff confirmation; footage showing Mass or comparable liturgical moments should be held from immediate use and treated as requiring direct verification or substitution.

Name the tempting imported assumption: the freelancer/legal/brand line that public visibility plus later editing fixes the issue. Explain that blurring faces addresses only part of the privacy risk and does not answer whether photography in that church context was acceptable in the first place.

Set a precise 12-hour sequence: freeze and label all church-interior clips; have one teammate review any captured signage, metadata, and website guidance; assign one person to contact church offices or staff for unresolved venues; have editors build a fallback cut using exterior and non-sensitive footage in parallel.

Explain why evidence is weighted this way: candles, front-facing service setup, and worshippers present are stronger cues than the absence of staff intervention; inconsistent websites increase the need for venue-specific checking rather than supporting a default yes.

Frame the memo to the director as a targeted risk-control plan that protects schedule and relationships: continue production on safer assets now, escalate only the church-interior material through the narrower verification path, and avoid overclaiming either unrestricted public-photo rights or a blanket ban.

Include a repair path if checks fail or responses do not arrive: swap in approved exterior/B-roll, remove unresolved interior service shots from the sponsor cut, and document the basis for excluding them so brand and legal understand it was a context-specific judgment rather than generic caution.

scenario: In Lagos, a newcomer is driving a company van carrying printed event materials and one overseas guest to a hotel briefing. They are late, the route is congested, and a traffic officer at a junction starts manually separating vehicles to clear one side first. The local colleague in the passenger seat is coordinating vendor calls and cannot take over driving.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: If we miss this hotel drop, the sponsor table opens without the badges. I still need to confirm the ballroom setup.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I’ll keep us moving and call ahead once we’re through this junction.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: There’s a manual control ahead. The lane markings stop making sense there when it backs up.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I see it. If they split the flow, I’d rather keep our van with the other event car so the guest and materials stay on one chain.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The second car is behind the buses now. Our printer is already waiting at the hotel entrance.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: If someone waves only us through, I’ll hold a moment and confirm before moving. In the last market I worked in, breaking convoy at a crowded point created pickup problems.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We’re at the front now. He’s pointing our van into the open side and sending the rest to wait.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I’m going to lower the window, explain we’re with the other car, and stay put until I reach our security lead so we don’t get separated.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The decisive behavior is culturally miscalibrated because the newcomer plans to delay and resist an immediate traffic officer direction in order to preserve convoy procedure. In this Nigeria seed, the officer’s real-time control of lane use and movement is a concrete legal authority, so the key execution axis is immediate public compliance rather than polite explanation or internal verification first.

scenario: A retail brand is activating a two-hour lunchtime promotion in central Nairobi. The crew plans to draw passersby from a fixed sidewalk spot using short sales calls and a portable speaker. No one has a sound meter, the permit packet is still in review, and the marketing lead argues that daytime activity in a busy commercial area usually gives more latitude than evening events near homes. You need to brief the crew now on the working rule until legal sends a final note.
question: Which guidance should anchor the briefing?

options.A: Treat the speaker as the main compliance issue: keep announcements brief and at a level that does not carry far enough to disrupt conversation beyond the immediate crowd.
options.B: Treat timing and surroundings as the main issue: daytime sales calls are workable in a commercial district, but avoid repeating them if the activation shifts toward mixed-use blocks later.
options.C: Treat measurement as the main issue: proceed with both voice calls and the speaker for now, then tighten or stop only if on-site checks show the sound traveling unusually far.
options.D: Treat the voice calls as the main issue: in the city center, do not use shouted selling lines at all, and keep any speaker use secondary and low enough not to dominate nearby public space.

scenario: You are the regional operations lead for a pan-African consumer brand. A product launch roadshow is scheduled in Accra in 12 days, with a dawn convoy, outdoor MC set, branded speaker trucks, and a Sunday evening thanksgiving service hosted by a partner congregation. The Ghana country manager says permits for traffic and venue use are moving normally, but several recent emails from venue staff and district officers use phrases like "sound levels should be managed this month," "keep activation quiet in the mornings," and "confirm whether percussion is essential." No one states that the event is blocked. Your Nairobi events manager argues these notes sound like routine urban noise compliance and proposes keeping the program intact while lowering decibel levels and filing an extra compliance memo. The sales VP insists the opening weekend cannot move because distributors and influencers are already booked, and the church partner expects public visibility. A legal colleague in London warns against cancelling religious or promotional elements without a clearly documented basis. You need to send a decision memo today that tells the team what to change now, what evidence to verify in the next 24 hours, and how to brief headquarters without looking indecisive or overreactive.
question: Draft the decision memo you would send. Specify: (1) your working diagnosis of what may be driving the local signals, based on the evidence you have; (2) the imported assumption or near-miss plan that looks reasonable but is miscalibrated here; (3) the exact changes you would make immediately to program sequence, sound use, and stakeholder coordination before full confirmation arrives; (4) the narrow evidence you would seek in the next 24 hours, from whom, and what findings would or would not change your plan; and (5) how you would brief the sales VP, legal, and the church partner so the team acts quickly without treating the issue as either ordinary city noise or a reason to freeze the whole launch.

rubric.point: Infers a time-bound citywide restriction affecting ordinary sound practices, not just venue-level decibel management.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer reads the signals as pointing to a broader locally grounded restriction that can override normal commercial and worship sound routines in Accra during this period; partial credit if it mentions 'sensitivity' or 'festival season' without operational implications; no credit if it treats the issue as standard permit or noise-threshold compliance only.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the attractive near-miss plan of keeping the program intact with lower volume and extra paperwork.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explains why a generic global noise-abatement response is too narrow here and would still misfire on the key issue; partial credit if it adds consultation but still preserves percussion, speaker-truck, or public worship amplification by default; no credit if it centers on decibel reduction, waiver-seeking, or legal memo coverage as the main solution.

rubric.point: Makes the correct execution choice on timing and sequence before full confirmation.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if it immediately redesigns the Accra program to remove or suspend the likely affected sonic elements first, especially percussion/high-profile amplified components, while preserving non-sonic launch tasks where possible; partial credit if it proposes broad delay of everything or waits for complete certainty; no credit if it keeps the original sound-heavy sequence pending confirmation.
