dialogue.text: The donor wants two images from today before 6 p.m. We can use the courtyard and arrival moments for sure, but I still need to know whether you'll try to capture anything inside.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll be careful. I was thinking one tight interior shot for texture, maybe the arranged table near the front, and then I'll stay out of everyone's way.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Inside gets sensitive fast, and the mãe de santo is tied up right now. Also, the team has already placed everything for later, so there isn't much room to adjust angles.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll avoid moving anything. If no one is free to brief me, I'll just take a quick close-up from where I'm standing so we don't miss the deadline.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We also need a short note for the donor on community hospitality, since they asked whether guests share what's prepared there.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Good point. If refreshments are already set out, I'll mention that visitors were welcomed with them unless someone tells me otherwise. That should read naturally.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Please send me your draft caption before posting. The driver is here in twenty minutes, so whatever you decide, keep it simple.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Will do. I'll keep the caption broad, grab that one interior detail shot now, and send you the text from the car.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer relies on generic visitor assumptions instead of calibrating to the Bahia terreiro context: he proceeds with a close interior shot of altar/offerings details without consent and assumes prepared items are for guest hospitality unless told otherwise, both of which conflict with the seed-specific rule about photos and offerings.

scenario: Your organization is producing a short documentary segment and visitor protocol for an interfaith travel platform. A multinational project team has three days to finalize the field plan for filming part of Qoyllur Rit'i in Peru. The executive producer in Madrid wants stronger footage and asks for a list of 'interactive access moments' that will make the segment feel immersive. The legal lead is mainly concerned with permits and crowd safety. A Peruvian logistics contractor has only confirmed transport, cold-weather support, and a contact for arrival coordination; they have not offered any interpretation of local expectations. Internal chat notes from prior travelers mention that groups come in under named community delegations, that certain figures on site manage order, and that visitors who 'act like audience members' can create trust problems even when they mean well. Budget is tight, weather windows are narrow, and the sponsor has warned that missing distinctive scenes could jeopardize renewal. Some teammates argue that the respectful global default is to request brief on-camera participation from whoever seems willing, capture close process shots from within the crowd, and rely on formal permissions plus visible courtesy to manage any concerns. Others worry that this could damage access, but no one can say exactly why from the material on hand.
question: Write a decision memo for the team lead that sets the field execution plan. Your memo must: identify the hidden cultural mechanism you think is operating from the evidence provided; name the most tempting but miscalibrated assumption in the current team discussion; specify exactly how the crew should position itself, seek access, and handle any people managing movement or order on site; and explain what effort the team should be willing to absorb to protect both the deliverable and local trust under deadline pressure. Be concrete about sequence, roles, boundaries, fallback options, and what you would and would not ask for on location.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the event as a community-structured devotional setting where outsiders must operate as guests observing an ongoing practice rather than as spectators optimizing content capture.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires inferring the mechanism from the evidence about community delegations, order-keeping figures, and trust risk, then translating it into operational consequences. Little or no credit for merely saying 'be respectful' or naming religion without changing field behavior.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the attractive near-miss plan of using generic permission-based access to create interactive or immersive footage.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires identifying why formal permission, willingness from isolated individuals, or brand-safe courtesy is insufficient if the crew still behaves like an audience or intervenes in the flow. Reduced credit if the answer only suggests 'ask more people first' or broadens consultation without changing the access model.

rubric.point: Makes the correct primary execution-axis choice on positioning and sequence: observe from the edges of activity, avoid inserting the crew into processional or devotional flow, and do not initiate participatory or staged interactions for content.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires concrete field choices about where the crew stands, what shots are ruled out, when to hold back, and how filming sequence follows the event rather than redirecting it. No full credit for culturally accurate facts applied at the wrong stage, such as planning respectful conduct only after entering the crowd.

rubric.point: Handles role-specific coordination with those managing discipline and order on site as functional authority over movement boundaries, not just as colorful local participants.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires assigning one crew member to monitor cues and immediately comply with direction on movement or proximity, with no debate in the moment. Reduced credit if the answer treats these actors mainly as interview subjects, visual assets, or optional contacts.

rubric.point: Shows motivational CQ through costly but targeted adaptive effort rather than intrusion or withdrawal.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires the team to absorb visible costs such as accepting less dramatic footage, longer waiting, extra reset time, or a narrower shot list in order to sustain trust and remain productively engaged. No full credit for energetic but intrusive persistence, respectful disengagement, or shifting the burden to locals to customize access for the crew.

rubric.point: Designs a bounded fallback and repair plan if sponsor pressure escalates or the crew misreads access in the moment.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires a practical fallback such as switching to observational wide shots, voiceover, off-site contextual material, or post-event explanation rather than pressing for closer participation; and a repair move that reduces presence and recenters on guest behavior. Reduced credit for vague 'pause and reassess' language without operational steps.

reference_outline: State that the pattern of organized community delegations plus designated order-keeping figures signals a setting where the crew should fit around an existing collective practice, not create participant-facing content moments.

Name the tempting imported assumption: if permits are in place and individuals seem willing, the crew can safely pursue immersive access through close interaction; explain why that would still mis-handle the situation.

Set the field sequence: brief crew before arrival, designate one boundary watcher, arrive with a minimal footprint, take observational positions, and allow movement patterns on site to determine where filming can occur rather than negotiating ad hoc inside the action.

Specify that no crew member solicits spontaneous participation, directs pilgrims for retakes, steps into organized group flow for better angles, or treats order-managing figures as performance elements; those figures are followed as practical authorities on spacing and conduct.

Accept visible costs as the right motivational move: give up some close-up or immersive footage, spend more time waiting for natural openings, and protect trust even if this weakens the sponsor's preferred shot list.

Use fallback options that preserve the deliverable without interference: observational footage from permitted boundaries, narration, ambient sound, interviews off the main activity path if appropriate, or contextual visuals gathered before or after peak moments.

Include a repair rule: if the crew causes friction or is redirected, comply immediately, reduce footprint, stop requesting access upgrades, and continue only within a guest posture instead of arguing from permits, deadlines, or production needs.

scenario: A museum media team in Peru is finalizing approvals for a short film about a village patron-saint weekend. The schedule includes a morning service in the church and an afternoon offering on nearby farmland, with many of the same families appearing in both. The local coordinator has submitted one packet signed by parish leaders and community authorities. Headquarters needs a documentation route today so the crew can travel tomorrow, and the archive team wants categories that will stay consistent across future projects.
question: Which approval decision should the manager make?

options.A: Approve one project file covering the full weekend, record both local sign-offs in that file, and avoid splitting participants into exclusive religious categories unless the community itself requires it.
options.B: Require two separate approval files, one for the church activities and one for the field activities, with distinct participant lists to keep the archive from combining conflicting religious material.
options.C: Approve one file for the outdoor activities, but open a second church-only approval file for anyone also appearing in the morning service so indoor religious participation is documented separately.
options.D: Route the whole film through the museum's general heritage documentation process, note the event as community culture rather than religion, and keep the archive categories broad to reduce classification disputes.

scenario:
You are the regional operations lead for a nonprofit rolling out a mobile water-testing unit in Tonga. The donor’s communications team in Australia wants drone footage, a blessing-style launch moment, and a same-week social media release because a funding board meets on Monday morning Sydney time. The local site manager in Nuku'alofa has sent a draft schedule that places equipment delivery on Saturday evening, a community launch at 8:00 a.m. Sunday near a church hall, and a volunteer football exhibition plus music after the speeches to attract families. A logistics vendor says shifting the launch to Monday will add overtime and may delay testing in two villages until Tuesday. In the message thread, several local participants sign off warmly but do not comment on the Sunday plan; one earlier district meeting note also begins and ends with short prayers. Your supervisor tells you not to 'overcomplicate this with culture' and asks for a decision memo within two hours that keeps the donor happy, protects relationships, and avoids public embarrassment. No one has yet announced the plan externally.

You must coordinate across the Tonga team, the Australian donor team, and the logistics vendor. Assume you cannot get a fully new legal opinion before the memo deadline, and you only have the current emails, meeting notes, and schedule draft.
question: Write the decision memo you would send to your supervisor. It must specify: (1) what parts of the current plan you will stop, move, or keep; (2) the exact stakeholder sequence and channel you will use in the next 24 hours; (3) how you will word the change to the donor team and to the Tonga-based team; and (4) what you will do to preserve momentum without treating the issue as a generic 'let's just ask locals more' delay. Your memo should identify the tempting imported assumption in the current draft and explain why your execution choices fit the evidence better.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden mechanism from scenario evidence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that Sunday in Tonga is not just a convenient weekend launch day but a day requiring practical non-activity constraints that affect event timing, public noise, recreation, work, and operational setup, using clues from the Sunday schedule and prayer-structured meeting notes. No credit for merely saying 'be respectful of religion' or naming Christianity without operational consequences.

rubric.point: Makes the correct timing-and-sequence decision on the core axis
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly stops or moves the Sunday launch and related operational/public activities off Sunday rather than merely softening them, shortening them, or rebranding them. Partial credit if it removes some obvious elements like music or football but still keeps delivery, launch, setup, or public activation on Sunday.

rubric.point: Rejects the polished near-miss plan
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer identifies the attractive but wrong assumption that a generic global weekend event plan can proceed with minor sensitivity tweaks, disclaimers, or optional attendance, and explains why that efficient compromise is miscalibrated in Tonga. Low credit if it proposes a courteous version of the same Sunday plan, such as keeping the launch but adding prayer, lowering volume, or making activities 'community-led.'

rubric.point: Shows behavioural CQ through visible coordination choices
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer chooses concrete channels, audience order, wording, and rhythm: first privately align internal decision-makers, then notify Tonga-side counterparts directly before any broad donor-facing or public communication, with wording that states a schedule adjustment clearly and matter-of-factly rather than debating local belief. Low credit for generic consultation, reply-all escalation, or publicly floating Sunday as an open question.

rubric.point: Uses prayer and meeting form appropriately without overextending it
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer treats prayer-structured meetings as evidence for how gatherings may be framed and therefore adjusts meeting/event format appropriately, such as allowing a formal opening or closing prayer in the rescheduled launch if local counterparts choose, without assuming prayer alone makes a Sunday event acceptable. Low credit if it uses prayer as the fix that preserves the Sunday launch.

rubric.point: Designs a concrete momentum-preserving alternative under pressure
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer preserves project progress by separating what can be quietly prepared before Sunday from what must not occur on Sunday, and gives a credible Monday or non-Sunday launch sequence that manages donor optics and village testing impact. Low credit for indefinite postponement, maximal shutdown of all work regardless of stage, or a broad 'wait for more input' answer.

rubric.point: Includes role-specific repair and risk control
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer anticipates reputational risk and assigns who will contact the vendor, who will reset donor expectations, and how to prevent accidental public promotion of the Sunday plan. Low credit for abstract statements about alignment or risk management without actor-by-actor execution.

reference_outline: Infer from the Sunday launch draft, public-event elements, and prayer-framed meeting notes that the key issue is not generic faith sensitivity but Tonga-specific restrictions on Sunday activity, so a Sunday public launch and related operational/event components should not proceed.

Choose the main execution-axis move: cancel or shift the Sunday launch, Sunday setup/delivery tied to activation, and attraction activities; move the public/community-facing launch to Monday or another non-Sunday slot, while tightly limiting any pre-Sunday preparation to non-public, non-disruptive steps that do not amount to Sunday business/event activity.

Sequence stakeholders behaviourally: first brief the supervisor with a firm recommendation, then contact the Tonga site manager privately and directly to align on the revised schedule and acceptable Monday format, then instruct the vendor on revised logistics, then update the Australian donor team with a clear alternative plan before any public announcement.

Frame donor communication around execution and reputational protection: say the current timing creates a high risk of misalignment in Tonga and public embarrassment, so the launch is being rescheduled while donor assets are preserved through Monday coverage or alternate pre-recorded material; do not present it as an open culture debate or ask the donor to choose.

Frame Tonga-side communication clearly and concretely: acknowledge the schedule adjustment, confirm the team is protecting community fit and the project’s standing, and discuss whether the rescheduled gathering should open/close in the locally appropriate meeting form, without treating prayer as a workaround for Sunday activation.

Reject the near-miss plan explicitly: do not keep the Sunday event by reducing noise, cutting football, shortening the program, or adding a blessing/prayer; those are plausible global fixes but still miss the decisive timing boundary.

Preserve momentum under constraints by offering a replacement workflow: use Saturday for permitted wrap-up only if already appropriate, hold Sunday free of launch/event activity, prepare donor messaging and Monday run-sheet, and start village testing immediately after the rescheduled launch or in a sequence agreed with the local team that avoids Sunday breach while minimizing Tuesday slippage.

Add repair and monitoring steps: stop any outgoing Sunday promotions, assign one owner for vendor rescheduling and one for donor reset, and check revised wording/materials so no remaining asset implies Sunday operation or entertainment.

scenario: A newcomer coordinating a visiting donor team in Niue needs to gather a few scenic clips and still attend a village service later that morning. The donor wants same-day social media material, and transport has already been booked. The local counterpart is focused on keeping the schedule intact and not inconveniencing hosts.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The van can take us past the west side before the service, then straight to the hall. The donor team still hopes for a few coastal shots today.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Great, I'll keep it tight. We'll stop near the shore for ten minutes, get a quick water clip from the path, and then join everyone at the service in formal clothes.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The choir starts exactly at eleven, and people will already be settling in by then. We should not arrive flustered.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll have the camera team ready beforehand so we can move fast and be seated before it begins. Once inside, I'll put phones away and follow what everyone else does.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Afterward, the elders want a short thank-you from the visitors, and the donor office keeps asking whether we can post something by afternoon.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll skip filming inside and keep the thank-you brief. To meet the deadline, I'll use the shoreline footage from this morning and draft the caption while we're waiting outside.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. The driver only has one route in and out, so timing matters.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then we'll stick with that plan: quick coastal footage first, quiet arrival, no devices during the service, and the post goes out later today.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer sounds organized and respectful inside the church, but the decisive behavior is still miscalibrated for Niue: on Sunday they plan to collect shoreline footage from a path by the water before the service, relying on a generic 'be discreet and punctual at worship' default instead of applying the stricter Sunday sacred-space restrictions around churches and nearby sea access during services.

scenario: Your team is finalizing a museum opening in New Zealand for a newly installed collection that includes ancestral material. The plan has a short welcome in the gallery at 5:30 and canapes at 6:00. For convenience, venue staff have staged glasses, plates, and a drinks station along one wall inside the gallery, to be rolled out after the welcome. The community adviser who reviewed the installation is unreachable until morning, but the event brief must go to catering tonight. Which briefing decision should you send?
question: Which briefing decision is the best one to send tonight?

options.A: Keep the reception in the gallery after the welcome, but remove the drinks station and serve only hand-passed items so food is not set down near the collection.
options.B: Pause all catering for this event and keep food service out of the entire wing until the adviser confirms whether refreshments anywhere nearby would create a problem.
options.C: Move all food, drink, plates, glasses, and serving equipment out of the gallery now, and run the reception in the adjacent foyer unless local review later reopens that room.
options.D: Leave the gallery setup in place, add a note in the program that refreshments are optional, and let guests choose whether to eat in the gallery or wait until they exit.

scenario: You are the program manager for a multicultural museum-tech team preparing a 48-hour pilot install for a regional heritage center in Australia. The pilot must be ready before a ministerial walkthrough, and your supervisor has already promised the client that the team can reuse existing on-site materials to stay within budget. During a site visit, you notice a locked glass cabinet is open for cleaning, and several carved items have been placed on a side table near a room that also contains old photographs, a fenced-off patch of ground visible through a rear door, and boxes labeled for temporary storage. No item is physically blocked from handling, and the venue operations coordinator says only that 'the back area is being reorganized' and asks for the install plan by 3 p.m. Your German facilities lead wants to move the carved items into the entrance display because they are 'already out and undocumented placement causes insurance risk.' Your Singaporean client-services colleague wants one approval email covering all movable objects and spaces so the ministerial route is not delayed. A previous message from the center mentioned that some materials on site are 'community-linked' and that final wording and placement should avoid surprises, but it did not specify which materials or areas this referred to. You have one local staff contact available before 3 p.m., but that person is not the formal signatory on the contract. By 5 p.m. you must send a coordination memo telling the team what can proceed today, what must wait, and who needs to be involved.
question: Write the coordination memo you would send by 5 p.m. Describe: (1) your working diagnosis of what the ambiguous site cues mean and what assumption you think your teammates are most likely importing incorrectly; (2) the exact sequence of actions you would allow, pause, or reroute before the walkthrough; (3) which person or role you would consult first, what you would ask them, and what evidence would or would not be enough to proceed; and (4) how you would brief your team so they can keep work moving without turning your uncertainty into either blanket delay or overconfident reuse.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that physical accessibility is not sufficient evidence for handling, moving, entering, or repurposing the items or nearby area.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers from the mixed cues that some objects/spaces may carry restrictions despite being visible or currently accessible, and treats access as ambiguous rather than permissive. No credit for assuming that open cabinet, side-table placement, or current cleaning status makes them available for reuse.

rubric.point: Identifies and bounds the tempting near-miss assumption.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly rejects the imported default that one general facilities/compliance approval or ordinary site access is enough to clear all objects and spaces for operational use. Partial credit if it notes risk in general terms but does not name the mistaken execution logic.

rubric.point: Makes the primary execution-axis decision on approval scope and sequence.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan separates immediate low-risk work from any touching, moving, display placement, storage transfer, or route use involving the ambiguous objects/area, and routes those decisions through the right permission path before action. No credit for broad site freeze, or for proceeding first and documenting later.

rubric.point: Uses metacognitive CQ by stating what can be inferred now, what remains unknown, and what evidence would change the plan.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer distinguishes provisional inference from certainty, names the key unknowns, and specifies what kind of confirmation is decision-relevant (for example, role-based local guidance or explicit permission tied to the specific items/space) rather than collecting generic reassurance.

rubric.point: Chooses a role-specific first contact and asks narrowing questions that reduce the right uncertainty.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer consults the available local contact first to map which items/spaces require special handling and who actually has authority over them, while recognizing that this person may inform the route but not substitute for final permission. Partial credit for 'ask locals' without specifying role, scope, or question design.

rubric.point: Designs a work-moving coordination plan under deadline pressure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo keeps unrelated pilot tasks moving today—such as digital setup, signage drafts not tied to those items, traffic-flow planning outside ambiguous areas, or alternative display placeholders—while pausing only the restricted-scope actions. No credit for the safest-longest answer that delays all preparation.

rubric.point: Briefs teammates in a way that prevents wrong-stage action by other functions.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer gives concrete instructions to the facilities and client-services leads about what they must not do yet, why one umbrella approval is insufficient, and what approval/documentation threshold is required before moving, entering, or repurposing anything ambiguous. Partial credit for vague 'be respectful' guidance.

reference_outline: State a provisional diagnosis: the carved items and adjacent area may be subject to culturally specific restrictions linked to object history, contact, burial-related association, or controlled access, so current visibility/open access is not enough to treat them as operational assets.

Name the near-miss: applying a generic museum/facilities default that accessible items can be temporarily relocated or covered by one compliance-style approval, plus the adjacent assumption that an available room or path is usable unless physically blocked.

Set the sequence: continue non-contact setup work; stop any touching, moving, storing, displaying, or routing through the ambiguous objects/space; do not include them in the ministerial path or entrance display until item-specific and place-specific clearance is established.

Contact the available local staff member immediately to identify which objects/areas are sensitive, what categories of restriction may apply, and who the recognized decision-maker is; treat this as mapping authority and boundaries, not as automatic permission.

Escalate next to the appropriate authorized local/community or institutional approver for explicit clearance tied to the exact items/space and intended action, because handling, entering, moving, and repurposing may each require separate permission judgments.

Tell the German facilities lead not to relocate the carved items for insurance/orderliness reasons yet, and tell the Singaporean client-services colleague that one blanket approval email is the wrong scope; approvals must match the specific object/place and proposed use.

Show metacognitive calibration by writing what is known now, what is only suspected, and what evidence would justify updating the plan; avoid both premature certainty and empty caution that halts the whole pilot.

Offer repair and contingency: if approval cannot be confirmed before the walkthrough, use alternative materials/placeholder displays and reroute the ministerial visit away from the ambiguous area, while documenting the hold and preserving trust with the center.

scenario: A newcomer is coordinating a short video segment for a community event in Oceania. The visiting donor wants shoreline footage before sunset, and the only clean camera angle appears to be from a side path near a ceremonial area. At the entrance to that path, a small bundle of coconut leaves has been tied across two stakes, while the printed event map does not mention any closure.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We have about twenty minutes before the donor car leaves. The main stage is crowded, so if you need a quiet shoreline shot, check the side path near the old meeting ground.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I walked over there just now. The path is empty except for a leaf tie across the entrance. Since the printed map shows it open, I think it's probably a temporary marker from setup.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The map was printed last week, and a few things changed this morning. We still need the clip before sunset if possible.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll keep the crew out, go in alone for two minutes, get the wide shot fast, and be back before anyone notices a delay.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The donor team is asking me now whether the shoreline footage is confirmed.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Tell them yes on timing. If that path stays awkward, I'll at least capture something from just inside the entrance so we don't lose the window.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right, I need to stay with the guests. Message me once you've decided the angle.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Will do. I'll make the quickest call on site and keep the schedule intact.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer misreads the tied coconut leaves as a flexible setup marker instead of a customary prohibition signal. The decisive error is the execution choice: treating brief, solo, low-impact entry as acceptable, when entry itself into an area under fono is strictly forbidden.

scenario: On Sunday morning in Niue, a field team needs shoreline footage and a short site walk before a Monday 8 a.m. briefing with senior officials. The team is already dressed plainly and can do prep work without filming if needed.
question: What should the team do next?

options.A: Take the faster route now, pass the church area before the service starts, and keep cameras packed until the team reaches the shoreline section.
options.B: Enter quietly at the rear for a few minutes, then leave once the service is underway and begin the shoreline walk after the opening prayers.
options.C: Use the inland route now for nonfilming prep work, then do the shoreline walk and any footage only after the service has ended.
options.D: Use the coastal route during the service, move through without stopping, and check with nearby residents on the way whether the passage is acceptable.

scenario: You manage rollout logistics for a regional public-health NGO. Next Thursday your multicultural project team will host a 70-minute community launch meeting in a village hall in Fiji for a maternal-health pilot. The donor wants photos and a same-day social post showing the launch happened on schedule before 7:30 p.m. Your Australia-based communications lead has drafted a standard run sheet that opens with a brief land acknowledgment, then the district health officer, then your project manager, then a participant story, with a buffet served as soon as the speeches end. The hall booking ends at 8:15 p.m., and the generator outside is noisy when restarted after shutdown.
question: Write a concise decision memo for your team that sets the meeting-opening and meal sequence. Your memo must: (1) diagnose what hidden local mechanism is most relevant from the facts given, (2) identify the tempting imported assumption in the current plan, (3) specify who you would verify, acknowledge, and sequence before the meeting and on the floor, and (4) explain how your plan controls schedule, neutrality, and relationship risk without turning into a generic 'ask everyone' or 'delay until fully certain' answer.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the operative mechanism as procedural authority embedded in shared community life, not mere private belief or optional courtesy.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers from the scenario that religious figures and ritual may have a formal place in meeting procedure and community authority in this Fiji setting; no credit for saying only 'be respectful of religion' or naming tolerance/inclusion in general.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the neutral-global near-miss plan.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly identifies the attractive mistake in the draft plan as treating religion as something to omit for fairness, and explains why that would misread the local setting; partial credit if it notes risk but still leaves religious elements as optional add-ons after the formal opening.

rubric.point: Applies the mechanism to the exact execution axis: opening order and meal sequence.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer makes concrete sequence choices such as verifying who must be acknowledged, ordering acknowledgments/speakers with government, traditional, and religious roles handled deliberately, and building prayer/grace into start/end or meal transition where appropriate; no full credit for broad consultation without a floor sequence.

rubric.point: Uses cognitive CQ by distinguishing relevant evidence from misleading process defaults.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer weighs the incomplete RSVP list, expected attendance of church figures, hall timing, and evening constraints as evidence that the team must infer a likely procedural requirement rather than default to headquarters SOP; partial credit for mentioning ambiguity without showing how it changes interpretation.

rubric.point: Assigns role-specific verification before the event.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer identifies a narrow verification route—for example, confirming with the field coordinator or host-side organizers exactly who must be acknowledged and in what order—rather than sending a broad open call or waiting for all invitees to reply.

rubric.point: Controls time pressure without stripping out the culturally significant sequence.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer preserves the key opening/meal elements while shortening elsewhere, such as tightening speech lengths or photo timing; no credit if it solves schedule pressure by removing the opening ritual/acknowledgment issue or by proposing indefinite delay.

rubric.point: Handles wording and stage scope precisely.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer shows that the acknowledgment/prayer issue affects the public meeting procedure itself, not just backstage hospitality or private side conversations; partial credit if it places the right idea at the wrong stage, such as only adding thanks in a printed program.

reference_outline: Infer that in this Fiji village launch, church leadership and Christian ritual may function as visible parts of formal community procedure, especially in openings, closings, and meals, not just as private preferences.
State that the imported near-miss is the NGO-style neutrality assumption: omitting religious procedure to appear fair would likely mis-sequence authority rather than create true balance.

Before the meeting, use a narrow verification chain through host-side coordination to confirm exactly which government, traditional, and religious figures must be acknowledged and in what order; do not rely on the incomplete RSVP list alone.

Revise the run sheet so the formal opening deliberately accommodates the expected acknowledgment order and any opening prayer if required, rather than inserting it casually after institutional remarks.
Build the meal transition around expected grace or closing procedure before service begins, instead of releasing people directly to the buffet on a generic event timetable.
Protect the deadline by compressing speech length, photography, and donor remarks, not by stripping out the locally significant opening sequence.

Explain the decision to teammates as a work-performance choice: the aim is to match local authority structure and procedural expectations with minimal disruption, not to favor one belief group abstractly.

Include a repair fallback: if a key religious or customary figure arrives after the planned start, pause before moving into the meal or main remarks and correct the acknowledgment/order publicly in a contained way rather than ignoring the omission.

scenario: In Taipei, a newcomer operations manager is helping a local colleague prepare a short briefing for headquarters after a delivery van blocked a marked crossing outside their building during the morning rush. A traffic officer had already redirected people through a side lane and left before they came downstairs. Headquarters wants a same-day note on whether the company should treat the incident as a facilities inconvenience only or send the images and timeline to the relevant office. The local colleague is focused on not overstepping, while the newcomer must decide how to act before the afternoon reporting deadline.

roles.local: Local colleague in Taipei facilities team

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: I pulled the loading dock photos and the guard's notes. The officer on site had people use the side lane for a few minutes, then traffic cleared. HQ wants our summary by three.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Let's separate what we know from what we don't. I'll note the officer's direction as part of the incident sequence, and I'll review the timestamps before we send anything.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The van belongs to a vendor we still use. If this goes into a regional deck, procurement may ask why facilities escalated it instead of just warning the driver.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I won't make it a public internal issue first. I'll keep the HQ note factual, and if the photos and guard log line up, I'll send the file through the normal external reporting channel rather than treating it as only a vendor conversation.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The guard also wrote down that two pedestrians hesitated and then crossed where the officer was pointing. We don't have everyone's names, only the vehicle plate and time.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: That's enough for a factual packet, not a conclusion. I'll attach the plate, images, and the guard account, and say the authority can verify the rest. Then I'll tell procurement separately that we're still expecting the afternoon delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: So you want to file it today even though the officer already handled the scene?

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Yes. The scene response and the follow-up record serve different purposes, so I'll do both pieces now and keep the wording narrow.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer's decisive behavior matches the Taiwan public-norm mechanism on two axes: treating the on-scene officer's direction as authoritative in the factual account, and using formal citizen-assisted reporting with concrete evidence for a suspected traffic violation rather than limiting the matter to a private vendor warning. The calibration is metacognitive because the newcomer distinguishes what is known, what remains for authorities to confirm, and still acts before the deadline.

scenario: A UK operations lead is briefing brand staff for a two-day transit promotion in Hong Kong at ferry piers and tram stops. Break coverage is tight, and several staff ask whether smoking can be allowed when they wait near boarding bays, especially if people are standing in a loose curved line rather than a straight one. The local agency wants one rule for all stops before call time.
question: Which policy scope should the operations lead set for the team?

options.A: Allow smoking unless it blocks boarding or draws complaints, and treat waiting lines near transit stops as a courtesy issue rather than part of the operating rule.
options.B: Ban smoking inside marked boarding zones, but allow it a short distance outside the markings even when riders are already assembled in a curved or staggered line.
options.C: Ban smoking once boarding begins and people start moving toward the vehicle, but allow it during the waiting period if staff remain at the outer edge of the group.
options.D: Ban smoking whenever staff are in a boarding area or holding a place in a line for transit, even if the line bends, spreads out, or lacks clear markings.

scenario: You manage a regional field-activation team preparing a one-day promotional campaign tied to a mobile wallet launch in Hong Kong. The campaign uses branded staff at three busy bus interchanges during the Monday morning commute to hand out QR cards and direct people to a nearby sign-up booth. Your supervisor in Singapore wants visible footfall and insists that long lines near the booth will make the campaign look successful in photos. A vendor from another market proposes a 'fast capture' tactic used elsewhere: have roaming promoters step toward approaching passengers, pull interested people out of the flow before they reach the stop, and create a separate priority line for people who scan first. The Hong Kong operations lead is worried about complaints after a prior activation drew criticism for slowing boarding, but has not given a legal explanation. Budget is tight, permits are already filed, and changing the site layout tonight will require extra overtime and a reduced photo team. Your team includes staff from Singapore, India, and the UK, and they are split: some want the fastest lead-capture setup, while others want to keep everything 'orderly' in a general sense without knowing how far to redesign the plan.
question: Write a decision memo for your team that gives a concrete rollout plan for tomorrow morning. Your memo must: (1) diagnose the hidden local mechanism shaping what is risky here, using only the scenario evidence; (2) identify the most tempting imported assumption in the vendor's plan and explain why it is miscalibrated; (3) specify the operating sequence, staff placement, and escalation boundary for the interchange activations; and (4) show what adaptive effort you personally will invest tonight and during the morning launch to keep the campaign on track without shifting the burden to local staff or simply canceling the activation.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that the core risk is not just social annoyance or brand optics, but entering a transport/public-order context where queue and boarding flow are treated as enforceable constraints.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that line discipline and boarding/alighting flow at Hong Kong bus interchanges must be handled as rule-backed operational boundaries. Partial credit for mentioning crowd sensitivity or commuter irritation without the stronger enforcement implication.

rubric.point: Rejects the attractive near-miss plan of using generic high-conversion street-promo tactics around approaching passengers and a priority side line.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explains that the vendor's plan is tempting because it boosts leads and satisfies photo/KPI pressure, yet misfires by pulling people out of queue order or impeding boarding flow in the transport setting. No full credit for generic statements like 'it may confuse people' or 'it might be seen as rude.'

rubric.point: Makes the primary execution-axis decision on timing and sequence: engagement must occur without disrupting existing queue/boarding order, not merely with friendlier wording.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer sets a concrete sequence such as placing outreach before queue formation zones, after passengers have cleared boarding/alighting paths, or at a separate area that does not create a competing line near the stop. Answers that keep the same line-adjacent tactic but add politeness, more signage, or verbal reminders do not earn full credit.

rubric.point: Designs role-specific placement and escalation boundaries for staff.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer assigns who monitors passenger flow, who handles outreach, where staff may not stand, and when activity pauses or relocates if boarding/alighting slows, complaints emerge, or crowding forms. Vague 'coordinate with the team' answers do not earn full credit.

rubric.point: Shows motivational CQ through costly, bounded adaptive effort by the respondent.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer includes visible personal effort such as taking the overtime hit to rework layout/materials tonight, briefing the mixed-nationality team on a narrower operating rule, arriving early to test placement, and owning live adjustments during launch. No full credit for simply telling Hong Kong staff to monitor, asking them to decide everything on site, or postponing action under the banner of caution.

rubric.point: Balances progress with constraint management instead of defaulting to the biggest, safest, or most consultative response.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer preserves the campaign objective in a narrowed form—e.g., reduced capture volume, relocated sign-up funnel, or changed photo expectations—while keeping the transport-flow boundary intact. No full credit for canceling the activation outright without showing why a tighter compliant design is still workable.

rubric.point: Uses evidence from the scenario to justify calibration under ambiguity.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer cites specific clues such as the prior complaint about slowed boarding, the bus interchange setting, morning commute density, and the proposed side-line tactic to support the decision. Generic 'learn the local culture' language or unsupported assertions do not earn full credit.

reference_outline: Infer from the bus-interchange setting, morning commute, prior complaint about slowing boarding, and the proposed queue-diverting tactic that this is a transport public-order problem with harder boundaries than ordinary promo etiquette.

State that the vendor's imported assumption is that queue handling is mainly an informal customer-experience issue, so creating a faster side line or intercepting passengers near the stop is acceptable if done efficiently; reject that assumption because it risks disrupting protected boarding order and passenger flow.

Redesign the sequence so staff engage only in a clearly separate zone that does not compete with the bus queue, and do not approach people once they are effectively joining or moving through the boarding flow.

Assign specific roles: one staffer watches flow and has authority to halt outreach, one handles sign-up away from the stop, one distributes materials only at approved positions, and no one steps into boarding/alighting paths or invites queue splitting.

Invest personal effort tonight by approving overtime for layout changes, resetting KPI/photo expectations with the supervisor, rewriting the staff brief, and owning the uncomfortable tradeoff of lower apparent footfall in exchange for a workable launch.

Invest personal effort during launch by arriving early, checking real passenger movement, enforcing the narrower setup even if conversion looks lower at first, and adjusting quickly rather than telling local colleagues to absorb the judgment call alone.

Set a repair/escalation boundary: pause or relocate immediately if staff see queue distortion, passenger complaints, or slowed boarding, and document the change as operational risk control rather than waiting for a bigger incident.

Keep the activation alive in reduced form rather than canceling by default: preserve lead capture through separated signage, QR distribution outside the queue path, and controlled handoff to the booth.

scenario: A newcomer renting a flat in Singapore has had two nights of dragging sounds and brief hammering from a nearby unit, once after 11pm and again before sunrise. He has an early client session tomorrow, wants the noise to stop quickly, and is trying to handle it in a way that feels measured rather than confrontational.

roles.local: Local teammate who grew up in Singapore
roles.newcomer: Newly relocated colleague renting the flat

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Rough night again?

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Yes. I logged the times, walked the corridor to make sure I had the right side, and now I'm running on coffee before tomorrow's client session.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: So you know which unit it's likely from?

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Almost certainly the one opposite the lift lobby. I spent an hour drafting a neutral note for the estate contact so they can pass it along without making my first month here awkward.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: You're trying to keep it low-friction.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Exactly. I also pulled together the timings in case I need to open a mediation request later. I'd rather make the process tidy than knock on their door half-asleep and misread the situation.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: What if it happens again tonight?

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll send the note first thing, use earplugs tonight, and only approach them myself if the building side can't settle it after that.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer shows real effort, but he places it in anonymous documentation and third-party handling before making direct first contact with the neighbour. In this Singapore noise-complaint sequence, the misstep is the channel and order of engagement, not his tone or diligence.

scenario: You are briefing front-of-house supervisors for a museum opening in Hong Kong. The entrance uses rope barriers, and visitors often line up outside before the doors open. Ten minutes before opening, a supervisor asks what exact first line staff should use if someone in that line lights a cigarette. Security can come later if needed, but the card must give one short line staff can say immediately.
question: Which wording should go on the briefing card?

options.A: Excuse me, if you want to smoke, please step a little farther from the doorway and keep clear of the entrance area before joining the line again.
options.B: Excuse me, this area is smoke-free; please leave the queue, finish your cigarette away from the entrance, and then come back when you are ready to enter.
options.C: Excuse me, smoking is not allowed while waiting here to enter; please put it out now or step away from the line.
options.D: Excuse me, this is a smoke-free entrance area; if you prefer to continue, please show your name and identification to the supervisor here.

scenario: You lead a multicultural operations team preparing a 10-day pilot at a Hong Kong transit-linked shopping complex for a new mobile preorder pickup service. The client wants the pickup point open before a holiday weekend and has rejected adding more staff. Your team includes a product manager from Germany, a service designer from Singapore, and a regional brand lead in Seoul. A draft plan proposes one fast lane for app users, one general line, and a host who can pull forward 'obvious quick pickups' to keep throughput high. In a previous walkthrough, the mall facilities manager objected to a temporary sign placed near the MTR-facing entrance, saying only that crowd flow there becomes 'sensitive very quickly.' A junior Hong Kong vendor also rewrote your draft customer script, removing a sentence that told waiting customers they could 'step aside briefly and re-enter near the front if they already paid.' The client is pressing for visible speed metrics, and your supervisor wants a single decision memo by 5 p.m. explaining the launch design, staff instructions, and what evidence you are using rather than escalating for more meetings.
question: Write the decision memo you would send to your supervisor. It must: (1) diagnose the hidden local mechanism shaping the queue design, using only the scenario evidence; (2) identify the most tempting imported assumption in the current draft and why it is miscalibrated here; (3) choose a concrete queue-management design and staff sequence for launch day, including where not to place discretion; and (4) explain how you would justify this plan to the client and coordinate the Germany, Singapore, and Seoul teammates without turning the answer into a generic 'be respectful and consult more' response.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the Hong Kong-specific mechanism as more than customer preference or etiquette
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that orderly queue access in this Hong Kong public-facing setting must be treated as a strongly enforced shared-access norm with public-order consequences, not merely as a service-style choice; partial credit for noting 'people care about fairness' without linking that logic to the operational seriousness implied by the scenario.

rubric.point: Identifies and bounds the tempting near-miss assumption in the draft plan
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly rejects or tightly limits the imported assumption that common global throughput tactics—pulling forward quick cases, allowing paid customers to rejoin near the front, or using staff discretion to optimize speed—are acceptable here; partial credit if it rejects only one tactic without naming the broader mistaken logic.

rubric.point: Makes the correct execution-axis decision on queue sequence and discretion
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer centers the design on preserving strict, visible first-come order within each clearly defined line, eliminates ad hoc front-of-line recovery, and assigns staff to direct customers before line formation rather than to reorder people once queued; no full credit for answers that keep a 'fast but fair' exception system or move the discretion to a later stage.

rubric.point: Applies cultural knowledge at the right scope, actor, and stage
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer applies the mechanism to the entrance-facing pickup flow, signage placement, host script, and launch-day staffing rules in this Hong Kong site; partial credit for accurate cultural knowledge used too broadly ('all of Asia') or at the wrong level (general brand tone, only back-end staffing, or private VIP handling).

rubric.point: Uses cognitive CQ by weighing ambiguous evidence and separating explanations
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer shows why the facilities manager's crowd-flow comment, the vendor's script change, and the transit-facing location together support a specific local interpretation over generic alternatives like efficiency, personality, or mall preference; partial credit for asserting the interpretation without comparing it to plausible non-cultural explanations.

rubric.point: Designs role-specific coordination for the multicultural team
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer translates the decision into concrete instructions for teammates, such as telling the German product manager not to optimize reported wait time through line-skipping mechanics, the Singapore designer to redesign signage around lane clarity rather than exception handling, and the Seoul brand lead to frame fairness/order as trust protection rather than just hospitality; partial credit for generic 'align the team' language.

rubric.point: Justifies the plan to the client under deadline and metric pressure
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer gives a concise business-facing rationale that protects launch viability by reducing conflict/escalation risk and preserving predictable access, while offering alternative metrics or controls that do not depend on front-of-line exceptions; no full credit for answers that simply delay launch, ask for more research, or maximize staffing beyond the stated constraints.

reference_outline: State that the key issue is not mere politeness but that this Hong Kong transit-adjacent public queue must be managed as an orderly shared-access system where visible line integrity matters operationally.

Interpret the clues together: the MTR-facing entrance, the facilities manager's sensitivity to crowd flow, and the local vendor removing re-entry-near-the-front language all signal that discretionary queue disruption is the real risk.

Reject the near-miss plan of boosting throughput through host discretion, quick-pickup pull-forward, or paid-customer re-entry near the front; explain that these are attractive global service tactics but misread the local boundary here.

Choose a launch design with clearly separated lanes only if each lane has unambiguous entry criteria from the start, fixed signage before customers join, and no staff authority to resequence people once lined up.

Assign staff to upstream triage and lane direction, not downstream exception handling: one person directs customers into the correct queue before entry, one verifies eligibility at the service point, and nobody invites customers to reclaim a forward position after stepping out.

Tell the client that the plan protects throughput by preventing disputes, bottlenecks, and reputational damage at a high-flow entrance; offer compliant metrics such as time-to-pickup within lane, queue abandonment, and mis-entry rate instead of 'customers accelerated out of order.'

Coordinate the team with role-specific guidance: product removes queue-skipping logic from the SOP, design rewrites scripts/signage to stress lane clarity and exact joining points, and brand frames the experience around reliable orderly access rather than personalized speed exceptions.

Acknowledge uncertainty without defaulting to delay: monitor line breaks, customer challenges, and staff improvisation during the pilot, and repair by tightening lane definitions or physical markers rather than introducing more discretionary exceptions.

scenario: A foreign sales manager in Shanghai is trying to recover a stalled hospital equipment registration before a trade fair demo next week. A bureau contact has stopped replying to formal emails, but a local distributor says the contact will attend a small dinner with several long-term partners that evening. The company has strict rules against side payments, and the newcomer must decide how to handle the next step without losing the relationship or the timeline.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The file is still sitting there. He ignored the last two status emails, but he'll be at tonight's supplier dinner. We only have six days before the demo team arrives.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I won't bring the paperwork to the table or ask him for a decision in front of everyone. I'll attend, keep it social, and ask our host to seat me near him so we can reconnect first.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That dinner is mostly old contacts and family-friend introductions. Finance also asked me this morning whether you need any special hospitality budget approved.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: No envelopes, no favors, and nothing tied to the file. I'll use the normal hosting budget, bring the product photos he asked about last month, and after we've talked a while I'll mention that our team will be in town next week.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: He may not answer directly there. If he says only that we should stay in touch, we'll still be short on time.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: That's fine. I'm not trying to close the matter at the table. If the conversation opens the door, I'll send a short note tomorrow through you and ask for a time to stop by with the complete file.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Understood. The host usually keeps the evening moving fast, and some guests prefer not to discuss business until late.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I'll keep the evening light and brief, stay until the host has made the rounds, and use it to re-establish the connection before any formal follow-up.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer aligns with the seed-specific mechanism by embedding the stalled approval discussion inside a relationship-setting first and deferring the concrete ask to later formal follow-up, rather than treating it as an isolated transactional request. The decisive axis is sequence and social framing: connection first, file later.

scenario: A mobility app is preparing short onboarding videos for launches in Japan and France. Both cuts currently use the same street scene: during a long wait, one pedestrian steps into the crosswalk while the signal is still red and several others follow. The production team can afford only one market-specific storyboard change before final sign-off.
question: Which approval decision best fits this situation?

options.A: Replace that crossing moment in the Japan cut with pedestrians continuing to wait for the signal, while leaving the France cut otherwise unchanged for this release.
options.B: Remove the red-signal crossing sequence from both country cuts and use the same waiting scene everywhere to avoid market-specific assumptions in a public-safety context.
options.C: Keep the red-signal crossing in the Japan cut but show several pedestrians moving together first, and revise the France cut to show a single early crosser instead.
options.D: Approve the same red-signal crossing sequence in both cuts, since urban pedestrians in either market may follow others once one person starts moving.

scenario: You are the regional policy lead on a multicultural launch team for an autonomous shuttle pilot in Singapore. The team includes a product director in the US, an operations manager in Germany, and a local public-affairs manager in Singapore. The shuttle is designed to run without active driving input on a fixed business-park route, but a trained safety operator will sit onboard during the first month. A government-facing briefing pack is due in 48 hours for a meeting with the Land Transport Authority, and the CFO wants the liability section simplified so procurement can finalize insurance and vendor contracts this week. In the latest draft, the US director assigned primary incident responsibility to the onboard safety operator 'because a human is present in the vehicle,' while the German operations manager added a note saying the vehicle maker, software stack provider, fleet operator, and onboard operator can be sorted out later if regulators ask. The local public-affairs manager has not objected directly, but has twice asked in email whether the application entity, assessment sequence, and incident-accountability table will be 'stable across Level-4 operation' before the pack is circulated externally. The CFO is pressing to avoid expanding the scope of the briefing because 'we already carry liability insurance and the operator can be the named accountable person for first deployment.' You cannot delay the meeting, and sending a vague 'we are still checking' memo upward will be seen as poor execution.
question: Write a decision memo for your team lead that recommends how to revise the briefing pack now. Your memo must: (1) diagnose what assumption in the current draft is most likely to fail in the Singapore context, using only the scenario evidence; (2) specify the exact liability and approval structure you would present in this version of the pack, including which actor should be foregrounded now and which actor distinctions cannot be deferred; (3) explain what you would tell the US director, German operations manager, CFO, and Singapore public-affairs manager in what sequence over the next 48 hours; and (4) state what remains uncertain, what evidence is already strong enough to act on, and what would trigger a later revision after the meeting.

rubric.point: Identifies the hidden failure in the current draft as treating human-presence or generic driver logic as the default accountability frame for this Singapore Level-4 pilot.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly diagnoses that the draft wrongly centers the onboard safety operator or ordinary driver-style road-rule logic despite evidence that the shuttle operates with automated control; no credit for vague statements such as 'check local regulations carefully' or 'liability may differ by country.'

rubric.point: Recommends a Singapore-specific liability structure that foregrounds the deploying legal entity rather than the onboard operator for Level-4 operation.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer states that responsibility in the pack should shift toward the corporate deploying entity because the automated system has greater operational control, while still allowing role-specific descriptions for other actors; partial credit if corporate responsibility is mentioned but the safety operator remains framed as the primary liable party.

rubric.point: Refuses to defer critical role delineation and instead specifies that the briefing must distinguish relevant AV actors before the authority meeting.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer says actor boundaries cannot be left for later and should be shown now in a clear accountability table or equivalent structure tied to deployment, technical assessment, operation, and incident handling; no credit for answers that merely call for a broad consultation or say roles can be sorted out after regulator feedback.

rubric.point: Includes the approval route needed now: the deploying legal entity must be presented as the applicant to the Land Transport Authority and linked to technical assessment readiness, not just insurance coverage.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer connects the application entity and technical assessment sequence as immediate briefing content and rejects the CFO's idea that existing liability insurance alone is enough; partial credit if either application route or technical assessment is missing.

rubric.point: Uses metacognitive CQ by separating what is already actionable from what remains uncertain, rather than becoming inert or overconfident.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer states that available evidence is already strong enough to revise the pack around corporate deployment responsibility, actor delineation, and application structure, while naming bounded uncertainties such as exact incident-allocation wording or later contractual allocation among firms; no credit for 'delay until all facts are confirmed' or for asserting certainty on details not supported by the scenario.

rubric.point: Provides a concrete 48-hour stakeholder sequence that recalibrates imported assumptions under pressure.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer gives an operational sequence such as first aligning the team lead and public-affairs manager on the revised frame, then correcting the US and German drafters with specific edits, then briefing the CFO on why insurance does not solve the accountability structure, and finally circulating a regulator-ready pack; partial credit for listing stakeholders without sequence or purpose.

rubric.point: Rejects the polished near-miss plan of using a cautious generic memo, broad consultation, or operator-named accountability as a brand-safe compromise.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explains why the tempting compromise is miscalibrated in this context: it preserves the wrong accountability anchor, treats insurance as a substitute for regime structure, or postpones distinctions Singapore authorities would expect; no credit for answers that reward the longest or most consultative plan without correcting the core frame.

reference_outline: Diagnose from the scenario that the current draft is built on a generic human-driver default: the safety operator is being treated as the primary accountable person merely because a human sits onboard, while the Singapore public-affairs manager's repeated questions signal that application entity, assessment sequence, and Level-4 accountability are the real fault lines.

Revise the pack now so the deploying legal entity is the central accountable actor for Level-4 operation, with an explicit role-delineation table covering the distinct AV actors instead of collapsing responsibility into the onboard operator.

State that the briefing must identify the legal entity applying to the Land Transport Authority and show readiness for technical assessment; keep existing liability insurance in the pack as necessary background but not as the main solution to accountability.

Tell the team lead and Singapore public-affairs manager first that enough evidence already exists to correct the frame before external circulation; use them to stabilize wording around applicant entity, actor delineation, and Level-4 responsibility before debating commercial preferences.

Then correct the US director's operator-centered assumption and the German manager's defer-until-asked approach by explaining that in Singapore the key execution risk is not general completeness but using the wrong responsibility anchor and postponing role clarity that should appear before the meeting.

Brief the CFO that naming the onboard operator and relying on existing insurance may feel efficient but is a near-miss because it does not match the expected regime structure; propose keeping contracts on track by narrowing the immediate revision to accountability architecture, application entity, and assessment pathway rather than reopening every contract term.

Use metacognitive calibration: act now on strong evidence about corporate deployment responsibility and separate AV regime logic, but mark limited open items for post-meeting refinement, such as finer contractual allocation among firms or exact incident-reporting language if regulators request adjustments.

scenario: A newcomer on a museum partnership team in Tokyo needs a few same-day images for a sponsor recap deck. The team is moving quickly before the venue closes. In the lobby and on the platform-style exhibit area, many visitors are casually taking pictures, and staff are busy guiding foot traffic rather than stopping anyone.

roles.newcomer: Marta, newly arrived regional communications manager

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The sponsor wants two photos for tonight's recap slide. We have about fifteen minutes before the school group exits, and the train-car exhibit gets crowded.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Got it. I'll move fast and keep it usable for the deck. I saw several visitors already shooting on their phones, so I'll work around them and grab what we need.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Please make sure we don't create extra work for the floor team. They usually stay focused on moving people along.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I won't ask them to manage the shot. I'll take one wide frame in the main hall, and for anything tighter I'll only use people who clearly agree and are standing with me for that purpose.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The sponsor especially likes images that feel lively and close. The school group is about to pass the old carriage display, and that area often looks strongest on slides.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll skip that as the hero image and take the crowd scene from farther back instead. If we still need a closer shot, I'll ask one of our adult partner volunteers near the entrance after this round.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. We need the files in ten minutes, so please send whatever you decide without a long review loop.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Will do. I'll send one wide lobby shot now, then a second tighter image only if it's from someone I've asked directly.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer calibrates to the Japan-specific mechanism by treating posted/public-space restrictions as binding even if others are casually taking pictures and staff are not intervening. The decisive behavior is the execution choice: using a wide crowd shot for the urgent need, while avoiding close identifiable images of sensitive groups and taking any tighter shot only with direct permission.

scenario: Your team is reusing a transit-health poster from another market for a two-week launch in Manchester. The station operator wants the local version by tomorrow. Their draft note says passengers respond best when sanctions are spelled out, but the site pack also distinguishes between areas where face coverings are formally required and areas where they are only requested by the operator.
question: Which briefing decision should you give the design team for the UK version?

options.A: Limit the adaptation to making the rule status unmistakable in each area and naming the responsible authority or operator, while leaving out added penalty amounts from the overseas template.
options.B: Adapt the poster fully for the UK by keeping the area-specific rule status and adding a prominent fine panel, since the operator has asked for a stronger deterrence cue.
options.C: Keep the poster standardized across the whole station by using one strong enforcement version everywhere, as a clear legal-style message is more consistent than varying by area.
options.D: Expand the adaptation by explaining the public rationale for face coverings in every area, but reserve explicit rule-status wording for the entrances where formal requirements apply.

scenario: You lead operations for a European events agency preparing a two-day investor roadshow in Sofia, Bulgaria. The venue contract was signed months ago by headquarters and includes a lounge area just off the main conference hall that the Bulgarian hotel sales manager informally described in email as a 'comfortable smoking corner for VIP guests.' Your German legal lead says many countries allow enclosed indoor smoking areas if ventilation is good, so the fastest path is to leave the setup alone unless the venue produces a written prohibition. Your regional sales director is pushing back because two major clients from Turkey and France both smoke and have already asked where they can step out during short breaks; he wants a frictionless guest experience and does not want the local partner embarrassed. The event starts tomorrow morning, printed signage is due in three hours, and your junior coordinator has drafted a floor map labeling the lounge as 'VIP Smoking Room.' You also know the event will include press, and the hotel has asked that any concerns be handled 'discreetly' rather than in front of guests. No one on your team is based in Bulgaria, and the local venue contact keeps replying with short confirmations but not detailed explanations.
question: Write the operational plan you would send your team today. Your answer must identify what you think is going on in this Bulgaria-specific situation, what tempting assumption your team is making, and exactly how you would handle the lounge label, guest communication, venue coordination, and escalation path before doors open. Be concrete about wording, timing, audience, and follow-up. Do not give a generic 'check locally and be respectful' answer; explain the execution sequence you would use under the deadline and why.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that the Sofia venue should be treated as operating under a strict public indoor smoking prohibition, not a broad manager-discretion or ventilation-based exception model.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers a narrow-rule environment from the Bulgaria context and acts on it operationally; no credit for vague statements like 'laws may differ' or for assuming enclosed hotel lounge smoking is probably acceptable until disproven.

rubric.point: Rejects the near-miss plan of keeping the VIP lounge smoking setup unless a written ban appears, and explains why that imported default is miscalibrated here.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly bounds the 'many countries allow ventilated indoor rooms' assumption as an attractive but wrong shortcut in this case; partial credit if it questions the assumption without changing execution.

rubric.point: Makes the correct primary execution-axis decision on timing and sequence: remove or stop the indoor smoking-room designation before guest-facing materials go out, then verify any lawful narrow exception rather than advertising first and correcting later.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if signage, floor map, and guest directions are changed immediately before event launch; no full credit for plans that keep the label temporarily, wait for more detail, or rely on a same-day soft warning while leaving public materials unchanged.

rubric.point: Uses behavioural CQ through calibrated visible action: private, direct coordination with the hotel on the specific lounge label and setup, paired with clear internal instructions on what staff should say to guests.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies who is contacted first, in what channel or setting, and gives workable staff wording such as redirecting guests to lawful outdoor options or confirmed designated exceptions; no full credit for abstract advice without actor-by-actor communication.

rubric.point: Sets an escalation and risk-control route tied to enforcement exposure for both venue and organizer, rather than treating this as a mere hospitality preference.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan notes inspection/fine risk and assigns a decision owner for documenting the correction and escalating unresolved venue resistance to legal/operations leadership; partial credit for generic 'document it' language without linking it to enforcement consequences.

rubric.point: Handles guest experience without reenacting the misunderstanding by offering a narrower alternative rather than preserving the indoor lounge for VIP convenience.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer proposes a compliant workaround such as directing guests to an outdoor area or a confirmed lawful designated facility, while avoiding public embarrassment; no full credit for overbroad accommodation that preserves the indoor room because clients are important.
