reference_outline: Infer from the Bulgaria setting and the ambiguous 'smoking corner' language that the safe operating assumption is a comprehensive ban in public indoor spaces, with only narrow designated exceptions rather than broad hotel discretion.

Treat the German legal lead's ventilation/enclosed-room logic as the polished near-miss: it sounds efficient and internationally plausible, but it should not control signage or guest messaging in this case.

Immediately pull the 'VIP Smoking Room' wording from the floor map, signage, and staff brief before materials are printed; do not publish a guest-facing designation that normalizes indoor smoking and hope to correct later.

Contact the hotel manager privately and directly today to state that your team cannot label or use the lounge as an indoor smoking room unless the venue can confirm it fits a lawful narrow exception; ask for the compliant alternative location to brief guests on.

Send internal instructions to front-of-house staff with exact wording and sequence: if asked, do not gesture guests toward the lounge; direct them to the confirmed outdoor area or other lawful location, and keep the message matter-of-fact rather than moralizing or debating.

Document the change and assign an escalation path if the venue resists: operations/legal sign-off, updated floor plan, and a clear record because organizer and venue both face inspection and sanction risk in a strict enforcement environment.

Balance relationship management by correcting privately with the venue and preserving client dignity, but do not let discretion, VIP status, or deadline pressure delay the visible behavioural change that removes the indoor smoking-room cue before doors open.

scenario: After a policy event in Manchester, a local operations coordinator and a newly arrived regional events manager need to get twelve visiting delegates onto an airport coach running from a busy public stop. The delegates already have prepaid QR tickets, one attendee has limited mobility, and the group is running late for check-in. Other passengers will also be boarding from the same stop.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The airport coach is due in about five minutes. This stop gets busy after conferences, and the driver scans fast once the doors open.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I’ve put all twelve QR codes on one sheet and asked everyone to keep passports out, so at least we won’t stall at the step.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Good. One delegate will need a steadier pace, and the others are spread between the bench and the shelter with their cases.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I’ll keep that delegate with me and pull the rest into pairs with their luggage now, so we’re not scrambling when it arrives.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: There are already people waiting from the last train, and this driver usually stops only briefly.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I’ll put our slower guest and one colleague where the boarding line is forming, and I’ll hold the rest just off to the side. Once those two reach the scanner, I can feed our remaining ten straight in behind them as one party instead of letting them get split up.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. We just need everyone on without bags blocking the pavement.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Exactly — I’ll keep the pavement clear, move the pairs up in one go, and stay by the front until the whole delegation is through.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer does useful prep, but the decisive misstep is the boarding sequence: using two delegates to establish a place in the public line and then inserting the remaining group behind them as a single party. In this UK transport setting, queue order can be a public-order matter, so the miscalibration is not tone or efficiency but expanding a privately organized group into an existing public queue.

scenario: A conference operator in Manchester is briefing temporary platform staff for two days of rail-replacement shuttle boarding. Some overseas attendees found the lane system rigid this morning, and adding more marshals at every stop will cost extra. The operations lead wants one boarding rule set for all stops before tonight's printed briefing goes out.
question: Which briefing decision should the operations lead adopt?

options.A: Use one rule set: let passengers off before boarding at every stop, and require joining the back only at stops where staff have already formed a visible line.
options.B: Use one rule set: require late arrivals to join the back at every stop, and allow boarding to begin during alighting at quieter stops if the doorway stays passable.
options.C: Use a flexible rule set: each stop supervisor can choose either a line or free-form boarding, provided passengers leaving the vehicle are given space first.
options.D: Use one rule set: where staff direct a line, late arrivals join behind it, and boarding at that doorway starts only after those getting off have cleared through.

scenario: You lead launch operations for a multicultural events team preparing a three-weekend street market in Porto, Portugal. The concept was copied from a successful rollout in another European city where the team handled sound issues by setting decibel caps, ending amplified music by 22:00, and sending a courtesy notice to nearby residents. In Porto, the proposed site is on a plaza bordered by apartment buildings, a small hotel, and a school that is in session on Friday mornings. A hospital complex is four blocks away. The sponsor wants daily live music because vendors say silent periods reduce foot traffic, and your regional director has already told headquarters that the Portuguese launch is “operationally aligned” with the earlier market model. Budget is tight, moving sites would reduce sponsor revenue, and the mayor’s office has not yet replied to a general inquiry sent by a junior teammate. Your Portuguese vendor coordinator says only that ‘the location mix matters more than the sound plan itself’ and then goes offline for the day. You have 36 hours to send a go/no-go execution memo, assign responsibilities, and brief teammates from Germany and Spain who are pushing to finalize the standard event pack without reopening scope.
question: Write the execution memo you would send to your team and director. Your memo must: (1) diagnose the hidden issue from the facts given, (2) identify the most tempting but miscalibrated imported assumption, (3) set a concrete approval and event-design sequence for the next 36 hours, and (4) show what extra effort you personally would absorb to keep the project moving without shifting the adaptation burden onto local partners. Be specific about which event elements you would freeze, which you would stop, who you would contact, what evidence you would require before approving sound-related activities, and how you would protect the relationship with the sponsor while controlling risk.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that the core problem is not generic noise management but whether temporary noisy public activities at this site can proceed at all under Portugal-specific local authorization conditions tied to nearby sensitive buildings and event pattern.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires inferring that the residential, hotel, school-in-session, and hospital-sensitive context changes the decision threshold and that some recurring sound plans may be non-approvable, not merely adjustable by volume or curfew. Partial credit for noting 'permits may be needed' without linking this to the exact site mix and recurring-event structure.

rubric.point: Rejects or sharply bounds the attractive near-miss plan of reusing the prior European market template with decibel caps, courtesy notices, and standard close times.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires stating why the imported SOP is insufficient or dangerous here even if it worked elsewhere in Europe. Partial credit for proposing both the standard plan and local checking in parallel without freezing the risky sound-dependent elements.

rubric.point: Sets the primary execution axis correctly by making approval/documentation come before committing to amplified recurring programming at the proposed site.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires a clear sequence such as: freeze public claims and music bookings, confirm site-sensitive facts, pursue the mayoral/special-license route if and only if justified, and redesign or relocate sound programming if approval conditions are not met. No full credit if the answer treats approval as a late compliance step after sponsor sales or programming are locked.

rubric.point: Applies the Portugal-specific rule to the right scope and timing, including the risk boundary around continuous or recurring noisy events near hospitals or in school buildings during school hours.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires operational consequences: daily or repeated live music cannot simply be assumed viable, and school-hour or hospital-adjacent recurrence must trigger a narrower plan or cancellation of that element. Partial credit for mentioning sensitive locations without translating them into design changes.

rubric.point: Shows motivational CQ through costly, bounded ownership rather than generic caution or withdrawal.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires visible personal effort under pressure: taking responsibility to escalate with the municipality, revising sponsor promises, obtaining site documentation, reworking programming, or absorbing status/time cost instead of leaving 'local colleagues to check.' No full credit for respectful but passive delay, or for pushing locals to solve the ambiguity alone.

rubric.point: Designs role-specific coordination that balances speed, hierarchy, and relationship maintenance.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires assigning concrete roles such as who gathers map/site evidence, who pauses vendor bookings, who communicates risk to the sponsor, and how the director is briefed so prior public commitments are corrected without blame. Partial credit for generic statements about teamwork or stakeholder consultation.

rubric.point: Uses evidence selectively rather than broadly, focusing on the facts that control the decision.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires seeking targeted evidence such as exact proximity to residences/hotel/school/hospital-sensitive uses, whether the school is operating during planned sound hours, whether the event is recurring, and whether exceptional circumstances can plausibly be justified for a special license. No full credit for proposing open-ended consultation or citywide sound benchmarking as the main next step.

rubric.point: Includes a repair and fallback path that protects sponsor trust without overpromising.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit requires a concrete fallback such as silent/vendor-only hours, non-amplified programming, adjusted timing, or alternative placement if authorization is weak or unavailable, and frames this to the sponsor as preserving launch viability. Partial credit for saying 'have a backup plan' without operational detail.

reference_outline: State that the deciding issue is whether noisy temporary public activities at this Porto site are legally/administratively permissible given nearby residences, hotel use, school-in-session timing, and hospital-sensitive context, not whether the team can simply manage noise levels well.

Name the near-miss explicitly: copying the earlier European market model with decibel caps, end-time limits, and courtesy notices is attractive under budget and deadline pressure but misreads the Portuguese approval boundary.

Set the sequence: immediately freeze amplified-music marketing, recurring live-performance bookings, and any promise of daily sound programming; collect exact site-use evidence; escalate directly for municipality-specific confirmation and special-license viability before approving noisy elements.

Translate the hidden rule into design consequences: recurring noisy events are the danger zone; school-hour activity and hospital-sensitive proximity require narrowing, rescheduling, removing amplification, or relocating that component rather than just lowering volume.

Show motivational CQ by personally absorbing friction: own the escalation, stay late to revise the pack, take the status hit with the director and sponsor, and do not leave the Portuguese coordinator as the sole cultural/compliance buffer.

Assign roles concretely: Germany teammate updates the standard pack and freezes noncompliant claims, Spain teammate prepares low-noise fallback programming, you handle municipal escalation and director memo, vendor coordinator validates site facts when back online.

Brief the sponsor in relationship-preserving terms: the launch is still moving, but sound-dependent elements are conditional pending site-specific authorization; offer fallback foot-traffic alternatives instead of a flat cancellation message.

Use a bounded evidence threshold for go/no-go: approve only after site-sensitive facts and authorization route are clear; if exceptional justification or mayoral approval is not realistically obtainable in time, strip recurring noisy elements from the plan rather than waiting indefinitely.

Include monitoring/repair: if approval remains ambiguous by the deadline, issue a revised low-noise operating model, document why the standard template was unsuitable here, and preserve future trust by showing disciplined adaptation rather than last-minute noncompliance.

scenario: At a Dutch secondary school, a newcomer operations manager is finalizing a campus-wide facilities memo before a board visit the next morning. The school leases one building but also uses the paved lane, bike racks, and a small terrace beside it for student circulation and lunch overflow. A neighboring property owner has already complained about mixed messages from different tenants, and the municipality has not yet replied about signage placement.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The board wants the facilities memo tonight. The main entrance is easy, but the side lane and terrace are awkward because students use them between classes and other tenants cross there too.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I’ll keep the rule clear inside our control: building entrances, the courtyard, and our own marked grounds. For the shared lane, I can add a polite note asking people to be considerate until the municipality answers.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The neighbor already said they do not want three different notices posted along that stretch. They want one workable arrangement, but we still need something in place tomorrow.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I’ll call them tonight and suggest one joint sign later, but for tomorrow I’d rather not extend our formal ban wording onto space that is open and shared. I’ll keep that part as guidance only.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Students also leave bikes there during breaks, and staff have asked where they should intervene if someone lights up while standing near the racks.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I’ll tell staff to redirect people once they step onto school property proper. If someone is on the lane by the racks, staff can avoid confronting them and just report patterns so we don’t overreach.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right, I need the final wording in fifteen minutes because security prints it before they lock up.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I’ll send it now with a strict ban for the building and our enclosed areas, plus temporary courtesy language for the lane and terrace while I keep working on alignment with the neighbor and municipality.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer invests real effort by calling neighbors and seeking a uniform arrangement, but the decisive execution is wrong for the Dutch rule: he limits enforceable action to clearly owned or enclosed school property and treats the shared lane/terrace as courtesy-only, even though associated areas next to or near the school that are used by the institution can fall within the institution's smoking ban and enforcement scope.

scenario: A mobility company plans a pilot in three European cities using cars that can handle stretches of driving on their own. After a low-speed collision during system-controlled operation, tomorrow's board pack must propose the next legal work sequence for launch, claims handling, and regulator outreach.
question: Which next step should the legal lead take now?

options.A: First complete the vehicle conformity dossier and safety-risk file for the regional approval pathway, then address city operating conditions and any compensation model once that file is settled.
options.B: First split the incident plan in two: avoid assuming the seated monitor was the acting driver during system control, and set compensation without waiting for fault findings; then sequence city operating checks.
options.C: First prepare a driver-accountability position for the seated monitor and align claims to ordinary fault rules, then refine the technical file and local operating conditions after the board review.
options.D: First secure each city's circulation and service permissions, then finalize the claims model after those talks, while treating the product safety file as the main basis for responsibility questions.

scenario: You lead a multinational policy team preparing a 48-hour briefing pack for the European board of a mobility company before a pilot hearing in Strasbourg. The pack must include a one-page incident-response model for crashes involving the company's Level 4 shuttle service in several European cities. Three weeks earlier, one shuttle struck a cyclist while the automated driving system was engaged, the remote supervisor had not intervened, and internal logs show the vehicle followed its current design parameters. No final regulator finding exists yet. The board chair wants a crisp rule for public commitments because journalists are already asking who pays and who is accountable. The U.S. general counsel is pushing for a clean driver-or-operator fault framework because it is simple to explain and aligns with existing claims workflows. The German product team worries that any language implying manufacturer exposure will trigger investor concern. The public affairs lead in Brussels argues that focusing only on payouts will look narrow after recent European policy discussions. You have one meeting tomorrow with legal, engineering, operations, and communications to lock the briefing language and workflow.
question: Write the decision memo you would send before that meeting. It must: (1) diagnose the underlying Europe-specific liability logic you think the board pack needs to reflect based on the facts given, (2) identify the most tempting but miscalibrated assumption in the current internal debate, and (3) set a concrete execution plan for the briefing on one main axis: how responsibility should be scoped across actors in the incident-response model. Specify what the pack should and should not say, which functions must be assigned to which parts of the analysis, and how you would justify that design under board pressure for simplicity and speed.

rubric.point: Diagnoses that a simple user-in-charge or operator fault frame is not adequate when the ADS was properly controlling the vehicle and acting according to manufacturer design.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer links the scenario facts to a mismatch between conventional criminal/civil fault logic and ADS-controlled crashes; no credit for merely saying the issue is 'complex' or 'shared' without tying it to the automated control facts.

rubric.point: Sets the main scope decision around distributed responsibility rather than a single blamed actor.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo operationalizes responsibility across at least manufacturers/design, deployers/operators, and compensation handling, with clear consequences for the board pack; partial credit if it mentions multiple actors but still centers the model on finding the individual at fault first.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the attractive near-miss of importing a generic global driver-fault default for message simplicity.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly identifies the clean driver-or-operator default as tempting under media and workflow pressure yet miscalibrated here; no credit if it accepts that frame with softer wording or hides behind generic 'wait for facts' language.

rubric.point: Translates the Europe-specific logic into concrete briefing content on compensation and scrutiny.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer includes both: a compensation approach that does not depend solely on proving user fault first, and a parallel line of analysis that examines manufacturer/product-design exposure; partial credit if only one of these appears.

rubric.point: Applies cognitive CQ by mapping the correct legal-cultural boundary instead of using a nearby but wrong rule.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer distinguishes this Europe-context logic from a generic legal SOP or another market's default and explains why the same facts change the liability framing here; no credit for generic compliance, empathy, or consultation language without that mapping.

rubric.point: Designs role-specific workflow for the next meeting and board pack.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if legal, engineering, operations/deployer, and communications each receive distinct responsibilities tied to the scoped-responsibility model; partial credit if roles are listed but not connected to different evidence questions or message boundaries.

rubric.point: Addresses the broader accountability expectation beyond post-collision payout alone.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer shows that the pack should frame compensation as only one part of the response and add a wider responsibility structure involving organizational learning, deployment governance, or policy/research responsibility; no credit for answers limited to claims handling.

rubric.point: Maintains speed without defaulting to the broadest or safest plan.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo gives a narrow, actionable board-ready structure that can be used within 48 hours; partial credit if it delays decisions behind more consultation, more data collection, or a maximalist review process that avoids the core scope choice.

reference_outline: State that because the shuttle was under ADS control and logs show it followed its design parameters, the board pack should not assume the user-in-charge or remote supervisor is the natural primary fault bearer.

Frame the incident-response model around apportioned or layered responsibility: immediate compensation pathway, manufacturer/design scrutiny, and deployer/operational review should run in parallel rather than waiting for a single human-fault finding.

Name the near-miss explicitly: the imported instinct to use a simple driver-or-operator fault template because it is media-friendly and already fits claims workflow; explain why that misses the Europe-specific liability logic in this case.

Direct legal to draft language that avoids premature single-actor blame, includes possible strict-compensation style handling for victims, and preserves product-liability analysis for the manufacturer side.

Direct engineering to produce design-behavior evidence on what the ADS perceived and executed, operations to document supervision/deployment conditions, and communications to use responsibility language broader than 'who pays' while avoiding admissions beyond established facts.

Include in the board pack that compensation is necessary but insufficient; the response should also show a wider responsibility architecture across manufacturer, deployer, policymakers, and researchers or safety-governance functions.

Use the Europe context as the decisive interpretive boundary: the same crash should not be briefed through a generic global fault-default template when the relevant local policy logic questions whether traditional fault categories fit ADS operation.

Add a calibration step for the next 48 hours: if new evidence later shows the ADS was not actually in proper control or that human override duties were breached, the responsibility map can be reweighted, but the initial briefing should not start from the conventional driver-blame default.

scenario: A newcomer on a travel media team is in Barcelona with a local coordinator. They need a few interior shots quickly for a same-day sponsor post after filming street scenes nearby. The newcomer wants to stay efficient and avoid bothering staff, but the shoot is inside a famous basilica with many visitors around.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We already have the exterior footage, but the sponsor still wants one strong inside image before noon. The queue is moving fast, and there are a lot of visitors today.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Got it. Since we were filming freely outside, I'll keep this light too—just a few quiet stills, no tripod, no flash, and I won't block anyone.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We only have about twenty minutes once we're in, and I need to rejoin the driver after that. The sponsor mainly cares that the post feels authentic, not staged.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Perfect. I'll work fast, stay off to the side, and make it look like a normal visitor capture so we don't create extra friction.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The sponsor also asked whether we can mention the location by name in the caption. They don't need video if that complicates things.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I'll skip video and keep it respectful—one or two handheld interior shots should be fine in a tourist site, especially if we're not setting up equipment.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right, once we're through, I need to send the draft upstairs quickly. Reception inside can be patchy.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I'll grab the images first and send you selects as soon as we're back outside.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer overgeneralizes from street-tourist photography to a church interior and decides based on a global lightweight-shoot logic. In this seed, the key is to apply site-specific interior rules for a religious setting rather than assume that quiet handheld stills are permitted.

scenario: A nonprofit is sending two expatriate program managers by car across Kinshasa for permit meetings. Their one-page transport brief needs a single line on police stops. The local partner mentioned that, this week, roadside checks may be reduced under a city instruction, but the security lead has also seen drivers taken to a station after being pulled over. Compliance wants the line to avoid endorsing improper payments, and the team leaves in an hour.
question: Which briefing line should be approved for the transport brief?

options.A: If stopped, assume the check may still be part of the city instruction shift; ask to continue unless shown a formal basis for the stop, then report the encounter afterward.
options.B: If a stop turns into being taken off-route for settlement, contact the senior host listed in the brief and treat the matter as unresolved until that person advises next steps.
options.C: If stopped, call the senior host listed in the brief as soon as the officer starts the interaction, before discussing documents, destination, or any request to move elsewhere.
options.D: If stopped, follow the officers to the station, pay only against an official receipt, and log the case afterward as a standard enforcement matter unless told otherwise.

scenario: You are the operations lead on a multinational mobility project preparing a two-week fuel-support pilot for contracted drivers in Lagos, Nigeria. The pilot starts in 72 hours, and your client wants a one-page field protocol tonight because a sponsor has already complained about delays and possible favoritism. The local subcontractor says drivers will often need to join public petrol lines during shortages, and disputes at stations could damage the brand if they are filmed. Your team is split: a UK compliance manager wants a strict rule that drivers should avoid any queue interaction that is not formally supervised because informal lines are too disorderly to trust; a UAE logistics manager argues that vans carrying medical supplies should be told to move ahead if they are larger and time-critical; and a Nigerian field supervisor has sent only neutral notes from prior shifts: drivers who stayed in line usually got served, people nearby reacted quickly when someone tried to bypass others, and two female drivers reported no special handling compared with male drivers. You do not have time for new field research before launch, but you can choose how to brief drivers, what exceptions to allow, and what evidence to monitor in the first 48 hours.
question: Write the core of the protocol memo you would send tonight. Your answer must: (1) state your working diagnosis of what is most likely governing these fuel-line interactions and what remains uncertain; (2) identify the most tempting but miscalibrated assumption in your team discussion; (3) decide the rule for driver behavior on queue position, claimed urgency, vehicle size, and interactions with other people in line; and (4) explain what evidence you will watch in the first 48 hours that would make you revise the protocol. Be concrete about sequence, wording, escalation, and limits rather than giving general advice.

rubric.point: Diagnoses an existing informal queue order among strangers rather than treating the setting as basically unstructured.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers from the scenario evidence that the line likely operates through observable unwritten rules and peer enforcement, and uses that inference to justify immediate operating guidance. Partial credit if it mentions uncertainty or possible local norms without converting them into a working operational read.

rubric.point: Sets the execution rule on queue position and exceptions in the correct direction.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if drivers are instructed to hold their place in line, not self-authorize bypassing, and not assume larger or time-sensitive vehicles can simply claim priority. Partial credit if the answer discourages conflict but leaves room for driver-created exceptions or vague case-by-case negotiation.

rubric.point: Rejects the attractive imported misunderstanding rather than amplifying it.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly identifies a tempting outside assumption such as 'public queues here are too disorderly to rely on' or 'operational urgency/vehicle size should override the line by default' and bounds it as a poor basis for protocol. No full credit for answers that merely say 'respect local culture' or that choose the safest broad ban on queue interaction.

rubric.point: Uses metacognitive CQ by separating what can be inferred now from what still needs checking.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer makes a calibrated commitment now, states remaining unknowns narrowly, and names specific disconfirming evidence that would justify revision. Partial credit for generic calls to monitor, ask locals, or delay decisions without specifying what uncertainty matters.

rubric.point: Designs concrete driver wording, escalation, and repair steps aligned to the hidden mechanism.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer gives operational moves such as drivers stating they are joining at the current place, refusing pressure to jump ahead without arguing status, escalating only if station staff formally direct a different order, and documenting attempted bypass disputes or sanctions from others in line. Partial credit for abstract advice about being polite or avoiding confrontation.

rubric.point: Interprets gender and identity evidence at the right scope.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer avoids building unnecessary preferential or protective queue rules around gender or outsider identity based on the scenario, while still allowing normal safety escalation for threats. Partial credit if it overgeneralizes from one identity category or adds broad exception handling unsupported by the evidence.

reference_outline: State a working diagnosis that the fuel line is likely governed by informal but real ordering norms among strangers, with social sanctions against bypassing, so the protocol should rely on that order unless an authorized station actor clearly redirects it.

Name the near-miss assumption: outsiders may default either to 'the queue is too chaotic to trust' or to 'larger/urgent vehicles naturally deserve priority'; both are attractive under sponsor pressure but misread the local mechanism.

Set the primary execution-axis decision on timing/sequence: drivers join where they arrive, keep position, do not negotiate ad hoc priority based on cargo or vehicle size, and do not attempt private side deals to move forward.

Give role-specific wording: drivers say they are taking their place in line, acknowledge others already waiting, and if pressed by colleagues or client pressure, explain that only explicit station direction changes order; supervisors back this stance rather than improvising exceptions by phone.

Apply metacognitive CQ by distinguishing current inference from unknowns: infer enough now to brief firmly, but track whether any stations consistently use recognized exception rules, whether enforcement comes from peers or staff, and whether company-branded vehicles trigger different reactions.

Specify 48-hour evidence triggers for revision: repeated staff-directed priority handling, consistent acceptance of narrowly defined exceptions, or contrary evidence showing that staying in order does not actually secure service or safety at certain stations.

Include repair and risk control: if a driver has already attempted to bypass and tension rises, instruct them to step back to the accepted position, avoid arguing entitlement, notify the supervisor, and log the incident for protocol adjustment rather than defending the original shortcut.

scenario: In Kaduna, a newcomer logistics officer is sent with the company van to buy fuel before a generator test for visiting auditors at noon. The station has a long line, tempers are rising, and the local operations assistant is coordinating by phone from the office because the van must return quickly.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: How far along are you? The auditors are already asking whether the backup generator will be demonstrated today.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'm at the station now. The line is wrapped around the block, but I can still make it if it moves.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: People have been here a while. If this slips much longer, the test window closes and Facilities will blame our team.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. I walked down the line and told everyone I'm with the company van for an audit deadline. I asked who came first, wrote plate numbers in order, and said I'd help make it strictly first-come-first-served so nobody feels cheated.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Hmm. And now?

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: A few men near the front objected and said I was rearranging things. I stayed calm and suggested we ignore side conversations and just follow the list from the back forward. I also told a woman who arrived after me that I'd put her exactly where she came in, same as everyone else.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Has the van moved any closer since then?

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Not yet, but at least I'm being fair and transparent. If they keep arguing, I'll ask the station staff to announce my written order so the queue resets cleanly.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer imposes a generic first-come-first-served reset and tries to reorganize the whole petrol queue publicly. In this Nigerian shortage-queue context, the queue operates as a social organization with existing hierarchy and role expectations, so the miscalibration is the newcomer's audience, sequence, and authority choice rather than politeness.

scenario: You are finalizing operating instructions for a one-night film event in Gaborone that uses a cinema complex and contracted shuttle buses. Bilingual smoke-free notices have already been printed for entrances, waiting areas, and vehicles. With doors opening in two hours, your local team is split on one point: should ushers and drivers personally address a person who lights up, or should they rely on signs first and contact security only if needed?
question: Which observation would most strongly justify briefing the front-line team to address the smoker themselves rather than treating this only as a signage or security issue?

options.A: At nearby shopping and entertainment sites, smoke-free notices are posted prominently in both English and Setswana at entrances, ticket counters, and other high-traffic public areas.
options.B: At several restaurants and bars in the same district, indoor tables have no ashtrays and staff direct smokers toward outdoor areas before guests sit down or order.
options.C: At the shuttle contractor’s depot, each bus and the passenger waiting bay display smoke-free notices clearly in two languages where riders queue and board.
options.D: During your site walk, cinema ushers and minibus drivers at comparable venues are the people who promptly tell someone to stop, without waiting for police or a separate compliance team.

scenario: You are a UK-based operations lead for a hospitality group preparing a three-night brand activation in Kampala. The local venue contract is already signed, the regional marketing director wants the site photos approved by end of day, and the sponsor has paid extra for a premium terrace experience because several invited guests smoke. A Kampala venue manager has sent a floor plan showing an indoor bar, an outdoor terrace directly attached to the entrance, and a boxed-off area on that terrace labeled for smokers. The draft signage package from London includes English-only table cards saying smoking is restricted to the designated area. Your Ugandan logistics coordinator has not objected, but in message history keeps asking whether the entrance flow, guest pickup point, and sign placement are "final-final" because printers must start in two hours. Legal review from London only says to "follow local law and display no-smoking notices." You cannot cancel the terrace concept without executive approval, and you need a plan today that the Kampala team can execute without a public confrontation with the venue.
question: Write a short action memo to your Kampala team and London stakeholders that sets the execution plan for the venue setup. Your memo must do four things: diagnose what is likely wrong with the current setup from the available evidence, identify the tempting imported assumption behind the current plan, specify the exact sequence of actions and who does what in the next two hours, and give the wording/channel you would use to correct the venue without creating avoidable relationship damage. Be concrete about placement, signage, smoking location, and escalation boundaries.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the operative problem as a setup-wide compliance issue, not just a guest-preference or signage issue.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that the on-site 'smoking area' and current entrance-adjacent terrace plan are likely noncompliant and require changing the physical smoking arrangement, not merely clarifying rules or adding disclaimers.

rubric.point: Rejects the attractive near-miss assumption behind the London draft.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly identifies and bounds the imported assumption that a venue can solve the issue with a standard designated smoking zone or generic smoking/non-smoking split; partial credit if it notices legal risk but still preserves an on-site zone as the default solution.

rubric.point: Makes the decisive execution choice on placement and distance.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the plan moves smoking away from the public-place footprint rather than leaving it on the terrace, by requiring a separate compliant location beyond the prohibited boundary or, if that cannot be confirmed immediately, treating the event as no-smoking on-site until a compliant off-area location is verified.

rubric.point: Translates the rule into concrete signage behavior.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer replaces English-only table cards and vague restriction language with clear, prominent no-smoking signage in relevant local-language-inclusive form and ties signage responsibility to the venue/operator execution, not just guest comms.

rubric.point: Uses behavioural CQ through calibrated channel, audience, and wording.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer chooses a direct but relationship-preserving correction sequence such as private call/message to the venue manager first, followed by written confirmation and stakeholder update, with wording that states a required operational change rather than a soft suggestion or public reprimand.

rubric.point: Assigns roles and timing under the two-hour deadline.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the next-step sequence is operationally staged: stop printing the current signs, verify physical distances/entrance boundary immediately, redesign sign pack, instruct the venue on revised layout, and escalate only if no compliant alternative exists before print cutoff.

rubric.point: Sets a narrow escalation and risk-control boundary.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer avoids overbroad delay or generic consultation and instead defines a specific threshold for escalation, such as inability to verify a compliant smoking location or refusal to change layout, while otherwise keeping the launch on schedule.

rubric.point: Penalizes plausible but miscalibrated alternatives.
rubric.score_rule: Answers should lose credit if they rely on generic politeness, ask locals broadly without an execution decision, keep the smoking terrace with better labels, use only English signage, issue a public correction first, or propose the longest/safest review loop without changing the setup.

reference_outline: Infer from the floor plan, terrace-at-entrance location, and 'designated smoker area' label that the current layout likely treats smoking as allowed within the venue footprint, which is the core problem rather than a mere communications gap.
Identify the near-miss logic as a UK/global-hospitality default: assuming a compliant venue can offer an on-site smoking section if it is marked clearly enough.

Immediate decision on the main execution axis: do not approve the terrace smoking zone; require either a verified smoking point outside the prohibited public-place boundary or run the activation as no-smoking on-site until that is secured.

Pause current printing, replace English-only restricted-smoking cards with clear no-smoking notices in locally usable language, and make signage prominent at the entrance and relevant public areas rather than only on tables.

Use behavioural CQ by contacting the venue manager privately first with firm operational wording such as: the current terrace smoker setup cannot be used, please confirm an alternative location outside the venue/public-place boundary now, after which send a written layout confirmation to all teams.

Assign roles: Kampala coordinator measures/verifies site boundary and sign placement, venue manager confirms revised guest flow, London marketing updates artwork immediately, operations lead informs sponsor that terrace hospitality remains but smoking cannot be accommodated there.

Set escalation only if the venue cannot verify a compliant alternative before print cutoff or resists the layout change; then escalate to the regional director for approval of a no-smoking event configuration rather than preserving the smoker zone.

Monitor execution by requiring revised floor plan/photo proof before approval and preparing a repair script for staff to redirect guests calmly if they attempt to smoke on the terrace or at the entrance.

scenario: A newcomer operations manager in Niamey is preparing a same-day promo ride campaign with a local transport coordinator. The print vendor has already sent mockups for stickers to place inside shared taxis and at the departure stand before the evening rush. The newcomer notices one mockup shows a driver with a lit cigarette and a child passenger in the back seat. There is pressure to approve the files quickly because the cars start rotating in less than two hours, and the coordinator is also worried about losing the discounted print slot.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The printer wants final approval in twenty minutes or we miss today's run. The stand manager already cleared the sticker size, but the driver image is still your call.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I saw the mockup. Since it's just a lifestyle image and not an actual vehicle rule card, I'll keep it for now and ask the agency later whether people here read that kind of scene literally.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The agency copied in a youth group last month on another campaign, so they may take time. Also, these stickers go inside the cars, not only on the station wall.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Understood. To avoid overreacting before we verify, I'll approve printing today but tell the vendor to swap that panel in the next batch if anyone objects.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We also have the mayor's visit at the stand tomorrow morning, and the drivers want everything installed tonight while the fleet is together.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I'll keep the artwork moving and note in my report that we're waiting on local feedback. I don't want to impose a stricter standard than necessary based on my own assumptions.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right, send whatever you decide to the printer before they close the file.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I'll release this version now and review the imagery once we've heard back from the agency side.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer makes a polished but miscalibrated choice by treating the issue as optional imagery pending feedback, instead of acting on already-sufficient local public-norm evidence for shared vehicles carrying nonsmoking passengers and minors. The decisive error is the execution axis of timing and scope: approving now for in-vehicle use, then planning to revise later.

scenario: Your NGO in Uganda is launching a one-page briefing line for field officers who help families access a public education support program. Compliance requires the line to avoid suggesting unofficial payments, but officers also report that applications often move only after a personal introduction or persistent follow-up. The country director wants wording that field teams can use this week without expanding the policy.
question: Which briefing line should be approved?

options.A: If a family’s application stalls, our team should make the follow-up calls through the official office route and named program contacts rather than asking the family to secure its own introducer.
options.B: If a family’s application stalls, remind them to use the published process, decline any side arrangement, and document irregular requests instead of entering local relationship channels around the case.
options.C: If a family’s application stalls, advise them to identify a trusted local contact who can introduce the case at the office, while keeping every payment and document on the formal record.
options.D: If a family’s application stalls, our team should first ask the family who already knows someone in the office, then join that contact chain to keep the case moving formally.

scenario: You are the regional operations lead for a Kampala-based health supply NGO in Uganda. A new convoy handbook for drivers must be finalized by tomorrow because a donor audit starts in two days and a senior director wants one standard rule sheet for all corridors. One section covers routes into two eastern Congolese cities used for last-mile deliveries. In WhatsApp threads and older trip reports, several local staff and partner drivers refer to periods of 'road courtesy.' Your Ugandan compliance manager has drafted guidance that treats this as a driver-behaviour issue and proposes a bold box: 'During road courtesy, model extra politeness, avoid horn use, and remind drivers to show patience and courtesy at checks.' A field logistics officer says the phrase matters for corruption risk and delay planning, but provides no full explanation and is now offline. The finance team wants fewer escort and delay contingencies because costs are rising, while the director wants language that looks anti-bribery and operationally simple. If your handbook misstates the term, drivers may either budget the wrong kind of risk or follow the wrong roadside instructions, but if you reopen the whole document you may miss the donor deadline.
question: Write a decision memo for your team that states how you will handle the 'road courtesy' section before release. Your memo must: identify the most likely mechanism behind the phrase from the evidence given; explain the tempting but flawed assumption in the current draft; specify the exact handbook change, who you will involve tonight, and what limited follow-up effort you will personally own despite the deadline; and show how you will keep the document usable for Ugandan staff while controlling legal, bribery, and schedule risk. Be concrete about sequence, wording, and what not to overclaim.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the phrase as a specific roadside enforcement arrangement rather than ordinary driver civility
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that the phrase refers to a temporary change in how roadside police stops are handled and links that to corruption or harassment risk; no credit for treating it mainly as manners, patience, or general safety culture.

rubric.point: Applies the mechanism to the correct execution axis: handbook wording and trip-risk planning
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the respondent changes the section so drivers are briefed on altered stop/checkpoint conditions, uncertainty windows, and anti-bribery boundaries, rather than adding generic courtesy instructions; partial credit if they identify the mechanism but attach it to the wrong stage or actor.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the attractive near-miss in the current draft
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly names the current draft's imported assumption as plausible but miscalibrated, and explains why a polite-behaviour frame would misbudget risk or mislead driver action; low credit if the answer merely says 'be culturally sensitive' or 'consult locals more.'

rubric.point: Shows motivational CQ through costly but bounded follow-through
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the respondent personally absorbs a concrete cost under deadline, such as staying late to verify with one or two targeted sources, revising wording themselves, or pushing a narrow addendum instead of abandoning the issue; no credit for offloading the burden entirely to local staff, postponing indefinitely, or reopening the entire handbook without boundaries.

rubric.point: Designs a role-specific coordination sequence under pressure
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer specifies who to contact tonight, what each person is asked to confirm, and how approvals are narrowed so the document can still ship on time; low credit for broad stakeholder mapping without sequence or for adding unnecessary reviewers.

rubric.point: Controls legal and anti-bribery risk without overclaiming certainty
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer preserves a clear no-bribe/no informal payment boundary while avoiding unsupported claims that all stops are suspended or that drivers should ignore police instructions; partial credit if anti-corruption is mentioned without operational consequences.

rubric.point: Keeps the final guidance operational for a Ugandan team working across borders
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the memo translates the interpretation into simple field-ready instructions for route briefs, contingency timing, and escalation channels for Kampala-based staff; low credit for abstract cultural explanation with no work-performance consequence.

reference_outline: State that the most likely meaning of 'road courtesy' in the eastern Congo corridor is not interpersonal road politeness but a temporary public-order arrangement in which authorities limit roadside police stops to reduce corruption or administrative harassment.

Replace the draft's courtesy-behaviour box with narrow operational wording: note that local reports may use the term for altered checkpoint enforcement conditions, so drivers should not reinterpret it as permission to pay, argue, or ignore lawful instructions, and planners should adjust delay assumptions accordingly.

Explicitly reject the tempting near-miss: a generic global driver-safety interpretation sounds brand-safe and simple, but it would misdirect attention to manners instead of stop patterns, corruption exposure, and escalation protocol.

Use a bounded overnight sequence: contact the field logistics officer and one trusted route partner for confirmation of present usage; ask compliance to review anti-bribery wording only; ask the director to approve a targeted addendum rather than reopening the full handbook.

Show motivational CQ by taking ownership of the extra effort yourself under deadline: stay with the issue, narrow the questions, revise the section personally, and accept a small time/status cost instead of pushing vague consultation onto local staff or leaving the flawed draft in place.

Set operational instructions for Kampala teams: pre-brief drivers that the phrase concerns roadside-stop conditions, not etiquette; keep incident logging active; escalate unusual stop demands through the named operations channel; maintain no informal payments.

Control uncertainty by avoiding overclaim: describe the condition as corridor- and time-specific local reporting, not a universal legal rule, and commit to a post-audit update once the field team confirms whether the arrangement is active on current routes.

scenario: A multinational mobility company is preparing a short submission for a parliamentary roundtable in South Africa on pilot rules for autonomous delivery vehicles. The note must be circulated that afternoon to an insurer, a municipal transport unit, and a road-safety NGO, and the local public policy lead wants it to sound workable without closing off debate too early.

roles.newcomer: New regional legal manager newly transferred from Europe

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: We need two pages by 3 p.m. People will quote the opening paragraph, so it has to travel well across the insurer, the city team, and the NGO.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I can get this done. I stayed up reworking our pilot note and I can keep the front page very practical: operator oversight, manufacturer duties, incident reporting, and a narrow pilot permit.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That may read cleanly, but the room is mixed. If the first page sounds too settled, some readers will stop there and not get to the nuance.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I'll add a boxed section saying the pilot should be reviewed with local stakeholders after the roundtable. I also booked twenty minutes with our claims adviser at lunch so I can stress-test the insurance language.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Helpful. Just remember the chair tends to ask very early whether the draft assumes the current road-law framework already fits these vehicles.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: I heard that, but if we lead with unresolved statutory questions, circulation may stall. I'd rather keep page one usable and move that point into a short second-page note, then recommend a later working group on any legislative amendments.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. Send me the first page as soon as it's stable and I'll see what reactions I can get before printing starts.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: You'll have it in forty minutes. I'll keep the headline implementation-focused and attach a brief legal note so we don't lose momentum today.

label: inappropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer shows real effort, but places that effort in preserving a globally familiar implementation frame while relegating the South Africa-specific threshold issue to page two. The decisive mismatch is the sequence and scope choice: treating current road-law categories as workable on the front page, instead of foregrounding that the pilot may require changes around the human-driver concept and liability rather than only later consultation on amendments.

scenario: At a pop-up credential desk in North America, your team is writing a one-line briefing for volunteers managing a long self-formed line before doors open. Supervisors will be tied up elsewhere, and the note needs to tell volunteers which person in the line is the most relevant reference point if someone steps into the middle and a dispute starts.
question: Which direction should the briefing use?

options.A: Treat the person immediately after the insertion point as the first relevant reference, and have volunteers anchor any quick check to that person's place in the line.
options.B: Treat the person immediately before the insertion point as the first relevant reference, and have volunteers anchor any quick check to that person's place in the line.
options.C: Treat the earliest person who visibly notices the insertion as the first relevant reference, and have volunteers anchor any quick check to that person's account of the line.
options.D: Treat the nearest volunteer or cashier as the first relevant reference, and have volunteers make the placement call themselves rather than relying on any one person in line.

scenario: You lead operations design for a multicultural team launching a temporary check-in and merchandise area at a three-day technology conference in Chicago. The team includes a U.S. venue manager, a Brazilian event producer, a German finance lead, and a Singapore-based CX analyst. You must send a same-day decision memo because the sponsor wants a visible setup approved by 5 p.m., the floor plan is already printed, and staffing is capped at four people per rush window. Two layout options are under debate: (1) three short parallel lines, one for each service point, which appears faster on paper and fits the sponsor's branding mockup, or (2) one winding line feeding the next open station, which takes more floor tape and forces a redesign of the sponsor's display wall. In a pilot test that morning, one volunteer stepped in halfway near a friend at the front; only the person directly behind the volunteer challenged it, while others watched and said nothing. The sponsor now argues that separate lines are more efficient and says that if cutting happens, staff should avoid getting involved unless several customers complain, because public intervention could look heavy-handed on social media. You need a plan that will be judged by U.S. teammates as competent operations design, not just polite cultural sensitivity.
question: Write a decision memo for your team that chooses the queue design and enforcement approach for the U.S. launch. Your memo must: diagnose the local interaction logic behind the pilot incident; identify the most tempting but miscalibrated assumption in the sponsor's proposal; specify the exact staffing, signage, and intervention sequence during rush periods; and explain why your plan fits the U.S. context better than a generic efficiency or neutrality approach. Be concrete about who acts, when they act, and what evidence from the scenario you are using.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden mechanism from the pilot evidence
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that the queue must be designed and managed around a U.S. fairness logic in which equal turn order matters and line-cutting is often challenged first by the person immediately disadvantaged, rather than expecting whole-crowd enforcement or treating silence from others as acceptance.

rubric.point: Chooses the correct queue structure on the decisive execution axis
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer selects one shared line feeding multiple service points and ties that choice to perceived fairness in this U.S. setting; partial credit if it mentions fairness but still allows parallel lines as the main plan because they look faster, more branded, or easier to staff.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the attractive near-miss
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explicitly identifies the sponsor's 'wait until several people object / stay neutral unless there is broad complaint' logic as a tempting but wrong imported assumption for this case; low credit if it accepts nonintervention, relies on crowd self-correction, or treats the pilot incident as too ambiguous to act on.

rubric.point: Applies the mechanism to the correct actor and timing
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer assigns staff to monitor the line entrance and respond as soon as a cut or side-entry appears, rather than waiting for escalation; it must connect this to the fact that the most directly affected person is likely to object first and should not carry the full burden alone.

rubric.point: Uses cognitive CQ rather than surface etiquette
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer distinguishes the U.S.-specific queue logic from generic customer-service efficiency, generic politeness, or a vague 'respect local norms' statement, and shows why the same visible behavior could be misread without the underlying fairness interpretation.

rubric.point: Designs concrete workflow and communication
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer gives operational details such as a single entry point, visible directional signage, a staff role at the head or entrance of the line, a brief intervention script, and a handoff rule to open counters; low credit for broad recommendations like 'train staff' or 'communicate clearly' without sequence.

rubric.point: Calibrates risk control under sponsor and timing pressure
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explains how the chosen design reduces public conflict and reputational risk while still meeting the deadline, rather than proposing the broadest or slowest consultation process; low credit if it defaults to postponing the decision, escalating generally, or adding excessive review that avoids the core choice.

reference_outline: State that the U.S. launch should use one visible shared line feeding all open stations because customers are likely to judge fairness by equal place in line, not just by throughput.

Use the pilot incident as evidence: only the person directly behind the cutter objected, which suggests that lack of broader protest does not mean the behavior was acceptable or that staff should stay passive.

Name the near-miss explicitly: the sponsor's neutrality rule assumes staff should wait for broad complaint or prioritize apparent efficiency, but that misreads how enforcement tends to localize to the immediately affected person in this context.

Assign one staff member to line entry/monitoring during rush periods, with the other staff at service points; the monitor guides arrivals into the single queue and intervenes immediately if someone joins mid-line or bypasses the entry.

Specify a short intervention sequence such as: stop the side-entry, redirect the person to the line start, acknowledge the flow issue without debating publicly, and resume movement quickly so fairness enforcement looks procedural rather than personal.

Add physical and visual supports that match the decision: floor tape for one queue, signs saying the next available station will call forward, and placement that makes the line start unmistakable even under crowding.

Explain cognitively why this is not just 'be respectful': the operational choice depends on understanding the local fairness logic and the likely enforcement pattern, not on generic event-management best practice alone.

Show calibration under constraints by noting that the redesign is worth the sponsor tradeoff because it lowers conflict, reduces accusations of favoritism, and lets staff resolve violations early without waiting for a public pile-on.

scenario: A newcomer on an Ottawa event team is overseeing a Saturday winter charity run. A sponsor wants the route marshals to create a lively send-off at 7:30 a.m. in a residential area, and city staff have warned only that neighbors complained last year about being woken early. Snow crews are still working nearby, the sponsor expects visible energy for social media, and the team must keep the start on schedule.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The sponsor keeps asking for a stronger start line atmosphere this year. We roll cameras at 7:30 Saturday, and the route begins beside apartment buildings. Last winter a few residents called in complaints.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: We can still make it feel energetic without adding a soundtrack there. I’ll move the pump-up piece to the indoor check-in tent, then have marshals switch to visual countdown boards once runners are outside.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The sponsor also suggested having the lead vehicle give a few blasts when the runners set off. They think it will read well on video.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Let’s skip that and cue the start with the overhead clock and raised flags instead. The plows already make enough presence on that street, and I don’t want us adding our own layer on top.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: That may look quieter than they want. We still need a clear launch moment, and I can’t push the start later because police closure times are fixed.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Then I’ll tighten the sequence: emcee finishes inside, runners are lined up outside in silence except for brief safety calls, and the camera team gets the visual cue sheet so they know exactly when the release happens.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Alright. There’s also a church two blocks over that may already be active by then, so the street won’t be perfectly still anyway.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: That’s fine. I’m only controlling what our event adds, so I’ll brief the marshals now and send the sponsor the revised run-of-show.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer applies the Ottawa-specific noise logic correctly by removing event-added amplified sound and vehicle horn use during an early weekend residential start, while not overreacting to other exempt or unrelated sound sources nearby. The decisive execution axis is controlling the event’s own noise-making methods and timing, not pursuing a generic 'all noise must stop' rule.

scenario: Your team is preparing a one-line volunteer briefing for a public arts venue in Toronto before tonight’s event. The building has three exits: a main entrance that opens directly onto a city sidewalk, a side door that opens into the venue’s own forecourt, and a rear staff door beside the loading area. The venue manager wants a single sentence volunteers can use if guests ask where they may smoke during breaks, and there is no time for a full legal review.
question: Which briefing line should be approved?

options.A: If guests ask, direct them away from every doorway; at the street-facing entrance, do not stop near the threshold, and use the city sidewalk beyond the frontage rather than the forecourt or rear exit area.
options.B: If guests ask, direct them to move well beyond every entrance before lighting up, including the street-facing doorway, and avoid using the forecourt or rear exit area for smoking.
options.C: If guests ask, the main entrance is acceptable once they are outside the doors on the city sidewalk, while the forecourt and rear exit should still be treated as no-smoking areas nearby.
options.D: If guests ask, send them to an outdoor spot that is clear of door traffic and visible to staff, using whichever exit is closest and keeping the pathways open for arriving guests.

scenario:
You are leading venue-readiness for a three-day public policy forum in Toronto. The event is hosted in a municipal building and opens tomorrow morning. Your team is multicultural: the facilities vendor is based in Germany, the guest-services lead is from Singapore, and the sponsor liaison is from the United States. The sponsor has complained that past events felt unfriendly to smokers, so your U.S. liaison wants to avoid any setup that looks punitive. At the same time, the building manager has warned that city inspectors sometimes pass by during large public events and that the host organization, not just individual attendees, could face complaints if the entrance areas are handled poorly.

You review the current setup at 6:30 p.m. the night before opening. There are temporary standing ashtrays placed a few steps outside two main doors because the vendor assumed people should have an outdoor place to smoke near the flow of arrivals. The printed entrance signs mention no-smoking indoors, but they do not mention where smoking is not allowed outside. The sponsor liaison argues that because the ashtrays are outdoors and easy to move, the team should leave them for day one and "adjust if anyone objects," since removing them now may trigger sponsor pushback and confuse guests. The guest-services lead suggests adding a staff script telling smokers to stay outside the building, without changing the physical setup until after the opening rush. You have one evening to issue instructions, update materials, and assign roles. You cannot redesign the whole plaza, and you do not have time for a full legal review memo.
question: Write the action brief you would send tonight to your team. Your brief must: (1) identify the key risk mechanism you think is operating from the facts given, (2) explain which tempting assumption in the current discussion you would reject or tightly limit, (3) specify the immediate sequence of changes you would make before doors open, including physical placement, signage, and staff guidance, and (4) state what you would treat as sufficiently certain to act on now versus what you would still verify tomorrow. Make your answer concrete enough that each team lead knows what to do and why.

rubric.point: Diagnoses the hidden compliance mechanism from the scenario facts rather than treating the issue as a generic indoor-versus-outdoor smoking question.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer infers that the risk zone extends beyond the doorway itself and that a person smoking just outside an entrance can still create a venue-side violation problem; partial credit if it only says entrances are sensitive or that local rules may be stricter.

rubric.point: Rejects or tightly bounds the attractive near-miss plan that leaves ashtrays near the doors and relies on later adjustment or generic 'smoke outside' wording.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer explains why 'outdoors is fine for now' or 'we can wait for complaints' is miscalibrated under Toronto conditions; no full credit for answers that merely recommend being polite, monitoring reactions, or asking guests to use judgment.

rubric.point: Makes the correct execution choice on the primary axis of physical placement and risk boundary before opening.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer directs removal of ashtrays from entrance/exit areas before the event opens and avoids creating or endorsing a smoking spot beside the doors; partial credit if it proposes moving smoking activity vaguely farther away without acting on the entrance boundary immediately.

rubric.point: Translates the diagnosis into role-specific operational steps for signage, staff scripting, and ownership.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer assigns concrete tasks such as updating entrance signs, removing or relocating entrance ashtrays, briefing guest-services on where not to direct smokers, and naming who confirms completion; partial credit for general coordination without role clarity.

rubric.point: Applies metacognitive CQ by distinguishing what is certain enough to act on tonight from what still needs verification tomorrow.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer shows calibrated reasoning: act now on the strong evidence that the entrance setup is unsafe/noncompliant, while identifying limited follow-up questions such as exact approved smoking locations or final wording checks; no full credit for broad delay, full uncertainty paralysis, or overconfident claims beyond the facts.

rubric.point: Handles pressure from sponsor friendliness, time limits, and cross-team assumptions without letting those pressures override the local mechanism.
rubric.score_rule: Full credit only if the answer preserves guest experience through wording or alternative direction while still changing the setup tonight; partial credit if it chooses the broadest or most brand-comforting plan but leaves the seed-specific risk intact.

reference_outline: State that the problem is not simply indoor smoking; the entrance/exit area itself creates the operative risk, so smoking beside the doors and placing ashtrays there is not a safe default even though it is outdoors.
Order immediate removal of ashtrays from the entrance/exit areas tonight and do not open day one with a doorway-adjacent smoking setup in place.
Revise entrance materials tonight so signage addresses the entrance area, not just indoor space, and ensure staff are not instructed to send smokers to stand just outside the doors.
Assign the facilities vendor to remove/reposition physical items, the guest-services lead to update the staff script, and one accountable owner to confirm the entrances are reset before opening.
Explicitly reject the near-miss assumption that the team can leave the setup in place until someone complains or that 'outdoors' alone is a sufficient compliance standard in Toronto.

Use metacognitive calibration: act now on the strong evidence already available, but note limited next-morning checks such as confirming the designated permissible location and validating final sign wording with the building manager.

Manage stakeholder pressure by explaining to the sponsor liaison that the change is a narrow entrance-control adjustment, not a hostile anti-smoker stance, and by pairing the restriction with clear guest direction rather than vague prohibition.

scenario: A newly arrived regional compliance manager in Mexico must decide how to handle a supplier's offer before a permit-related site inspection. The plant needs the inspection this week to avoid a shipment delay, but the supplier representative keeps framing the offer as help for future coordination as well as the current visit.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: The inspector is scheduled for Thursday, and our customs window is tight. The supplier's representative said he can 'help smooth things' and asked whether we want him to host coffee for the municipal team before they come.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Let's not approve anything around the visit itself. Ask him to send the exact agenda, who would attend, and whether this is tied to Thursday or part of his normal client program.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: He replied quickly. He says he likes to stay close to officials and clients year-round, and if we let him handle this one well, it will make later permits and utility issues easier too. He also mentioned a holiday basket for our office next month.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: That changes the read for me. Please decline both the coffee setup and the basket, and tell him all contact about the inspection stays in the formal channel. If he has documents for Thursday, he can send them to our shared compliance inbox today.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: Understood. He may feel brushed off if we make it that formal right away. Do you want me to soften it and say we'll revisit after the inspection?

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: You can thank him for the offer, but don't leave the door open for later favors around permits or offices. Keep the message short and practical so we don't turn it into a relationship discussion.

dialogue.speaker: Local
dialogue.text: All right. I'll send that now and copy procurement only. We still need the inspection materials by end of day.

dialogue.speaker: Newcomer
dialogue.text: Good. If the documents arrive cleanly, we proceed. If anything else comes bundled with 'future help,' pause and forward it to me before answering.

label: appropriate
brief_reason: The newcomer correctly updates when the offer shifts from a one-off courtesy to reciprocity aimed at building an ongoing useful relationship with officials and the company. The decisive culture-specific move is distinguishing relationship-building favors from ordinary logistics, then closing both the current and future-favor channel while preserving task progress.

scenario: A fleet company is launching same-day deliveries in Colombia. During pilot runs, drivers reported three kinds of roadside interactions: a marked patrol officer redirected traffic around roadworks, a uniformed civilian at a municipal checkpoint asked vehicles to pull over for document review, and a private parking contractor at a loading bay warned that trucks refusing his on-the-spot "corridor fee" would be reported for an added penalty. Operations wants one short sequence for the driver briefing card before Monday's rollout.
question: Which sequence is the best one to place on the card?

options.A: Follow directions from the marked patrol officer, decline the municipal civilian’s stop until police arrive, then pay the loading-bay fee if needed and dispute the added penalty later through the city contact.
options.B: Follow circulation directions from the marked patrol officer, stop for the municipal civilian’s document check, then ask the loading-bay contractor to cite the written basis for any charge and report the incident through dispatch.
options.C: Ask dispatch to confirm each roadside instruction before complying, let the municipal civilian record the vehicle details while waiting, then request a supervisor review before discussing any loading-bay charge.
options.D: Follow the patrol officer’s detour, stop for the municipal civilian’s review, then pay the loading-bay charge under protest, collect a receipt, and challenge both the fee and added penalty after delivery.
